AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister would tell us what terms of reference were given to those who are studying boundary waters pollution.
To which particular reference is my hon. friend directing my attention? Has he the Rainy river one in mind?
No, I am thinking of the great lakes reference.

I will be very pleased to deal with that one, and perhaps this will give me the opportunity of discussing a matter that is of great concern to border communities, and particularly to areas such as the city of Windsor.
As I said earlier today in answer to a question asked by my hon. friend, the international joint commission is conducting investigations on water pollution under three commission references from the two governments.
On October 7 the commission was requested to study the problem of pollution of lake Erie which borders the southern portion of the county of Essex, the county in which I live. This is the area where the constituencies of Essex South, Essex West and Essex East happen to be. At the same time the commission was asked to investigate pollution of the waters of the Red river at the international boundary, and to make a similar report to the governments with recommendations for any measures which they might regard as appropriate.
Under the third reference, the commission is now preparing a report to the governments concerning pollution of the Rainy river and

lake of the Woods. In addition to these three current investigations, the commission since 1951, as my hon. friend, the minister of national health and welfare knows-and he has had a lot to do with these things-has maintained surveillance of water quality conditions in the connecting channels of the great lakes. I refer to the channels such as the Detroit river, which joins lake Erie and lake St. Clair and which borders the city of Windsor.
The commission has also been authorized by the two governments to maintain supervision over boundary water pollution in the St. Croix river basin in Maine and New Brunswick. If any hon. member would like the particulars of these I will be very happy to deal with them.
Let us have them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With regard to the situation covering the Detroit river area, lake Erie and lake St. Clair, it may be recalled that following complaints I made in this house some time I think in 1948 or 1949, steps were taken by both Detroit and the city of Windsor for a submission to the joint commission concerning air pollution in the Detroit-Windsor area, which might be attributed to vessels plying the Detroit river. A recommendation to broaden the reference term to the advisory board, allowing it to make recommendations respecting other major sources of pollution in the area was, however, rejected by the United States. In 1954 a technical advisory board on air pollution was established which conducted atmospheric studies in the area, and reported that the air was being polluted and that the many vessels plying the river were a contributing factor to the situation.
The minister of national health and welfare will recall-
Thank you.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: that he himself made a report to this house in respect of the interim report of this advisory board.
That is twice.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
A smoke abatement program was inaugurated with the voluntary co-operation of vessel owners, operators and their associations.
I did not catch the interjection of my right hon. friend.

The interjection was
simply this. That is twice the minister has referred to the hon. member for Perth as

the minister of national health and welfare, and I appreciate it very much.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should like to remind my right hon. friend that the hon. member for Perth was the minister of national health and welfare during the time that my right hon. friend was the head of the government.
But not today.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The technical advisory board also continued studies of possible remedial measures to present to the international joint commission in April, 1957. Certain recommendations which it proposed to incorporate in its final report were presented. Criticisms of its draft proposals were made, and amendments to it were drafted over a period of time. The final report of the technical advisory board was submitted to the international joint commission, as my friend the hon. member for Perth will recall, at this October meeting in 1959. The international joint commission presented its recommendations to the government later, on May 31, 1960.
One of the recommendations provided for the establishment by the joint commission of a board which would continue surveillance on a voluntary basis of air pollution from vessels plying the Detroit river. This has been accepted by both governments, and has received the support of the government of Ontario.
The other recommendations of the international joint commission report, which are now under study, call for the following. First, the adoption of standards for smoke emission, described by the technical advisory board, and incorporated in the commission's final report. The standards are to go into effect as soon as the governments have worked out the legal and administrative details necessary to enforce them. Second, during the interim period the new standards are not to apply to handfired coal-burning vessels. Third, that all costs incurred in converting vessels in order to meet the new standards are to be borne by the owners of the vessels. This marks an example of the progress being made in trying to meet the very serious problem in the area covered by the Detroit river.
As a further follow-up on the recommendations of 1961, the Department of Transport, it will be recalled by the former minister of transport, the hon. member for Three Rivers, who sits with the right hon. gentleman, put through an amendment which enables the
Supply-External Affairs government to regulate air pollution from ships plying Canadian waters within one mile of land. The regulations under this act were gazetted and will be found now in the Canada Gazette as P.C. 1964-324. The regulations apply, first, to smoke emissions by ships while they are in Canadian waters within one mile of land and, as so many of my constituents who live on the banks of lake St. Clair know, this represents a very important step. Second, so far as non-handfired vessels are concerned, the regulations are more stringent than those recommended by the international joint commission in the 1960 report. Third, so far as handfired vessels are concerned, a special exception is made in the case of the Detroit river to bring the regulations in line with the main I.J.C. recommendations. Fourth, penalties are provided in the form of a fine not exceeding $500 or a term of imprisonment not exceeding six months, or both fine and imprisonment. Fifth, although steamship inspectors under the Canada Shipping Act are provided with powers of inspection it does not follow that special administrative procedures will be set up by the Department of Transport to enforce the regulations, as was explained at the time by the Minister of Transport.
So far as Canada is concerned, Mr. Chairman, the adoption of these regulations puts into practice the recommendation in the report of the joint commission recommending that smoke emission standards should go into effect as soon as the governments have worked out the legal and administrative details necessary to enforce them. In other words, the Canadian government is now in a position to approve the recommendations. Recommendations of the commission are normally approved jointly by both governments. However, on the United States side of the boundary there are no corresponding regulations of general application measuring up to the I.J.C. standards.
The reason for this is largely that the United States federal government has virtually no authority, it is alleged, in the field of air pollution, although this situation was remedied somewhat in 1963 with the passage of public law 88206. This legislation permits federal financial assistance to regional air pollution control agencies and also allows the federal government to take direct action when the health or welfare of the citizens of one state is endangered by air pollution from another state.
There is now proposed a new reference to the I.J.C. for study of air pollution in the

Supply-External Affairs Detroit-Windsor area. In May of 1963, as a result of complaints made by the hon. member for Essex West supported by my colleague, the member for Essex South and myself, the department made representations to the United States department of state through our embassy in Washington requesting prompt relief from air pollution originating on the United States side of the Detroit river in the vicinity of Zug island and Ecorse. So far as can be determined, the Great Lakes Steel Corporation with a plant in Ecorse, which is near Detroit, is primarily responsible for this situation. Smoke from this plant pollutes the atmosphere in the west end of Windsor and in La Salle in Sandwich west. When making representations to the state department I pointed out that preparations for a reference of the matter to the international joint commission were going forward on our side.
These represent important ventures by the international joint commission with regard to what quite properly has been referred to as a serious condition of pollution in the air resulting from several of the causes I have mentioned. This matter of pollution, of course, is not confined to the great lakes, and to the extent that the international joint commission on the Canadian side is able to prosecute studies it will have at least a persuasive effect in both countries. The house may be assured that the commission will undertake its responsibility to see that these matters are properly studied. Remedial action can then be taken by those authorities primarily concerned, when it comes to giving effect to recommendations. The authorities in the case of Canada are the provinces with their responsibility in property and civil rights. But some provinces may take the position that the cost of giving effect to the remedies suggested is one they cannot bear alone and in that event, of course, consideration has to be given as to what action can be taken to bring about the necessary and desired results.

Mr. Chairman, the committee has been treated to a disquisition on a subject that does not come up at all under the particular item we are dealing with and I can only assume that what was said by the hon. gentleman was said in a desire to impress his constituents with the action taken in regard to a problem that is not before us at all. As a matter of fact, as I listened to the hon. gentleman reading his statement and pouring forth that volume of words, I could only conclude that when he really gets under a full head of steam he pours forth over the


air, whether polluted or not, a volume of words in search of an idea.
That was very apparent because what we are dealing with and what he has not dealt with is the question of what is being done about water pollution. Interesting as it is to hear of what has been done in connection with a problem that is not before us, I now return to the subject under consideration, which is Canada's share of the expenses of studies, surveys and investigations of the international joint commission including studies and surveys of the midwestern watershed, Canada's share of the expenses of the international St. Lawrence river board of control, Canada's share of the expenses of the St. Croix river reference, Canada's share of the expenses of the proposed Alaska-Yukon rivers reference, Canada's share of the expenses of studies of boundary waters pollution and Canada's share of the expenses of the Champlain waterway reference.
The minister, of course, has not dealt with the questions that were raised and I now ask him to return to the subject with some greater regard to what is before the committee than he has shown up to the present moment and to tell the committee what, if anything, has been done by the international joint commission in connection with the subject of water pollution, which we are dealing with at the moment. How many technical advisers are there in the Canadian section? What is the nature of the work they are doing? Interesting as his disquisition on the subject of air pollution may be to himself and to his constituents, and also generally, that is not the subject before us at this time; but I presume he brought it up because he has no information on the questions that have been asked him.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am glad my hon. friend is interested in the problems that face the area from which I come. I had been asked a question about pollution-
About water pollution.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -and I dealt with air pollution, but since my hon. friend wishes me to go on I am very happy to deal with water pollution.
That is fine.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I approved a note following which the governments of the United States and Canada recognized that the waters of lake Erie, lake Ontario and the international section of the St. Lawrence river

were being polluted by sewage and industrial wastes discharged into these various bodies of water. I pointed out that the provisions of article 4 of the boundary waters treaty signed on January 11, 1909, set forth that boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other side. It provides the two governments with a justification for agreeing upon a joint reference pursuant to the provisions of article 9 of the treaty.
The commission was requested to inquire into and report to the two governments upon the following questions: First, are the waters of lake Erie, lake Ontario, and the international section of the St. Lawrence river being polluted on either side of the boundary to an extent which is causing or is likely to cause injury to health or property on either side of the boundary? If the foregoing question is answered in the affirmative, to what extent, by what cause and in what locality is such pollution taking place If the commission should find pollution of the character just referred to is taking place, what remedial measures would, in its judgment, be most practicable from the economic, sanitary and other points of view, and what would be the probable cost thereof?
Now, the answers to those questions will provide suggested remedies for what is admittedly a serious situation.
What is the date of that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is dated October 7 of this year.
In the conduct of this investigation and otherwise in the performance of its duties under this reference, the commission can utilize the services of engineers and other specially qualified personnel of the technical agencies of Canada and the United States and will, in so far as possible, make use of the information and technical data heretofore acquired or which may become available during the course of their investigations. I cannot give my hon. friend the exact number of professional and technical people who will be engaged on this particular study. I asked for this information at noon, but as yet it has not yet been finally determined, although the work has begun.
The two governments, I am happy to say, are agreed upon the desirability of extending this reference to other boundary waters in the great lakes basin at the appropriate time. These studies do take a considerable length of time to make, but they will be carried out
Supply-External Affairs in accordance with a schedule that has not yet been announced. The commission is asked to advise the governments when, in its opinion, such action is desirable. When the commission will have made its report the two governments will be in a position to consider what remedial steps can be taken.
My hon. friend asked me about some of the expenses involved in these studies. Canada's share of the expenses of studies, surveys and investigations with regard to the various projects are as follows for 196465: in the case of the mid-western watershed, $7,500; for our share of the expenses of the international St. Lawrence river board of control, $10,000; our share of the expenses of the St. Croix river, $500; for the proposed Alaska-Yukon rivers reference, $5,000; Canada's share of the studies of boundary pollution to which I have been referring, $13,000; for the expenses of the Champlain waterway reference, $2,500, making a total of $38,500. Now, this appropriation provides for the various investigations, studies and surveys undertaken by the commission under the various references and obligations to which reference has been made.

If I understood the minister correctly, he stated that the reports that might be made by the joint commission would be of the type that could not be acted upon by the government of the United States as such. He implied these were matters that would have to be acted upon by the various states concerned. Has the minister, as Secretary of State for External Affairs, held any discussions with the governors or officials of these various states to bring to their attention the problem that does exist and explore the avenues that might be available to meet these problems?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In the case of the state of Michigan I, myself, did talk, when I was minister of national health and welfare, with the then governor of the state of Michigan.
What year was that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That was in 1956; I believe that was when these studies were brought in. As Secretary of State for External Affairs, I have had correspondence with Premier Robarts of the province of Ontario who, as a result of an arrangement that has been made, has been dealing with this matter, through one of his ministers, with the present regime in the state of Michigan. I presume, although I would have to ask about this, that with regard to the situation in Quebec,

Supply-External Affairs there could be action taken by the corresponding governing bodies.
Am I right, then, in assuming the minister, as Secretary of State for External Affairs, has not taken up this matter with the particular states involved?
No; as Secretary of State for External Affairs, I take this up with my opposite number in the government of the United States who, in turn, communicates with the appropriate person in the state body.

Mr. Chairman, since we are considering the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words on the deepening of the Richelieu river.
We all remember that, when the previous government was in office, some hon. members of the province of Quebec, particularly the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) who was assigned very important diplomatic duties in Africa -which duties are keeping him away from the house today-as well as the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin), took a very active part in the debates and made every effort to try and convince the government that it was not only urgent but essential to go ahead with the deepening of the Richelieu river, so that an inland water route could be established between the harbour of Montreal and New York city.
However, since the Liberal government took office, we have noticed that those two hon. members have not said one word on this matter. At that time they were clamouring in order to convince the Canadian people that the deepening of the Richelieu river was essential.
I would like the hon. minister to comment on this project. I would like to know where the surveys stand and if the hon. minister is still receiving representations from the two ministers I mentioned more particularly and from those in that electoral district who are interested in that canal project.
Would the hon. minister inform us on the progress of the negotiations, and tell us if the project is practicable, or if this was just a balloon sent up by the people in opposition, when the Conservatives were in power -those who are now in a position to implement this project-so as to play on the emotions of the people?
I would like to know the intentions of the minister on this matter.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member very well knows, many members on all sides of the house became interested in this matter. The Associate Minister of National Defence, in particular, was highly interested.
This is the situation: The investigation is completed, but we have not yet received the report of the commission. As soon as we receive that report, we will be in a position to study the facts; and I am referring not only to the Canadian government, but also to the government of the United States.
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for the rather vague information he has just given us, but I would like to know when we can expect to get the commission's report?
That is a good question.
When does the minister expect the commission to report on that matter and how long is it since the technical survey has been completed?

Mr. Chairman, I do not know; I am not a member of the commission. It is never easy to ask a judge when he will give his decision. That is a matter which comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the commission, but I will inquire.

The reason I raised this question today is because it is one of the most important problems with which Canada must deal, not only the government but all of us. I well recall the many statements which have been made by the minister on the importance of this problem. Today he has indicated that he was advised by hon. members representing areas in close proximity to the constituency he represents in parliament. I would have thought that one so well versed in this problem and so aware of its detrimental effects would have taken action before 18 months had gone by, since this government came to office. Consider the length of time which has elapsed between the date this government came to power and the date action was taken, that is, on October 7 and 8. It is evident that the government has been most lax in discharging its responsibilities in connection with this increasingly serious problem.
We have been told there has been no intensification of the studies which have taken place with regard to this matter. The minister has shown by his answers today that no

discussions have been held directly with the state governments across the line. I must say I am deeply disappointed at this lack of action. Anyone who takes notice of the activity going on along the St. Lawrence and the great lakes today on our side of the border cannot but realize that more action and more attention is required than the government is giving to this subject. At the present time it is clear that it is likely to become even more extensive and that pollution will be even greater in the years ahead. Now is the time to intensify this work in all phases, not only the necessary studies but the action which has to be taken. I wish to say very sincerely that I am disappointed in the minister because of the lack of attention he has given to this matter.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member is disappointed and I am sure his disappointment is sincere. But when he understands what the constitutional arrangements are he will I am sure realize he has been ill-informed in the interesting remarks he has just made.
Shortly after the present government came to office it undertook to communicate with Premier Robarts. I regret I do not have any correspondence, but I will be glad to table it next week, with the consent of the province concerned. We communicated with the premier of Ontario several times with regard to this matter. I am not complaining about the co-operation I received from Premier Robarts, because we did receive co-operation. It was necessary to have the co-operation of the government of Ontario. Perhaps the hon. member does not realize that, when the international joint commission undertakes these projects, it does not do the work itself; it has to use the technical services which are available, and in a case like this these are largely the technical services of the province. The water belongs to the province. The assistance of the officials of the province is essential in order to carry out the engineering assessments which have to be made.
So there has been no delay on the part of the federal government and I am not suggesting there was any delay on the part of the province of Ontario. They have a lot of work to do and I am sure Premier Robarts acted as readily as he could in the circumstances.

I hope the minister is not trying to pass the buck to the premier of Ontario or of any other province. This is a matter which requires leadership at the federal level if progress is to be made, and we
Supply-External Affairs expect this kind of leadership from hon. gentlemen opposite-the kind of leadership they said they would give to this country.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member knows I would not pass the buck.

I rise at this time because I, too, am interested in this serious problem which is before the government and before all of us in this country. I wish to congratulate the right hon. Leader of the Opposition for having brought this subject up for consideration. As set out in this item, Canada's share of the expenses of studies of boundary waters pollution amounted to $13,000 last year, with provision for the same amount this year. This pollution problem has markedly increased during the past year and I submit, in consequence, that the item before us is totally inadequate to enable us to meet it properly and carry out the work required.
Let hon. members consider the damage being done to our tourist industry, as well as the piteous state of the fishing industry not only in lake Ontario but in all the other great lakes as well. I submit this item should be ten times the amount set out here, and I advise the minister that he would be doing his duty to this country if he were to protect himself and his department by setting aside adequate funds to perform this task effectively. In my opinion he should leave 'this item open to make it possible for him to come back to this parliament, in a few months time, and secure approval for the expenditure of more money to be used in the fight against this flagrant pollution of the great lakes.
I would point out that I brought this question of the pollution of lake Ontario to the attention of the government on June 18 this year. Hon. members will find that I spoke then, as reported on page 4443 of Hansard, concerning the pollution of the lake by oil emissions which, we suspect, came from ships-ships from other countries which are now steaming up the new waterway and whose masters seem to think, when they get into lake Ontario, that they are back in the ocean again and can open the seacocks of their vessels and emit oil waste or any other type of excess chemical they do not need aboard. I also put this matter before the government on September 24 last, as reported at pages 8407 and 8408 of Hansard. At that time I placed before the government the plight of the commercial fishermen of lake Ontario. I would like to see some progress made in this connection lay this government that claims

Supply-External Affairs they are so interested in cleaning up the situation that exists.
I would now refer you, Mr. Chairman, to the Kingston Whig-Standard of September 22, 1964, where some words of wisdom are contained in an editorial. This newspaper claims that we are not adequately enforcing the laws that we have in this country with regard to pollution. I would quote just briefly from the editorial:
The real trouble, we suspect, is that the authorities have not yet appreciated that we have a war on our hands and that the time tor polite notes of admonition has long since passed.
I am sure all hon. members in this house will agree with those sentiments. I believe we must intensify the fight against this problem; and we cannot do it with a puny $13,000 which is, we might say, hidden away in the estimates. Had the right hon. Leader of the Opposition not brought this matter to the attention of the house it probably would have slid into oblivion, like a great many other measures of this government. I think we should stop the flow of raw, untreated industrial by-products and effluents into our lakes and streams. The minister has mentioned a question that was posed by, or for the international joint commission, namely, is there pollution coming from one side of the international boundary line that is adversely affecting and damaging the other side. I claim that there is. Pollution is obviously coming from every watershed that drains into lake Ontario; all our small rivers are polluted before they ever reach lake Ontario. This applies in both the United States and Canada.
We should stop effluents, as I say, and industrial pollution reaching our streams. We should also see to it that industry which uses water in their processes return the unconverted portion of this water to our lakes and streams as pure as it was when they took it out. That is possible today, I would advise the minister. There was a time, not long ago, when I believe that was not possible; but it is possible now and action here should be taken in this regard. We should also prohibit insoluble detergents being passed into our streams. We should make a continuous and concentrated study of the chemical content of all soaps, detergents and cleaning materials being marketed, to ensure no insoluble toxics are passed into our streams. We should review whatever anti-pollution laws have been promulgated by this country and the United States; and since the great lakes waters are common to both countries, the anti-

pollution and conservation laws for the protection of the purity of waters and for the protection of the fish population ought to be exactly the same in each country. I would remind the minister that he should use his good offices to see that this is done. He should see that these laws are uniform, so that when they are enforced neither country is outside the pale of this common legislation.
I will not take up any more of the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, but would remind the minister and his department that the people bordering the great lakes, those in the great lakes basin, are watching to see whether something good is done to abate this nuisance that affects so adversely all the people of this country, namely the pollution of our public and international waters.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter I wish to raise in connection with this item. If I understood the minister correctly, he referred to health and one or two other factors arising out of pollution as the basis for the studies that are now taking place. I wonder whether the minister would tell us if the studies taking place at the present time go so far as determining the effects of the pollution on our fishing and the tourist and recreational value of these waters.
Mr. Chairman, these studies are comprehensive and I would think they would take this matter into account; but I want to make sure before I give a definitive answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I was waiting to see whether any other hon. members cared to make remarks on this last item of this part of the minister's estimates. I was wondering whether the minister would consent to our reverting to the first item of his estimates and reopening it, for one purpose and one purpose alone; that is, the opportunity of hearing a report by the hon. member for Red Deer in connection with his recent trip to Africa. This would be the only opportunity we would have of hearing a report from the hon. member for Red Deer, and it is certainly a matter of great interest to members of the house and the people of Canada. I think it would be very discourteous of the members of this house if we did not provide an opportunity for the hon. member to make a report on his trip to Africa and his representations to His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Ethiopia, Dr. Kenyatta and others. Would the minister consider doing this?

Mr. Chairman, I think this is most unusual. I believe we should finish the estimates, and then my hon. friend could address himself to this point. We are on a particular item now. This question is concerned with another item. I think we have to deal with each of these items as they come along. The hon. gentleman was here this morning, and we could have dealt with this question on item 35, which was before the committee at that time.
No.
Yes. We were on item 35 this morning, dealing with the external aid program of the government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Where have you sent him now?
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member kindly resume his seat. The Chair would like to bring to the attention of the committee that there is a particular vote before the committee a the moment, and the discussion which has just taken place between the minister and the hon. member for Oxford is certainly not relevant to that vote. If it is the intention of the committee to discuss the possibility of reverting to an item which has already been passed, I cannot see how it can be done under vote No. 40. The minister has replied to the suggestion made by the hon. member, and I would suggest that we go on with the item before us at the moment.

I am, of course, completely in Your Honour's hands and would welcome suggestions from Your Honour as to when I may make this request of the minister and do it, of course, within the rules of the house. I used this particular moment to do it because I thought, since we were in committee and rather free and easy, perhaps Your Honour might overlook a small breach of the rules. However, I would be very happy if Your Honour would suggest when I may raise this matter and make a formal request of the minister to reopen item No. 1 of his estimates, so we may have the opportunity of hearing the hon. member for Red Deer.
I am sure there will be plenty of opportunity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this procedure may be a little irregular, but if we pass these estimates it will be too late, of course, to make the request of the minister. I know the minister is in a co-operative mood so we
Supply-External Affairs thought he would welcome this request. I am foregoing a 30 minute discussion on water pollution in order to make it possible for this request to be accepted.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What a choice.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the house would like me to desist from that discussion but in view of the special circumstances-and they are special circumstances-I would be willing to take this course. Had the hon. member for Red Deer returned yesterday he could have spoken on item 1. He has been a special emissary abroad and we do not know-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. My hon. friend does not, of course, want to make a mockery of the rules of parliament. We are discussing the estimates of the Department of External Affairs and we are dealing with a particular item. When we began our deliberations this morning the hon. gentleman had the chance to raise this matter, at which time it would have been perfectly in order, under item 35.
That is nonsense.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend says that is nonsense, but that is true. All he need do is to look at item 35.
External aid.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course; that is the item precisely. That is not what we are on now. I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that we ought to dispatch the business before us and my hon. friends can take whatever other procedures they wish. I see the hon. gentleman is not in his seat. He travelled for a long time yesterday but I am sure he will be available. In any event, I thought I had satisfied my hon. friend by the comprehensive statement I made last night, and he suggested that I did not need to proceed any further with it. I thought 1 had given all the explanations he wanted. In any event my point of order is clear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The minister has raised a point of order which is along the line the Chair has already taken. Members of the committee know as well as or better than the chairman that we have to be guided by the terms of standing order 59(2), which says that discussion in committee must be strictly relevant to the item before the committee. We are now on vote 40, and certainly the Chair cannot see how under vote 40 there

Supply-External Affairs can be any discussion of the subject matter raised by the hon. member for Oxford.
May I speak to the point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Well, it does seem to me that the matter is very clear. A point of order has been raised and has been dealt with already by a few hon. members. The Chair has given an opinion and really it seems to me that we would make better progress if we were to limit our discussion strictly to the matter before us.
The only reference I wanted to make was this. After all, a matter of procedure like this is a matter of common sense. This morning-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, a point of order has been raised and you have listened to two speakers. I suggest that we should not allow a mockery to be made of this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Rosthern sought a moment ago to address the Chair and the committee on the point of order. I believe the point of order has been ruled upon and it does seem to me that the hon. member would want to abide by the suggestion made by the Chair that the subject to which he is now referring cannot be discussed under vote 40.

Then I rise on a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman. The only reason I wanted to refer to the point of order was that a matter of procedure is really a matter of common sense. The hon. member for Red Deer was in the house this morning but no one would have thought of asking him at that time, after the journey he had just completed, to get up and make a report to the house at once. I have asked a question on the matter of pollution which is now before the house, with regard to which the minister said he would try to get information. Perhaps in the interval we could hear a report from the hon. member for Red Deer on this other matter and deal with it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member for Rosthern said that he was addressing the Chair, not on a point of order but on a question of privilege. Could the minister answer the last question regarding the reference which was given the commission, and whether it went so far as to permit them to determine the effects of pollution on the fishing, tourist and recreational values of these waters?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said that the reference of the commission was comprehensive, and I believe would include that; but I do want to make absolutely sure and I have not the information before me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Before the item carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to know whether the minister is sure about this. This is a very important matter.

I have read the terms of reference and I pointed out their comprehensive character. They are directed to the study of whether the pollution is likely to cause any injury to health or property on either side of the boundary; and if that question is answered in the affirmative, to what extent and in what locality is such pollution taking place. These are the terms of reference.

Although the general terms of reference were well intentioned it might have been better to spell them out in more detail so the commission knows exactly what they are doing in this regard. I see the minister is smiling when I say that. He should not smile because he himself has been unable to determine just what this reference which is before us today means. After all, the fishing industry is an important industry to Canada. The tourist industry is an important industry to Canada. The recreational value of these rivers is also important to the Canadians who live along the waterways, and the Canadians who will live along the waterways in the years ahead. I should like the minister to give some thought to broadening the reference given the commission in regard to this matter, because as I read what he has read to the committee today I do not think the terms of reference give the commission any express instruction along that line.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I simply want to say that the terms of reference are broad; but I fully agree with the hon. member about the recreational importance of these waters to the tourist industry. I would assure him that the study

of pollution in the waters around Essex county enables me to say there is no finer tourist centre and no finer recreational centre than the county of Essex.

Item agreed to.
L 12a. Loans to the government of India to finance the purchase in Canada of aircraft and associated spare parts and equipment in accordance with a financial agreement entered into between the government of Canada and the government of India, $1,367,100.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This is a matter then of external aid?
No, it is not; it is a matter of military assistance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is India part of Canada, then?

This is a matter of military assistance to India. My hon. friend may recall that questions were asked in this house about military assistance to India at a time when it was dealing with difficulties involving one of its neighbours. Canada agreed to make a loan to India in the amount of $12 million to provide for the purchase of Caribou aircraft and also to provide a further loan to cover the interest bearing charges of this loan. On March 9 the government approved a special intergovernmental loan to India in an amount not exceeding $12.5 million to cover the purchase of 16 Caribou aircraft and related spare parts, and equipment for the Indian air force. The cabinet decision stipulated that the loan would bear interest at the normal commercial rate of 5J per cent but would be accompanied by a grant sufficient to defray half the interest charges up to a maximum grant of $2 million. In the fiscal year 1963-64 expenditures under this loan amounted to $11,132,982 and the unspent balance of $1,367,018 lapsed. It is necessary to submit, therefore, for revote, an amount of $1,367,100 in order that funds will be available in the current fiscal year to enable the government's total commitment to be met.

There are not many members in this house who would question the accuracy of the minister's report about that hon. member's travels abroad, and he did give us a rather full report last night. The minister will recall that we expressed some surprise that there was no one within

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to know, when the hon. member for Red Deer appears, just what the situation is in Africa, and how close he came to the centre of the trouble area. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank my hon. friend, the member for Burnaby-Richmond, for his forbearance. I should have dealt with his question last night.
First of all, may I say on the population problem to which he referred, that this was discussed at the United Nations general assembly and has been previously discussed at the economic and social council. The Canadian government did register an abstention on the matter. I hope my friend will realize that in registering that opinion, rather than voting for or against, the delegation was acting on instructions.
However, I listened to what my hon. friend had to say last night during his constructive and well articulated statement, and we will give attention to what he said. I will not say at this time what our attitude will be, because I want to give more consideration to this matter. As the hon. member will realize, there are many considerations involved, some of which he touched upon last night in a very clear way.
I know the hon. member regards this matter as important. He has played a significant part in planned parenthood organizations, and I respect his sincerity in this matter as I am sure he understands mine.
At this time I should like to make a brief reference to what the hon. member said about foreign service officers' pay. He was in a position to know something about this because he himself was in the department. Foreign service officers grade 1 now receive starting salaries from $4,860 to $6,060 per annum. The lower figure is for those who simply have the basic qualifications, while the top figure is for those with doctorates or equivalent academic qualifications. There are

three or four intermediate salaries offered, according to qualifications and experience.
The hon. member may be interested to know that the foreign service officer competition now taking place seems to have been successful in terms of the number of applicants. There will be interviews this year of over 300 applicants, which is almost a record. This speaks well for the interest that the young men and women of Canada have in the foreign service.
With regard to the particular item before the committee I should like to say that this represents a complete new program in Canada's external aid policy. The new loans in the amount of $50 million this year or $150 million over a three year period represent a very important new aspect in Canada's external aid program. The motives are the same as those which for the past 14 years have motivated Canada's outright grants.
Initially the terms are expected to be comparable with those of the international development association, that is, a 50 year maturity period with 10 years grace, non-interest bearing and with a service charge of three quarters of 1 per cent. The development loan program will be directed toward countries now eligible to receive Canadian bilateral grant assistance and in addition will permit a further Canadian contribution to economic progress in Latin America in close co-operation with the international development bank. My hon. friend will remember that last week we announced that $10 million had been apportioned, which represents a departure in the form of assistance by Canada to Latin American countries. Negotiations with regard to this loan and all the other loans that will be made under this vote will be carried on with various countries.
In short, parliament is being asked to provide under this vote for a new instrument to provide assistance. The loans are based on bilateral negotiations based in turn upon a consideration of projects that can best be assisted in this way. I think this represents a very important departure. It is one that was not established first by Canada but we are among the first to use this kind of assistance apart from the United States which I believe was the first country to embark on this type of program.

I have just one question I should like to ask the minister before we take advantage of the opportunity to hear from the hon. member for Red Deer. Is the minister in a position to confirm the press report, which I presume he must have had
Supply-External Affairs at his disposal, that 800 Belgian paratroopers are based on Ascension island ready to land in Stanleyville to save the lives of the white hostages held there by the rebel government of the Congo? Apparently these troops arrived at Ascension island a few hours ago with the permission of the government of the United Kingdom and are ready to attack Stanleyville if necessary. I wonder if the minister can confirm that report, because it might be helpful to the discussion?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there are many things about this matter I could confirm but as my hon. frend, who has had a very deep and penetrating experience of foreign affairs, knows, you do not disclose intended strategy. I know it is in the newspapers but my hon. friend will realize there are many things in the newspapers which are accurate. There are many things that might be in the newspapers which are not there. There are plans to try to relieve these unfortunate hostages and I will wait until the proper moment to disclose all the other steps that are being taken to try to relieve the situation. I am sure my hon. friend, with his deep understanding of these problems, will understand why I take this position.

Mr. Chairman, the press report indicates that this move was officially announced by the Belgian government and I was wondering whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government have been informed and whether this report is correct, because it might make some difference to our discussions.
This matter is one that is not under the control of any one government, either the Belgian government or any other.

Mr. Chairman, this type of answer does not add anything at all either to the knowledge of the house or to assuage the feelings of the Canadian people. The question asked by the hon. member for Oxford is one that should be answered. Is there a basis for this report? Is the Belgian government in this announcement placing before the world as a whole information that is not correct? I simply cannot understand this assumed attitude-I do not quite know how to describe it-of pretence on the part of the minister, that for him to give information like this which is already known world wide would be harmful under the circumstances. This is nothing but nonsense on his part and he knows it. If he had been asked for information as to courses being taken which are

Supply-External Affairs not known to mankind as a whole, one could understand his attitude; but for him to raise himself up and stand on an altar of pretence in a matter such as this certainly is in line with the regular course followed by the minister in dealing with external affairs. We are interested in knowing if there is a foundation for this report. I have had some experience too in this regard and I should like to know what the minister would have done when he was sitting over here at the time we were in office and anyone on the government side had chosen to give that kind of answer.
Does my hon. friend want me to answer that question?
If the hon. gentleman will wait, I am asking for information now and we have a right to have it.
Oh, oh.

Oh, I know that those hon. gentlemen sitting opposite choose to live in an atmosphere of ignorance, but the rest of us want to know what is going on. I ask the minister to give this information. Let us at least have a picture that he has some appreciation of what is going on, for certainly the press has been very definite and clear in this regard. I am not asking him to tell us what other courses of action the government may have in mind. The government has undertaken several courses of action in this regard and they have all blown up in its face. Finally India has been called upon by the United Kingdom and two other nations, the United States and Canada, to exercise its diplomatic facilities so that apparently as of this moment, with India called in, all that has taken place heretofore has not been successful. We are not asking the minister to give information that is secret, but certainly for him to adopt an attitude of mystic silence in regard to a matter that is known to everyone through the press is not in keeping with the responsibilities of a minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I see that the hon. member for Red Deer is now in the house and this item is broad enough to provide him with the opportunity to give us the benefit of his experiences in Africa and to tell us about his attempts to be helpful in the matter of the release of these missionaries from Stanleyville, and also the other objectives of his mission. I was wondering whether we should not have the opportunity of hearing from him.

Mr. Chairman, before the member for Red Deer proceeds I should like to raise a point of order in view of the discussion we have had about his trip and having to do with the remarks he may make. In view of the fact that the member for Red Deer went to Africa at government invitation, under government auspices and at public expense and presumably returned the same way, I wonder whether or not the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government are now willing to accept responsibility for all that the member for Red Deer may say to the committee this afternoon?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know what will be the full purport of what the hon. member is going to say.
Has he not reported to you?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He has made a report to the government. I want to say that we are grateful to the hon. member for Red Deer for what he has tried to do in a most difficult situation, affecting the freedom and security of a good many Canadians and many others from other countries.

I am not arguing about these latter comments of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If he is not willing to take responsibility for what the member for Red Deer now says as a result of his trip, which was made at the invitation of the government, under government auspices and direction, and paid for out of public funds, then I think we should pay no attention to what the hon. member for Red Deer says, but only to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs is willing to take responsibility for.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I want my hon. friend to know that I have the fullest confidence in the execution of this mandate by the hon. member for Red Deer.
But you do not take responsibility for what he is prepared to say.
Sit down.

If I may speak to this point of order; surely it must be obvious to members of this house that any report which the hon. member for Red Deer is making is one for which the minister is going to be responsible, as a report to the minister and not particularly to this house.

At the outset, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I am very pleased to note the interest of various mem-

bers of the house in the situation that presently centres around the insurgent held territory in the Congo, the capital of which is Stanleyville. Unfortunately, it seems to me that public opinion with regard to this very serious crisis is not too much aroused. It is only a matter of 50 years ago or less when a few hostages held in this way would have been the cause of a world war. Today we have something over 1,000 people being held as hostage under blackmail for political and military purposes. Unfortunately the world does not seem to care too much.
I am not speaking, nor do I make any pretence to speak, on behalf of the government as I report briefly on the situation as I see it. I do count it a privilege to have been entrusted with the responsibility of trying to do something for those in this situation, not only for the relief of some 33 Canadians who are amongst these hostages, but on behalf of the 16 countries that have nationals in the Stanleyville area. I say it was a privilege not only because of the fact that, as a result of my experience in Africa it was felt that I might be able to perform these duties in a way that a person not having these contacts and this experience might not be able to do, but it was a privilege because of the general good will and respect in which Canada and Canadians are held in Africa and across the world. At this point I must say that I come back feeling very proud of the fact that I am a Canadian with the hope and the wish that Canadians in Canada could do an equally good job in getting along with each other and meeting their home responsibilities as Canadians outside Canada obviously are able to do.
This situation relating to the hostages is a very difficult one. It is very difficult because of the complexity of the Congo situation. It is very difficult because, should I or any other Canadian in some position of responsibility make a false step or make a comment which could be misinterpreted by those who are responsible for the welfare of these hostages, it could mean the difference between life and death for them. I am sure therefore that every member in this house will understand and appreciate this situation and will be willing to accept the fact that it may not be possible to say everything publicly that might be said or that one might be thinking.
Now, briefly, the situation in the Congo is this: a large area in the northeastern and eastern part of the country during recent months was taken over by insurgent Congolese, sometimes better known as the rebels,
Supply-External Affairs a name which is strenuously objected to by most African leaders today. This, again, adds to the complexity of the situation. The insurgents have set this up as the people's republic of the Congo. In taking over this area, they have taken into their custody something like 1,000 foreign nationals who represent 16 nations. I might just identify these nations. They are the Argentine, Haiti, the United States, Canada, Great Britain, France, Belgium, Switzerland, Greece, Italy, Pakistan and India, and then four African nations, being Kenya, the Cameroons, the Upper Volta and Nigeria. These are foreign nationals carrying passports who were there on some particular assignment.
You may ask how other African nationals are there. It is the result of the fact there was working in this area of the Congo a number of United Nations agencies. I refer to the World Health Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization, UNESCO and the United Nations technical assistance program. The purpose of these people being held as hostages is to further strengthen the political and military position of the insurgent authorities and forces. The situation became critical when the Congolese government forces, that is the military forces of the democratic republic of the Congo, began to close in on the Stanleyville area. These military operations, briefly, are encircling around the north, around the south, up along the eastern border which is known as the Uganda frontier, and then southwest in a pincer movement. Only a few days ago they took over the city of Kindu and several other towns farther along.
As this military operation closes in, the real problem develops as the rebel authority begins to break down. I am sure that the position is much more dangerous so far as these hostages are concerned from these radical elements within the rebel area, one of which is known as Lajeunesse, than it is from the rebel authorities themselves. It is for this reason that, should any mismove be made in so far as our efforts are concerned, and I speak now of the efforts of the 16 nations having nationals there, it could mean the slaughter of these people.
Canada has taken the initiative in trying, one, to get the international Red Cross into Stanleyville; and, two, through the facilities of the international Red Cross to arrange the evacuation of these hostages. In taking this initiative the government of Canada asked me if I would make this trip because it was felt that I happened to know personally many of the African officials on the

Supply-External Affairs eastern side of Africa where contact is maintained with the rebel Congolese. I did so because it seemed to me there might be more hope of getting into communication with the rebel authorities.
I would say to those who have been interested or who have been critical of my going in the first place that it had been the original plan that during the recess I should make a trip which would involve a survey of what was being done in Africa under Canada's aid program, particularly as it relates to some of the African agencies attempting to co-ordinate the African development program. It so happens that the headquarters of these organizations are located in Ethiopia. One is the economic commission for Africa, more commonly known as the E.C.A., which is an agency of the United Nations. It is the aim of the E.C.A. to coordinate all the aid programs of the various friendly countries and at the same time to bring about a degree of co-ordination in the economic development of those countries to which the aid is directed. This is a reasonable and practical approach. Another organization concerned is the organization for African unity. I may say that this organization has been a dream of the Emperor of Ethiopia for many years, and when I served his government we used to spend many hours discussing how it could come to pass. So we have been familiar with it from its inception. In addition, and connected with the E.C.A. but functioning as an autonomous organization, is the African development bank which held its formative convention in Lagos, Nigeria a few days ago. Then, there is the United Nations technical assistance agency with headquarters in Addis Ababa.
It was thought that, because of my familiarity with these various organizations, my experience might be put to good account, not for the benefit of the Liberal party, as I understand, but for the benefit of Canada and her external aid program. Since we did not have a recess, as we had expected at one time, plans for this assignment were delayed, until the crisis in the Congo due to military pressure reached a point where there were justifiable fears for the wellbeing of Canadians who were being held as hostages.
Briefly, the following is a summary of what has been done to gain the release of these hostages. A few weeks ago the organization for African unity set up a special ad hoc conciliatory committee for the Congo. This commission was charged with responsibility

for trying to work out an answer to the complex political problems of the Congo. Because this organization was in existence, it was felt that the only sensible approach to the rebels would be by way of this ad hoc commission. When I first arrived in Africa I had an opportunity to discuss this with Mr. Nkrumah, the president of Ghana and, in particular, with his foreign minister who is a member of this ad hoc commission which I have just mentioned. I soon found out in discussion with them and with officials of some other countries who had a good deal to do with this commission that the general attitude in the minds of many Africans toward these hostages was: "Let them remain there; if they can do some good in stopping the dropping of bombs from Congo military airplanes provided by the United States, or the advance of mercenary soldiers who, reportedly, are paid out of Belgian funds, they will be performing some useful purpose; but if the presence of the hostages fails to do this, let them all die together."
This is the very difficult attitude with which we were faced. While I did not agree with this attitude-it is contrary to all humanitarian reasoning and certainly it is in contravention of any of the Geneva conventions which have been signed-it is one which is, nevertheless, held by a great many representatives of the African countries. What did we do after this? Without going into all the details, may I say that we used our knowledge of the situation and the contacts we had with various individuals to appeal to two of the older men of Africa, both of whom are held in great respect and both of whom have shown they understand the responsibility of democratic government and humanitarian dealing between peoples. One of them is the Prime Minister of Kenya, Mr. Jomo Kenyatta, the chairman of this ad hoc commission. In appealing to him we felt we were making a direct approach to the rebel situation because he had been authorized to deal with the Congo situation. We consulted with many individuals in Kenya as well as with the governor general Mr. Malcolm MacDonald. We were given an assurance that the lives and well-being of these hostages were guaranteed by the rebel authorities.
We then approached the Emperor of Ethiopia on the same basis. I might say I presented to Mr. Kenyatta a telegraphic letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the effect that it was the hope of Canada that he, Mr. Kenyatta, would use his good offices to intervene in this hostage

situation. As we discussed the matter with the Emperor of Ethiopia it became evident that this elderly gentleman, who is regarded with such great respect across the world and who is looked on by other Africans as more or less the founder of modern Africa, possessed a deep understanding and appreciation of the issues which were involved. So the weight of the influence of these men was added to the appeal made to the rebels, first of all, to allow the Red Cross to enter and, second, to permit the Red Cross to arrange for the evacuation of the hostages.
In all these discussions Dr. George Hoffman, who is delegate general to the international committee of the Red Cross in Africa, was present. He had found it impossible to reach some of these senior authorities. Thus we were able to assist him and, in return, his presence lent weight to the argument we were putting forward, namely that this situation must be dealt with on humanitarian grounds and separated entirely from the political aspect. I may say that in addition to this general appeal for intervention and consideration on the part of the two elder statesmen of Africa I have mentioned, we came up with the idea that it would be a very good thing if the nations which had nationals among the hostages could get together to form what we called, for want of a better term, a concilium in order that they as a group, rather than unilaterally, might present their request for the objective we had been endeavouring to secure through direct negotiation. I am pleased to say that in the latter days of the negotiations both in Kenya and in Ethiopia I was joined by one of the most experienced Canadians in the Congo situation, Mr. Michel Gauvin who is a senior officer in the Department of External Affairs. At the present time he is in Nairobi more or less leading this effort to get these nations together and in recommending that the good services of India might be used, because India has a number of nationals involved as well.
This is the point at which we left and came home. We came home for the purpose of passing through Europe and contacting as many of the nations concerned as possible to encourage them to take part in a joint appeal.
All of us are sorry that it should be the case, but as those who know something about the situation realize, it was not possible in the present circumstances to gain the outright release of these hostages. The rebels were not willing to release them. Every means of persuasion has been used. Direct contact has 20220-654
Supply-External Affairs been made through the representative of the rebel authorities, a man named Thomas Kanza, who spends his time outside the rebel held area of the Congo negotiating for and representing the Stanleyville authorities. I would be most happy if I could report to the committee that we were able to gain the consent of the rebel authorities to meet the Red Cross and grant the evacuation of these hostages. They apparently do not intend to do so. As the military situation worsens, it is obvious that they have more reason and are more intent on keeping control of these hostages than ever.
I might just say in summing up this matter which I have briefly surveyed that as I left Addis Ababa the day before yesterday I issued a statement which was intended to emphasize again the purpose of my visit and the desire and will of the Canadian government. I might say before I read this statement to the committee that we received word just a couple of hours before we released the statement that Dr. Carlson, the American medical missionary who had been condemned to die, had been given a reprieve. We felt this was a very definite step in the right direction. We were encouraged by it and we made this statement with the intention that it might further encourage consideration by the rebel authorities to grant amnesty to the hostages. I will now quote from this statement because I think it is of interest to all of us and, as it has been released to the press, it is a public document:
As I leave Africa to report to the government of Canada on my mission, I believe it is only fitting that I should set the record straight with regard to the purpose and the results of my mission as it relates to the hostage problem in the Congo.
I came to Africa at the request of the Canadian government in order to contact a number of friendly governments and exchange views with them on matters of mutual concern.
Particularly as it relates now to the new African organizations:
Within my terms of reference, I was requested to deliver to the Prime Minister of Kenya, Mr. Jomo Kenyatta, in his capacity as chairman of the ad hoc commission on the Congo, a message from the Honourable Paul Martin, the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada, expressing the concern of the Canadian government for its nationals in the Congo who are in the area of Stanleyville and about whom we have had no news since the start of hostilities last July. I was instructed also to see His Imperial Majesty Haile Selassie I, whom I know personally, having served in Ethiopia from 1943 to 1958, and to call on the secretary general of the organization of African unity, His Excellency Diallo Telli.
In reply to Mr. Martin's message which I delivered, Prime Minister Kenyatta assured me that he had made several appeals to the Stanleyville authorities and in response had received assurance

Supply-External Affairs
that the foreign civilians in Stanleyville would not be harmed. In a subsequent telegram he expressed the hope "that the lives of the persons concerned"
*-those in Stanleyville-"will not be in danger".
I was received by His Imperial Majesty, the Emperor of Ethiopia, on four occasions. The Emperor expressed grave concern over the fate of the Canadians and other foreign nationals held as hostages. I likewise discussed the matter with the minister of foreign affairs, Ato Ketema Yifru who, on returning from Kenya where he had conferred with Prime Minister Kenyatta and other Kenya officials-
Perhaps I might break in here to say that the first action the emperor took in this regard was to send his foreign minister, along with other senior officials, with myself back to Nairobi to carry on these negotiations. Coming back to the text of the statement:
-informed me that he also had been assured that there was no reason to fear for the lives of the foreign nationals held by the insurgent forces. During the past week end this has been re-emphasized by Mr. Thomas Kanza, the representative in East Africa of the Stanleyville authorities who on several occasions has given his firm assurance that the hostages were in no danger and there was no reason to fear for their lives.
Yesterday-
That is, the day before I left Ethiopia:
-I met His Excellency Diallo Telli, who told me Mr. Kenyatta was doing everything humanly possible for the protection of foreign nationals in Stanleyville. Mr. Telli referred me to Mr. Ken-yatta's statement to the effect that Stanleyville authorities had given him assurance that foreign nationals were not in danger.
Might I just say, Mr. Chairman, that the reason I reviewed this as I did was to place the responsibility for the well-being of these hostages back on the individuals who had given me those assurances. I felt it would again place some degree of responsibility- at least the maximum which we could obtain -for their safety on the individuals who had given me these assurances. Continuing with this text:
During the course of all these discussions I continually emphasized the fact that my purpose in urging the release of the hostages through the international committee of the Red Cross was solely on humanitarian grounds, and should be considered as such apart from all political implications. I explained that Canada would very much like to see the African nations, particularly those represented on the ad hoc commission of the organization for African unity to use whatever influence they had on the Stanleyville authorities to allow the international committee of the Red Cross to be permitted to enter Stanleyville in view of the imminence of an attack by the forces of the democratic republic of the Congo. I explained that the holding of the hostages by the Stanleyville authorities is in violation of all international conventions and that they are being denied even the good offices of the international committee of the Red Cross.

I believe that this statement had some good effect, because very shortly after the text had been presented to the Ethopian minister of foreign affairs and to the secretary general of the organization of African unity by Mr. Gauvin-that is, two hours after I had left- a further message was sent by Ethiopia to Mr. Kenyatta urging him again to contact directly the Stanleyville authorities and emphasize the importance that the lives of these hostages be carefully safeguarded. A second effect of this was that I believe it speeded up the agreement amongst the member nations of this so-called concilium in such a way that today they have met in Nairobi and have agreed to ask India to take the lead in making their appeal. I think this was a very wise decision; I believe that India can have a great deal of influence.
I might briefly close my remarks, Mr. Chairman, by referring briefly to the situation that obviously is disturbing to all of us in so far as concerns the report that Belgium has placed certain troops on the Ascension islands ready for military intervention in the Stanleyville area. I know nothing about this, no more than any of us do who may have seen the report in the newspapers. On the other hand, it is the Belgians and the Americans who have the greatest number of nationals at stake, there being something over 700 Belgian nationals and some 60 Americans, a fair proportion of them being consular representatives which the rebels themselves have said are being held in confinement. I neglected to say earlier that the Canadian hostages, unlike the Americans, Belgians, Italians, and I believe one other nation, are merely being held under house arrest or compound arrest. I do know something of the concern of these nations for the large number of their nationals. We held many discussions with representatives of these two governments as well as representatives of other governments concerned in the area; but whether or not there is any truth in the story that the Belgian government has decided to take this action, I do not know. I merely refer to this because I can well understand their fear as the forces of the government close in in the Congo. Again, Mr. Chairman, may I emphasize to hon. members of the house that the situation is extremely critical.
It would be a terrible blow to the peace of Africa; it would be a very difficult situation for the organization of African unity, and it would further complicate the very difficult situation existing in the Congo, not to mention the atrocity it would represent on

any basis of humanitarian thinking, if these people should be destroyed. Therefore what we say and what we have done, and what will be said and what will be done, before the situation is cleared up is something which must be taken with the greatest of concern, forethought and carefulness, bearing in mind that any misstep might result in the tragedy that we are all so concerned about.
Let me say in closing that this experience has been a privilege for me. In spite of some of the criticisms which have been made, if the situation were to arise again where I might be asked to carry out such an assignment I would be very happy to do so. I cannot emphasize too much to the members of this committee the regard in which Canadians and Canada are held, not only by the nationals of Africa but by all those with whom we came in contact. By offering our good services and taking the initiative in an effort to free these hostages we were doing something which perhaps no one else could have done, and I am sure all members of the committee will understand this.
I could go on and make a few remarks about external aid but I think I might do that a little later on, if it is considered relevant, as at this time we are closing our deliberations on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. I will just leave this statement as it relates to the hostages by itself, because we do not want to do anything to detract from the urgency and the gravity of the situation.
Item agreed to.
