speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The committee will now proceed with the examination of the 20220-654J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration estimates of the Indian affairs branch, vote No. 15. This item is to be found on page 62 of the blue book, the details on page 65.

Mr. Chairman, I had the opportunity on another day when these items were before the committee, as did other hon. members, to make a few comments, but since that time there has been another development in the field of Indian affairs which I think is worth a comment or two. Incidentally, I understand that just within the past few days-the move may still be taking place -the Indian affairs branch, along with other offices under the minister's jurisdiction, is moving into a brand, spanking new building. Many of the personnel are there already. I hope the atmosphere of freshness, vigour and newness which exists in this new building will also have some effect on the minister and his officials, so that they may come up with fresh, invigorating approaches and policies in regard to Indian affairs.
Since the last time these items were before this committee a federal-provincial conference has been held on Indian affairs. This was a conference from which the native Indian people were excluded. Because of the exclusion of the very people whose rights and freedoms were being debated in that conference there has developed a very large degree of resentment against this government and against the provincial governments for participating in a conference held behind closed doors, and for discussing and debating and doing heaven knows what else with Indian affairs and the rights of the people themselves.
The reason given by the minister for holding this conference in secret was that it was a dominion-provincial conference, and dominion-provincial conferences have traditionally been held behind closed doors. This reasoning may be sound if this conference, as with conferences in the past, had been about fiscal arrangements, taxes, statistics or dollars and cents, but at this particular conference the federal and provincial governments were not dealing with cold, inanimate statistics but with human beings, a group of human beings incidentally who populated this part of the world countless thousands of years before Europeans ever dreamed it existed. This conference dealt with our first Canadians and their basic rights, their fundamental freedoms, their position under the law and the whole field of their social activity.
I echo, Mr. Chairman, their resentment as being excluded from this conference. They do not know what went on behind these

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration closed doors and I do not know that they will ever know. But certainly they should be fully advised if any similar conferences are held in the future. Regardless of the expressions of view of certain provinces the minister should insist, in his position as minister responsible for the provisions in the British North America Act concerning Indians and the land reserved for Indians, that any future conferences should be open, and that the native Indian people should be able to sit in on, participate in and listen to what is taking place with respect to their rights and freedoms. Because, as I said earlier, these native people are not statistics or taxes or cold, inanimate objects; they are human beings for whom we should have a far higher regard than was the case with this particular dominion-provincial conference.
Incidentally a suggestion was made in connection with conferences which I think the minister should reject or say something about. This was the position taken by the province of Quebec-what the other provinces said I cannot say at this stage:
The Quebec delegation believes in the need for future federal-provincial conferences following the present one.
In our opinion, these conferences should be held not only between ministers but also between the senior officials.
It could be left to the federal government to convene these conferences but. in our mind, the provinces should play an active part in their preparation and especially in setting up their agenda.
I suggest to the minister that even though Quebec is his own province he should reject that sort of proposal, because all it does is carry on the proposition that these conferences which take place in secret represent the form of conference which should be followed in the future. The minister should tell the native people that he made an error in holding this last conference behind closed doors, excluding the native Indian people from it, that he does not wish to repeat that error at any future conference, and that so far as his government is concerned future conferences will be open to the native people.
It is true that following the conference, both as the communique mentioned and as the minister himself said in reply to questions in this chamber on November 22, there have been continual references to the idea that consultation should take place with the Indian people before anything is done. I submit that consultation will mean relatively little to the Indian people unless they are told fully, openly and honestly what the positions are that were taken by the respective

provincial governments behind those closed doors.
The proposition is being held out to these native people that they might be in a better position by accepting the jurisdiction of the various provincial governments. One of the things the native people will be concerned about before accepting that proposition is the attitude adopted by this, that or any other provincial government. They do not know what that attitude is and they will not be able to discover the attitude expressed at these conferences. How are the native people going to know what the position was that was taken by the province of Quebec at that conference? How are they going to know what are the proposals the province of Quebec put forward at those discussions? How are the native people in Alberta going to know what the government of Alberta proposed at that conference? If the minister continues to say that what went on at that conference is privileged and cannot be disclosed, then the native people will never find out.
I do not intend to single out the province of Quebec, but I do happen to have some information about the representations it made at that conference. I should like to refer to one other proposal made by that province about education, and this is of vital concern to the native people of the province of Quebec. This will also be of concern to the native people of other provinces, if a similar proposal was put forward by other provincial governments. Let me read part of this proposal:
The province of Quebec gladly accepts the proposal of the federal government to the effect that, when feasible, the Indian reservations be incorporated in the school districts of the province, providing, evidently, that the Indians contribute, one way or another, their fair share toward educational costs.
When reading between the lines, what does that mean to the Canadian native people? I do not intend to give my interpretation of it, but shall state only what the native people feel and fear as a result of this proposal. They are afraid their Indian reserves will be incorporated in the school districts, and a land tax immediately imposed for educational purposes. These lands will then be liable to seizure and sale, if the native people are unable to meet the school taxation which might be levied.
The minister did say that there was a protection in this regard in the British North America Act. I wish he would expand on that and indicate where that protection is, or what led him to that conclusion. There is a

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
protection section in the Indian Act to the effect that Indian lands are exempt from taxation, except those taxes which may be levied by the bands themselves for their own purposes. However, I remind the minister that laws have been changed before in respect of Indian affairs, and because there is now a protecting section in the Indian Act is no guarantee that it will remain, regardless of what the minister has said.
And if jurisdiction is transferred to the provinces your statement is even more accurate.

If jurisdiction is turned over to the provinces the whole protection is gone, and the Indian people will be at the mercy of heaven knows what.
The key point of all this discussion is that proposals were made by the minister and his government which still remain secret. Behind those closed doors various provinces made proposals which also remain secret. While there was some reference to the proposals by the province of Saskatchewan contained in a Regina newspaper, and I recall also seeing something in a newspaper about what the province of Manitoba suggested, these were selected references of what took place at these discussions.
You are now going to commence a program of conferences with native Indian people to discuss with them whether they will accept provincial services such as welfare, health measures and education. Can you stand up now and say that at that same time there will be a full and honest disclosure by the provinces of the proposals that they put forward at those closed door conferences? It is not the final agreement that may be arrived at between the federal government and the provincial governments that is of importance to the native people, but rather what is in the back of the minds of the provincial government officials. We owe it to these native people to tell them freely and honestly all about the detailed discussions which took place at those meetings, if the provinces will not do so. We owe it to the native people of the various provinces to be honest with them and declare fully the intentions of those provinces.
The minister will appreciate even more than I that the native people have grounds for continuing suspicion of governments, and I am not referring alone to his government. As long as these suspicions exist, that there is something underhanded taking place, the minister will not be in a position to make
any really progressive steps in the field of Indian activities. This is one thing which must be cleared up before the minister can hope to develop anything worth while for the native people. The governments must have open, honest and frank discussions with them.
One other point of concern to Indian people to which T should like to make reference is the manner in which these conferences are going to take place. At page 9652 of Hansard, the minister stated that he was going to give clarifying explanations about this matter, and then said:
This consulting procedure will operate at two levels.
First, in every province of Canada, there shall be held a conference to which all Indians will be invited-
Does that mean that in the province of British Columbia there will be facilities available for more than 40,000 Indian people to congregate in one place?
Who is going to be responsible for the financing of the transportation of native people to these conferences? The minister talks of a conference in each province, so presumably there will only be one in each province, which will be held at a central location. Unless the public treasury is willing to finance the travelling of native Indian people so they may attend these conferences it will mean that the points of view which will get across at the conferences will be those of the native Indian people who live closest to the conferences and will be able to attend because their transportation costs will not be great. It will be the point of view of those bands who have a sufficient amount of money in their treasuries to pay the expenses of their representatives. It will not be a broad, general, representative point of view.
I think the minister owes it to the country and to the native people particularly to explain in great detail the mechanics by which these conferences will be held, how the native people are going to get there, where the conferences are going to be held, how long they are going to last, what procedure will be arranged for the discussion of ideas, what procedure will be used to reach conclusions at the conferences. Will there be voting by the people there or will there just be some sort of gathering of opinions and an attempt to assess the reaction? All of these mechanics and fine details need to be explained as soon as possible so that the native Indian people will know just where they stand with respect to these conferences. Then the minister went on to say:

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
After this consultation and provided the Indians agree-
I have just dealt with that point. How are you going to determine the extent of their agreement, by vote, or what is going to take place?
-that such provincial services would be des-sirable, there shall be a second method of consultation: the bands will be consulted-
I am omitting some words in order to retain continuity of thought.
-that is, the councils of those bands will be consulted in order to ascertain if they wish to take advantage of a program to be established in a province-
And so on. We want to know in greater detail just how this consultation procedure is going to operate. Will there be mechanics for voting set up? Will there be in the case of the bands, as I suggested earlier must also be done at the conferences, a full, honest and open expression of what is in the minds of the provincial governments so that it may be determined whether or not there are any nefarious schemes involved in this transfer of administration? These are details that the bands also want to know about. The minister went on to say:
Third, it was decided at the conference to set up, in each province, a standing Indian affairs committee which will be consulted on any administrative question concerning the Indians.
How are you going to set up these administrative committees? Are they going to be selected by the Indian affairs branch? Are they going to be selected by the minister? Are they going to be selected by the provincial governments? Are they going to be elected? Are the native Indian people themselves going to choose their own representatives on these standing Indian affairs committees? What is the fine definition of the word "consultation"? The Indians are vitally concerned about this point. "Consultation" runs throughout the whole aftermath of the dominion-provincial conference where, if anywhere, consultation should have taken place.
It is very easy to consult with someone after you have made a decision as to what you are going to do. The dominion and provincial governments can come to some agreement and in fact may well have come to some agreement behind those closed doors. I know that the native people are not merely going to accept the bland statement of the minister about consultation unless they know what consultation means. Does consultation mean that you are going to be bound by the decision of the native people or, as has been the case so often in the past, does it mean


you are merely going to speak with them about a certain subject matter and then go ahead and do what you like anyway and try to look for support?
It has not been beyond the activities of Liberal governments in the past to attempt to hand pick native Indian people who support their point of view in order to use them as a consensus in making changes with regard to Indian affairs. I was going to say that this was what the present Minister of Transport did, but it probably was Walter Harris who was the first minister of citizenship and immigration. In any event, this is what the Liberal government did with regard to the amendments to the Indian Act in 1951. Their consultation procedure involved hand picking native Indian people who they knew would support them, and then saying that the opinions they expressed represented the consensus of the Indian people:	"We have
consulted them and they have told us this and we are going to put it into effect." The amendments to the act in 1951 were a most disgraceful and arrogant show of a desire to control all Indian affairs from the ivory tower of the minister's office, because it was at that time the minister's power was extended so that the native people could do practically nothing without first obtaining the permission of the minister.
I was reminded of this when I heard the message program over one of the radio stations at home. This is a public service to some of the remote villages. On this program the Indian agent or Indian superintendent, as he is now called, gave permission to a lonely couple in an Indian village whose child had died to proceed with the burial of their child. This sort of thing is ridiculous. Over the message program the Indian superintendent gave permission to Mr. and Mrs. So-and-so to go ahead with the burial service for their child who had died.
The 1951 amendments gave the minister virtual power of life and death over the native Indian people and their band councils. That is not the type of consultation the native people want now and its is not the type of consultation that any member of the house wants for the Indians, if he thinks seriously about the matter. I think it is up to the minister to explain in full detail what he means by consultation and what democratic processes are going to be put into effect and are going to be guaranteed so that the native people will control their own destiny, and so that some politician will not control them

merely because he happens to think it is the wise and smart thing to do.
There are many other things I mentioned earlier, about which I should like to talk, which involve details of the activities of the Indian affairs branch in my own riding of Skeena. However, we have agreed to confine consideration of the remaining estimates so that they will be completed by next Friday and I do not want to transgress the opportunity and right of other members to comment on some of these matters. But because the minister has not had the opportunity so far I would urge him to take all the time he requires to reply, not only to my proposals but to those that other members have made on the various occasions that the estimates have been before the committee, in order that we will have a full explanation of the attitude of the department and the minister, and so that the Indians will not be left in the dark and will have as complete and understanding as is possible of the manner in which the government intends to deal with their rights. After all, as I said earlier, they are human beings and deserve perhaps a far greater degree of consideration in this parliament than any other group of human beings in Canada. I am including the Eskimo people in this reference. We should be prepared to give them this consideration.

I have a few comments to make on this item, some of which I have delayed for some time. I did not speak on the first item of the minister's estimates because I thought it might be wise to wait until now so that my comments could be concentrated. First of all, I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the newly appointed assistant deputy minister. I know of his work in Alberta and I am sure he will bring a great measure of satisfaction, experience and knowledge to this department. As a matter of fact, this appointment did not go as far as had been originally suggested in the joint committee report on Indian affairs. At that time I believe we considered the establishment of a separate department. However, this move goes a long way and it is long overdue. I am happy to see that the move has been made and the position is occupied as it is.
It is quite obvious, as the hon. member for Skeena has said, that the government is now giving serious consideration to what are, in effect, very drastic, very sweeping changes in the administration of Indian affairs. In doing so they will tend to shift jurisdic-
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration tion, responsibility or administration or possibly a combination of all three. This, of course, is indicated in the press communique released following the conference the hon. member for Skeena mentioned. Let me make it quite plain that this was also a matter to which we referred in the joint committee. Personally, I believe this is a move in the right direction. There were a number of briefs presented by Indian bands indicating concern about the possibility, which was posed to them during a meeting of the committee, of a change of jurisdiction from the federal to the provincial government. My own view is that it is not right that we should have two sets of laws pertaining to groups of people in this country and that the ultimate, most desirable result, will be to have, as circumstances permit and people themselves require, jurisdiction put into the hands of provincial governments so that there will be an integration of the rights and responsibilities of the people of Canada.
Having said that, I must say that we must move with the utmost care, the utmost caution, not only to see that equity is done but to give the appearance of doing equity. In our dealings with the Indian people in the past, this has not been the case. The suspicions which they have indicated they possess are suspicions which they are certainly entitled to harbour because of what has happened in previous years. There must be the most careful, sympathetic consideration given in each instance to each band, each group, each section, each district and each area. It must not be done by wholesale regulations issued from Ottawa and bearing on all parts of the country.
We have to make it crystal clear that there will be no compulsion, no force of any kind. Any changes which will be made will only be made after the fullest consultation, discussion and advice. In the final analysis, the choice will be the choice of the Indian people themselves. I have had some experience with the Indian people in my area, and there are many thousands of them there. I can think of a number of cases in which departmental officials have attempted to compel these people to have closer contact with the white people with a view to fitting them into the white man's world. These conditions were not acceptable to the Indians within the area, as was proven by the results. I am not going to go into the details, but there is not the slightest doubt but that there are as many problems as there are Indians. Perhaps there is not an Indian problem so much as there are many Indians who have problems.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
It is obvious to me therefore, Mr. Chairman, that consideration is a condition precedent to what I propose to deal with subsequently. I am not raising the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in, I think it is the Sikyea case, otherwise known as the case of the lame duck, but I want to extract from that case the fact that by a decision of the territorial court of appeal, which was confirmed in the Supreme Court of Canada, the Indian treaties have now been relegated to a position where they have very little legal effect. I do not think there is any question about that. The statement made by Mr. Justice Johnston, who delivered the judgment of the territorial court of appeal after hearing the case at Yellowknife, indicates that this is the situation. I feel this is going to have the effect of increasing the existing suspicions that so many of the Indian people have with regard to the rights which they feel should be theirs under the terms of these treaties, and as to the intentions and policies of the white man, particularly the white man's government.
This, in turn, is bound to have some effect on the proposal of the government in connection with the Indian claims commission. I believe the terms of this commission are now being considered. In my view, they will have to be substantially widened from those originally contemplated. They will have to be made more equitable, and benefits extended to people and situations which were never originally contemplated when the first measure was being introduced. There is no doubt at all, Mr. Chairman, about the fact that this decision downgrading the Indian treaties and the benefits which they were intended to confer upon the Indian people, is going to be detrimental. Certainly, as a result of the decision the use of the word "treaty" becomes absolutely meaningless. These treaties do not have the effect of treaties.
It does not do any harm to refresh our memories by examining some of these treaties very briefly to ascertain just what was said. I think that this was done very well by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories when he was speaking on these treaties some time ago. I have here a treaty which affects the Indian people in a very large area of northwest Canada. One particular section which I think is of interest reads as follows:
And Her Majesty the Queen hereby agrees with the said Indians that they shall have right to pursue their usual vocations of hunting, trapping and fishing throughout the tract surrendered as heretofore described, subject to such regulations

as may from time to time be made by the government of the country, acting under the authority of Her Majesty, and saving and excepting such tracts as may be required or taken up from time to time for settlement, mining, lumbering, trading or other purposes.
This section should be read in connection with a letter which accompanied the treaty because it indicates the frame of mind with which the Indian people approach the execution of these treaties, and makes even more unfair the conditions which now have been attached to the treaties and the effect which they are having. I have here a letter dated September 22, 1899 sent to the superintendent general of Indian affairs in connection with the signing of this particular treaty, treaty no. 8. I should like to read this paragraph from the letter-the agent who negotiated the treaty is discussing the difficulty he encountered when he was negotiating on this matter of hunting and fishing privileges with the Indians.
Our chief difficulty was the apprehension that the hunting and fishing privileges were to be curtailed.
How right the Indians were in having those apprehensions.
The provision in the treaty under which ammunition and twine is to be furnished went far in the direction of quieting the fears of the Indians because they admitted it would be unreasonable to furnish the means of hunting and fishing if laws were to be enacted which would make hunting and fishing so restricted as to render it impossible to make a livelihood by such pursuits.
But over and above the provision, we had to solemnly assure them that only such laws as to hunting and fishing as were in the interest of the Indians and were found necessary in order to protect the fish and fur bearing animals would be made and that they would be as free to hunt and fish after the treaty as they would be if they never entered into it.
In addition, some consideration should be given to the appreciation the Indian people had as to the effect of these treaties. The white man believed in the personal and private ownership of land, but the Indian had an entirely different concept. This was made very plain during the meetings of the joint committee at which we heard a most interesting witness, a Mrs. Worthington, who has had a lot of experience and done a lot of research. At page 108 of the transcript of the evidence given before the joint committee in the year 1959 this interesting paragraph appears:
The tribe are tenants and in a sense trustees. The Indians may have granted loans to the whites. They possibly granted rights to pass overland, to lend the whites use of land, the right to cultivate it, to use its waters, animals, birds, fish, but with the expectation that at the end of the loan the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
whites would return the land, the waters, and that the animals, fish and birds would be replenished, the scars healed.
Of course, this conception came into conflict with the use of the land made by the white man. After the treaty had been signed, the white man felt himself free to deal with the land as he saw fit. There was no true meeting of minds. What the Indians thought when they agreed to these treaties was not what the white man thought. And, of course, the recent decisions in the Supreme Court of Canada confirm that the white man's view is the one which must prevail. For these reasons I submit that when the Indian claims commission is established the minister and his officials should give the most careful consideration to the requests and to the briefs which I am sure the Indian people are presenting. Let there be no stone unturned in the effort to ensure that the terms of reference to this commission will be wide enough to ensure that all legitimate complaints will be dealt with fairly and equitably. I think, too, that in all justice the government should consider amending the Indian Act so as to place these treaties in a far higher category than that in which they have been placed as a result of the recent decisions of the supreme court, and requiring the courts to give effect to such a clause. I know we have to be reasonable. We cannot turn back the clock and give the Indians back what they once had, even if that were desirable. But I think we must start immediately to put them in a position they would have enjoyed but for the effect of downgrading the treaties.
I wish now to make a suggestion in connection with education. There has been established in the last year and a half in the northern part of Alberta a vocational training school which, while it is open to all young people, was specially designed to permit the Indian peoples of northern Alberta and the territories to receive a trade training which would enable them to find a place in society. It has been found that many of the Indian boys and girls attending this school are not equipped scholastically, although grade eight rather than grade nine has been accepted as being the minimum standard required for individuals, to deal with the subject matter being taught. It was suggested in a brief submitted to the Department of Labour, copies of which I believe I sent to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, that a number of satellite schools be set up throughout the area so that the young people who would ultimately be going to this training school might receive better training than in the past 20220-655
and consequently, when they did arrive at the school, would be better able to profit from the instruction given to them. I have made a point of visiting this school on several occasions. Excellent work is being done there. The principal, Mr. Bill Thomas, is a full blooded Indian who has had a notable career in business, industry and education. He is doing a wonderful job and it was inspiring to watch these young Indian people equipping themselves, side by side with white people, with skills which will serve them well in their careers. However, in order that best advantage may be taken of the facilities offered by this school it is necessary that the additional step I have mentioned should be taken. I suggest that the minister and his officials establish liaison with the Minister of Labour whose department is charged with responsibility in connection with these vocational schools, so that an educational program may be made available.
Finally I wish to say something about agriculture. There are a number of areas in the north country where the Indians might well avail themselves of opportunities to take up farming. Unfortunately there is one hindrance; they find they are unable to take advantage of credit facilities such as are generally available today under the terms of the Farm Credit Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the bill recently passed by this house, the farm syndicate machinery bill. The reason is that the Indian people have no title to their land; they farm only under a certificate of occupation. Consequently they are not eligible for credit under any of the various bills I have mentioned. I suggest that the minister should give serious consideration to this problem and consider whether arrangements could not be made to enable the Indian people to have access to credit of this type in order to improve their farms, purchase machinery and help themselves attain a higher standard of living. The opportunities afforded to them should be brought in line with those afforded to white settlers in similar circumstances.
There is one other matter I should like to mention. I asked the minister a question on the orders of the day about ten days ago- whether or not when he proposed to make adjustments in connection with the transfer of jurisdiction and responsibility in connection with Indians to the provincial governments he thought it would be necessary to do so by bringing a measure before parliament to have an amendment made to the Indian Act. His answer was that it was not necessary. I
10348	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration realize this is not the occasion on which to enter into an argument as to the law, but I have reason to believe that if the changes which are now contemplated are of the nature which appear to be outlined in the press release, in the communique, there will have to be changes in the Indian Act. I believe the executive does not have the power to make these changes. From the viewpoint of legality, therefore, I think it is essential that the matter be brought into the house, and I believe that from the viewpoint of propriety as well changes of this nature should be considered by parliament and not merely by the executive.
The hon. member for Skeena a moment ago referred to the question of taxation. I think that is dealt with, if I recall correctly, by section 86 of the Indian Act, which in fact prohibits the taxation of lands of Indians, individually or in bands, in Indian reserves. But as one goes through the Indian Act section by section it seems quite apparent that sweeping changes of the kind contemplated, having in mind that the federal government is charged with the sole and exclusive responsibility under the British North America Act for matters relating to Indians, would not be possible without there being first secured the approval of parliament. I would urge the minister and his legal advisers to make quite certain, before these changes are brought about, that they are doing something by executive decree which they have the right to do, because I have grave doubts whether this right exists.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the minister because I hope to hear him reply at length to the comments of the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Peace River; but as an honorary chief of the Ojibway band of Christian island, in the southern part of Georgian bay-an honour that I share with the hon. member for Simcoe East-I have been asked by the band to make a simple request of the minister of citizenship. I would point out that you do not use the term "immigration" when you are speaking of the Indians of Canada and addressing the minister. I have been requested to ask the minister of citizenship if he will consider granting $6,000 to the Ojibway band of Christian island for the installation of a marine telephone line from Cedar point to this island. They have occupied the island for several hundred years. This is one of the finest Indian reservations in the country, and they are absolutely cut off from the rest of Canada by a


stretch of water of 1J miles. The nearest telephone service to them is a municipally-owned line in the township of Tiny, with 235 co-operative subscribers. We are unable to spend $6,000 to bring in one or two telephone lines to Christian island, and if the Indian affairs branch would appropriate only $6,000 for this purpose, it would help the Indian band immensely.
Under vote 15 we are voting money and authorizing the minister of citizenship to provide instruction and supervision and to furnish materials in respect of Indian commercial activities. These Indians on Christian island are now operating a commercial pheas-antry; they raise 4,000 or 5,000 pheasants a year. The hunting season is open seven months of the year, from September 1 to March 31, and yet would-be hunters from Hamilton, Toronto, Oshawa and large urban centres in central Ontario are unable to get in touch with them by telephone. There is a radio-marine telephone, which has been in operation for about two years, in the Indian agent's office to communicate with Midland; but you cannot talk to the island except during the hours when the office of the superintendent of Indian affairs on the island is open, and it is not open during week ends, when most of the hunting is done.
For an expenditure of merely $6,000 the Indians on Christian island would be put in touch with thousands of would-be hunters who are willing to spend money on the island in their pursuit of pheasants for seven months of the year. It would also give direct access to the mainland. They are now leasing cottage property sites on the island, which is becoming big business. As vote 15 covers advances by the minister for commercial activities of the Indians so they may be selfemployed, I strongly urge that he give consideration in the current year to spending $6,000 for a marine telephone cable from Cedar point to Christian island Indian reservation in the southern Georgian bay.

Mr. Chairman, I will take only a couple of minutes. My interest in the Indian dates back quite a long time. In the days of the 'flu epidemic back in 1920, as a result of the discovery of a number of very serious situations throughout the province at that time it so happened that it was ascertained that Indians dead, alive and dying were all occupying the same beds. The end result was that my father, although he had a very large family of 11 living children at that time, took three Indian lads and helped to raise them. As a matter of fact, they grew up with the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
rest of the boys, including myself. Further than that, in the lumber business operation it was our privilege to have in the Babine lake area a complete crew of Indian lads working in the saw mill industry. We found them to be a little bit on the irresponsible side, naturally, because it was not in their makeup to stick with the job for any length of time. However, this was solved very simply by having the chief become responsible for seeing that we had a crew every morning. Believe me, there was no doubt in the world that every morning we had a full crew-* maybe not the same ones, but we had a full crew every day, because the chief made sure that if one Indian disappeared another took his place.
Over the years I have been advocating that we get into a situation where we can somehow have one jurisdiction. I am glad the government is looking into this proposition and working-we hope all the way-with the Indians themselves to accomplish this very, very desirable result. Previous speakers have dealt very fully with this question and I want to commend the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Skeena on their speeches today and the questions that have been put. We will be looking forward with interest to the answers that will be coming forward to some of these questions, and there is no need to deal with them further at this time, Mr. Chairman.
The important thing, in my view, is that whatever society needs to do in order to carry on, if there are some things that society is going to deprive the Indian of, let us see that the Indian gets something better in return. This is possible, surely. I think it should be borne in mind at all times that if for some reason in the development of society some things have to be taken away from the Indian, we should return to him more than we are taking away. This is quite possible, of course. With those few remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would like to see the estimates passed. I am sure several hon. members would like to take part in the debate this afternoon. I would just like to say thank you to the government for their apparent interest, and I would ask them to pay very close attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Skeena.

Mr. Chairman, I have but a few observations to address to the minister responsible for Indian affairs, and they have
20220-655J
to do with an Indian band in my area, the Weymontachie.
A few weeks ago, I got in touch with the minister to try and provide those Indians with decent accommodation. During a visit I made to the Sanmaur area, where their reserve is located, I noticed that their accommodations were-no, I would not say poor-just nonexistent. Their village dates back to some 50 years and the houses are even older, so that those Indians prefer, even right in the middle of January, to live in tents. Conditions there are almost inhuman.
I, therefore, asked the minister to press this affair and find a solution to the housing problem facing this Indian band.
The radar station located but a few miles from where this Indian band lives was closed recently. I then suggested to the minister that this Indian band be established in that abandoned radar station. Those Indians could take advantage of appropriate schools and even of a hospital, and benefit from all necessary services. The minister told me that after consulting with some high officials who deal with those Indians, he had come to the conclusion that it was impossible to transfer them to that location, because they could not be provided with the education and other necessary services. I wonder then what are these essential services which are not to be found in Parent.
Eventually these people will have to be moved because I know that the Quebec government intends to build a hydroelectric dam in that county and that part of that area will be flooded. Therefore, we have to think about relocating that Indian reserve. I would like to ask the minister if he has given serious consideration to finding a solution. If the solution I have suggested is not agreeable to him, I would urge him to find another one, because it is essential to provide suitable accommodation for that Indian band as soon as possible, as well as educational and medical facilities, in short, all that is necessary from a humanitarian point of view.

Mr. Chairman, at this hour I almost hesitate to take part in this debate, but for a number of years I have looked forward to saying something about the Indian affairs branch of the department, and on each occasion seemed to find myself in much the same position in which I find myself today. However, I should like to say a few things and I will try and be brief, so that
10350	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration others who may want to make a few remarks may do so.
There are a few Indian reserves in one part of my riding, and every time I visit them I must say I am appalled at the conditions I find there. When I look at the estimates of the department over the years going back a considerable period of time, I am appalled at the amount of money spent and at the little positive result we have seen. I believe the purpose of the department, if it is anything, should be to create a new dignity for and respect toward these native people of our country. I cannot help but ask the question whether or not we are achieving that today, with the expenditures we are making and the way they are being used.
In saying that I am not being critical of those who work in the department. One has only to visit any of the reserves in my area to realize that something more is needed. I believe one of the things which is needed is a greater sympathy for the Indians, greater independence for them and a less paternal outlook on the part of the department, as well as perhaps a little more co-operation with those agencies which exist locally to try to help these people. I understand that at the present time it is very difficult indeed for an individual on a reserve to secure assistance in a case where he is the boss of the enterprise he is trying to manage. I know the situation with regard to this particular matter. There are many who perhaps are not ready for that full measure of confidence that the department would like to give; but there are some, and an increasing number, who I believe could be given much more confidence than the department and its officials are giving them today.
As I talk to those who have been very close to reserves in years gone by I get the impression that this situation seems to be getting worse with the passage of the years, and that there has been some deterioration in the character of those who might have become very good citizens of our country. I believe one of the essentials is to create a spirit of initiative, a sense of self-respect and pride; and I want to leave the thought with the minister that perhaps a partial answer to this might be to encourage some resettlement of those who are desirous of such resettlement, without any loss of treaty rights presently existing. This might give them a better opportunity to take part in the life of the community in a province or in the country at large. From speaking to some of them I find they are very disappointed at the way


some of their fondest hopes are neglected, sometimes discarded, by officials of the department, including officials of the department in Ottawa when a matter is sent down to headquarters for decision.
I believe that we have a good staff generally, but in recruiting staff for the department I think more consideration should be given to a preference for people who have proven through experience that they have sympathy for and the understanding of the Indian people. These people are found in any area where there is a reserve. I believe that if these people are recruited to the staff of the department and given a little training and instruction, though they might not have much formal training otherwise, they might get a grasp of what is the department's policy, which I hope of course is one which will give more and more responsibility to the individual on the reserve.
Other hon. members have dealt with other various aspects of this matter and I will not go over them. I will not mention any personal cases which may have come to my attention, though there have been one or two. I should like to see the department try to give these people the same opportunities they would give anybody else in this country, and this can only be done by giving them more responsibility than that which the department seems to be prepared or able to give them today.

Mr. Chairman, I sincerely hope that the estimates of this department will get through today, and I am sure many hon. members agree with me there. I will not be too lengthy, but like the hon. member for Peace River I should like to congratulate the new assistant deputy minister, Mr. Battle. On many occasions when we were attempting to work out Indian problems on the reserves in the constituency of Bow River he was extremely helpful. He is one official who at that time, while working in that area, was liked and respected by the bands of Indians. I hope in his position now he will be able to exercise some influence upon the department of Indian affairs.
I was very impressed by the speeches made by the hon. members for Skeena and Peace River, and felt that they touched upon an important problem facing the Indians, particularly in relation to these so-called conferences. As pointed out by both those speakers, when we are considering amendments to the constitution affecting Indian rights we should keep in mind the Indian treaties which were signed by officials of Canada and the Indians.

I have in my hand a copy of the book "John A. Macdonald, the old Chieftain" by Donald Creighton, from which I should like to read one paragraph, because of its reference to these treaty rights. I have sent photostatic copies of this paragraph to all the chiefs of the various reservations in Alberta because it emphasizes some of the history behind the treaty of 1886. This is what Creighton says about John A. Macdonald, the old chief. Macdonald had left Winnipeg early in the day in the year following the completion of the railway, and Mr. Creighton writes:
But the darkness of the long summer day had already fallen when the train finally pulled up at Gleichen, the little station, east of Calgary, in the heart of the Blackfoot country. Chief Crowfoot, who in the dark days at the beginning of the northwest rebellion had pledged the loyalty of his tribe to Macdonald, was waiting, a little on his dignity, for he had been led to expect the visitors nearly three hours before; and it was not until very early the following morning that the Indians, who had come to the rendezvous in full force, began to assemble for the pow-wow. The lesser chiefs-Old Sun, Eagle Rib, Medicine Shield, Running Eagle, Little Plume-sat about portentiously in full war-paint and feathers. Crowfoot alone was in his oldest clothes-in memory, he informed Macdonald, of the dead Poundmaker. His face, with its well shaped features and fine lines, was shrewd and proud and intelligent. He told the listening Indians that Macdonald was the "biggest man" they had had among them for a long time. He begged Macdonald to banish the fears of the Indians for their children's nourishment and welfare. Then the Indians did a dance, and presents were distributed; and Macdonald gave Crowfoot a dark broadcloth suit with silk facings-a proper suit of mourning.
It is only about two weeks ago that I stood in a hall at Gleichen on the Blackfoot reservation in the very place where John A. Macdonald met Chief Crowfoot.
When the people at that time signed these treaties they understood that certain rights would be guaranteed. I was very pleased at the way the hon. member for Skeena referred to the so-called consultations. It seems to me the kind of consultation we should have if, as I think we do, we have respect for these treaties, is by way of plebiscite. As the hon. member so ably stated, the proposed consultations would be with hand picked individuals, whom the department, the minister or others, wanted because of the influence they might have on programs to be outlined.
I should be very disappointed if this government placed the administration of Indian affairs under the jurisdiction of provincial governments, because this administration is one of those things delegated by section 91
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration of the British North America Act to the federal government. Certainly these rights should not be used to satisfy the desires and ambitions of certain provincial premiers. After all, these rights are based on treaties. Last evening we heard discussion about giving $350,000 to Indonesia. I wish we could persuade the officials of some weekly magazines or newspapers to send their representatives across this country to take photographs of the homes in which our Canadian Indians are living. Several newspapers have suggested that I am extreme in the language I use. Perhaps what is extreme to some is not extreme to others. I have visited the reserves at Morley and at Gleichen, and with the exception of the new housing development which is progressing very slowly, these people live in hovels.
And they are the best.

The hon. member suggests that those are the best homes. If they are, I should not like to see the worst.
It is all very well for the minister to smile, and I am not blaming him by any means for this situation which has existed for a long time, but the Indians are living in destitute circumstances, and let us not forget that fact. I see an hon. member shaking his head. If he has any doubts about what I am saying I invite him to go there and see for himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are not smiling at what the hon. member is saying, but at the way in which he is saying it.

You were shaking your head as though you were not in agreement. I hope you are in agreement, because the situation there is appalling. Their standards of living, even under the most native conditions, was much better than has been the case since our arrival.
These people are paid $5 treaty money per month. That amount was established some 100 years ago. What effect has the inflationary trend alone had on the value of that monthly payment? What is it worth today? Just as a matter of interest I consulted the dominion bureau of statistics about a lawsuit in which a $30,000 judgment had been given, and was informed that it would now be worth only $25,000. That would indicate there has been a decrease in the value by at least one fifth, and one can readily see the change in value of the $5 treaty money over the 100 year period.
If we are going to wage that war on poverty talked about so often by the President of the United States and others, we should
10352	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration establish one of our battle lines on the reservations of this country. I do not wish to speak in incendiary terms, but if there were more of these people and they were organized, we would be faced with a rebellion in this country. No other class of people in this country would put up with the poverty and standard of living we find on these reservations.
Changes are constantly being made without consultation with the native people. Two hospitals to which the women went to have their babies were closed without consultation. These women must now travel to hospitals elsewhere. While I realize some changes must be made, the Indians find that they are being made at great inconvenience to them. How is an Indian husband receiving his $5 per month expected to take his wife from the reserve at Gleichen to a hospital in Calgary to have her baby? Sometimes he is even forced to beg a ride from other people. These are the actual circumstances that these people must accept. Not one word of what I have said is exaggerated and I have never before described these circumstances in the kind of terms I intend to use this afternoon. The circumstances are disgraceful.
If a newspaper editorial writer wishes to write another statement to the effect that Eldon Woolliams speaks in extreme language, let him send his newspapermen to these areas to observe for themselves the poverty stricken conditions and disgraceful circumstances under which these Indians are forced to exist. I am not now referring to the housing development which was commenced under the Conservative administration-and even it moved very slowly. There are only a few houses completed and I do not know who chooses the families to live in them. I do know, however, that the majority of homes occupied by Indians are nothing more than hovels. We constantly refer to and talk about missionaries going to underdeveloped countries of the world where the inhabitants are living under substandard conditions. We had better look to our own backyards, because they certainly need cleaning up.
In reference to Indian claims, let us immediately set up a program so the Indians can bring their claims before a proper commission. Surely that could be done quickly. There is a case now pending with reference to the Blackfoot reserve involving several million dollars. I do not know anything about the facts, but do you know what the chief of the Blackfoot reserve tells me? He tells me that the documents he wants to prove the claim have been refused him day after day.


Some people say they have disappeared entirely so that their claim will never be proven. How does the department deal with these people?
I hope that Mr. Battle, with the sympathy I know he has for these people and who understands the circumstances, will exercise his influence so that in that regard they will receive better treatment. There are things that should be said in this regard. The whole of the rights of the Indians are based on treaties but, as the hon. member for Skeena said, how can the Indians trust the white man? These treaties were signed and certain rights were guaranteed the Indians. Certain standards of living were guaranteed them. You may say that there are always two sides to these matters; but these people who are living with us and among us as Canadians and with Canadians, are the real Canadians, and we have reduced them to a standard of living lower than that of the peasants 50, 75 or 100 years ago in certain places in Europe and Asia. So we have an obligation to the Indians.
There is just one thing I should like to say about the kind of consultation that should take place. Let us give the Indians a plebiscite before changing the jurisdiction. Let us give them a standard of living that is realistic. Let us see that they receive the treaty money about which they talk. We talk about a contributory pension plan but it will not affect these people because they have nothing to contribute. To be realistic they should be getting at least $50 a month and the kind of homes that will enable them to live in dignity with their families. I say, set up the claims commission immediately, respect their treaty rights and let us declare war on poverty among the Indians. This may be one of my shortest speeches but I have never been more sincere. Let us have something done in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I want to speak at length on this topic and I am not going to have the time to do so now. I want to raise what I think is the major problem in connection with the Indians. It is a problem that has not been touched upon in this debate and I have not raised it before because of a natural hesitancy in connection with the subject. But I have come to the conclusion that it is the most vital problem in connection with the Indians. I have seen it in depth in my own part of the country. It is the factor that is demoralizing the situation more than anything else and destroying most of the progress. I am not making these remarks with any bravery in bringing this matter out into the open, but I believe we have got to talk about it and we have got to ascertain the position and stance of the Indian affairs branch with regard to it. We have got to find out how they are going to meet it. It may be we will be told it is perhaps not the main problem throughout the country but only in the part of the country I represent.
I am talking about the problem of alcoholism, overdrinking and all the consequences and difficulties that flow from it. We are beginning to take a greater and greater interest in the Indians. I am, as a member of the house, and I have at least 7,000 Indians in my riding. There are a number of reserves and also a great number of Indians who are nomads. I have increased my knowledge but at the same time decreased whatever confidence I had in my own ideas or in the ideas of the Indian affairs branch to move with speed to meet the problem.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
There are two matters that are never talked about but which seem to me to be central, and the major one from my point of view is alcoholism and drinking, and the effect of drinking upon these people and their place in society. The other is a very controversial subject that is touched on occasionally. I refer to the whole question of religion, the religious approach and the relationship of the religious communities, mainly Anglican and Roman Catholic, to the Indians on their reserves and in the missions.
In my own travels I have never encountered any missionaries or other people working with the Indians for whom I had any disrespect. I have a tremendous admiration for some of these people whose lives are full of hard work and filled with frustration because of the inadequacy of response, either in religious or social terms, to their teaching and the work they do. But if we are going to have a realistic appraisal of the Indian situation it seems to me that we need to know more accurately what the effect is of the religious association with Indians across the country, and we simply have to know much more about the problem of alcoholism and drinking.
I want to give some examples to indicate why drinking is a problem. Many of you may remember that a few years ago the regulations regarding drinking in Ontario were altered so that Indians could play the part of normal citizens in the use of beer parlours and so on. At that time I was one of those who believed very strongly that they should have this right. I did not want to see them segregated from the same opportunities that all the rest of us have, and I have not changed my opinion in that regard. But when I go to communities such as Sioux Lookout, Armstrong, Nakina, Beardmore, Macdiarmid, Heron Bay and other places in my riding and see some of the consequences of the opening up of opportunities to drink, when I see the extent of all the difficulties that follow from this overdrinking, it makes me realize that, in a way, this is a crime that our free society with its mores and practices commits, because of the effect upon these people who have not really been a part of this society and have not been brought up in our tradition.
Recently at a certain place in my riding- I am sure some of the people in the Indian affairs branch will know about this-a considerable spending program was completed for a school and teacherage. Almost before the carpenters had cleared out, nearly every window in this new building was broken and
10354	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration other damage was done. By whom was it done? It was done by teen age girls and young fellows. I do not know what the police court evidence may disclose, but I understand a couple of them are now in jail. This was the result of drinking. It was not a random incident in that particular location. There have been thousands of incidents like this.
Just a day or two ago there was an annual meeting or pow-wow when the treaty money was handed out and a new band council was picked. Within two days the chief was in the hospital, after being almost kicked to death by his fellow councillors of the band. All of them had been involved in a big drinking session. This is incident No. 2. I could name, in connection with that group of Indians, many others, perhaps dozens of incidents like this which indicate the breakdown in morality.
One of the most shocking things that happened in my constituency happened to one of the simplest and noblest characters I have met, a Roman Catholic priest. He was attacked by Indians who were drinking. This man had laboured in the community and had given a great deal to it. However, aroused by the noise and tumult of this kind of session, things exploded and went too far. How you get an analysis of the effect of this kind of drinking upon Indians, I do not know.
May I just give one last example to point out to hon. members what is involved, and the difficulties of the Indian affairs branch? I received a letter from a young Indian couple to the effect that winter was coming on, their house on the reserve was completely inadequate, and could I ask the Indian affairs department to do something about it. I went to see the young couple. It was a long drive of 150 miles through the bush. I got there to see them sitting in their house. You could see the dust from the yard blowing through the cracks in the house, and I got very worked up about this, to think that the branch had done nothing for them. They gave me this story. They were a very contrite, soft spoken couple and I accepted their story. Incidentally, there was nothing wrong with the young man or young woman; they were not crippled. I spoke to the Indian affairs branch, and was told they had provided the couple with paint, Ten-Test and all the materials necessary to fix up their house. The branch had trucked them in all that distance. What had this young couple done? They had taken the material almost as soon as the one truck was off the reserve, carted it away and sold it. What followed was that they


went on a week long drunk and left their children alone. As a consequence we had the children's aid people coming in.
This state of affairs is desperately serious. It is at the core of almost every problem I know of in relation to the Indians in northwestern Ontario. If the minister knows anything about the Indian situation, he will know that they are in as desperate a situation as anyone else anywhere. There is a breakdown here that relates to work. A couple of years ago, I talked with some of the Abitibi foremen up near a place called Auden. They had tried to work some Indians into the pulp cutting operation. Auden is up in the north corner of lake Nipigon. The reports from the union stewards and the foremen agreed that these Indians were able-bodied and strong enough to do this type of work. They have all the skill. But what happened? After they had worked a few days and there was a bit of money piled up, a cheque came along. As soon as the cheque came along, they took off. In this particular case of which I am speaking, they had not paid their union dues. They just took off, and they were gone for several weeks. Their money lasted them that long. A couple of them finally came back, and they were in very bad shape because again they had been off on a long boozing session. They could not understand why the company was hesitant about hiring them again. The company did hire them again and the very same thing happened as soon as the first cheque came along.
Two years ago, I visited another Abitibi camp down near Regan. Again, there is an Indian reservation near there called Mobert, and this has been one of the busiest cutting areas Abitibi has had. There are over 100 able-bodied men and I do not know how many women on that reserve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I promised to make a statement at the beginning of this week respecting the administration of the Canada student loans plan.
On Monday and Tuesday, November 16 and 17, officials responsible for administering the Canada student loans plan in all the participating provinces, together with representatives of the province of Quebec and the territories, met in Ottawa with officials of the Department of Finance for the purpose of reviewing the operation of the Canada student loans plan. This was the first opportunity for such a general review since the initiation of the plan last September.
Provincial representatives expressed the unanimous view that the plan has met a real need for a large number of students. Many students attending universities and other institutions this year would not have been able to attend in the absence of the plan. Many other students, who might have managed to attend without the benefit of the plan, are able to devote more time and attention to their education because their financial burdens are now less demanding. In spite of its late start, the plan has already proved to be an outstanding success.
A total of 29,000 students had received certificates of eligibility for loans as of November 13. The average loan under these certificates for the academic year is about $680, for a total amount of approximately $19.8 million, representing 73.3 per cent of allocations for the loan year ending June 30, 1965. I ask the permission of the house to include in Hansard a table which gives the breakdown of these figures by participating provinces and territories.

subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am pleased to report that students are making effective use of the plan to a greater extent than was expected when the plan was discussed in advance with provincial officials last summer. With few exceptions the loan certificates are issued by bodies already accustomed to furnishing student aid. This has greatly facilitated speedy implementation of the plan and minimized risks of overborrowing and abuse.
As I reported to the house on July 14, we expected that financial provision would be ample, based on the assumption that approximately one student out of three might make use of the plan and that the average loan would be about $500. I added, however, that if perchance actual needs outran our expectations we would bring the matter back to parliament. In practice, financial provision on this basis is proving about right in some provinces, rather more than sufficient in a few cases, and less than sufficient in two provinces.
In the discussion of subjects put forward by the provinces at last week's conference it became apparent that many of their administrative problems were the result of varying traditional practices in handling student aid, and a general desire emerged to seek a greater degree of harmony in these practices. To this end it was agreed that special reports would be prepared during the next two months on three subjects; the criteria for judging student needs; questions relating to students from one province making use of loans under the plan in another province; and the whole

question of standards and criteria for the designation by provinces of educational institutions under the plan. It was agreed that pending consideration of these reports there would be no basic change in present practices. I should add that representatives of the province of Quebec will be associated with these studies.
I have already mentioned the fact that the financial provision for this year is proving adequate or more than adequate in the case of all but two provinces, where the demand for loans is outrunning the allocation made under the act as passed by parliament this summer. In these circumstances many students, particularly those who had postponed making financial arrangements for the second term of the academic year, could be faced with the interruption of their education because of financial difficulties. The government has considered this situation and decided to seek approval from parliament to increase the guarantee authority of the Canada Student Loans Act in the current loan year by $8 million, this amount to be available for allocation to provinces upon application to meet additional requirements in the loan year ending June 30, 1965. A special item for this purpose is included in supplementary estimates "C" for 1964-65 which have just been tabled. At the present time it is expected that only two provinces will exceed the provincial allocation for this year. Accordingly, if this turns out to be the case, less than one half of this proposed additional provision is likely to be utilized.

The alternative payments under the act to a non-participating province relate to actual disbursements by the federal government in the administration of the act. Such payments will, of course, automatically rise to the extent that enlarged allocations are utilized.
I should emphasize that the special financial provision which the house is being asked to consider will apply only to the current loan year and will not alter the provincial allocations for subsequent years as now provided for in the act. I have outlined the nature of the studies which provincial and federal representatives have already undertaken. Against the background of these studies, a more general review of the Canada Student Loans Act, of the loan limits which it provides and of the formula on which those limits are to increase year by year, will be made when the full results of the current year have been collected and reviewed.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members will welcome the success which the student loans plan has achieved in meeting the financial needs of so many students across Canada in extending their education and training. This has been due in no small measure to the fine spirit of co-operation shown by provincial educational authorities and lending institutions.

subtopic: STUDENT LOANS-STATEMENT RESPECTING OTTAWA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has listened with a great deal of interest to the statement just made by the minister with respect to the administration of the student loan fund. As he has said, certain difficulties have arisen in connection with the administration, and I am very happy to know that apparently the conference last week was prepared to deal specifically with those administrative problems.
I had hoped that possibly the minister would make some statement with respect to scholarships in connection with the student loan fund, but I presume that is a matter which we can look forward to at some not too distant date, because it is certainly something which the people of Canada expected of this government when it took office.
The minister referred to the three points which I understand were agreed upon last week, and I think it is well that there has been some hopeful agreement in that connection. However, I am sure all hon. members have heard of the difficulties which have arisen as between the provinces with regard to the means test basis. Some provinces have been much stricter than others in that regard. I know one province which, because of the
Student Loans Plan
short time available, is still using the application form which they provided for their own student loans years ago, and is much stricter than under our regulations or what should be our regulations. This brings up the old problem of reconciling the prerogative of the province which administers education with the responsibility of the federal government which pays the bills. It is well to know that careful study is being given to this matter.
Then there is the further problem of the residential qualifications that certain provinces require. I had a rather pathetic case the other day, and I am sure many hon. members have had such cases over the last few weeks. In this particular case the man happened to be in the armed forces, but he might have been in any other employment. He was transferred from one province to another, and was told that in order to get a loan in the province to which he had been transferred he would have to be a resident for a year. He could not get a loan from the province he had left because he was no longer a resident there. This question of residence must and should be dealt with in order to clarify this ambiguity. This difficulty affects only a few, it is true. The great majority of students are realizing a great deal of help from this legislation. However, there are these two points respecting the means test and residence which need to be ironed out, and a degree of co-operative federalism should be attained in the near future.
In so far as the standards of educational institutions are concerned, this is something that has been with us for a long time. We have it in connection with university grants. I am sure there is machinery available by which the problem can be ironed out, and we look forward to some standardization on that basis. The other day I had a case of a student going to the United States, and of course he could not get a student loan. I believe a loan was obtained later on. All these matters are bound to arise, of course, in connection with a measure which is in its preliminary stages. We appreciate what has been done for the students so far, but there are many other difficulties which have to be ironed out. I hope they will be ironed out in this conference to which the minister has referred.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the opening statement which I intend to make relates to the functions of my department generally and to two aspects of the activities of my department.

The Department of Justice-

subtopic: REPORTED POST-SYNCHRONIZATION OF FILMS IN FRANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED POST-SYNCHRONIZATION OF FILMS IN FRANCE
speechtext:
Yes.

In a general sense the Department of Justice comprises several branches or sections of the public service which are the responsibility of the Minister of Justice.
The strictly legal functions are discharged by the law branch. I should mention also
20220-656^
Supply-Justice
the Bankruptcy Act administration, the Combines Investigation Act administration and the Parole Act administration.
The minister is, moreover, responsible for the administration of the Supreme Court of Canada, of the Exchequer Court of Canada and of the penitentiary system.
The Minister of Justice is also responsible to parliament for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the restrictive trade practices commission.
He also has jurisdiction in matters of patents, copyrights, trade marks and industrial designs.
Under the Criminal Code the attorney general of Canada is attorney general as concerns the Northwest Territories Act and the Yukon Territory Act.
I intend today to make some remarks concerning that function of my department having to do with the administration of the penitentiaries and our projects in the field of reform.
During the last few years the Canadian penitentiary service has experienced important progress. However, in order that such progress be rational, the government thought it appropriate to approve in principle a new development program, the implementation of which would take place between 1964 and 19/3. This program I intend to explain briefly to the house today.
The primary function of the Canadian penitentiary service is to protect society against individuals bent toward crime, and this through preventive detention and reform training during imprisonment. These measures should reduce recidivism but, in the long run they increase the normal costs of penitentiary operation; on the other hand, they should return to our society, as useful citizens, people who, otherwise, might be a threat to it.
In order to ensure adequate reform training for the inmates, the following requirements have to be met: surveillance, physical and body needs, education, as well as economic, psychological, moral and spiritual needs.
Consequently, the inmates will be scattered in various institutions, according to the requirements of detention and security.
The training program in every institution will be prepared according to the needs for reformation of the inmates.
In each region in Canada there will be organized a penitentiary system comprising the following institutions: special detention

Supply-Justice
institution, maximum security, medium security and minimum security institutions.
In each of the four regions the following will also be provided for:
(a)	reception centres to be used for purposes of reception and diagnosis so the inmate can be sent to an appropriate institution;
(b)	institutions for juvenile delinquents, medium security type, to be used for the detention and training of inmates from 16 to 25 years of age;
