speechtext: I wonder whether I could interrupt the minister briefly. I am not trying to embarrass him in any way, but he has been speaking about young offenders and I should like to ask him a question. Some months ago a return was made showing the number of young offenders held in custody in our penitentiaries. Are they still in the penitentiaries? Has there been any change in that situation since the return was made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED POST-SYNCHRONIZATION OF FILMS IN FRANCE
speechtext:
I have no figures as to changes. There certainly or probably must have been changes by way of promoting young prisoners from one institution to another, because to the extent that accommodation is available it is the policy of the penitentiaries system to try to detain young offenders in these specialized institutions. But there may not have been substantial changes, and this is precisely why we are providing for those types of institutions in each region which I know the hon. member understands and agrees are essential.

(c)	hospitals for the purpose of offering medical and psychiatric services; finally
(d)	a kind of institution yet unknown in Canada: predischarge centres to house inmates who have almost completed their full sentence and who, consequently, must be reintegrated ipto society.
Each institution will have facilities to apply programs of activities offering inmates occupations, constructive pastimes, religious services, contacts with their families, with social agencies and with representatives of the public, a classification process, education and technical training.
The plan will be achieved in two stages: the first phase, which is already begun, will extend from 1963 to 1967; the second, from 1967 to 1973.
According to a comprehensive survey of the trends of institution population in the past, it is anticipated that the inmates will number 8,500 in 1967 and 10,500 in 1973.

The accommodation needed in the years to come will depend on the increase in the number of inmates and the need to keep apart certain types or certain classes of inmates. The type and the number of institutions to be built will depend on the need to separate, the degree of danger that they represent and the need to offer a special training to certain classes of inmates.
The immediate purpose is to set up for 1967 a uniform detention and training system in each of the four regions in Canada so that each inmate can be confined with a degree of security desirable and so that each can take advantage of the training most appropriate to his needs. The policy restricting the maximum population of each institution to 450 will be maintained. The treasury board has already approved substantial expenditures to provide for the carrying out of that project.
A special detention unit has been built and is already in operation at the British Columbia penitentiary and three more will be built in Dorchester, N.B., St. Vincent de Paul, Quebec, and Millhaven, Ontario.
In 1965, the construction of a maximum security institution will get under way at Ste. Anne des Plaines, Quebec, and in 1966, the construction of another institution will start at Millhaven, Ontario.
A medium security institution is being built in Cowansville, Quebec, and recently a contract was awarded for the construction of a medium security institution in Springhill, Nova Scotia.
In a few months, tenders will be called in order to undertake the construction of two other medium security institutions, one in Warkworth, Ontario, and the other in Drumheller, Alberta. An institution for the treatment and training of drug addicts, male and female, is under construction in Marsqui, B.C.

At this point I wish to recall that in January last the then minister of justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, announced that in the fiscal year 1965-66 a new prison for women would be constructed in the vicinity of Cornwall, Ontario. Developments in the penitentiary service since that time lead to the conclusion that the construction of a new federal prison for women should be postponed for some years.

subtopic: REPORTED POST-SYNCHRONIZATION OF FILMS IN FRANCE
speechtext: That is the best way to get Chevrier out of the basket he was in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED POST-SYNCHRONIZATION OF FILMS IN FRANCE
speechtext:
This is the best way to be objective and have justice done.

The average daily population in the existing prison for women at Kingston, Ontario is 120 inmates. Of these more than 50 are narcotics addicts from western Canada. At the present time a new narcotics addict treatment institution is being constructed at Matsqui, British Columbia. When completed in September, 1965 it will provide accommodation and training facilities for 150 female inmates. At that time the female narcotics addicts from western Canada will be transferred to the new institution, where they will have the benefit of a program of treatment and training especially designed for their needs. The female narcotics addicts of eastern Canada will continue, that is for the present, in the women's prison at Kingston.
There is a conflict of opinion on the question of whether the narcotics addicts can best be rehabilitated through a treatment program involving addicts alone, on the one hand, or through a program of training involving association with non-addicts. The Matsqui experiment will make it possible, over a period of three or four years, to determine which technique is more effective. Accordingly I propose postponing the construction of the new prison for women until the results of the Matsqui operation have become apparent.
The prison for women at Kingston has accommodation for 150 female inmates; 50 inmates can be confined in bright, modern rooms constructed, I am pleased to advise hon. gentlemen across the way, in 1960. With the opening of the Matsqui institution and the transfer to it of some 50 narcotics addicts from western Canada, the result will be that the great majority of females confined in the prison for women can be accommodated in modern, clean surroundings. As for those in the small minority, great care will be taken to make such use of the remaining accommodation as will assure the fairest and best possible treatment in every respect.
In the general program, the additional construction that will be required to achieve the 1967 objective is as follows; four new reception centres and three reception centres to be developed from existing facilities; three minimum security institutions; three new medical and psychiatric centres and a fourth to be developed from existing facilities; four prerelease hostels to be obtained by using existing houses owned by the crown or by purchase; administrative facilities for two maximum security complexes; the modernization of certain buildings in three of the existing maximum security institutions that are an integral part of the new program; two
Supply-Justice
staff colleges, one in the Quebec region and one in the western region, to replace present inadequate facilities for the training of penitentiary service officers.
If the foregoing program of institutional development is carried out, it will mean that by 1967 Canada will have a federal prison system that will rank with the best in the world. It will mean a conclusive end to that oft quoted slander that, by the United Nations standards, Canada ranks 44th among the nations of the world in so far as the quality of its prisons is concerned. In anticipation of the completion of the development up to 1967, plans are being made for developments during the period 1968-1973.
There is, of course, no way of determining accurately at this time whait our 1968-1973 requirement will be. It is to be hoped that the reformative program for inmates now being carried on and to be further developed in penitentiaries will reduce recidivism. If this happens the number of institutions required during the period in question will be fewer. On the other hand, there may be some other sociological factors at work that might increase the number required over what is contemplated as a result of past experience. The provinces may develop their probation services further, with the result that committals to penitentiary may be lessened. The operations of the parole board may result in more paroles and in fewer penitentiary committals than has been the case thus far. Amendments to the Criminal Code may result in fewer penitentiary committals.
Whatever happens, there is nothing inflexible about the proposed program. The penitentiary service will prepare, in June of every year, a statement of penitentiary population with predictions of accommodation and training requirements based upon the experience of the preceding ten years. On the basis of this study there will be a prediction of requirements for the succeeding ten years, upon which can be based the penitentiary service estimates for the succeeding fiscal year and forecasts of requirements for the ensuing four or five years.
This method of operation, if carried into effect, will have the twin result of ensuring that our penitentiaries do not become overcrowded and, therefore, less effectual, and planning for the construction of an institution can be carried on at least three years prior to the time when the institution will be required.
Buildings are, of course, essential for the custody of inmates. However, the determin-

Supply-Justice
ing factor in so far as the reform of the inmate is concerned is the quality of the training program that he receives. Effective training of inmates can only be carried out by competent staff. It is with the objective of improving the competence of staff that the penitentiary service has, within the past year, required every newly recruited officer to receive three months of induction training. Formerly no such period of specialized training was required.
It was to achieve this standard of training that a new staff college was recently opened at Kingston, Ontario, and existing facilities were converted to staff training purposes at St. Vincent de Paul, Quebec, and New Westminster, B.C. The program calls for construction next year at St. Vincent de Paul of a staff college that will provide similar facilities to those that are now available at Kingston.
I said earlier that the construction program which I have outlined is not inflexible. I intend to take into full account the representations and submissions which will be made to me in this connection by specialists and other knowledgeable citizens and organizations. In this respect I wish to repeat that it is my intention that two committees be established without delay.
A resolution is being placed on the order paper providing for the establishment of a special committee of the house to look into and report upon the state of penitentiaries throughout Canada. If established by the house this committee will have full occasion to visit Canadian penitentiaries, interview inmates, ascertain the physical accommodations such as kitchen facilities, sanitary conditions, medical, dental or other services. It will have access to the plans already completed as well as those being developed for our construction program. As the committee will have power to report from time to time, it will be able to submit views even for the purpose of possible modification of our short term construction program.
A second committee, which will be a special committee of experts in many ways similar to the Fauteux committee, will be appointed by the government to study, report and make recommendations upon the whole corrections field in Canada. This will include such matters as arrest, bail, personal recognizance, remand and detention pending trial, sentencing, detention under sentence, rehabilitation methods and instruments, probation and parole. The study of that specialized committee will, of course, involve all

aspects of the criminal law which are related to the matters which I have just enumerated. That second committee will have the benefit of both the interim and final reports of the parliamentary committee.
Through these two committees all those interested in the field of correction and penal reform in Canada, and who wish to make their views known, will have ready access to the government before the formal statement of an over-all philosophy and policy of Canadian correction is made.

Before leaving this question, I wish to recall that lately the personnel of the penitentiaries was the object of many unfair and unkind criticisms in the press and in radio and television reports. Those criticisms followed the statements made by a former inmate of the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, convicted of having been one of the leaders during the riot which occurred there in 1962.
That man was mistreated at that time, and when the incident was brought to the attention of the commissioner of penitentiaries, the latter appointed an independent commissioner to investigate this matter.
After a serious inquiry, the investigating commissioner stated in his report that eight officers belonging to the personnel were involved in that affair. The report also showed that the officers had thus acted after flagrant provocation.
The report also stated that five of those officers either had left their jobs or had been suspended; the report recommended disciplinary action against the other three. That measure was taken.
The conduct of those eight officers is not typical of that of the officers in the penitentiaries branch. Most of the penitentiaries officers, and there are more than 3,000 of them, are patient and devoted men who perform difficult and dangerous duties under difficult circumstances. Those persons do not deserve to be criticized by the Canadian public; they deserve our gratefulness.

In respect to the matters with which the combines branch of my department is concerned, I wish to make a few comments about the act itself. It is my view that the Combines Investigation Act should be considered at all times as an integral part of the economic policy of the government of Canada, and should have a definite role to play as part of that policy. As the government's economic policy develops, the principles declared in the

Supply-Justice
legislation ought to be reviewed from time to time to ensure that they are making their optimum contribution to the over-all economic policy for Canada. I intend, therefore, to consider whether or not the substantive provisions and the procedural machinery in the legislation require any revision to bring them into line with the needs of our developing economy and of the general economic policy of the government.
One important matter to which I wish to give serious attention in this respect is the extent to which it might be possible to support legislation in this field under the head "trade and commerce" in section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, so as to give greater scope for the application of non-criminal remedies in enforcing the act.
As the committee is aware, the present legislation has been upheld as constitutionally valid by the Supreme Court of Canada on the ground that it is criminal law. The fact that proceedings under the act in the courts are criminal in nature poses particular problems in enforcement and creates considerable rigidity so far as adjusting monopolistic situations is concerned. I therefore am exploring the extent to which it may be within the power of parliament, without necessarily abandoning the criminal law technique, to extend this legislation into the non-criminal field with a view to providing additional and more flexible remedies for dealing with unwarranted restraints upon competition.
As an example which I have already cited to the house on a previous occasion, I have in mind that the greater use of injunctive remedies could, in many circumstances, bring about perhaps more quickly and more effectively necessary adjustments to correct restrictive situations. Indeed, a start has been made in this direction by the administration having obtained in several recent cases injunctions without prosecution under the present criminal provisions of the Combines Investigation Act.
I should like to emphasize that I am stating here merely what general consideration I am giving to these matters, and I am not announcing any decision as to government policy. However, as I have informed the house already, certain recommendations in this field are now the subject of discussion between myself and my colleagues in the cabinet, and any decision arising out of such discussion will be made known in due course in the proper way.

Here I should like to add a word concerning the disclosure of investigations carried out by the director, especially in view of the keen interest some hon. members have shown for the application of the Combines Investigation Act in particular cases.
As hon. members know, whenever I am asked if the government has undertaken or will undertake an investigation under the Combines Investigation Act, I always answer that the matter will be brought to the attention of the director of investigations and research, under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, and that the director will take whatever steps the act requires, but that in accordance with the usual practice, no information will be supplied to indicate whether an investigation has been undertaken with regard to a particular group of companies or individuals before such information appears in a published report.
That policy has been followed for many years by the various ministers of justice and it is in keeping with section 28 of the act which stipulates that any inquiry under the act shall be conducted in private, except that the president of the restrictive trade practices commission may order that all or any portion of any proceedings before the commission or any member thereof shall be conducted in public.
Parliament has protected the public interest in the judicious application of the act by requiring that the director, who is a high official, enjoying a high degree of independence, should undertake an investigation each time he has reasons to believe that the act has been or will be violated. The director can also be activated, if I may use that word, through a proper request made by six Canadian citizens or the Minister of Justice. The public is well informed at all times about the administration of the act through the periodic reports of the restrictive trade practices commission, special inquiries, court proceedings and the annual report of the director which has to be submitted to parliament.

It can be taken for granted that the director makes a satisfactory preliminary examination of any complaint he receives to determine whether he is required by the law to undertake an investigation. The procedure is the same for any merger brought to his attention, whether or not a complaint has been laid.
However, it would not be in the public interest to reveal, before all the facts have been evaluated, including the arguments and explanations presented by the parties concerned, any information concerning an investigation carried out to determine whether individuals or corporations have broken the law.
To act otherwise would almost necessarily be prejudicial to public interest for two main reasons: it would impair the orderly conduct of the investigation and serious injustices could be committed against those whose conduct is being scrutinized because the general public could conclude too early, before it is in possession of all the facts, that the people concerned must be guilty since an investigation is being carried out. I suggest that such a state of things would be contrary to our concept of the sovereignty of the law.
Two main aspects of public interest have to be reconciled: the policy of parliament, as reflected in the law, which requires that all investigations be carried out confidentially, except in those cases where the law provides for publicity, and the interest of the public which requires that the latter must be sure that the administration always carries out its obligations conscientiously and efficiently and that cases of public interest, within the meaning of the act, are handled judiciously.
Naturally, it is most important that hon. members be on the alert so as to be in a position to recognize any situation which should be looked into. Quite properly, they should constantly draw the government's attention to particular situations and they should seek to ensure that the government remains aware of the importance of applying efficiently the Combines Investigation Act. Still, the immediate disclosure of the director's activities in particular cases is not necessary to enable the house to fulfil its supervisory role, in view of the publicity provided for by parliament in the act.

In five years and eight months of the federal parole board's operation, 11,614 inmates in various institutions have been let out on parole. Of these 11,614 inmates on parole, only 1,137, or 9.7 per cent, returned to jail. Of those who returned to jail 585 only returned because they broke the law again. The other 552 had their paroles rescinded because they broke the parole regulations under which they were released.
Of course, when you speak of parole you cover the question of lifers. It is most interesting to note that of those who were sentenced to life imprisonment or who were sentenced to death and had the death sentence commuted to life imprisonment, only 11 have had their paroles revoked or forfeited. There are at present 183 persons on parole who received a life sentence. To the best of my information not one of the lifers ever committed another offence; they merely broke the regulations of their parole. As I have mentioned, out of some 11,614 inmates released on parole in five years and eight months only 9.7 returned.
How many parole officers have we in the federal service? We have 28 parole officers in the federal service scattered among the ten field offices across Canada. The parole officers under the control of the federal parole board which gave authority to release over 11,000 men on parole are employed in ten field offices across Canada as follows: five in Vancouver, two in Edmonton, one in Prince Albert, two in Winnipeg, four in Kingston, three in Toronto, seven in Montreal, one in Quebec, two in Moncton and one in Halifax. I ask, Mr. Chairman, how are you going not only to make the parole system work but expand it? Do not forget that it costs around $2,800 a year to keep an inmate in a penitentiary, whereas a parole officer can handle between 34 and 50 men. The ideal number is 34 or 35 but he can handle up to 50. For the price of one parole officer you can handle 35 men; and on the basis of the record of the parole board since January 1, 1959 you can save about 90 per cent of them. Do we have to wait two years for the report of a royal commission to find out we need more parole officers and that the 28 in the ten field offices across the country are not enough? No. I know for a fact that if the minister would just ask for a report, if he has not already got it from the parole board, the parole board and the 
chairman can tell him immediately what to do.
There may be regulations governing parole which require to be amended; perhaps a change in the act itself is required. But something should be done because the government's policy in some regards is crazy. I have in mind a young man-a young scamp, that is what he is-who comes from a very good family in Vancouver. I know his parents well. He got into trouble, serious trouble, and landed more than once in jail. On the third occasion he broke down, became a mental case, and was transferred to the insane asylum. There they did a marvellous job and brought him back to a good approach, a good attitude and to good health. And what do we do with him? We put him back in the British Columbia penitentiary.
I saw this young man two months ago in the penitentiary looking forward to going out on what is known as the SNAP program which deals with narcotic offenders. May I say that I compliment the government for this new move and for the success of the first SNAP program experiment. But this man did not make it. One month ago that boy broke down and now he is back in the mental institution once more. I received a report a few days ago and the treatment he is receiving is bringing him back mentally. When Essondale says there is nothing more they can do, that he is fine, what will happen to him? Will he be sent back to the B.C. penitentiary? If this is the case, my guess is that he will break down again and perhaps he will never come out of the mental institution to which he will be once more committed.
These are things known to your officials, Mr. Minister. They are the sort of things which should be corrected now in order to save lives and the taxpayers' money. These are some of the matters we are asking you to think about and to do something about now, instead of waiting two years for a royal commission report. There are other things which can also be done. Speak to your commissioner of penitentiaries who has had years of experience. He knows the wardens and he knows the penitentiaries, and he knows the psychiatrists in those penitentiaries. Is the minister going to wait and perpetuate the situation presently existing, which is the most stupid and asinine policy I know of? Psychiatrists are employed on a part time basis. There are around 800 to 850 men in the B.C. penitentiary. There is a medium security prison at William Head and a minimum security prison at Agassiz. What can one psychi-

atrist employed half time do for 1,000 men? The majority of these men he is never able to see. Those he does see he sees for only a few minutes, and psychiatric treatment, Mr. Chairman, requires more than a few minutes.
I would ask the minister to talk to those psychiatrists, as we who are interested in this matter do. Talk to Dr. MacDonald in the British Columbia penitentiary. He told me three months ago that there were many sex offenders there requiring attention. There should be full time psychiatrists at that penitentiary, in which case 55 per cent of those in jail for sex offences would never come back again. He said they need three or four psychiatrists in every penitentiary and if that were the case over 55 per cent of the sex offenders and the mentally unbalanced would not be anti-social any more. But no, we would rather spend $2,800 a year to keep a prisoner in the penitentiary than give the parole board a few more parole officers or employ psychiatrists full time. Admittedly we might have to pay $25,000 or $30,000 a year for a psychiatrist, but if 55 per cent of the sex offenders did not come back to prison you would not only save lives but you would save the money of the taxpayers.
These things are known to the minister's officials; and I know they believe in what I am saying. Why did we only get generalities, platitudes and promises for the future from the minister when he spoke at the introduction of his estimates this afternoon? We are asking him for action now, not for some vision for the future. As 1 said this afternoon, I could have closed my eyes and thought to myself "My golly, that is the same speech I have been hearing now from ministers of justice for the 11 years I have been in this House of Commons, on the subject of penology". Now is the time for action, and we did hope we would get it from the present Minister of Justice.
I see my time is running on, Mr. Chairman, and very soon it will run out, so although this is a subject very dear to my heart I am not going to carry on, as I could, for hours, if I had the opportunity, to speak about narcotics and the need for forensic clinics. But I would mention what is said to me by every psychiatrist I have spoken to who is interested in penology, and that is that money and lives can be saved if there is segregation between the young and the old, the new offenders and the old offenders, the narcotics and the sex psychopaths.
I should like to conclude by using the minister's words. I have been interested in

all these wonderful speeches which the minister has been making over the past two months across the country. I am very grateful that he has been so kind as to send me a copy of these speeches. I should like to read from a speech made by the Minister of Justice on November 5, 1964 at Montreal to the Canadian club as follows:
If I were to reproach those who today condemn our prisons, I would tax them with restricting their censure to merely a small part of our correctional system. You, who in your various professions, form a virtual parliament of Canadian corrections, can measure this failing better than anyone; you know that at stake is the entire treatment of delinquents, their entire treatment right from the prevention of juvenile delinquency to after-care, not to mention sentencing, probation, imprisonment, rehabilitation and parole. For in spite of considerable recent progress, our correctional regime remains in many ways disorderly, reactionary and inhuman.
Those are the words of the minister on November 5, this year. He also said this:
But it must be observed that, in the long run, punishment promises society no real security. The only lasting way to prevent offenders from falling back into crime-unless we imprison them all for life-is to change their anti-social attitude.
Mr. Chairman, I conclude by drawing the minister's own words to his attention, particularly where he says that our correctional regime is disorderly, reactionary and inhuman, and that the object is directed toward rehabilitation and parole. speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister of Public Works today was with regard to
10420	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the construction of the Prince Edward Island causeway, a matter upon which there is confusion and uncertainty resulting from diverse and differing statements from ministers of the crown.
According to Time magazine of October 9 the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) said that it-
-is certain that construction will start by 1966. There's nothing in the reports to indicate any delay or any discouragement. We have a schedule and I am completely confident it will be met.
One has to read the papers regularly to hear progress of this undertaking, since one finds little on the records of parliament. On November 21 the Charlottetown Guardian had a headline "Causeway Construction Slated for 1965 Start?" The story is more interesting, if less revealing, than the headline. It is an account of a Liberal meeting in Kings county where the guest speaker was the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). I quote from the newspaper account:
Mr. Pickersgill did not make a long reference to the causeway. He said there was absolutely no question now about the causeway being built. He said he hoped to see the project actually under way next year.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-P.E.I. CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION START
speechtext: Don't you?

maintopic: TRANSPORT-P.E.I. CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION START
speechtext:
I hope so; my colleague hopes so; a hundred thousand islanders hope so. But we would like a little more than hopes.
It is significant that the minister who has departmental responsibility, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) has not said 1965, like the Minister of Transport, or 1966 like the Solicitor General. He has made a consistent and sustained contribution of silence to this vital question.
Throughout the years when our party was in power the present Minister of Transport was frequent and constant in his interrogation of the government. He used to rise and ask about the feasibility report, and when it was going to be tabled. Frequently he would ask if the causeway was under construction. He was fortunate that he was never asked to put these questions on the order paper, like I have been. But now, after being 19 months a member of the government I would have thought that more than hope would have been voiced by him. I would have thought a definite statement, not of hope but of policy and of plans would have been made-a firm announcement; the kind of statement the former prime minister made in the house when


he rose and pledged his government to build the causeway.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-P.E.I. CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION START
speechtext: What happened to that?

maintopic: TRANSPORT-P.E.I. CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION START
speechtext:
I hope the minister will contain himself. I have listened to many things from him for many years and I was able to restrain myself from interruptions, which were very easily prompted.
The former government was often criticized for not producing reports fast enough. Now we have a situation where this report has been available for months, but it is not being revealed. It is not being released, nor is the government indicating what plans it has, based upon the information which it admits it has had for a long time. We have had no information as to what type of work will be done and when it will begin. There is nothing about the interesting suggestions of a very reputable organization headed by Mr. Margison. There is nothing about the possible effect upon rail travel.
Except for newspaper releases and short statements at political meetings, all is silence on this great subject, one of the greatest things as far as the maritime economy in the region is concerned. With regard to a place where transportation problems have always been of the most compelling urgency we find a dreadful lack of official assurance, of official statements from the government by the minister who has the responsibility for this vast project, about which so much was done by the preceding government. I invite the minister to lift tonight a little of the veil of secrecy and state in this house officially where the project stands.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschatelets (Minister of Public Works):
maintopic: TRANSPORT-P.E.I. CAUSEWAY-INQUIRY AS TO CONSTRUCTION START

The first phase of preliminary studies has been completed; a detailed report has been turned in, and also two sets of designs have been submitted by the consultant engineers. This report establishes without any shadow of a doubt the feasibility of this project both as regards the engineering and economic aspects. This report and the designs are now before the government. I have said several times, and I repeat tonight, that this project is under very active consideration by the government. Having said that, I do not want to comment any further on the matter except to say that I have read the statement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) as re-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF JUDICIAL INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not see how the government could have done other than it has done, namely to offer a judicial inquiry into this matter which was raised in the house yesterday. The surprising thing to me is that it should have been necessary to bring this to the attention of the house before the government decided to initiate the inquiry.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that in my opinion the terms of reference which the minister has suggested are far too limited. As I took them down in rather scratchy notes, the minister said there would be two items in the terms of reference, namely whether or not there was sufficient information available to the minister when he received the R.C.M.P. report to warrant the laying of a criminal charge; and second, whether there is any further evidence at the time of the judicial inquiry which would warrant a prosecution.
It seems to me there is a much wider aspect of this case which ought to be looked into now, and that is the whole procedure which was followed by the minister and the government in dealing with this matter. Here was a minister of justice who, if I remember the dates he mentioned yesterday, around August 14 was told by the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. that a counsel had been faced, in one instance personally and in another case by telephone, by two executive assistants to two cabinet ministers. In the one case he was offered a bribe and in the second he had been subjected to intimidation in order to go easy on an application for bail by two men who were subject to extradition proceedings on behalf of the United States in connection with a narcotics charge. Now it is also apparent from the statement that has been made today that this allegation by a prominent counsel of

the city of Montreal involved a member of this house, the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister.
When the minister received the report on September 18 he had all this information before him. The minister decided, on his own, that there was not sufficient evidence to warrant prosecution. I say, Mr. Speaker, being as charitable as it is possible to be, that here was an allegation by a highly respected lawyer, a member of a reputable legal firm in the city of Montreal who had nothing to gain by making this allegation and, on the contrary, was only doing so to safeguard his own good name, and who must have known that in making this allegation he would be dragged through an investigation. Certainly there was every reason to believe that his allegations were true.
From the minister's statement yesterday it is perfectly clear that this matter was not referred either to the law officers of the crown in his department or to the crown attorney of the area to see whether they thought there were grounds for prosecution. Instead the matter was dropped, and would not have been raised again if it had not been raised in the house yesterday.
I think we are entitled to some explanations, and certainly a judicial inquiry ought to bring out some of the facts. For instance, the secretary or executive assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration left the employ of the minister around October 1, two weeks after this report was given to the Minister of Justice. Was he fired? If he was fired and if there were sufficient grounds for firing him, surely there were sufficient grounds for prosecuting him.
Yesterday the minister did not give us any further information, although we pressed him, regarding whether or not there was any person higher up involved. Now it it admitted that the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister was involved in this investigation. Surely the house has a right to know, and the country will want to know, whether the Minister of Justice transmitted the contents of the report he received from the R.C.M.P. on September 18 to the Prime Minister. If the Prime Minister knew, and has known since September 18, that the parliamentary secretary was involved in this investigation, why is it that only today, on November 24-

Mr. Speaker, in view of all that has taken place I think we can only regret that it is difficult to find complete honesty in politics.
I think that the announcement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) of his decision to hold an inquiry in that matter is certainly a sound one. I can only urge the

Judicial Inquiry Established minister to carry out a complete inquiry into that matter so that no doubt can subsist in the minds of the members of the House of Commons and of the whole Canadian people as to the implications that could spring from the allegation made yesterday by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
It seems to me, after listening to the discussion yesterday, that there is definitely grounds for an inquiry, and a very serious inquiry, since confidence in politics is involved and since that confidence has been quite seriously shaken by the policy followed by this government since they came to office. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) I must state that we are far from being satisfied with the terms of reference of this inquiry.
The inquiry will be, especially under the terms of reference announced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), entirely contrary to the principles of impartial justice.
The minister states that the purpose of the inquiry will be to determine whether the department was right or not in not lodging a complaint when the report from the R.C.M.P. was received.
The inquiry will hence determine the action of the minister on receipt of that report from the R.C.M.P. Now, on receiving the report the minister decided not to lodge a complaint immediately. What happens to the role of the Minister of Justice? His efforts will tend to prove that he was right in not lodging a complaint and that there is not sufficient evidence. By the same token, it can be seen that apart from this role he will have another more serious part to play, which will be to try and justify the innocence of those against whom charges were laid, so that his own role, which was not to take action, will be justified.
In that inquiry the minister will attempt to justify his refusal to prosecute or lay charges against those presumed responsible.
Obviously the role of the Minister of Justice will be then quite contrary to that he usually assumes in the normal discharge of his duties. The duty of the Minister of Justice is to set up inquiries, to lay charges against those
[Mr. Lessard (Lake St. John) .1
presumed guilty, but in that inquiry, if the Minister of Justice wants to justify his action not to prosecute those individuals, he will definitely have to try to prove their innocence. Under the terms of reference the minister did set out himself, his duty and his role will be to prove that two individuals are innocent which is not his role but rather an opposite role to that he has to play.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that the terms of reference of the judicial commission whose establishment has just been announced is nothing but a smokescreen set up by the Minister of Justice who is trying to hide the facts and play a role which is not his, that is to exonerate the accused.
The matter raised by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is a serious one; in fact, it is much more serious than it would seem on the face of it. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out, two executive secretaries to ministers are involved. One of the parliamentary secretaries to the Prime Minister even felt compelled to resign. We do not ask for that much, since he is presumed innocent until proven guilty. However, he felt he had to resign and it is reported today that one of the two executive secretaries has been fired. The minister announced an investigation on the actions of those individuals, but not on the question of whether he was right in not bringing the matter before the court.
So, that is what I think of the announcement made by the Minister of Justice. The terms of reference that he formulated are absolutely contrary to the impartial application of justice. In my opinion the minister should ask instead for a complete investigation on everything that took place in this matter, including the telephone calls as well as the threats and the amounts of money involved. That is what he is there for, in any case, as he just stated.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. Yesterday, as reported on page 10410 of Hansard, I put the following question to the hon. member for Lapointe:
Does the hon. member feel that it Is a more serious matter to accept contributions from the S.I.U. than to work for Jos. Bdgin who is a notorious criminal and who has been charged before the courts?
I recognize that I have expressed myself more strongly than I intended to because Mr. Jos. Begin is not a notorious criminal. What I intended to say is that criminal charges have been laid against him, that they are before the courts and that the hon. member for Lapointe worked for this man for $50 a week.



The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
I.	Grant in respect of the net operating amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service, $85,900,000.

Mr. Chairman, mindful of the fact that we have many departmental estimates to pass in a short number of days my few remarks will be fewer than usual. I am sorry my colleague from Digby-Annap-olis-Kings is not able to be here, though I do not suggest I am continuing his remarks. He has enough problems to deal with without bearing the responsibility for anything I might say.
The impressive statement of the minister on Friday, November 13, indicating it is not such an unlucky day as some may think, was
10436

Supply-C.B.C.
full and interesting, and I was impressed at the emphasis he put upon what he chose to call the spiritual side of our Canadian life. We should remind ourselves that for a nation, as for an individual, life is more than meat, and the body more than raiment. While we all know that in our time life is becoming easier, it is our responsibility to give leadership in fields other than material. He said our cultural life was anaemic. Perhaps it is; but I am optimistic enough to believe that it is viable, that after an assiduous search for our identity we have found one. Now it is up to us to nurture and nourish our cultural development.
Much of what the minister said the other day was not new. Much was a recapitulation of plans and projects which have been under consideration or in progress for years. A good deal of it was of a very general nature. Despite this, however, his statement was important, useful and on the whole encouraging, and I congratulate him upon it.
I should like to make a few brief comments on one or two of the subjects he dealt with. I do not intend to spend any time on the affairs of the C.B.C., because on interim supply many of us made our comments with regard to that important body. Had the estimates come before us earlier we would have made them in connection with those estimates. I do hope that at another session of this parliament, if there is one, we may all have an opportunity to deal with this vital subject in a period of time commensurate with its interest and importance.
In the first place, I think putting all the cultural agencies under one roof, as the minister describes it, constitutes a good and useful step. I should like to advocate strongly the establishment of a standing committee on cultural matters. I believe much would come from the establishment of such a body. Third, I believe, and I hope the minister believes, that we Canadians must devote far more of our budget to cultural matters. The minister, with all these agencies under his umbrella, has a tremendous opportunity and an immense responsibility. Fourth, I believe far more use could and should be made of the queen's printer, or perhaps of the queen's publisher, to popularize the cultural activities and aims of our nation.
I believe too that larger budgets and greater programming autonomy should be provided for agencies such as the archives and the others the hon. gentleman mentioned in the latter part of his statement. I only

wish I had more time in which to discuss the public archives, which is the institution I know so very well, but I can pay a tribute here to the wonderful effort which has been made in recent years in encouraging historical research and revitalizing our interest in our past. Sixth, I should like to endorse the intention to proceed with consideration of the establishment of a national research centre for the humanities and the social sciences. I believe this is a most commendable and worth-while field of study. We have the national research council as a splendid example of what the government can do in this area of science. Surely in the social science realm the need is even greater.
With my seventh point my sermonette is at an end. In the words of a great man whose death we mourned and recalled just the other day, a nation is judged not only by the men it produces but by the men it honours. This brings me to a subject I have often raised in this parliament; the failure of Canadians and, I believe, of this government to give proper attention to our history and to the great men of our past. We are heading toward the sesqui-centennial of the birth of our greatest founding father, Sir John A. Macdonald. This event takes place on January 11. We are looking forward to celebrating the centenary of confederation in 1967. Let us take the first step in 1965 by celebrating in a full and fitting way the birth of the leading figure in the confederation movement whose centennial we will soon be marking.
I invite the minister to stimulate the interdepartmental committee which he said the other day has been established. In the process he might get somebody to provide an answer to the very simple question I placed on the order paper on August 18, namely whether the government had any plans-whether it was consulting with the government of Ontario, the city of Kingston, and so on-for participation in ceremonies honouring the anniversary of the birth of our first prime minister. Perhaps he could approach his colleague the Postmaster General about the issue of a commemorative stamp, the first of a series, it may be hoped, by means of which we could honour many men, including George Brown, D'Arcy McGee and others for whom appropriate celebration dates will be arising soon.
As far as I know nothing has been arranged except a dinner at Kingston to honour the birthday of Sir John A. Macdonald. I think the centennial committee is playing some part in that celebration. Perhaps the minister, if

he cannot get me an answer to my question, might get me a ticket to the dinner. This is something on which I would commend him most heartily; but surely the government, this parliament, which itself in such an impressive way commemorates Sir John A. Macdonald, should be giving a lead. Part of our trouble is that we are always so reluctant to enthuse or emote about the things which have made this Canada a good and worthy country.
Regretting that I have not time to say a great deal more, I wish the minister well in his efforts. I think he is a good minister. I hope I will be able to say this with greater enthusiasm as he produces more. In this connection I would urge him to keep in mind this need to pay tribute to our great men and honour our national founders. Let him give leadership in this regard. I shall be interested in what happens on January 11, and I shall expect to see his hand there in celebrations worthy of the man and worthy of our country.

Many hon. members have taken advantage of this opportunity to comment on the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I intend to devote most of my remarks to the activities of the national film board.
First of all, though, I should like to say a word about the minister himself. I had intended to congratulate him on being the man from the Pearson team chosen to drag the wagon of culture. Someone behind the curtain remarked that we should be no longer speaking of "the Pearson team" but of "the Pearson gang". I do not know how the hon. gentleman would fit in with the gang.
I am pleased that he has this job and I hope he will be able to move quickly beyond the statement of policy he presented when the estimates were first brought before the committee. I notice that most people seem to think this statement was a good start, but there have been suggestions that it represented a hazy start. One of the drawbacks is the great hesitancy on the part of the people of Canada to consider a minister of culture. It seems too highfallutin', too fancy, too eggheadish, too corny, even, for Canadians. Nevertheless, in effect that is what the minister is, and the sooner the government sets out to give weight to the whole concept the better it will be.
The C.B.C. has been much in the news lately, largely because of programming. There has been a great deal of discussion in this house about the relationship between parliament and the corporation. We are waiting, as we usually are for some reason or other 20220-660^
Supply-C.B.C.
in connection with the C.B.C. and broadcasting matters generally, for a report, in this case the Fowler committee report. One of the gaps in our thinking as politicians is our inability to come to grips with the whole question of the grey areas of the relationship between the crown corporations and the government. I was reading J. K. Galbraith's analysis the other day of what a public corporation should be and his whole point was that it had to be completely clear of intervention and interference so far as its administration is concerned. But the important thing was to have the objectives of a public corporation open for discussion and perfectly clear, and it seems to me that this is the predicament of the C.B.C. at the present time.
The objectives of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are no longer clear, and it seems to me they have been changed partly because of a hardening of the arteries within the C.B.C., which is now a middle aged and rather frumpy institution which has lost a great deal of its zest. Also private industry and the opportunity of watching United States programs has pretty well changed its objectives and indicates one of the main theses supporting the tremendous amount of money which is given to the C.B.C.
The whole concept of the C.B.C. has been that it provided the main bones of the broadcasting service in Canada. The plain fact of the matter is that it now no longer does this. It shares it with the private stations in both radio and television and it shares it also with the 60 to 75 per cent of the people of this country who are able to watch United States programs on television. This it seems to me, has really been the cause of the questions raised in many minds about the scale of financial support which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation gets.
This support has increased tremendously. If you go back to about 1945 or 1946 I believe it had a budget of $5 million or so. Now the budget is more than 20 times that, and the scale of contributions from general revenue is up over the $70 million mark. The situation has changed and the C.B.C. is no longer the main agency through which the majority of people get their radio and television. As a matter of fact radio is now a very minor element, not a major element, in terms of listening hours put in by Canadians. Television seems to get its major audience in most places where the audience is split or the program competes for an audience, or

4.	What is the "entertainment" concept of national film board policy? Is it primary? I sent that letter to the minister requesting the establishment of a committee. I gather that he felt it best to get the requested information from the head of the national film board, and he forwarded that letter. He did not reply to me in terms indicating that he took my request with any seriousness on his part as the minister. He did send me a reply which was prepared by Mr. Roberge.
I have discussed this personally with the minister and I do not intend to quarrel with him here, but one of my main disappointments is that when someone presents a request, with an analysis, he should reply in something other than the form of an answer from the head of a particular agency. The reason I might have expected a reply from the head of the agency is just that such would be normal; but surely if the minister is in charge of the over-all policy and its operations it is his responsibility to examine the questions put to him and make some comment.
I have heard that the head of the national film board and the minister are very close friends. Perhaps there is such a relationship between them that they speak with one voice, but I suggest to the minister that if he wants to be fair to opposition politicians he should speak or make some comment about the suggestions made.

In any event, Mr. Roberge was kind enough to send me copy of a memorandum to the Secretary of State with respect to a letter from me. This is the answer:
I regret that owing to circumstances beyond my control I have been unable to let you have earlier my comments on Mr. Fisher's letter to you dated September 10, and I trust that both the member for Port Arthur and you will not have been inconvenienced by this delay.
Then he states:
While it is not for me to say whether or not a parliamentary committee should be constituted to look into national film board matters, I do feel that a meeting with the member for Port Arthur could provide him more rapidly with the information necessary to reach a conclusion on the various points he raised, more particularly on page 4 of his letter to you. I would be quite prepared, with my colleagues in the management of the board, to go into these questions at Mr. Fisher's convenience, if he could spare a day or so for that purpose.
This invitation is all very nice, but one of the things I have learned as a politician and opposition member is that the best thing you can do is to keep away from the formal apparatus of a civil service or a department or an agency unless you are dealing with it either in a parliamentary committee or with the minister or the senior political official responsible present. By "political" I mean an elected person. I appreciate the invitation but I am not particularly interested. As a matter of fact, I have received most of the information I present as a critique from members or people who work for the national film board or have a very close relationship with it, and I would not raise these questions if I did not feel they should be considered seriously by the government, not just by the head of the national film board. But Mr. Roberge goes on:
I appreciate Mr. Fisher's interest in what we are doing and how we are going about it. We are not indifferent, I may assure you, to the concern expressed by Mr. Fisher with respect to our community operations in Canada as distinct from our other activities at home in the theatrical and television areas and our operations abroad.
Here is a lovely sentence of gobbledegook:
Considering all the factors affecting our role here and abroad, and resources are one of those factors, I sincerely believe that we have, over the years, maintained a reasonable balance.
Shades of Alphonse Ouimet. That is what A1 always comes up with, this reasonable balance thing. How do you argue with it? He goes on to say:
On all fronts, the demands have been, and still are, greater than our resources.
They certainly are. If you have got a director who starts with a short and turns it into a feature film because he is away from

home base, you really have got demands on your resources. There is no question about that. He continues:
In terms of effort and funds, community films and their distribution as a distinctive sector have not and are not receiving the "poor relation" treatment. I would say that on the production program for this current year, more than 20 new films in English and more than 10 new films in French are, in our opinion, particularly suited for community use-and this does not take into account other new films which are released first on television or in the cinemas and which then are placed in community distribution. An analysis of the current productions and of our releases in the last years would indicate that films "which handle social and economic problems" are not the exception in the board's program.
I am not going to accuse Mr. Roberge of lying because I do not think he thinks he is lying, but he is not giving a true statement of the situation as I see it. I do not know whether the minister has looked at the catalogue of films listed as available for distribution by the national film board in 1963, but I would challenge him to take a look at it, run through it and see just how old many of the basic series are. For example, the ages of the child series is seven years old, the adolescence series is seven years old, the mental mechanism series is 14 years old, the accidents do not happen series is nine years old.
And so it goes. In other words, much of the very best that has been produced by the national film board in the functional documentary area has become out of date, and anyone who has shown films eight, nine or ten years old, particularly in a field such as safety, knows just how out of date these things can become. Furthermore if they are in areas where there has been a fairly keen distribution you need a fairly large stock as well as having the older series brought up to date.
Order. The Chair does not wish to interrupt the hon. member but I understand the item before us is the vote for the C.B.C., not the national film board.
The minister will explain.

Mr. Chairman, when I made my general statement more than a week ago I covered the eight cultural agencies and at that time invited members of the committee to make any comments they might want to make on this so-called first item. Therefore I think the hon. member is quite in order.

I want the minister to examine and go through the catalogue with Mr. Roberge and reassure himself with regard to
Supply-C.B.C.
whether I am wrong, because I do not believe I am. I cannot find better evidence of the national film board's feeling with regard to the production of serious, functional documentaries than the fact that so many of these films in their major series are out of date, and on top of that so comparatively few new ones are being produced.
I have here the quarterly reports of the national film board on the production of films and other visual materials for the periods ended March 31, 1964, and September 30, 1964. I have gone through these and again it is a most discouraging record if you are interested in having the kind of material you can take to groups of various kinds out in the communities, who want something serious and substantial.
I was reminded of that national film board production a couple of weeks ago, which all television reviewers thought was so beautiful, about the unmarried young lady who becomes pregnant. It is all done very delicately and the acting is very good with all the latest technique. But the only message seemed to come at the end when in a great tizzy she grabbed the telephone, called her boy friend and said, "I am going to have a baby", and then slammed down the phone. Having seen the problems of showing films to teenagers and youth groups such as the girl guides out in the communities, I can just imagine how useful this particular national film board production, with its I am going to have a baby, drop the telephone kick, is going to be when it is distributed. Yet here was a production that made use of excellent directing talent, contained some wonderful acting and I am sure involved substantial expense. It is a perfect illustration of the kind of fetish in programming that has become an obsession with many people in the national film board and with, I think, bad effect upon its primary purpose. I continue with Mr. Roberge's letter:
We are conscious that the need is to take into account the ways in which films are actually used today and to supply films for those types of uses-films with substantial content and on subject matter of contemporary interest and value. In fact we are working along those lines-
That is good to know.
-and, to that end, are seeking the best assistance we can find. For instance, on September 16, 17 and 18 a small conference on films was held in Saskatoon, convened by the film board and attended by senior people from the extension departments of the Universities of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I just want to make one comment in that regard. The way Mr. Roberge puts it you would think that the film board had taken

Supply-C.B.C.
the initiative. That is not true. That meeting was called because the extension departments of most of the universities in western Canada were fed up with the national film board and its lack of touch and lack of liaison. But the way this is put it suggests that the national film board took the initiative. Mr. Roberge goes on to say:
I am now considering proposing to the members of the board that a national committee of some kind be set up to advise us on matters pertaining to adult education. As you know, a considerable expansion is taking place in adult education and a decisive role appears to be played there by university extension. Between 1957 and 1962, enrolment in extension has almost doubled.
This is what people have been telling the national film board for a number of years, and finally it has got through. At this late date Mr. Roberge has decided that he should now consider a national committee of some kind. I should like to point out that this is typical of the fact that the national film board has been proceeding along lines that have been taking away from its primary purpose. He goes on:
For several years, a Canadian education association-national film board committee has advised us with respect to films specially intended for school use. We have followed the same pattern on the French side; a joint committee has been set up with l'association Canadienne des educateurs de langue frangaise.
My information on this point is that over several years this so-called committee has met no more than twice, and I have the information from one person who took part in one of the meetings that it really did not get anywhere, and it certainly has had nothing of substance to put forward.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I bring to the attention of the hon. member the fact that his time has expired, unless he has leave to carry on.
Agreed.

I ask for about 10 or 15 minutes. I would appreciate it very much if I were given that time. I should like to continue with Mr. Roberge's letter:
There is a greatly Increased potential in community and educational films. There lies the board's traditional strength. While not detracting from our other duties, I am sure my colleagues and myself wish to emphasize and strengthen our work in these areas.
Well, where are the films? Where are these productions? There is a paragraph here concerning my local area which I will skip. I thought it a little bit of effrontery to tell me that the circulation of films is increasing

there. I certainly hope it will, and there is no reason why it should go down when there is a very devoted national film board man there pushing them.
Then, he goes on:
Mr. Fisher refers to film councils and to public libraries. In that respect, I would like to state in general terms that there is throughout the country an increase in film activities conducted through public libraries. Without implying that there exists a direct relationship between them, I would also like to say that while the number of film councils has remained quite constant, we have noticed that in the changing milieu and because of changes in the audio-visual and community fields their role is being modified. In my opinon, the film councils' role will, in coming years, find in many instances a different level. However, this is a matter under review and I am not prepared to say anything too precise about it at this time.
Well again, Mr. Roberge is not very precise or he is considering something. The facts, as I understand them, are that public libraries, particularly in Ontario and the western provinces, have built up a framework that is almost fundamental for the distribution of film. The cry at the moment is not so much for a different distribution system as it is for films. They want more functional, documentary films; films with a purpose; didactic films; films that explain some of the problems of our times.
I will just finish off Mr. Roberge's letter. He says:
Before closing, I would like to put the record straight on Don Owen's statement that his film "Nobody Waved Goodbye" just grew into a feature film production without our knowing about it.
This is really entertaining.
This is the ebullient statement of a young director who did not, I can assure you, operate with the complete independence his statement quoted by Mr. Fisher does suggest. The fact that the subject of his film grew was apparent to both hs producer and management. It was a management decision to produce the film at a longer length than that first contemplated.
I am not going to ask for a committee of inquiry into something that is within this area, the running wild of a film. However, Mr. Roberge is not kidding me, and I do not think he is kidding anybody when he says that the subject of the film grew and was apparent to both his producer and management. I do not believe you get a young man making the kind of statements Mr. Owen did, not to one reporter but to several at different times, indicating that he just went to Toronto with a bunch of film, on his own, and the first thing they knew he had a feature length film without his bosses knowing. I quite appreciate Mr. Roberge feels that he has

to cover up, but I am not accepting that answer at all.
I continue to quote from the letter:
Mr. Fisher points out too "the stories that come to him of the increasing split among the board's people in Montreal between the French and English sections". In the board, as almost everywhere in Canada, this is a delicate matter.
Well, it certainly is a delicate matter.
If, in this respect, the board were to be considered the "microcosm" of Canada, I venture to say that the whole Canadian situation would, at this time, appear to be quite sound and reasonable.
Well, I agree that they are still operating in the same building and that, I suppose, is an achievement. So far as I know, that is about it, in terms of the situation with regard to language.
I should like to add that I had some anxieties last year, but considerable improvement has taken place and, if left alone, the present equilibrium will be conducive to good results and relative happiness.
That is all I am going to read from Mr. Roberge's letter. This last point, the fact that there is a split between the French and English wings of the film board in Montreal is something I am not prepared to put forward any evidence upon. All I know is that it has come to me repeatedly, and the indications are that this split is not only a language split. It is a split between producer attitudes in terms of the fact that French Canadian producers are working as a result of the stimulus of their own city and the new techniques, and have gone much farther in this new, avant garde kind of film making. It is very easy to appreciate the excitement that they are generating amongst themselves. However, I think it has tended to divorce them in their purpose from the traditional, the functional kind of production that gave the film board a name in this work.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I think that in order to complete the record the hon. member should put the last short paragraph of the letter on the record.

I will certainly do that.
Should you wish me to report in detail on all the points alluded to by Mr. Fisher, I shall endeavour to do so. Should you require further information, do not hesitate to let me know.
I did not deliberately leave it out. It was just to shorten things. I happen to feel that Mr. Roberge is a competent administrator, in his way, of the national film board. If I am pillorying him here it is only because I believe that he is befogging the purpose, 20220-861
Supply-C.B.C.
what I consider to be the central purpose of the national film board, which is to produce good, functional documentaries that have a distribution out in the country beyond the theatrical and television circuits.
Is there anything to say why they should have any place beyond television?

The hon. member asks if there is anything to say why they should have any place beyond television. I would assume that in his own area he knows that all kinds of groups cannot get around a television set.
No, why should there be any area beyond television?

Now you are on a very good point. I wanted to make these points that are put together by someone who has a relationship with the national film board, but in language which I have adopted or paraphrased.
There is a distinct danger of the national film board becoming oriented predominantly to the will expressed by some of its film makers rather than to the needs of its audience. I suspect that this is revealed by the great tendency in our films for manner to prevail over matter. Reversing the healthy relationship between these elements, the preferences are for subject matters to be increasingly dictated by the purpose of the film maker to provide film adventures rather than by the demands to maintain a story relationship. Consequently the policies currently being advocated, although presented without drama and in part legitimate slogans of aesthetic national idealism are essentially offering an environment of licence for film makers.
Performance and organization: by projecting discussion of internal national film board policies into the national arena and turning them into public dialogue, is both improper and dangerous. The national film board itself is increasingly coming to be influenced by the reflections of a narrow circle of critics, cine club critics, aesthetics and process film makers rather than those average viewers who seek a film more consistent with his problems of living than with the creation of an aesthetic division that assembles around the assumption that prestige in the film world amounts automatically to widespread public approval. The national film board has been living increasingly on past capital and good will in so far as a very large section of the Canadian public are concerned. The only prestige which counts in the long run is a prestige that is inevitably Canadian and associated with a creation in

Supply-C.B.C.
which the national film board has an important role to play. The steady distortion of the purpose by the alteration of this role could reduce the N.F.B. from its significant place in a Canadian society to that of an art factory concerned largely with its own prestige in a narrow film world, and this at a time when the real world faces us with most critical and complex problems. Already the national film board has begun to lose ground in an audience area where formerly it was successful.
Those points it seems to me, contain the guts of the criticism I have made and want to make of the national film board. I say that despite all the praise paid to the 25th anniversary of the national film board, the board is in serious difficulty in terms of its purpose, its allocation of resources and its direction.
If I had more time I would like to read other contributions. For example, I have a translation here put forward by the French association professionale de cinema which I think is very germane to the points I have raised. I know the minister has a copy and I assume he has looked at it, and later on in this debate I want to come back to this topic of the national film board.
There is a quotation from Jacques Maritain I want to read. Perhaps it is a little too arty to slip in here, but he made the point in one of his studies of philosophy that man is confronted by two separate concepts, that of artistic value which relates to his own work, and that of moral values which relate to his being a man. He says, about these two autonomous worlds, art and morality, that each is sovereign in its own field. The problem arises from the fact that these two worlds cannot ignore and disregard each other, for man belongs in them both as an intellectual maker and a moral agent. Therefore since an artist is a man before being an artist and is not an abstract impersonation of art coming down from an Appollonian separate heaven, the autonomous world of reality is superior to the autonomous world of art. "There is no law against the law on which the destiny of man depends."

At the present time the corporation's planning in radio takes into account all areas of Canada with a population of more than 500 which could be served by one transmitter.
