I do not know how many hon. members watch television, but there is virtually no live Canadian programming in the prime hours over station CJOH. What we get are old films, canned murder mysteries and westerns, purchased cheaply from the United States. I am not criticizing the owners of CJOH if they can get away with it, but I do suggest that in terms of developing a Canadian identity and in terms of the promises which they voluntarily made to the B.B.G. they have welshed, virtually 100 per cent, on their promises.
They promised that at least once a week they would show live dramatic programs, and that at least once a month one of those programs would be produced in Ottawa, using Ottawa actors and producers. To my knowledge station CJOH has never had a live dramatic program, and certainly never one that was produced in Ottawa.
They promised that they would give an award to the best Canadian playwright for a play produced in Ottawa. Of course they have never lived up to that promise.
They promised, in view of the fact Ottawa has a very large percentage of its population which is French speaking, that they would televise as much as ten hours a week in French. Recently when they were checked up on that by the student newspaper of Ottawa university their answer was that they had looked into the matter but they could not get the advertisers to make it worth while. When they made these promises to the B.B.G. they did not mention any condition that they
Supply-C.B.C.
would do this only if they could get the advertisers to pay for it.
Not one of these promises has been kept. Station CFTO in Toronto owned by that great Canadian patriot and citizen Mr. Bassett promised it would spend more than 25 per cent of its estimated gross revenue on live talent. Well, I venture to say that it has not spent 5 per cent of its gross revenue on live talent unless one includes in the cost of live talent the cost of televising football games. I am in favour of football. I like football and I like to watch football on television. But this certainly was not what Mr. Bassett promised the board of broadcast governors when he was applying for the channel in Toronto.
Especially when Kapp is passing for Vancouver.

Similarly, the owners of station CFTO promised they would be televising performances by the Toronto symphony orchestra, that they would be televising "live" ballet, that they would be televising concerts of serious music. None of this has ever been done and I think the Canadian people and members of this house must bear all this in mind when they compare the schedules which, in fact, are offered with the standards of programming which the C.B.C. carried on so effectively before the private companies were permitted to enter this field-standards which the corporation has been obliged progressively to reduce as a result of this competition.
Station CFTO promised it would make available to its viewers a wide selection of Canadian programs of an artistic and dramatic nature. Its sponsors undertook to produce "live" dramatic plays. Of course none of this has been done. What we are given, as Canadian content almost exclusively over the private stations and over C.T.V., are quiz programs of the lowest type in terms of their appeal to those interested in any program content which would make them think.
Similarly the channel in Winnipeg promised to televise discussion groups, music by symphony orchestras, and so on. It undertook to give an opportunity to the ethnic groups in Winnipeg, of which there are many, to illustrate their various cultures; it promised to televise their music, their dancing and their folk art. None of this has ever been accomplished. I could go on for a long time. But these are some of the things which the applicants for private channels promised

Supply-C.B.C.
the board of broadcast governors. These applicants were interested primarily in making money, but I am not blaming them for that. Similarly, the C.T.V. network submitted to the board a list of no less than 45 programs which the sponsors said they were ready to produce both for Canadian consumption and for distribution around the world-programs dealing with sport, with life outdoors and with wildlife, with games of all types, with the work of dramatic groups, and so on. Few if any programs of this type have been available. I know the owners of the private stations and of the network will probably say they have been unable to do these things because they have not been able to make enough money. Indeed, I believe this is why the board of broadcast governors has gone easy with them and has failed to press them to keep their promises.
But, Mr. Chairman, this was not just a private arrangement made between private applicants and a body without official status. This was a promise made to a government board representing the people of Canada and I am naive enough to believe that such promises should be lived up to, whether they are made by ordinary citizens or by the big owners of private television stations and networks. Not only have the promised programs failed to materialize but pressure has been placed on the C.B.C. to lower its standards in order to meet the competition which these people are providing. This is why we must take a serious look at the reasons why the board of broadcast governors have not done the job which was given to it by the legislation setting it up.
It is true we will not have time to discuss these questions in detail to the extent that their importance makes desirable. It is true, as the minister will no doubt tell us, that a committee headed by Mr. Fowler has been appointed to look into this question. I have a great deal of respect for Mr. Fowler and I am hopeful we shall get a worth-while report from him. I wish, however, I could really believe we shall see more action as a result of the report which he will be submitting within the course of the next four months than we saw in connection with the last Fowler report. What has happened in recent years, and this has been the case whether Conservative or Liberal governments have been in power, has been the gradual erosion of the ability of the C.B.C. to do the job which it has to do, and which it was required to do the day it was set up by a former Conservative government back in the thirties. tMr. Orlikow.]
The corporation has tried to carry out these obligations, but their discharge will be increasingly difficult unless the same standards are applied to its competitors as are applied to the C.B.C.
It is important we should look at what these private stations are doing. Some people think that having given them a licence we simply let them put on what they please. But private radio and television, the latter, particularly, are not in the same position as are other private businesses. If 20 different individuals want to open up grocery stores in Ottawa, Winnipeg or Montreal, nobody will question their right to do so; they will either make a go of it or not, on the basis of the amount of business available. But it is obvious to anybody who gives the matter thought that there is a very definite limit to the number of television channels which a country with a population the size of Canada's can permit. The limit would be two in most cities, or possibly three in the largest cities; four if one includes French and English channels. When parliament has set up a regulatory body, surely we can expect that body to select from among the applicants for licences those who propose to give to the Canadian people the best, the most educational, the most entertaining and the most provocative programs. If the regulatory body makes that choice then I expect them to exercise some type of supervision. If the B.B.G. had ever exercised supervision, with the exception of the supervision it exercised on the televising of the Grey cup last year, then I do not know about it.
It seems to me that having given the present operators of private television stations the right, as I said earlier, to spend money, they probably forgot about it and instead of becoming a regulatory body as instructed under the act they became the friends, the protectors and lovers of private television stations and networks. The public is not getting from the B.B.G., and therefore from the Canadian government, the B.B.G. being a creature of the Canadian government -perhaps not this government but it is a creature of the Canadian government-the kind of protection to which it is entitled.
I hope that it will not be November 24 next year before the parliamentary committee to look into radio and television is set up. I hope it will be set up early in 1965. I do not think it is necessary for the parliamentary committee to wait to be set up until Mr. Fowler and his associates make their report. I hope the committee is appointed early in

the new session and that it gets down to business right away. I trust we will hear from the C.B.C. a report in much greater detail than we have here. I agree with the minister that he is not responsible for the decisions on programming by the C.B.C. but I hope a parliamentary committee will have an opportunity to hear a thorough and complete report from the C.B.C. in explanation of some of the things they have done.
I am not thinking of censorship. It may be I do not like a particular play or program. I can say-it is no secret; I have said this to the people working on particular programs -that I am not enamoured of the program "This Hour Has Seven Days". I did not like the Rockwell interview, not because I think the C.B.C. should not run that kind of interview but simply because I believe Rockwell represents no one in the United States. In my opinion the only reason for putting on that interview was as a means of sensationalism, as a means of getting viewers. I think the C.B.C. needs viewers and exciting programs, but they should not stoop to putting on what I consider cheap sensationalism. But that is my personal opinion and I am not suggesting for a moment that any member of parliament or the minister in charge should interfere with individual programs put on by the C.B.C. Last week they put on an Ibsen play. I watched it and I did not like it. I noticed that the television critics in both Ottawa newspapers thought it an excellent play. That is understandable, because people react in different ways to different programs. I like football, but many people think there is too much football carried on television. I hope the C.B.C. continues to make its own decisions, but I think it is time that they came before the parliamentary committee, told us what they have been doing, what they are planning for the future, and gave us an idea of what this will cost. I do not for a moment believe the C.B.C. loses money. I call the expenditure of money for the C.B.C. the development of a Canadian identity. I want to remain a Canadian; I do not want to be a citizen of the United States.
Would the hon. member allow a question?
Certainly.

The hon. member said he does not consider the C.B.C. expenditure a loss of money, that it is an expenditure on behalf of culture. Would he explain to us where the culture was in the program "This Hour Has
Supply-C.B.C.
Seven Days", when Rockwell said that F. D. Roosevelt was the biggest communist the world has ever seen, with the exception of his wife?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member asked a question which indicates he has not listened to me, or if he has, has not understood a single word. I think I speak in language which 99 per cent of the people understand. I said I am not going to set myself up as a judge of which C.B.C. program is good and which C.B.C. program is bad. The C.B.C. puts on a great many programs which I suppose the minister and I would consider culture. I do not know what the hon. member for York-Humber would call them, but he can speak for himself. The C.B.C. also puts on programs which are not culture but information. They put on discussions and programs which I would only classify as entertainment.
My point is that it is the function of a television network, whether it be a private network or a public network, to offer a well rounded variety of programs to its viewers. Until the last year or so I think the C.B.C. did this very successfully, and if the hon. member wonders how successfully he just needs to look at the list of former C.B.C. writers, producers, actors and performers who sang and danced and have now moved to the United States or to Great Britain where they are able to earn anywhere up to ten times what the C.B.C. pays them. If the hon. member does not know of whom I speak I will be glad to give him a list on a later occasion.
This is what I think the C.B.C. should do, and it is also what I think private networks should do. When you look at a private network program you will see quite a bit of time is spent, so far as Canadian content is concerned, on news and public affairs. Is there a single member here who would suggest that these news programs come anywhere close to those of the C.B.C.? They are not even in the same league. These stations have what they call public affairs programs. They have a program which is put on once a week in which my colleague from Port Arthur is master of ceremonies. I think it is a good program and I wish they would show it in my home city of Winnipeg, but they do not. There is a program every night in which Pierre Berton is master of ceremonies. I do not always agree with him, particularly when he is foolish enough to suggest he will vote Liberal, but I think he is a pretty provocative person and I give him credit for his program, even though it does not originate in the city of Ottawa.

Supply-C.B.C.
Having given these two examples I challenge anyone either inside or outside the house to show the Canadian people what other public affairs programs the private networks are putting on on a regular basis. Where is the use of Canadian talent? Where is the use of Canadian performers? Where is the use of Canadian journalists or professors who can speak on public affairs? They just do not exist on private networks. The same thing has happened with regard to the other things they promised the B.B.G., and therefore the people of Canada, that they would do.
May I say in closing that the parliament of Canada, which represents the people of Canada, ought to take a very close look at the thinking which went on in the formation of the C.B.C. For the benefit of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, who made a bitter and I think completely unwarranted attack on the C.B.C. several weeks ago, I should like to quote some words to him about the C.B.C. used by a former prime minister of Canada in 1932, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. These are the words of Mr. Bennett.
Hear, hear.

I am not sure the hon. member will applaud after he hears the quotation.
Mr. Bennett said that Canadians have the right to a system of broadcasting from Canadian sources equal in all respects to that of any other country, that this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence.
Hear, hear.

Obviously the members for Jasper-Edson and Bow River have forgotten, if they ever read the thoughts of Mr. Bennett about the needs of Canadians, the kind of organization which the C.B.C. has been in the past. The hon. member for Digby-Annap-olis-Kings has been a great supporter of the C.B.C. I wish those hon. members would read his speeches, particularly when their speeches have been so consistently and persistently in recent years an attempt to cut that organization's throat.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would remind the hon. member that his time has expired. Does he have leave to continue?
I will be able to complete my remarks within two minutes, Mr. Chairman.
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the kind of question I have raised today, which is basic to the needs of Canada if Canada is to survive as an independent nation, can be discussed in the very near future.
We on this side of the house have raised various matters and must accept our share of responsibility for taking up many long days during this session, which we hope is now approaching its end. We do not have sufficient time at our disposal to discuss in detail the activities of the Canada Council and other cultural and educational efforts of the government. As far as radio and television are concerned, we do hope that early in 1965 we can have a serious, detailed and careful consideration of the problems that beset these media in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I may be permitted to add a very short footnote to the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, and I should like to do so for the benefit of my hon. friend, the member for York-Humber.
Not too many weeks ago I tried to listen to that member when he was making a rather impassioned speech on the general subject of how the C.B.C. was attempting to cram culture down the throats of Canadian people. I would now remind that hon. member that one day not too long ago I wanted to listen to a program of entertainment on either radio or television, but I discovered that four of the five radio and television services in Ottawa which are part of the C.B.C. network were carrying the world series baseball game, and when I turned my television to the private station it was covering a football game. I thought at that time warmly of the member for York-Humber and felt that at some suitable time I should suggest to him that if we are having any kind of culture rammed down our throats by the C.B.C. and the other stations, it is the culture which pertains to football, hockey and baseball.

Mr. Chairman, in rising at this time to make some comments about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's expenditures, and I note that the minister responsible is in the house, I would like to state that only this afternoon I and other members of this house became aware of a supplementary estimate which was tabled yesterday in relation to the Department of Transport. This supplementary estimate amounts to $1 and could have a profound effect on the operation of private stations and the C.B.C. Is it the

intention of the government to allow a detailed debate about this supplementary estimate in the Department of Transport estimates, through which an effort is being made to place community antenna television under the supervision of the board of broadcast governors, or is this to be allowed to whistle by when the Department of Transport estimates are being considered? This subject must be debated in detail. This move will have an effect on the operations of the C.B.C. and private broadcasting stations, so is this the time to consider it, or should a lengthy debate take place during our consideration of the estimates of the Department of Transport some time presumably between now and Friday evening? I should like an answer to that question before I continue my comments in relation to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Mr. Chairman, the house leader is present at this time. This item is not within my responsibility, so I do not think a discussion about it could properly take place at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item to which the hon. member alludes is, I believe, item 50c of the Department of Transport, so it would properly be discussed when the committee is considering the estimates of the Department of Transport.

I am happy to receive your comments in this regard, Mr. Chairman, because I know that when that supplementary estimate comes up for discussion, during our consideration of the estimates of the Department of Transport, many members of this committee from all parties will wish to take part. This represents a drastic change which will affect public and private broadcasting services, if and when it is put into effect. I will reserve my comments on that subject until the estimates of the Department of Transport come before us for consideration, I hope before the end of this week. Only one item in those estimates has been passed to date.
At this time I should like to emphasize as strongly as possible that this House of Commons does not have much opportunity of showing any responsibility for the actions of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, because of the manner in which we are told not to question the C.B.C. about this, that and the other thing, as it is independent in its operations and parliament must allow it to go its merry way.
Supply-C.B.C.
The estimates as they relate to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are very interesting to members of parliament. The main estimates appear at page 54 of the blue book where vote No. 1 is shown as:
Grant in respect of the net operating amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service (details, page 55)
Page 55 is the next page, and one finds details of this expenditure of $85,900,000. Exactly 26 words including numerals give the details of this expenditure. Those words and details are:
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-
Vote 1-Grant in respect of the net operating amount required to discharge the responsibilities of the national broadcasting service (20)	$85,-
900,000. (1964-65)
Those are the details of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation expenditures, yet we are told on page 54 that the details are to be found on the opposite page. Those being the complete details given to members of parliament, one can understand easily why the members are provoked by the lack of responsibility shown by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to a body which is asked to fork over $60 million, $70 million, $80 million or $85 million in a given year, and in this case more than $100 million. We are not being asked to vote only $85,900,000 as shown on page 55 of the estimates. If you turn to page 516 you will find there a tricky little entry under the heading, "Loans, investments and advances, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation". The number of the vote is L10 and it reads as follows:
Loans to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the purpose of capital expenditures subject to terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, $14,250,000.
How in the name of heaven the government can make a loan to a crown corporation which has no means of repaying that loan except by a parliamentary grant, and call it a loan, is a euphemism, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings called it a few days ago. Under the heading of "Loans, investments and advances" we are being asked to lend $14,250,000 to the C.B.C., and I ask you where the money is going to come from except out of the current expenditures of the government at some time in the future? Why can this expenditure of $14J million not be included in the main estimates along with the $85,900,000 that is shown on pages 54 and 55?
I must say that having sat here for many months and having listened to the answers,

Supply-C.B.C.
that are given to questions regarding the C.B.C., I wonder whether I am legally right in commenting on the C.B.C. even tonight. I presume my first function should be to congratulate the government for the speed it has shown in bringing down the C.B.C. estimates. Last year we discussed the C.B.C. estimates on December 21, 1963, when the expenditures for nine solid months had already been made and there were only three months to go. I have a quotation here in my notes from the member for Algoma East in which he points out that the great responsibility of parliament is to examine the proposed taxes that a government may impose on the people and that these proposed taxes must be examined before the money is spent and before the taxes are laid on the backs of the people.
Last year the C.B.C. had already spent nine months of its allotment before parliament even had an opportunity to speak on the matter. Yet nothing was done. A number of us participated in the debate but the money went through without too much obstruction. The C.B.C. figures that members have had their say and they have got their money, so what is there for the C.B.C. to complain about? This year we have advanced the date from the 21st of December to the 24th of November. This is real progress. The C.B.C. has only spent eight months supply money before any discussion of their expenditures which are crushing the taxpayers of this country to death unnecessarily.
There are so many facets to the public and private broadcasting world today that it is difficult to know where one can speak most profitably for the taxpayers of the country who have to carry this load of $100 million to supply the C.B.C. We do believe that a little bit of responsibility by the C.B.C. to the House of Commons would be appreciated. They not only do not give us any details with regard to the expenditures they are going to make but they go their own sweet way in their programming. I will not comment on their programming, as I look at television and listen to radio very little. My objection to the C.B.C. is that it should not be in business at all.
Many years ago the federal government built the Rideau canal. I was born on the banks of the Rideau and I was raised on the banks of the Trent in the city of Peterborough. These two canals were built at government expense. The Glassco report recommends that they should be sold, or turned over to the province of Ontario as tourist attractions because they are of no future value to the fed-

eral government. I maintain that in the course of progress things that were satisfactory 30, 40 or 50 years ago are not necessarily so today. If these two canal systems that were so vital to the well-being of Canada in years gone by are now to be dropped by the federal power and offered to the provincial authority as tourist attractions, I say that the day of public ownership of national radio and television networks is past.
The government got into the field of radio in the 1930's, as I mentioned in another speech in the house, in order to protect the six channels that had been allotted to this country by international agreement in the very early days of radio. The government felt that if these six channels were allotted to individuals they would be offending scores and scores of people who would like to have these six channels, so in order to shut off criticism from scores of applicants for the right to broadcast privately the federal government decided to create a radio commission and broadcast on these six bands themselves. At the same time, however, they gave the right to private stations to broadcast in the farthermost parts of the country. Radio was so new in the early thirties that no one was aware of its potentialities or possibilities and it was thought that private stations in the far flung reaches of the country would not offend the stations on the bands in the central part of the country. The net result has been that with private stations allocated to certain areas and public stations to the larger cities we have had a private system growing up alongside the government stations, but as these two systems have been growing side by side the private stations have been paying their own way while the C.B.C. has been dipping into the pockets of the Canadian people more and more.
I have mentioned to the house before and I can only repeat tonight that as the national network of the C.B.C. expands and extends itself the competition which it provides against the printed communication media increases and increases. In the discussion of the proposed CATV service it has been brought out that the government is adopting the attitude that they must protect existing Canadian television stations and must see that they remain profitable. Has the government made any effort to see that the magazines and newspapers of the country remain profitable by forbidding television and radio stations to spring up in their communities?
The history of print media in this country over the past 30 years shows magazines sus-

pending publication month after month and year after year. Many big newspapers are no longer in existence because of the competition for advertising provided by the C.B.C. which is supported by the government all the way. I have complained on behalf of the print media of this country before that the advertising rates charged by the government system do not measure up to the cost of operation. A private publisher of a magazine or newspaper must secure an advertising rate high enough to cover his cost of production. On the other hand, the C.B.C. can go out and quote whatever rate it wishes and whatever rate the advertiser will pay. Then the advertiser, who is getting a cheap subsidized rate from the C.B.C., can turn around and tell the printed media publisher, "I am getting a cheaper rate from the C.B.C. than you are offering when I consider the number of families I reach per $1,000 spent".
This government subsidized competition is really strangling the print media business in the Dominion of Canada. But what does the federal cabinet care? Their only concern is that the now established radio and television stations shall not have any competition from other stations, as shown by the ruling with regard to the London application yesterday, and the wording on the CATV proposal shows they do not want any CATV competition for the television stations and radio stations now in existence.
In this country which is described by many speakers as one of free enterprise, why does the government show so much concern for the existing stations as to put newspapers and magazines out of business? Why does the government show so little concern for the print media that are forced to go down the drain because their advertising revenues are being sucked off into government subsidized television and radio stations?
Speakers today and during interim supply debates have been trying to get a committee or commission to investigate the C.B.C. There is no doubt that such a commission is long overdue. There are many Canadians who would like to get answers from the C.B.C. The members of the House of Commons are really provoked when the Secretary of State stands up and in reply to questions states, I will pass it on to the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that is the end of that. A week later when members ask another question we are told it will be passed on to the C.B.C. and if they have a reply, it will be brought back. Of course, when they do not have a reply, it is not
Supply-C.B.C.
brought back and that is the end of that. If we had a parliamentary committee and we could get replies from the C.B.C., I am certain many interesting facts and figures could be adduced for the guidance of members of parliament. We are asked simply to vote $85 million or $100 million toward the operation of the C.B.C. without any explanation.
Now, there are a number of questions that we might ask. I have just received from C.B.C. headquarters information to the effect that the cost of the new head office building in Ottawa was $3,100,000 and that the new furnishings cost $35,000. This is a total of $3,135,000 for the building and furnishings out on Riverside drive in what I believe is called Confederation heights. Anyone would think that a $3,135,000 building would have some class. However, I am advised that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation held a program committee meeting, in which they called in the vice presidents and all their auxiliary help, at the Seigniory club down on the Ottawa river. Is not a $3 million building on Riverside drive suitable accommodation for the C.B.C. program council meeting?
Not enough class to it.

The C.B.C. is seeking to reach the mass market, not the class market, I understand. Why do they, in their efforts to reach the mass market go to the Seigniory club? It would be very interesting to know why that meeting of the program council could not be held here in the city of Ottawa in a building that was opened during the past few months and which cost the taxpayers of the country $3,135,000. Frankly, I believe the reason they went to the Seigniory club was that they want to live in the style to which they have become accustomed since they got on the C.B.C. payroll. This is simply one question that we might like to have answered if the government would appoint a committee to investigate the operations of this bloodsucking behemoth that is drawing off more and more money every day.
Then, I should like to know the truth as it relates to a statement that has been bruited around the country that the C.B.C. spent $87,000 to send a camera crew to China. You remember that Mr. Faibish, after he had done the necessary work for the minister of agriculture in the previous administration, left the Department of Agriculture, went to the C.B.C. and wound up in China on a seven weeks tour. They spent $87,000 on the China expedition. Some programs have been placed on C.B.C. showing that China expedition. I have been told that the French network of the C.B.C.

Supply-C.B.C.
refuses to run the picture. I should like to get an answer to that statement. I am told the French network feels it is a little on the communistic side, and also that they would like to send a French camera crew over to China to take pictures of the Chinese because the English camera crew does not take good pictures of the Chinese. This is the story in C.B.C. circles, and I should like to get a direct answer to it. I hope we will not be told that the matter will be taken up with the president of the C.B.C., period, period, period.
I mentioned once before in speaking about the profligate hand with which the C.B.C. throws money around, that the newspapers of Canada did not send any representative of their own to the Holy Land when the Pope visited Palestine some months ago. The board of directors of Canadian Press, which is a co-operative organization of all the newspapers in the land, decided that the visit of the Pope to the Holy Land could be adequately covered by having Reuters news agency in Europe report to them, plus the Associated Press of the United States. Then, the larger Canadian newspapers could buy the official foreign services of such organizations as the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times or the Chicago Tribune, all of which operate news services under their own name. However, this did not apply to the C.B.C. As I reported before, the C.B.C. sent seven or nine people over to Palestine to record the visit of the Pope to that country.
The most interesting backlash of that visit is that we are now advised a French camera crew and an English camera crew arrived in Palestine unknown to each other to cover the visit.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Would he be willing to tell us if the French network was prepared to televise the program which he is now describing?

I trust that my next few words will cover that subject.
I wanted to report to you that C.B.C. personnel have advised me that when the English camera crew and the French camera crew found that they were in Palestine together, they agreed that the French would shoot silent French footage and the English camera crew would shoot silent English footage. If you can tell me what silent English footage is compared with silent French foot-

age in Palestine, I would appreciate getting the information. I do not want to be told, we will ask the president of the C.B.C. and if he deigns to answer the inquiry such as you are making we will pass it on to you. This is a report that comes to me from several people who are well placed and well able to give me the information that I am passing on to you.
Now, I have remarked on the irresponsibility of the C.B.C. in not giving us an explanation of the vast expenditures they are making year after year. I think it is absolutely ridiculous-I cannot think of a stronger word -the way the C.B.C. flouts the good name of the parliament of Canada. In 1962, the immigration department of this Canadian government issued a stop order against George Lincoln Rockwell being allowed to enter Canada. There were good and sufficient reasons for that order being issued. The present government reinforced the order of 1962 which had been made by the previous government. This means that two consecutive Canadian governments had issued an order prohibiting the entry of George Lincoln Rockwell into this country. Why, then, in the name of heaven has the C.B.C. the right to spend taxpayers' money sending a camera crew down to Washington to interview Mr. George Lincoln Rockwell in Washington, put it on tape and bring it back to this country? If the immigration department has forbidden the man to enter the country, I do not believe that taxpayers' money should be spent in sending a camera crew down to see him because he is not allowed to enter this country.
Then, the immigration department of this country took a chap by the name of Sands off a plane from Chicago, I believe, at the Toronto airport. They said he was non persona grata in this country and he was sent back to Cleveland, Ohio, on the next plane leaving for the United States. There is a cease and desist order against this chap, or there was at the time, forbidding his entry into Canada. We pick up the C.B.C. on Sunday night and find they have brought this gentleman-I will use the term loosely in this case -to the United States-Canadian border on the Rainbow bridge at Niagara Falls. Despite the fact the immigration department of this government has said the man is non persona grata, they give him the national network at taxpayers' expense. They even photograph the international boundary to show that the C.B.C. would not allow Mr. Sands into this country. The immigration department will not allow him into the country, so we will just keep

him across the painted line and give him a national network show in Canada at the taxpayers' expense. If that shows any sense of responsibility, then I do not understand the meaning of the word.
I ask this question bluntly: The C.B.C., at the taxpayers' expense, has made a monkey out of the department of immigration. Are they planning to bring Harold Chamberlain Banks up to the Rainbow bridge and photograph him across the border in order to make an ass out of the Department of Justice? There should be some sense of reason and decency shown in the operations of the C.B.C., but we have got few examples of that recently.
During the last few days hon. members have been reading quite a bit about a charge from Winnipeg, Manitoba, regarding young boys who have signed some papers, and their fathers complain that when they want the boys to jump from one junior team to another they are informed that they signed papers when a mere lad, and they are stuck with those papers from now until the end of time
You may wonder what this has to do with C.B.C. estimates. I would like to point out that there is a revolution coming in free broadcasting of sporting events on radio and television because the professional athletes of this continent and of Great Britain are fed up to the teeth. They entertain people sitting in their homes thousands of miles away, and they do not get a single, solitary cent for the entertainment they provide these people.
There is now a move afoot to unionize these athletes. Everyone knows that the owners of professional football teams, the owners of professional hockey teams and the owners of professional soccer teams-I am thinking of Great Britain now-are fighting the unionization of players hand and foot, tooth and nail, but it will not be stopped because the players feel that when they entertain tens of thousands, and even hundreds of thousands of fans, sitting in their own homes, they should be recompensed for the services they are rendering the public through the means of entertainment.
There is an editorial in the Globe this morning entitled "Bondage". It is quite a nice editorial and it compliments the government on its intimation that there is going to be an investigation into these charges out of Winnipeg. But I can tell you there is no combine in the pro-sports world, none whatever. Nothing is signed, never has been and never will be; but when six owners get together one will say, "Jack, when I pick up a 15 year old boy in Winnipeg who looks pretty promising
Supply


I will let the central office in Montreal know about it and you leave the family alone." Another one of the owners, walking around quite casually, says "We would not like to interfere with your property." That is the word they use, "property", so "bondage", as the heading of the editorial, is very good. Then another club owner says, "I have found a very good hockey player in Wetaskiwin. I will notify the central office in Montreal that this boy is going to be our property," and when the other five gentlemen owners of the hockey teams hear this they do not go near that chap.
No, there is no combine, not at all; there is nothing to break the combines law; it is just a gentlemen's agreement.
I have been in the newspaper game in Canada all my life. There is no combine in Canada with respect to the employment of people by newspapers, but I know newspaper chains that will not hire a man from another chain or from another paper. Of course there is an understanding but there is no combine. There is just an understanding that "if you leave my writers alone I will leave your writers alone. Anyway, why should you bid that man $10 a week more to drag him across to your paper when all I will do is raise my bid to $15 and then you will go up to $20? This is ridiculous. Why should the newspapers cut up one another?" Why should they offer the experienced help more money? The only person going to gain on it is the employee.
There are some employers who do not approve of that, but in the hockey business these men have no combine, no trust. They just do not bid against one another, so that thereby the players' remuneration would be greatly increased. The television and radio world is going to be revolutionized and more and more players in the baseball world, the football world and the hockey world will demand that they be shown only on either theatre, television or closed circuit television where the public will have to pay to see them perform.
Perhaps hon. members think that day will never come. I remember the junior member for Halifax making some comments a little while ago in which he said sports spectaculars could never be taken from the people, that they belonged to the people. That is a very nice phrase to coin, but what about the players?
In the city of Toronto today you can not only see pro hockey players playing on the ice at Maple Leaf Gardens but you can go to theatres in the city and pay admission, and

Supply-C.B.C.
there you can see the players playing on big screens. The away from home games are shown this way in St. Catharines, Hamilton and Toronto, and so long as the crowds remain at capacity in the Gardens, and so long as the theatres are selling out for theatre television the free broadcasting-any more than 75 miles and further away-will continue because it is through the free advertising that the C.B.C. gives hockey that it has reached its great popularity in this country today.
A royal commission, or preferably a parliamentary commission investigating the C.B.C. would turn out the facts to show how much it costs to broadcast a national league hockey game across Canada from coast to coast. You people may think it is those sponsors whose names are shown on the screen or which are heard over the air who are paying the full shot of the program. You could not be further from the truth. If they were paying the full costs of these sports spectaculars from coast to coast they would only be able to sponsor about two games a year.
The C.B.C. underwrites a tremendous portion of the sports spectaculars broadcast from coast to coast. It would be interesting to know whether sponsors of the Grey cup games and the N.H.L. hockey games are paying what are known as spot advertising rates or full program rates for the advertising they put on the air. Many of us who are experienced in the field are certain they are paying close to spot advertising rates rather than full program rates for the sports spectaculars with which their names are identified.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee agree that the hon. member should continue?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: For how long?
Oh, let him go.
I can sit down now.
Go ahead.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee for its consideration. I was just remarking that it would be wonderful to know the amount in millions of dollars of free advertising that the C.B.C. has given to such businesses as professional hockey and professional baseball. Why does it not give that same kind of free advertising to

other businesses in the country-the sale of furniture, the sale of automobiles, the sale of houses, the sale of pleasure boats? Why confine its free will advertising to sports businessmen and not support the whole commercial field throughout the Dominion of Canada?
I regret that I do not have more time to speak about the C.B.C. Frankly I think it ridiculous that on the 24th day of November we are discussing the expenditures of an organization that is going to take $100 million from the taxpayers of the country. There will be possibly two hours consideration of the matter and, come Friday, everything goes through in one mass vote without any further consideration; and a year from now somebody will say, "Oh, the C.B.C. was thoroughly considered, you remember, on November 24 last. Three or four fellows got up and talked about it, and that was that."
There has got to be a committee appointed to investigate the operations of the C.B.C. Its cost to the country today is greater than the cost of the C.N.R. The C.B.C. has asked for $100 million and C.N. is asking for $67 million. Some elections have been fought, won and lost in this country on the expenditures of the C.N.R. when they were little more than one half the cost of the C.B.C. today, yet when the C.B.C. estimates come up people get up and say, "This is terrific. This is culture. It is the best."
But the submission of the association of Canadian radio and television actors to the Fowler commission shows that 64 per cent of the programs on C.B.C. radio and 64 per cent of the programs on C.B.C. television are entertainment. Yet we hear all this stuff about culture, culture, culture. As I asked the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, what culture is involved in describing a great president of the United States as the biggest communist the country has ever seen, with the exception of his wife? Yet that is what was sent out from coast to coast not too long ago, and that is what the Canadian taxpayer had to pay for.
I regret exceedingly that discussion of the C.B.C. estimates is being so completely and thoroughly choked off. Since I have used up the time allotted to me, and even a few extra minutes, I will thank the committee for the consideration they have shown and keep to myself my reflections on the degree of thoroughness with which parliament is allowed to scrutinize public expenditures.
May I call it six o'clock?
I wonder whether the hon. member would agree that we should try to conclude these particular estimates so that we might get on to others.
Surely the hon. gentleman does not expect the committee to complete before eight o'clock a study of the estimates he listed last night?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, just these. Then at eight o'clock we could go on with a new department. I understand the hon. member wishes to speak.
Yes, but I do not wish to penalize everyone who is here now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Go on.

Well, I want to make a further point I had in mind in connection with the national film board. It is my information that the division between employees of the board recently reached a stage where opposing briefs were presented to the head of the organization. I should like the minister to check this and confirm my information. I should like to know whether these contending opinions were referred to the board itself and what opinions the board may have expressed on them, or what opinion the head of the board may have taken with regard to them.
The other point I want to touch on-and I take some pleasure in doing so, because I see some representatives of the C.B.C. sitting in the gallery-is an incident of which I think we should all be thoroughly ashamed in the House of Commons. It relates to the treatment given by the C.B.C. to the man who produced the Pearson film. I think it is one of the most disgraceful episodes in parliamentary history and I think we all share in it, including the Prime Minister- perhaps, particularly, the Prime Minister.
This is not a question of whether or not the film should be shown. Assume the C.B.C. has the right to make the decision it did. But when the C.B.C. made that decision its officials uttered what were in effect slanders upon the ability and technical prowess of the person who produced the film. The reason they gave for not showing it was its technical or intellectual inadequacy, or words to that effect. That is fine. But they publicized these reasons to the extent that the reputation of the man who produced the film, Mr. Ballentine has been placed in a very bad light. It is only natural that in the circum-
Supply-C.B.C.
stances Mr. Ballentine should seek to obtain some form of redress, some opportunity to prove particularly by using the film, that he is not as incompetent as the C.B.C. labelled him. There is the story of his efforts to buy the film, for example. He offered $35,000 for it. But the C.B.C., loaded with the $17 million that the hon. member for York-Humber was talking about, is not interested in $35,000. If indeed the C.B.C. really believed this film to be inadequate and lacking in intellectual grasp, one would suppose they would be prepared to accept the $35,000 offered not only by Mr. Ballentine but by other people. At the moment though this is not the point. They made statements about this man's reputation and capacity, and let them stand; and they have been niggling and petty and small about giving him the opportunity to get and use the prints in order to put forward his case.
I have all the correspondence which passed between Intervideo and the C.B.C., largely with Captain Brooks, and there could not be a stuffier kind of correspondence than the pomp of those answers; there could not be anything better put, to my mind, than the simple request that the C.B.C., in view of the fact that they had damned this man in his professional capacity, should at least give him the film so as to demonstrate that he had some answers on this particular question. He received a request from a famous museum and film gallery in the United States, the Huntingdon museum, to show his film. He asked the C.B.C. to release him from the very narrow contract terms which had been arranged at the time when there was no understanding that the film would not be shown on television, so that people might have an opportunity to see it at this place where, in a sense, the reputations of film producers are in many ways determined. What was the answer he received? The C.B.C. would not accede to this request but was willing to let him have other pieces of film he had produced for them to show on this occasion. I cannot thing of a sillier or more backward answer-an answer which seemed to prove some kind of fear on the part of the C.B.C. beyond my understanding.
I am convinced that the Prime Minister of this country wanted the damned film shown. Perhaps there is some great integrity in the C.B.C. demonstrated by not acceding to that point of view or to what was obviously the wish of parliament. As far as I am concerned, and as far as Mr. Ballentine is concerned, the

Supply-C.B.C.
issue whether it should be shown on television or not is dead. The fact remains that here is an individual whose reputation has been smashed as a result of the refusal of the C.B.C. to use this film. Yet they niggle, they whine, they cheat, they waffle all the way through in the face of his attempts to get free use of the print so that he can take it to the people across this country in order to show he is not the incompetent, the emotionally immature person the corporation has labelled him.
We in this house have permitted the C.B.C. to behave in this way and I think it is a disgrace. Members can say all they please about political influence. Maybe the Pearson film was an issue; maybe it was not. Certainly it made headlines. The fact remains we have this big, stiff, swell-headed organization with a bunch of arrogant people at the top- damned arrogant-who have knocked the little man on the chin and who are refusing to give him a fair shake. I just want to let those people in the gallery, those big shots in the C.B.C., know, having looked at the correspondence and followed this case throughout, how I feel about it. Maybe they have an argument in support of their decision not to show the film for various reasons. Maybe there was no political interference. I do not really care any more. But they should have nothing but shame for their conduct with regard to this particular film-their action in refusing to sell it and let this producer have his "go". I think we should all be ashamed of what the C.B.C. has done in this connection.
I should like to close my observations on this subject by saying that I think the Prime Minister shares the blame even more than the rest of us do. After all, it was he and fundamentally his reputation on which this whole thing balanced. I am pleased to find that the sort of resentment and malice I happen to feel in this regard is not shared so much by Mr. Ballentine, who perhaps is larger in spirit than I. But if I were he I would feel terribly let down by any prime minister who would not take some step, even if it is just the persuasive one of getting the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to sit down and talk sense about the matter over the table. It is pretty disgraceful to have that sort of situation in your head office in this country.
I am sorry to have been so extreme in expressing this point of view but it seems to me that anyone reading this correspondence and following this "Mr. Pearson" film incident through cannot help but be ashamed

that we have such stiff backed, swollen headed, arrogant types at the head of a corporation who would treat any small individual in this way. It is as though they are taking out on him all the meanness which has been generated in them because of the boobs pulled by their organization over this "Mr. Pearson" film. To me it is regrettably pathetic that a giant organization with a budget of over $100 million a year should continue to have such a narrow and malicious point of view toward an individual who is doing what is really, in effect, in money or in other terms, a relatively small job for them.
The last point I want to touch on in connection with the C.B.C. is to remind the minister of a meeting I had with him last year with some representatives from my area regarding the extension of television service to the Geraldton-Longlac area. This matter seems to me typical of the kind of frustrations expressed by the hon. member for Churchill and those of us who have spent seven years trying to see an advancement in the policy of extension of service both through the C.B.C. and at the encouragement of the B.B.G. When this delegation came to see the minister, frustrated and fuming after spending an hour with Mr. Ouimet and Mr. Fraser, he assured them that the government would look at the problem of extending services to see whether this would not be possible, since Mr. Ouimet had told us that for a sum of $20 million to $25 million television service in Canada could be extended in a blanket coverage. I have never had an answer from the minister to those representations, and if he checks the file he will see I followed up with a letter which specifically asked him about this matter. But still no indication of the position of the government in this regard. This is basically the same question asked by the hon. member for Churchill.
More than that, Mr. Chairman, when we met representatives from the C.B.C. last winter they told us that within a month or six weeks they would have received some bids or quotations on a potential satellite transmitter in the Geraldton-Longlac area. That is many months ago. We are now almost to Christmas and it is still impossible to get any kind of firm answer from the C.B.C. The last letter I had from them was about two weeks ago and the whole matter is still up in the air. This is typical of my experience through the seven years in which I have had

dealings with the C.B.C. in terms of extension of service.
There is a beautiful castle erected in honour of Mr. Ouimet on the outskirts of Confederation heights, about which our friend from York-Humber was talking, and I have often wondered what is done there. This seems to me a good question to ask. Certainly minor attention has been paid either to budgeting or planning for an extension of service in the way the members of parliament have been asking for seven or eight years. They never seem to be able to live up to their deadlines in terms of the introduction of projects. At one place, Terrace Bay, they promised a better, low power relay station one year ago, and I doubt whether the damned thing has been put in yet. At least, I had a letter the other day indicating that it had not. There is always this kind of delay and procrastination in projects, putting them over to some future date.
This matter may seem particularly in contradiction with the fulsome phrases extended to the C.B.C. by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North. My comments are directed toward the function of the C.B.C. as a program producer and apply to the substantial administrative weakness of the C.B.C. and lack of flexibility in responding to questions which we have asked as parliamentary representatives, having nothing to do with programming. So this is not interference with their programs. I should like to ask the minister about the public accounts hearings. Did the minister read what Mr. Ouimet told us at the public accounts committee a couple of months ago, in the summertime? Mr. Ouimet, obviously reluctantly, undertook to provide certain information for the public accounts committee, and urged both by the Auditor General and the members of the committee he undertook that this information would be provided. I still have not heard about it. I do not know where the information is. I had assumed some of it would be in the next annual report of the C.B.C., which is one of the most uninformative documents one can find. I notice our financial critics are always analysing the annual reports of companies, whether they are good or bad, and I wish they would look at the C.B.C. reports, because if they did so they would find out how well things can be cloaked. Any report which can figure out to a quarter of a cent a day how much each one of us contributes as a taxpayer to the C.B.C. as so-called shareholders, and yet cannot give us a more in-
Supply-C.B.C.
formative picture is, it seems to me, a bit of a cover up job.
My point is that in my experience the C.B.C. has been very lax in providing members of parliament, or parliament, or parliamentary committees with information and material. The president of the C.B.C. may remember that a few years ago he was before the broadcasting committee, and at that time I was one of those who was most anxious to have all this information. I am sure he will remember how he fought the battle from point to point and from day to day before giving any information about the cost of programs. Finally he did. I hope we will not be faced with the same kind of point to point resistance to the provision of information in connection with the figures before the public accounts committee for which we are asking. Let me tell the minister, and through him the C.B.C., that several of us on that committee do not intend to let the C.B.C. fall back into any of its old attitudes in failing to provide this information. We would ask him to inform us now whether he has any information as to when the C.B.C. will provide this information, how it will provide it and what sort of distribution it is going to get.
That concludes the remarks I wish to make, Mr. Chairman, and I thank the committee for its patience. Before I finish completely I want to mention one point in connection with the argument made by the hon. member for York-Humber about hockey players. I think generally I agree with him, but he is not completely accurate when he says that there is just a gentlemen's agreement existing. There are forms which are signed. Perhaps they would not stand up in court but the fact remains that forms are signed which tie a youngster through the amateur ranks and so on. I remember the son of a friend of mine who had a host of hockey scouts hovering about, and as the boy approached his sixteenth birthday a few years ago they all wanted his signature so that they could wire Clarence Campbell and get him registered in order that he would become their chattel.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

I would ask the hon. member for Port Arthur, does he consider a signed document which is an agreement between a player and a hockey team the same as a combine signed by six owners? I made

Supply-C.B.C.
reference to a combine signed by six owners; I said nothing about players' contracts.

1 can see the hon. member's distinction but I was only making the point that they give the impression that the whole thing is a gentlemen's agreement. I think if anyone wants to check on the business of professional sports organizations, he should look at the reserve clause, and if he really wants to look into the situation he should read the reports of the United States House of Representatives committee chaired by Mr. Cellar of a few years ago, before which Clarence Campbell and all the baseball and football magnates appeared and gave evidence.
I just wanted to put that on the record in case someone reading Hansard at a later time might wish to pursue the subject.

Mr. Chairman, just before you call vote 1 I should like to deal with some of the points raised during the course of this discussion.
In the first place, the hon. member for Port Arthur has spoken at length about the film board and the chairman. As far as I am concerned I do not intend at this stage to defend the film board, which has gone on winning international awards, or Mr. Roberge, who has proven over the years to be a very highly competent administrator and a devoted public servant.
I do not think either that the hon. member has read or carefully studied my speech, in which I said improvements were desirable and that the chairman and members of the board were conscious of this situation. I went on to say, and I think this covers a lot of the points the hon. member has raised, as recorded at page 10084 of Hansard of November 13, 1964:
They have begun a reappraisal of the institution itself and they are reviewing its programs and operations in several fields of activity in the light of current demand of course, but also of its national purpose and the relative importance of the functions assigned to it by parliament.
As an agency at the service of Canada and its people in the fields of information and culture, the board has already decided to strengthen its program for community audiences, and to undertake a survey and analysis of its distribution operations in Canada, with a view to identify and evaluate more precsely its audiences, in relation to their needs and to the purposes the board pursues.
While the present situation may need some improvement, as the hon. member has said, the board is already conscious of the changes that have taken place recently and over the years. It is already aware of new needs, and

is trying as fast as it can to meet those new needs.
It is the old needs that I was worried about.

The hon. member may have brought his criticisms too late to the board. In any case, I am quite sure the board will be happy at some later stage during the next session, if it is found desirable at that time, to appear before this standing committee on cultural affairs, if we decide to set up such a committee.
Three hon. members have raised the problem regarding the extension of the services of the C.B.C. Of course, as far as alternative service is concerned, there is a freeze at the present time, and this freeze will be maintained until we get the report of the advisory committee.
Where there are no services at the present time, the extension of services is of course a very important matter to those who are not covered. There is, however, a question of priority in the extension of services where they do not exist at the present time, and also a priority in other fields of services.
Like French in Toronto.

These decisions were taken a few years ago, as the hon. member is aware. So the whole question of financing, both short and long term, of the C.B.C., is before the Fowler committee at the present time. I am hopeful that we will get its report early in 1965, at which time, when priorities have been determined both by the committee and by the government, I will be happy indeed to give immediate attention in terms of government decision and policy to this important question.
As the hon. member for Churchill has suggested, I am sure the Fowler committee will, as we will, give special consideration to the possibility and desirability of establishing a special grant for this purpose.
I will certainly present the proposals that were made this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay West to the national museum and to the film board, in so far as the Columbia river project is concerned. It would be very worth while to try, as much as we can, to save objects of value which are there, and also to record, on film, this great river in its present state.

I should now like to say a word about the suggestion made this afternoon by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm

(Mr. Pigeon) who intimated that the government should, at this time, institute a royal commission on the C.B.C. and broadcasting.
The hon. member must have forgotten that last May 25 I announced on behalf of the government that a three member committee would be asked to look into all aspects of broadcasting. The investigation is now under way. The terms of reference of the committee are very wide and will not be limited in any way. The committee also has unrestricted authority. It is empowered to call as witnesses any organization or individual who is interested in this problem, it can examine briefs and investigate the C.B.C., private stations and the B.B.G. I fail to see what the establishment of a royal commission would add; in my opinion, it would just be duplication.
Will the committee publish a report?
Mr. Chairman, I have already announced that the Fowler committee report would be made public as soon as it has been received by the government.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister one further question arising out of his remarks about the Fowler commission report. It is my understanding that one of the advantages of having the deputy minister of the Department of the Secretary of State, and having that minister's former executive assistant secretary as members of that small group, not holding open hearings, was so that this report could be obtained quickly and would form the basis of government policy. Is that right?
Yes.

I am not interested in whether the report of this commission is published quickly, or immediately made available. The important thing is when the decision is made by this government, and when it will be in a position to lay down new policy guide lines or even legislative changes as a result of the report.
The spectre of waiting for a report in English and French, this sort of coming forth like a royal commission document and then being commented upon across the country is not, it seems to me, what we understood we were going to get from this particular committee.

Mr. Chairman, the last time I discussed this with the chairman of the committee he told me he was hoping to have
Supply-C.B.C.
the report completed by the end of March. If this turns out to be so I am sure it will give ample time to the government to make up its own mind and to present legislation at a fairly early stage of the 1965 session.

In relation to the question just raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur and having regard to his earlier remarks concerning the establishment of priorities in the extension of service to areas not now served, I should like to ask the minister whether this means that no government action on this question can be contemplated until March? I might say to the minister that it is only through exercising considerable self-discipline that I for one, and I imagine quite a number of other members who are in a similar situation, have refrained from commenting or raising questions at length on this subject. Many of us have experienced the frustrations referred to by the member for Port Arthur.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose that this is unavoidable. I think the government has not lost any time in this field. When we came into office we felt very strongly that we needed a new look at the whole field of broadcasting. We certainly needed a new look at the whole problem of short term and long term financing of the C.B.C., especially in view of the new need for consolidation projects in Montreal, Toronto and elsewhere. As was made quite clear this afternoon, there are limits to the activities of the C.B.C. and there are limits to the amount of money that parliament can provide to the corporation for the whole of its operations. It seems to me that the Fowler committee should have the chance to look at all the new needs that the C.B.C. will face very shortly in order to decide some order of priorities among those different needs. It seems to me it would be relatively unwise as far as we are concerned to proceed at the present time without a general plan.

Mr. Chairman, the minister just said that there are limits to the money that the government can supply to the C.B.C. I should like to ask him whether at $100 million for the current year we are anywhere near the limit?
This is not for me to say, Mr. Chairman. This answer will be provided by parliament.

After listening to that answer all I should like to say to the hon. member for York-Humber is that I hope he knows

Supply-C.B.C.
more about what parliament means than I do. I should like to ask the minister this question. As I understand the timing of things, the budget of the C.B.C. for next year has been approved and has gone through treasury board very recently. I understand it is done every fall. Can the minister now give any indication whether there is any flexibility in that budget in order to allow for more extension of services next year rather than putting a lot of money into the Montreal and Toronto white elephants that the corporation wants to erect?

Mr. Chairman, I will certainly look into this matter very carefully. As the hon. member knows, there are some delays in proceeding now with these consolidation projects and perhaps this will leave some money available for this other very desirable purpose. The budget of the C.B.C. has not yet been considered and approved by treasury board.
