We have reached a stage in the discussion of the estimates when some of us would like to ask questions of the minister rather than indulge in lengthy remarks. Having been in the chamber at 7.30-
Here is the minister.

-I felt we were getting into the position of having to deal with members of the government in relays. For that reason it may be a little difficult for us to bowl them down when they come in refreshed after a more extended recess than most of us had.
I have been trying to assemble the various pieces of material which I got ready on a number of previous occasions in the hope of making a few remarks and addressing some questions to the minister on the estimates of the Indian affairs branch. I listened with a great deal of attention to the minister's speech upon the administration of the branch. I do not recall everything he said, perhaps even he may not, but on listening to his remarks I got the impression that what he was suggesting as a program to meet the needs of Canadian Indians had a familiar ring. This led me to do some research on earlier discussions which took place in the house on this subject, particularly with respect to recommendations from parliamentary committees.
In this connection I would like to draw the minister's attention to one of the recommendations in the report of the 1948 joint committee on Indian affairs, a recommendation which was not included among his recent proposals. It is to be found at page 189 of the minutes and proceedings of that committee, and is a recommendation to the house:
Your committee recommends that the rules of the House of Commons be amended to provide for the appointment of a select standing committee on Indian affairs.	,
I am firmly of the opinion that it would have been the better part of wisdom had this recommendation been acted upon long ago, so that now we would have the machinery through which to give regular consideration to the problems faced by our Indian people. I hope the minister will consider these recommendations made by our predecessors in this house in 1948.
I find there were some other recommendations made by that 1948 committee which closely resemble the subject matter of the speech made by the minister when he introduced his estimates. For example, again on page 189, the committee had this to say:
Your committee therefore recommends that the government consider the desirability of placing on the agenda of the next dominion-provincial con-

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration ference, for consideration by the provinces, the following matters: education; health and social services, fur conservation and development and Indian traplines; provincial fish and game laws; provincial liquor legislation; validity of marriages solemnized by Indians.
The year 1948 was not the last year in which a committee of the house and the Senate met. In the report of the 1961 committee we And the following recommendation on the subject of health and welfare. It is recommendation No. 6.
(a)	The question of transferring health services for Indians to the provinces should be discussed at a dominion-provincial conference, but the present health program should be continued and extended until such time as this can be accomplished.
(b)	Provincial welfare legislation and services should be used for the benefit of the Indian population.
And so on. So in 1948 and 1961 we find committees putting forward proposals very much along the lines of those made by the minister in his speech introducing the estimates of the Indian affairs branch. I point this out to remind the hon. gentleman that a few months ago I did suggest in a speech made in this chamber that what we really require is a crash program. I am certainly not placing upon the shoulders of the present minister responsibility for the fact that the recommendations of the 1948 and the 1960-61 committee have not been implemented-they are still in the discussion stage at dominion-provincial conferences, and in secret, as my hon. friend from Skeena pointed out. Nevertheless I believe the hon. gentleman has very little time in which to do the things he is talking about.
Some of the modest increases proposed in certain items of the estimates of the branch are in the right direction. The proposal for a community development program, while extremely modest and, in my opinion, inadequate in its scale, is nevertheless a move of the right kind. I hope the minister can offer some explanation of the relationship between one aspect of these estimates and one of the statements he made in the course of his speech. The minister said, and I quote his words, that we shall need to considerably strengthen the branch staff in this field. I have tried to understand the estimates as laid out in detail, and as far as I can see the total increase in the establishment of the department for which provision is made is in the order of two or three persons out of a total of more than 600. Can the minister explain to us the relation between the proposal in these estimates to provide for wages and salaries

showing little increase as against past years with his opening remarks to the effect that there is a need to considerably strengthen branch staff? Does the minister believe that the provision of two or three people represents a considerable increase ,in the staff of the branch? Depending on the kind of answer the minister has to give me to this question, I may or may not have further questions to put to him later in this regard.

I think this is a good opportunity to comment on the many remarks made last Friday by some hon. members about the administration of Indian affairs.
Of course, I will not have enough time to discuss in full detail the particular problems raised by those who took part in the debate so far, but I feel that I should give explanations on a number of general problems which have been raised, especially by the hon. members for Skeena (Mr. Howard), Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett).
First of all, I would like to deal with what was called the transfer of jurisdiction as proposed by the government, that is, the transfer of the jurisdiction to the provincial authorities.
I only wish to state once more what I often said in this house-and this for the information of the committee-that at no time did the present government consider transferring this administration or jurisdiction to the various provinces. Even if this government considered such a transfer of jurisdiction, it would be totally illegal because under the constitution at it exists, no power reserved to the central government or to a provincial government may be transferred to another level of administration, since such a measure on the part of the central government or of the government of a province would be declared ultra vires, that is, overstepping the powers to them granted by the constitution. Therefore, the central government cannot transfer its jurisdiction respecting Indian affairs to a provincial government.
Second, the federal government would act against the constitution which gave the central government the power to legislate respecting Indian affairs, and I believe that in certain cases it would be contrary to the powers which were assumed by the crown when it signed treaties with the Indians, to transfer certain powers respecting Indian affairs, to the provinces which, in the opinion of some persons, could fulfil, better than

the central government, those responsibilities toward the Indians.
But there are other reasons beside the traditional respect of the central government for the constitution,, in regard to its obligations towards the Indians. The federal government is aware that it has a duty, a responsibility to all the Indians in this country, that is to help them to reach the goal everybody is looking forward to, namely the complete independence and control of their own affairs.
I feel that all Canadians wish that before the centennial of confederation, all the Indians in this country will be able to enjoy, as soon as possible, all the privileges and advantages the other Canadians now enjoy. Then those Indians will be able to say proudly: We belong to this Canadian nation, to this Canadian confederation the centennial of which we are going to celebrate in 1967.
It is because we are conscious of that task that we do not want, for any reason whatever, to give up the powers granted to us by the constitution and which, as I said earlier, are sanctioned by several treaties with regard to the Indians in our country.
But that having been said, and in view of the fact that we are conscious that the Indians themselves, in various numbers, are anxious to benefit like the other Canadian citizens from some services now provided by the provinces, it was thought that the time had come to submit both to the provinces and the Indians the project dealing with the extension of some provincial services to the Indians who wanted them. That gave rise to the idea of holding a federal-provincial conference on Indian affairs.
As you know, that same matter had been discussed by a committee which sat last fall, at the time of the federal-provincial conference on fiscal matters, and after a debate within that committee, the wish had been expressed to hold a full federal-provincial conference to deal only with problems related to Indian affairs.
As we know, this conference had originally been planned for last May but, for various reasons, it was postponed until fall. We were very happy to welcome to Ottawa the delegates from the various provinces to discuss with them, not the problem of the transfer of jurisdiction, but the attitude of the various provincial governments toward the Indians' problems.
I know some delegates suggested that we invite the Indians themselves to this conference, inasmuch as problems concerning them
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration directly were to be discussed. We all know that the conference was held without any Indians being present, and as I have already said to the house, the government did not wish to invite the Indians to this conference, for the following reasons:
That conference, of course, was not held to make any decisions with regard to any program which might affect Indians, and this is so true that the problem of consultation was put as first item on the agenda of the conference. We were, indeed, very much aware that any change, even with regard to the so-called extension of provincial services, would have to be submitted to the Indians in the first place, and that it would not be advisable for the federal government to conclude an agreement with any province, or to introduce a system which would apply within the country, without the Indians having been consulted and having stated their position, even as to the details of each program.
That is why the consultation principle was put as first item on the agenda.
What was the result of this conference, from the point of view of consultation? We decided, we of the federal government-and the provinces agreed-that from now on systematic consultations should be held in Canada with the Indians; that it did not suffice to greet a group of Indians to be able to say: The country's Indians accept this or that program, this or that legislation. There was going to be, for the first time in Canada, what has been called a consultative organization. I know Indians have appeared, singly, in groups or in bands, before the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs.
I know also that through our officials the Indians could express their wishes and claims to the department or to the government. But everyone deplored the fact that there was not in Canada a system under which the Indians could regularly, especially in connection with the details of the programs, express their views and wishes.
The central government and the provinces agreed unanimously on the need for consultation with the Indians and recognized two principles in that respect.
First, that consultation must start at the level of the Indians themselves, that is to say that the Indians, wherever they live in the country, whatever tribe they belong to, whatever ethnic community they may belong to, must be able, through duly selected representatives, to express to the central govern-

ment or to a provincial government, if need bp, their wishes, complaints and opposition.
Therefore, consultation among all the Indians was the first principle. But, as I have already said in this house, that consultation would be related to the second point which I will develop later on.
That consultation would take place at the regional level or, as it were at the provincial level, but in regard to Indian affairs, we always refer to regions that correspond approximately to provincial boundaries.
Regardless of the recommendation of the consultation given by the Indians and their representative in this form, it was recognized that no decision could be forced on any particular band. Therefore, a new level of consultation was needed-a more traditional one -the council of the band which retains its right to reject or accept any provision which might apply within the area or the province.
. Therefore, those two kinds of consultations have been accepted in a general way by the central government, which told the provinces: With you, if you wish, or alone, we shall, in each area of this country, establish Indian advisory committees to which every problem of importance in respect of Indian dffairs will be submitted. You will give your advice to the government and decisions will be made in the light of those consultations. But this consultation will not necessarily be binding on all bands in the territory, which shall remain free individually. In other words, these bands will remain free to accept this consultation or this decision of the majority of the Indians in the area, or to accept a special status.
It is because we wanted the provinces to express their views on the principle of consultation that we thought-and that is one reason-that a federal-provincial conference at government level should be held before submitting any program directly to the Indians.
The second principle was that nothing should be done concerning Indian affairs without preliminary discussions with the Indians themselves and with the provinces concerned about the problems which could arise by extending provincial services. One of the conclusions reached was that everything that had been discussed at the conference should be reconsidered at a conference with the Indians, in every region in the country. I think In am now answering the hon. member for Skeena who was concerned about the Indians having to decide on some programs without

knowing what stand would be taken in that connection by the province in which they lived, since Indians did not attend the federal-provincial conference.
But since the conference recognized the principle whereby there would be consultations at the regional level and the provinces themselves, jointly with the federal government, would have to submit to the Indians their views on extension of education, welfare, health and community development services, precisely because that consultation with the Indians was to be held at the regional level, it would be at that level that the program in which the central government and the provincial governments were interested would be submitted to the Indians.
Therefore, that is another reason why the Indians were not called upon to attend this conference whose purpose was merely to support the principle whereby, there would be submitted, at the regional level, any particular program which would show some degree of flexibility in relation to other programs which could be established in other regions of the country.
You may say that some financial problems were on the agenda of that conference. That is true, but it was merely in order to ascertain the reactions of the provinces concerning what could happen in a certain district should a special educational or welfare service be extended to the Indians, how the provinces could participate in those programs, and what financial problems would arise should such services be extended.
In the other fields, there was merely an exchange of ideas, and those discussions will be resumed at the level of each and every province and region.
Hence, it can be said that this federal-provincial conference on Indians was merely a first step, a precedent in the frank and open discussion between, on the one hand, the central government which has full responsibility over Indian affairs, and the provinces which, through the school boards or municipalities, are already engaged in the extension of some Indian services, and that gives rise to some problems.
It was immediately realized that it was necessary for those provinces to make their reactions known so far as the financial aspects of that conference were concerned.
That is the story of the federal-provincial conference which, in my opinion and in the opinion of most of the participants, was a success. It resulted in two major effects: a consultation system was set up, and it was

recognized as a principle that a general service extension plan could not be established in this country, but that there had to be a particular agreement with each province, after consultation with the Indians of that province, who would be consulted collectively and, after that, individually, within each band.
A second general point which was raised during the discussion on Indian affairs estimates is the problem of the Indian claims commission. I merely want to say this: even if the government was blamed for proceeding slowly with the establishment of that commission, I am not so much concerned with that criticism, because the delay is the result of a systematic consultation, of course not with the same methods which will be used in the future, but a consultation which was carried on by mail. My predecessor had sent at that time letters to all the provinces, to all Indian associations in the country, to all Indian bands, asking them for their comments on Bill No. C-130 which had already been tabled in the House of Commons and was in relation to the setting up of an Indian claims commission. It would have taken a lot of time for each and every one of those Indian groups to start working seriously, to study the aspects of that legislation and after that systematic work, we began receiving briefs and recommendations.
There are hundreds of briefs, some much more elaborate than others, but we made a systematic study of all those briefs and recommendations.
Following that study, we have now brought a certain number of reforms or amendments to Bill No. C-130 regarding Indian claims. We hope that very soon we shall be in a position to bring before the house a bill to amend Indian claims.
Those were, Mr. Chairman, the two main points brought up during the examination of my estimates, first, the federal-provincial conference and the whole problem of consultation with the Indians and, second, the problem of Indian claims.
I realize that other points have been raised by various hon. members. I would be very glad to send my comments to each of them individually on the points they raised while discussing my estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister's statement on the two points with which he dealt, namely the federal-provincial confer-

I fully agree with him that this is a matter which has to be dealt with on a regional basis or among the Indians within each province. Therefore I will confine any questions I have on this aspect of his remarks to my own province of British Columbia.
I think I can say without fear of being contradicted by any of my Indian friends that there is a generally accepted desire among the Indian people in the coastal region of British Columbia to be treated the same as any other citizens of the province in respect of services such as education, health and welfare and so on. Can the minister tell me what the attitude of the government of the province of British Columbia was? Is he in a position to say whether that government is prepared to enter into a suitable arrangement or whether a suitable arrangement has already been worked out with the provincial government in respect of the provision of these services if, as a result of further consultations which the minister indicated will take place provincially, the Indian people themselves confirm what I feel to be their desire to have these services rendered under some more direct form of provincial administration?

Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier, no general program was set up at that federal-provincial conference, neither for the whole of Canada nor for any particular province.
I do not have the right, of course, to disclose the stand taken by each of the provinces, but what matters most is not so much what a province's representatives might have said at that conference but what will be said when the provinces and the central government meet and the provinces express their views. That is when a particular program, for British Columbia for instance, can be submitted to the Indians in British Columbia and a consultation can take place with the Indians of that province.
I think it is in keeping with the general spirit of the federal-provincial conference to wait until those conferences and consultations have been held at the provincial level to really know what particular programs will be submitted to the Indians in each of the provinces.

I should like to ask the minister whether a report from British Columbia I read recently is correct. Mr. Chairman, as a matter of fact, I am told that in British Columbia, it is hoped to be able very soon to bring the welfare payments to the Indians up to the level of the welfare payments that are now being paid to the other citizens of British Columbia.

the welfare payments in any province be the same in the case of the Indians as in the case of the other citizens of that province, with this provision that in none of the provinces should the welfare payments be lower than they are now.

Is this provision contained in the estimates now before us? I read the announcement about the same time that the latest supplementary estimates were tabled and I looked for an item in those estimates but did not see one. Is there already provision in the estimates we are discussing?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration confined his remarks to the federal-provincial conference and the claims commission as if those two items covered all the problems of the Indian people. I want to say a word or two about the problems of the 5,000 to 8,000 Indians on five reserves in my riding. I rise in my place because I feel I have a duty to these people and so far the minister-I should like to have his attention-has not given any intimation whatsoever as to what his department intends to do with regard to a program on the reserve for these people.
What are the problems that should be solved? On these reserves you will find that the Indians do not have any feeling of ownership. In turn they are not given an incentive, as white people are under our free enterprise system, to go out and earn and save their money. If we are going to start to solve the problems of these Indians on reserves we have to introduce a system of farm management to deal with the problems that exist there. You have to give these people a feeling of ownership and the feeling that when they work on the land on their reserves they will have something to show for their efforts. At the present time no program has been worked out by the department.
I want to congratulate the minister on promoting Mr. Battle to the position of head of Indian affairs. He is a very fine man and I wish to congratulate the minister on having made that appointment. But at the same time, without encouragement from the minister, without encouragement from the top, even Mr. Battle will not be able to put measures into effect that will give the Indian the incentive to put his best foot forward and give him

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
the feeling that he is operating under a free enterprise system. As it now stands, it is apparently a socialist system, a 100 per cent communist system, on each one of these reserves. This is where the problem arises. I wonder if the minister has thought through this problem? I wonder if the members of his department have gone into these reserves and thought about these things from the point of view from which the Indian is forced to think of them? Many people criticize the Indian and say he is shiftless; that he will not take care of his affairs; that he will not put his best foot forward. This is not true; if he had the incentive to do it, he would. Put any white man in the same position as an Indian, and he will not do any better than the Indian. The white people who are governing these Indians, who are controlling them or guiding them, are not providing proper leadership.
What I am trying to say to you is to think about this problem and adopt a constructive program to deal with it. I have heard nothing from the minister that would lead me to believe he has any program in mind along the lines which I consider to be most vital for the solution of these problems. There is the whole problem of schools, education and health. You can lump them all together, if you wish. Certainly, if you are familiar with the Indians you will know that they want a square deal in connection with education, health and other problems. I do not believe they are getting it now. There is just too much squalor and all the rest of it on these reserves.
We can go ahead and double the foreign aid program for the minister of external affairs; I have no objection to that if we can stand it financially. At the same time, however, I believe that our aid should start at home with our own people, the Indians and the Eskimos. I notice that this vote is around $60 million or $70 million. Our foreign aid for this last year was jumped by more than $75 million. Why could not more money be put toward taking care of our Indians and Eskimos and less for the people in foreign fields? It is all well and good to do this, but there has been a strong minister of external affairs who had the ear of the treasury board or somebody and so has been able to get a doubling of his foreign aid program. What is the justification for it in relation to the requirements of these Indians? I say to the minister who is listening to me that this Indian appropriation is the vote that should be doubled under which more services should be given to our Indians. Let us cut foreign aid programs unless we can afford to do both.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, but I did want to put my own views on the record.
I hope the minister will give consideration to the type of program which he intends to implement on these reserves and start from first principles, that is the problems of the Indians and how those problems are going to be solved.

Mr. Chairman, the other day I introduced the subject which I thought was the No. 1 problem of the Indians, one of which we are not proud, and that is alcoholism and drunkenness. Shortly after that time I was speaking to the hon. member for Athabasca and he suggested to me that this is just a symptom, not really a cause of anything. I understand his reasoning very well. You only have to look at the difficulties created by alcoholism in our own society, where almost any community has an organization of alcoholics anonymous and in most larger towns and cities in eastern Ontario we have an office of the alcoholic research foundation spreading information and prepared to give assistance right up to psychiatric assistance to people who are suffering from alcoholism. I think most people in the educational realm are worried about the problem.
Recently I have been deluged by letters, as I am sure other members have, from people who are concerned about the promotion of alcohol and the amount of advertising on television, particularly in connection with beer. The whole content of this advertising seems to be to make drinking a kind of fun thing, an okay thing to do, a thing at which athletes and socially prominent or worthwhile people in the community spend their time. This is an aspect of the problem of drinking as it affects our society in the main, and our record is nothing of which we can be proud. I think we know enough about our own situation as it exists on parliament hill to realize that very few of us are in a position or have the sort of clearcut integrity to be our brother's keeper in this particular regard.
But I come back to the problem as simply and as bluntly as I can. Except for the Indians in the north who are nomadic and who are unable to get to substantial sources of drink, who have not yet developed skills in brewing their own, the largest single difficulty we encounter in northwestern Ontario with the Indian problem is drinking. Now, whether it is a symptom of their dissociation from our society and our culture, whether it indicates bad treatment on our part, this re-
10476	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration mains the central problem. The thing that bothers me is that you can go through the estimates and you can find $84,000 for burying destitute Indians who have died; you can look, and I have looked at every bit of publicity I can find that ever came out of the department at various times, and all you get are comments that touch on this matter peripherally.
I think it all comes down to the fact that we are embarrassed to talk about the subject. We are embarrassed when talking about it to our Indian friends. I admit the very same weakness. I remember going to one band and taking notes of a meeting that lasted for about five hours. I got 60 different grievances. Later, when I had these grievances explained to me, and they covered the whole range from the fact that an illegitimate child was not registered within the band to the fact that somebody could not get unemployment insurance or the welfare allowance was not big enough, I found that in case after case the grievance hinged on the fact that there was too much drinking in a family and, as happens repeatedly, a child had been left inadequately cared for and drink was at the root of it.
Just recently a young friend of mine who is a children's aid worker and who is studying for the ministry, a very able boy and not a sissy by any means, because he has been an excellent football player, landed into a reserve to check on a couple of children. The children's aid were concerned about whether or not they were getting the proper care. He found the child, less than a year old, just a mass of scabs, with maggots around in the bed and no responsible adult taking care of it-just a couple of children. Where were the parents? They had gone out on a drunk in town, and they had taken it too far and had been thrown in jail.
This is not an isolated thing. I am not talking about something that happens once every week or once every month. The minister and his officials should be aware-the men on the local scene are-that this is constant among almost every Indian group in northwestern Ontario, and one of my colleagues from B.C. tells me it is the greatest single problem there.
The very least one could ask is that the department should have some analysis and appreciation of the problem. It is an extremely difficult one and should be faced up to. We need to have some advice from the alcoholic research foundation of the provincial government. We need some advice from a


group such as Alcoholics Anonymous to see if they have any suggestion about how their particular method of meeting this problem might be translated into the reserves and the Indian situation in general.
I do not expect any thorough or complete answer from the minister. All I ask is that he accept that this is a major problem and that he give some indication the branch is prepared to do some studies on it. From the number of papers that are presented I know we have anthropologists and sociologists working on many problems. In fact I remember reading a most interesting study dealing with a comparison of the Indian community and Eskimo community up at the mouth of the Mackenzie river, and with the social attitudes and responsibilities of both. I was most impressed with the kind of analysis conducted by the man who made that study. It is people such as that who must go into some of these band and tribe situations and see whether it might be possible, working with the Indians themselves, to get some kind of movement towards temperance, or to achieve at least a realization that alcoholism and over drinking, bootlegging and home brewing are some of the worst factors in demoralizing and ruining the situation as it exists at present.
One of the really tragic parts of this concerns individual reserves comprised of a couple of hundred people, who send 20 or 25 of their children away to boarding schools for example at Fort William or Spanish. When the kids move away they get discipline. They are set within some kind of ideal and a philosophy, usually a religious philosophy. Their care is complete and I have no complaints about it. But at the end of the school year the kids go back to the band and quite often the first thing they see in their homes, which are mostly shacks, is a can on the stove with a bunch of yeast, raisins and sugar brewing away. They return into an atmosphere where the biggest worth-while thing the adults can think of is to go on a rollicking drunk on Saturday night.
Hon. members may say I am exaggerating the situation. Maybe the minister and his officials think so and, if they do, I am prepared to take them on a tour through my area, to talk to some of the Indians and to some of the people who work with them, who can confirm that this is the situation. I finally reached the stage a few weeks ago of feeling there was no use ignoring it any longer. I felt that any time an Indian band brought a problem to me that touched on welfare or jobs, one of the great dilemmas I had to face

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
was this whole question about drinking and the irresponsibility which it engendered.
There are a couple of good communities in my area. I know some of the Indians at Pickle Crow gold mines who have fitted in very well there, and my information is that they are good employees and are worth-while people in the community in the sense of total responsibility. I know that at Heron Bay the Ontario Paper Company for a number of years has encouraged men of the tribe to work on the flume where the logs go shooting down to the shore of lake Superior for delivery. The company has turned up a number of good workers and this has had a considerable effect on the reserve.
If one looks at that particular reserve and its housing, where the same basic provisions apply as over at the other side of lake Nipigon, it can be seen that band has a much higher standard in home furnishings and the kind of material comforts that tend to mean so much to all of us. They also have a higher attitude toward education for their children. I know economic opportunity also fits into this, but too often it is brought to ruin by drinking, and by the fact that too often in our bush communities the Indians live on the periphery, and their touching point with white society is usually in the noisiest of beer parlours or at the bootleggers.
I am not going to deal further with this particular point. I insist it is the most serious problem I know of in connection with the Indians. We have to face it openly and we must ask many of the Indians to face it openly.
Another point I want to touch on with the minister relates to the Department of Industry and the Department of Labour. We have designated areas to which special tax incentives are given, depending on whether a particular area qualifies under a formula, worked out by the Department of Labour, based on its unemployment statistics. The minister may be aware that most of the Indians in northwestern Ontario are not on the unemployment rolls or unemployment statistics. They just do not figure in the majority of them. Therefore they do not play any substantial part in determining whether the unemployment statistics are up or down.
This becomes important when you get into a situation such as one in my riding where there are two Indian reserves adjacent to the village of Longlac. A large United States plywood concern has expressed interest in establishing in that community, but of course it is looking around at other places where it 20220-663J
would have the advantage of a designated area tax incentive. Longlac has been seeking to see if it can qualify as a designated area but it finds that although it has serious unemployment, particularly among Indians, the formula has been determined in the main by the unemployment and employment statistics of the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William, 180 miles away. This is obviously unfair because the lakehead unemployment and employment situation is not a reflection of the situation at Longlac.
I understand the Department of Industry has been inflexible on this matter. I have talked about it to people in the department of economic planning and development of the provincial government, who say that three times they have raised this issue strongly with the federal government and got nowhere. I ask the minister to look at the situation closely as it applies to the community of Longlac because that plywood mill, if it should be established there, would mean much employment for the Indians on those two reserves.
I mention this in particular because a few of the Indians on those reserves have regular employment with the sawmill that is run by the Kimberly-Clark Pulp and Paper Company. This may seem to be an isolated problem, but it opens up one of the difficulties about economic development. We have a whole host of agencies involved in this, federal and provincial, but it seems to me it is very difficult to get any co-ordination or co-operation.
The last point I want to touch on relates to members of parliament who have a considerable number of Indians in their constituencies. It is apparent to me that despite the general interest each of us has in the Indian problem, there are no more than 20 or 25 members who have a substantial number of Indians in their constituencies and who get these problems brought to them in great detail. Offhand I can think of the hon. member for White Bay-Grand Falls-Labrador, the hon. member for Churchill, the hon. member for Skeena, the hon. member for Fort William, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and so on; but the number is not large.
I suggest one of the things we might do, in order to achieve a closer understanding on our part of the branch's problems, is that the minister arrange some kind of informal meetings, possibly a special informal committee, that could get together on several occasions during a year and have a rundown from the officials of the branch on Indian problems. It seems to me this would save considerable time for us when we come to consider these

Some may say: Is it not the responsibility of the member to deal with the branch? But I could be writing or telephoning the branch almost every day in connection with Indian matters, and one is engaged in a great many things. It seems to me that this special effort should be considered by the branch in order to keep us better informed.
Another thing I should appreciate as a member with a considerable number of Indians in his constituency would be a copy, at least several times a year, of any major decision taken in connection with the Indians in the region in which I am most interested. Mr. Chairman, before we take up another item I should like to come back to an extremely important point mentioned by the hon. members for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) and Skeena (Mr. Howard) last Thursday. They made a comparison between the estimates of Indian affairs and the estimates of the assistance to underdeveloped countries.
I think that the question asked by the hon. member for Macleod is a very good introduction to the program I announced in the house, namely the community development program concerning the Indians.
I think that to increase indefinitely the amount of money allocated for the various Indian reserves in the country is not the proper solution. All those who have experience in Indian matters and all hon. members who have followed closely the development of their reserves, in their own ridings, know very well that even if the government were to decide tomorrow to double the amount allocated for the the Indian reserves in the country, that would be no solution to the Indian problems that every hon. member is facing, no matter where they sit in the House of Commons. That solution was already


found, not by us, but by all those who experimented with what is called community development, which means that when one group has problems, in some society, the best way to solve that problem is to make them realize that they must themselves take a good look at their situation to find a way to improve their own lot. That is the experience we are trying to apply in the development of Indian affairs.
The amount of $3,500,000 may seem little, but we must not forget that the amount will be used to pay the salaries of community development experts. The regular expenditures for Indians will appear in the estimates already before the committee and they amount to some $60 million.
I believe that with $60 million much can be achieved for the Indians, especially if this amount is increased by a special budget of $3,500,000 for community development to be spread over a period of three years.
Specialists could be hired to help the Indians examine their position and devise means of improving their lot. After the Indians have studied their problems and drafted programs to their convenience and in conformity with their wishes, then the amounts that can be allocated to them will be useful and will allow them, on a long term basis, to develop their own initiative and assume their normal rank in the Canadian society.
This amount of $3,500,000 seems small, but it will allow us-according to the experiments conducted by our own department at the provincial level and by other countries- to eventually solve the problems facing the Indians.
I just want to say a word about the extremely important problem raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur. I refer to alcoholism in our country's Indian territories. I should like to tell the hon. member that we are greatly concerned about this matter. We are anxiously awaiting a report from the Ontario body which has been studying this problem for approximately four years and which is called the alcoholism and drug addiction research foundation of Ontario. We hope it will soon be in a position to submit a report to us on that subject.
On the other hand, we are doing all we can to provide Indian services with specialists on all the problems of alcoholism one could find on the Indian reserves. Such specialists would be of great use to us.
Now, a suggestion was made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, namely to set up a committee made up of members having a

large number of Indians in their ridings to discuss administrative problems with the officials of the Indian affairs branch.
My assistant deputy minister, the director of the Indian affairs branch, tells me that he would be very happy to co-operate with all hon. members of the house and to give them information beforehand-since that is another point raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur-about all the new programs that might deal with the country's Indian affairs.

As another member who has a large number of Indian reserves in his riding I, too, am deeply interested in this subject, particularly in the educational aspect.
I well recall that back in 1958 hundreds of Indian boys and girls in my constituency did not have the opportunity to attend school at all. I am pleased to say that in 1963, however, there was not one Indian boy or girl in my constituency who was not reasonably near a school. I am happy to find we have succeeded in reaching these children. However, in some cases there is great difficulty in getting these children to school. Great strides have been taken in connection with the integration of schools which are now providing instruction both for Indian children and for others. This was a wonderful step forward. But there is great difficulty in securing transportation to schools on the reserves themselves. Buses have to be provided by the Indian affairs branch, and great difficulty has arisen in this connection. I also found great progress in the integration of the Indians in our public schools.
One great disadvantage to the Indians is that in some parts of the north we are taking away their livelihood and have failed to provide alternative provision for them, such as fishing, trapping and hunting. We have taken such a large portion of this activity away from them with our tourist trade and we have not made alternative provision for them. Therefore the Indians find it very difficult to make a living. I realize we have increased three times the number of houses on Indian reservations but we have not gone nearly far enough. I also realize it is a great problem. I admit we have made great strides to increase the number of houses, but we have only scratched the surface of the problem.
I also found in the southern part of my constituency that the Indian population which
has a chance to farm or to raise livestock are willing in this day and age to go ahead with this activity, but we have only made a start in this direction. One speaker mentioned the Colombo plan, and I am sure we could do much more by way of providing equipment and encouraging these people to make their own livelihoods. The people in the northern parts of the country live differently from those in the southern part, which is why I am interested in what we have done to compensate the Indians for their loss of livelihood. In the Cold Lake area we have deprived the Indians of their livelihood through the construction of the bombing range there. We have also never fulfilled our part of the bargain by repaying these people for what we have taken from them. I have noticed that when we have given the Indian population the chance for progress they have taken it, and I am happy at the increased opportunities provided for the education of our Indians. But I am sure we must go a lot further yet.
Another difficulty I have noticed for our Indian farming population is that many are unemployed because they cannot obtain loans. We make provision for them to go into other fields of endeavour, and to do so they are forced to take their children out of school. This makes it difficult both for the children and for the parents. I have particular reference to the Indian families which work in the beet fields. In such cases a whole class at school can be upset. Perhaps the teacher was making great progress with the children of a family which goes to work in the beet fields, taking their children with them. In such cases they have no chance to attend school and possibly the whole year is wasted. I have seen what the Indian people will do if we would only help them. I have seen this particularly in the north where we provide them with saw mills, planers and materials for house building.
The drinking habits of Indians have been mentioned, but I do not think that they are any worse than those of the white man. In my constituency a lot of these Indians have only just obtained permission to go into beer parlours, so one might expect some problems; but it is amazing how they begin to conduct themselves in many cases better than the white people. The big problem is that we are not getting enough housing accommodation for them. We are not making enough provision to enable them to commence farming, or purchase livestock and machinery. If we are to reach the stage where these people take

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration their rightful place in the economy we must make greater progress than we have; and this should be forthcoming in view of the little which has been done in the past few years.

Mr. Chairman, I will follow tlie example of the hon. member for Meadow Lake and make my remarks brief and to the point. I should like to confirm what my colleague from Meadow Lake has said, that the improvement on reservations the last few years has been noticeable and I think we should strengthen the gains which have been made. But because there has been gain it does not mean that we should be satisfied. Tonight I propose to make one or two suggestions, which I hope will be practical and acceptable not only to the minister but to his officials.
First of all, to give weight to my arguments I have to refer to the circumstances existing in my constituency, in which I have eight reservations. These reservations are on land along the Qu'Appelle river, with one exception south of Broadview. Some of the land on these reservations is fairly good land for farming, and much of it is exceptionally fine land for pasture. So far there has been no good reason why the Indians should develop this agriculture land or these pastures. I do not intend to go into the reasons, which are purely local and well understood by the Indians. I want to make my positive proposal in the interest of pushing forward the efforts of the Indians on these reservations, who are making an effort to improve their lot, without very much help. This proposal has to do with encouraging those on the reservations who are now making serious efforts to get into grain farming. Fortunately for them the crops over the last three years have been good and they have been able to finance any improvements which have been made from the surplus grain which has been sold. At the present time they are encumbered by the fact that because the reservation land cannot be used to borrow money they cannot move into commercial farming operations like the rest of the farmers, because of their inability to borrow money on the land which belongs to the reservation or to the band.
My suggestion is that wherever an Indian farmer has demonstrated to the satisfaction of his band, to his neighbours on the reservation and to the farmers close by that he is a successful farmer, the Indian affairs branch, either by backing this Indian farmer's loan with the Farm Credit Corporation or by making the money available itself, give the farmer an opportunity to prepare a program
to show the Indians affairs branch and the band concerned that the money invested will not only return interest but that he will pay the capital back and increase his own capital at the same time. I know that several Indians on each of the reservations in my constituency are prepared to sit down with competent Farm Credit Corporation advisers and work out such a program, and if they meet the rigid test of the corporation's supervisors then I believe this backing should be given.
I should like to remind the minister of a similar situation existing in other countries besides our own in connection with young people. Young people on the farms in general, both in the United States and Canada, who have no parents to support their applications for loans from various government lending agencies are, generally speaking, unable to get loans. The exceptions are that certain sections of the farm improvement loans act of the United States make it possible for young people to go to local banks, and if a number of local farmers agree that the young person concerned has a chance to farm successfully and they sign their name to that effect, the young person is given credit as if he had land and assets. In the beginning they had to pay a deposit of $50, backing up their claim that these young farmers were worth-while individuals and deserved government assistance. This worked so well in several districts in the United States that the neighbouring farmers are no longer being asked by the banks to put up the $50 deposit.
This is the kind of legislation we must consider in relation to the Farm Credit Corporation's lending operations. We could allow local farmers, if they are willing, to put down so much money to indicate their good faith and judgment that the young farmers involved would not make mistakes and would be able to pay back the loans plus interest, while at the same time substantially increasing their standard of living. I suggest this type of operation could take place to the benefit of Indians on reservations, provided their neighbours, who are, after all, the best judges of their ability to farm, were willing to back these young Indian farmers as being capable of operating commercial and selfsustaining businesses. In view of the fact the Indians cannot use land on reservations as collateral the Indian affairs department could by this means provide the necessary collateral.
The other alternative is that the band councils could recommend that certain Indian

farmers on reservations are deserving of this type of assistance, and become a signatory to a loan backed up by the Indian affairs department, making a deposit to show good faith, and this signature could then be used as collateral by the Farm Credit Corporation.
To summarize the suggestion I am making, Mr. Chairman, we should now take the next step in relation to young Indian farmers, who are making an honest and sincere effort to improve their standard of living. If they can come up with a practical proposal, indicating that they can not only pay back the principal but the interest, while at the same time improving their standard of living, satisfying the farm credit supervisor, but due to the fact that the Indian cannot use his land as collateral, the Indian affairs could then provide the necessary assistance.
I would estimate that there are perhaps five to eight farmers per reservation in my riding who could meet the qualifications required to obtain the signature, and the deposit of $500 from the Indian bands, on the understanding that if the farmers were not successful the band would lose the $500. I think that would be a reasonable enough provision to secure any assistance advanced, and I feel that we should take this step to help these Indian farmers become self-sustaining.
I am personally aware of a young Indian farmer who, with a loan of $15,000, having at the present time 230 acres under cultivation, could increase his cultivated acreage, add to his herd of beef cattle, which is a fine one, and within 18 months to two years arrive at the end of the year with a net income of $4,000, after paying expenses. That is as good an income as any average farmer can expect in this country under those circumstances.
If we could put family after family into an operation of this kind, giving them that type of net income, even though it might only apply to five or six families per reservation, we would be assisting these Indian families and by their example do more for the other Indian families on the reservations than we could do by any amount of persuasion.
The Department of Agriculture has assisted a great deal in this particular area by using 45,000 acres of these Indian reservations, after making a tour of them with the band councils, and putting them under administration and operation by the P.F.R.A. They have assisted in putting cattle on these lands, paying the usual six cents per day per head, thereby increasing the cattle population. Under this agreement between P.F.R.A. and the Indian
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration bands the Indian gets first right to put his cattle on these pasture lands, which will eventually carry 9,000 head. Using very round figures this means an increase in income to these four reservations of approximately $1,500,000 per year. I should mention that Indian people take readily to beef farming operations because there is no intensive labour type operation involved, and they can work a few months in the wintertime feeding their cattle, then put the female stock out to pasture and work the land growing enough fodder to carry the remainder through the winter.
Mr. Chairman, this operation would not only be self-liquidating as far as the department is concerned, but would assist family after family to establish respectable selfsustaining businesses. That in brief is the first proposal I should like to make.
I had hoped that I could cut my remarks short at this stage by asking the minister to indicate that he and several of his officials will discuss this type of operation with me to see whether we can make an experiment in a few cases to prove to the minister and his department that this proposal will work. I hope the minister will be kindly in his attitude toward my suggestion.
The second type of operation I should like to describe today relates particularly to hay lands. The Department of Agriculture, through its P.F.R.A. operations, controls the movement of water down the Qu'Appelle river. In controlling this water sometimes it is necessary to dam up the river and flood some of these Indian reservation lands, destroying their economic possibilities as far as the Indian people are concerned. They are at those times not able to obtain full use of their hay lands. I believe the Indian affairs department could work with the P.F.R.A. officials in controlling the flow of water so as not to dam up the water during haying seasons, enabling the Indians in this area to take full advantage of the tremendous productivity of this land now subject to almost annual flooding. The P.F.R.A. officials have been very good in this regard, without any kind of pressure being put on them at all. They have carried out a voluntary survey of these areas of the Indian reservations, particularly the Muscowpetung reservation where the Indians have already done a lot of diking work. These people would like to co-operate with the Indian affairs department to organize this operation in such a way that the hay can be stored, and then, at the time of the
10482	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration inevitable shortage of hay, which will come within the next two or three years in Saskatchewan, it could be sold first of all to the Indian reservations, which are building up their cattle herds, and then to the neighbouring farmers.
Once again in this way with almost no expenditure on the part of the Indian affairs branch the revenue of the Indian bands could be added to, to the extent of $20 per ton for 3,000 or 4,000 tons of hay per year. That would provide a tremendous increase in revenue to these Indian bands.
Mr. Chairman, these suggestions are not impossible things. In fact, the expenditures are very small in respect of the second proposal, and none at all in respect of the first, except the amount required to back the credit. I hope that I can discuss these ideas personally with the minister at some time.
Finally, I should like to remind the minister that he made an announcement in the house not long ago about his negotiations with the provinces. I have discussed this proposal with some of the bands in my area. I have presented the arguments for and against, and have found that many Indians in my electoral riding have expressed a willingness to consider this proposal fairly. They realize that in some cases they probably will have to pay taxes, and also provide a right to certain services in the province of Saskatchewan. I cannot indicate for certain what the final outcome will be, but I can say for all bands in my area that they will consider the minister's proposals fairly. Naturally they are concerned, because they feel their long term rights cannot be tampered with, and the province of Saskatchewan has guaranteed that there will be no such infringement on their traditional rights. I think we must accept the fact that the word of the government of Saskatchewan is good.
The point that does worry them a little bit, of course, is the proposal in regard to roads. They know that they will have to expect to pay municipal taxes for their share of the roads through their municipalities. It may well be necessary that the Indian affairs department will have to consider that any cost in this regard is in fact a tremendous investment in social capital, particularly in the early stages. I feel that a little bit of help should be given in the earlier stages of the plan. Indians are also very much interested in the proposal to go in with the school districts, as far as nearby town schools are concerned. They are very interested in obtaining

the same social welfare services as the rest of the people in the province.
They know quite a bit about hospitalization and medical care and this point worries them a bit. If some ambitious young Indian boy or girl leaves the reservation at the present time and gets a job in the nearby town, which I think they recognize is the only future for them, the minute they go off the reservation they lose their right to the payment of hospitalization and medical care if that applies. This causes many of them to be frightened about leaving the reservation. When they go to the nearby town they have to learn about a new type of civilization and they are somewhat frightened about the fact that they are not covered with respect to the payment of hospitalization unless they are paying into the government scheme.
I think we should encourage the movement of these young people away from the reservations by providing that for a period of two or three years after they leave, their hospitalization premiums will be paid for them so they will not feel they are forced to go back to the reservation because of fear about not being covered for hospitalization.
These are small matters but I have tried to be constructive in putting them forward in the hope that by a slight change of attitude we can continue this mixing of the cultures of our country and help the Indians to make the necessary adjustment. At the present time in my constituency approximately half the children on most of the reservations go to the nearby town schools while the other half attend the reservation schools. I think you will find gradual acceptance of the fact that there is a slightly better standard of education in the town schools and that the tendency for them to go to these schools will increase.
Finally, I wonder whether the minister would provide me with copies of the brief presented by the provincial governments at the federal-provincial conference in which each province lays down its position with regard to what it will do for the Indian. I have the one for Saskatchewan and I should like to get them for the other provinces. Second, the Indian affairs branch provided a very fine briefing book for the discussions at the provincial level and I should also like to get a copy of that. If the minister can provide me with these documents I will be very happy.

I must say that my fear is based in part at least on my own observation of the present situation in the operation of the Indian affairs branch, and in this connection I should like to draw to the minister's attention yet another quotation from his opening speech on the branch which is related to the question I raised earlier and which he did not answer. The minister said:
The present staff can only do so much. There is a need to strengthen the operations of the branch in both the field and support services. More highly qualified staff are required to do the job.
I ask the minister again to relate that statement to the fact that, unless I have missed it completely in my study of the details of the estimates, there is no provision for more staff, more people to do the job. I had hoped to raise this point earlier in the discussion but did not have the opportunity. However, I would point out that I have had in my files since December 21 of last year the answer to an order paper question I asked on the subject of the office of Indian commissioner of British Columbia, and the staff of one of the agencies which operates within the boundaries of my own constituency.
If one makes an analysis of the complement, he certainly cannot help but come to the conclusion that there is some validity to my suggestion that we are in a position where we have the generals but have not got the staff in the field. Apart from the normal clerical positions in the commissioner's office in British Columbia, we have provision for an engineer and a supervisor of construction. I do not want to take too long going over all the details, but I would point out that there seem to be three part time construction foremen.
If I understand the return correctly, in the field of welfare we have only one trained welfare officer for the whole of the province of British Columbia. To take the west coast agency as an example, we find that in the field we have a superintendent and an assistant and two members on the clerical staff, a clerk and a stenographer. In addition we have a captain engineer to operate the agency vessel which goes up and down the west coast of Vancouver island. It is pointed out in this return, and I know this from my own observation, that when the agency vessel goes on a trip up the coast to the reservations a crew of three is required for this vessel under federal government regulations. Who are the crew? There is the captain engineer, and then the agent superintendent and his assistant have to perform the duties of the crew. They may not mind doing this too much, although I think there might be some question whether some of the steamship regulations are not being bypassed. But, more important, who is left in the superintendent's office? There are two clerks, and a clerk-stenographer.
In that one agency there are enough people who have been a part of the welfare case load to require more than the full time service of one social worker under provincial welfare standards, which are none too high in British Columbia. Yet as far as I can gather the only social worker for the whole of British Columbia is in the Indian commissioner's office in Vancouver.
I have a number of questions I should like to raise but to me this is a vital thing because I have seen money go down the drain on housing construction programs because supplies have been shipped up the coast and have been left lying on the beach until they rotted. Nobody was available with the necessary skill to give some direction in getting the construction of the houses started.
I have again drawn the minister's attention to the thousands of dollars that have been wasted on the reserve at Opitsat in respect of water supply systems. Each time it has been a case of too little and too late. It has been a case of sending good money after bad, and there is still no adequate water supply system there. I could go on and name other instances. This is the reason I raise these two questions with the minister. Is he convinced that he is going to be able, under this proposed community development program, to get the people out in the field where the job needs to be done? Second, what if anything is he doing to meet his own statement that the present staff can only do so

In concluding, Mr. Chairman, I note that the hon. member for Skeena and I believe the hon. member for Macleod, have related what we are doing for our Indian people to what we are doing in the field of external aid. So far as I am concerned, we need to do both. When I was at the parliamentary conference in Malaysia last year, one of the delegates from the United Kingdom, a delegate who was in the then government party in the United Kingdom, was able to say before that conference that the United Kingdom was devoting 1.5 per cent of its gross national product to its external aid program. I should like to tell the minister, in view of the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Macleod, that if we could lump together our external aid program and our internal aid program in relation to Indians and Eskimos so that for this combined purpose we were spending 1.5 per cent of our gross national product I would be much happier about the situation in both fields than I am at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I will not keep the committee very long but there are one or two things I wanted to say on these estimates.
Filibuster.

No, it will not be a filibuster; I am not that ambitious. I merely want to make some suggestions with regard to our trade policies in the future. I believe that our whole concept of trade should be changed in the light of developments in the world today and that there should be some consideration taken of our responsibilities and our opportunities with regard to the underdeveloped areas of the world. In fact, if policies of this sort were employed, I think it would amount to an [DOT]extension of the Canadian economy which would make it that much easier to deal with some of the internal problems with which we have been dealing earlier this afternoon.
As was stressed again and again by the international conference in Copenhagen this year, the gap between the developed and underdeveloped areas is widening and deepening. There appears to be little being done at the moment to close that gap. I suggest we have to base our trade now on a much more sophisticated basis than we have in the past. We have, as it were, to build up some credits for the future in our dealings with areas that are slowly trying to come into the twentieth century. Nor do I think we should allow political considerations to stand in our way of advancing the credits that will be required, in the first instance, to develop trade.
I have in mind, for instance, the position with regard to Cuba. While it is true we have, ever since the revolution, conducted trade in a rather delicate manner with Cuba and with one watchful eye on Washington, we have not really undertaken anything massive in the way of help for developing the economy of that country which might well help solve some of the tensions that now exist in the western hemisphere, if we were prepared to do that. The same thing is true, I believe with regard to the Middle East. If we were prepared to deal with the Arab countries in the same way, I think we might find we were beginning to reduce some of the tensions in that area. There are such things as the Jordan river development to be considered, which will require immense help from the western world. Should these be undertaken successfully we would be on the way to solving the festering sore that lies in the midst of our troubles in the Middle East, the Arab refugees.
Before long we may find ourselves with unsaleable volumes of wheat, and before that time comes we should be preparing the groundwork for future markets. Nor should
Supply-Trade and Commerce we consider this a philanthropic gesture. We often speak of that when talking about things such as the export of $350,000 worth of flour to Indonesia. Actually it is of equal benefit to the prairie wheat farmers, and I am sure their interests were of equal importance to the government in its decision in that regard.
So far as I am aware no one is yet in a position to estimate how massive an expansion of this credit program the Canadian economy could carry. But I would remind the committee that in 1939 we also had no idea just how heavy a load the Canadian economy could bear, and we astonished ourselves and the rest of the world by finding what a tremendously heavy load our economy was able to bear from its own resources.
I would suggest that in this new war- and to my mind even more important war- against poverty, ignorance and hunger throughout the world we have an even more important challenge facing us than we had in 1939. I would hope the government would begin to regard our trade policies as part of the responsibilities of Canada, as one of the affluent countries of the world, to try and win this war against poverty, and to remember that as we do so it is not a philanthropic gesture, it is a gesture of straight self-interest and self-survival.
I would like to see the government being considerably bolder in its estimate of what the Canadian economy can afford in the way of credits to the underdeveloped areas of the world, so that we may build up for the future further possibilities of trade for the vast volumes of goods and materials that an automated industry will, before long, confront us with. Because, make no mistake about it, this is one of the problems we are going to face in the next few years or decade-what to do with the enormous avalanche of goods a modern industrial community will supply us with. The rest of the world is going to be in desperate need of them, and I suggest we should now be placing its peoples in a position where they can take advantage of the enormous capacity of North America and other developed parts of the world.
But to do so will need a complete break with the traditional idea of trade for immediate profit, immediate return, trade for the immediate balance of payments problem, trade for the usual 19th century purpose of making a profit in the immediate future. I shall of course admit that if we do this we shall probably have to do as much violence to the more sacred cows in the free enterprise pasture as we did during the war. This does

Supply-Trade and Commerce not disturb me at all, because I have noticed those free enterprise cows are poor milkers to start with, and they preserve most of their milk for the owners of the pasture.

This is the only point I wish to raise. I think it is the one which most seriously concerns us in connection with the department now under review.

I should like to make a few brief comments in the time available tonight on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. They are directed to the action taken by the government during the past year, first with regard to the relaxation of the quota on imports of turkeys and second with regard to the Durum wheat situation a few days ago.
I think the action taken on each of these occasions indicates to some extent the attitude of the government opposite and are part of a trend. Already we can see the effects of this laxity or carelessness upon the agriculture industry of this country.
With regard to the quota, it has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as well as by his colleague the Minister of Agriculture that the United States took strong exception to the fact that these quotas were in effect. I would remind him that they were in effect for five years during which time the United States took no action whatever and there was no reason to think there would be


any change at this time. I believe what has happened reflects a certain carelessness on the part of the ministry.
The decision with regard to Durum wheat is another which strikes at the very heart of what agricultural people as well as governments in Canada over the years have been trying to achieve in international agreements, particularly international wheat agreements. The danger of the situation arising out of the action which has been taken cannot escape the minister's attention because it is of concern to anyone who is interested in the price of grain.
Another matter I wish to mention briefly has to do with seasonal embargoes on imports of fresh fruit from the United States. Many people engaged in this industry in Canada tell me they feel these embargoes should be put into effect three weeks or a month earlier than they are. At the present time United States surpluses are placed on our market where they fill up storage immediately prior to the embargo taking effect, and this works to the detriment of the local market.

I believe the minister was about to rise on the first item. I did not want to delay matters because I am sure he is anxious to get his estimates through. But perhaps he could answer some of the questions which have been asked.

Mr. Chairman, during the several days on which my estimates were discussed I took a careful note of many of the questions and suggestions made by hon. members. Indeed, I have with me a very large file in which I have recorded the comments and suggestions made. It would take me quite a little while so I propose to leave the matter, and if any hon. member would like to ask me a question on some other occasion or address a letter to me I would be very happy to supply the information.
May I answer the question asked tonight by the hon. member for Parry Sound-

Muskoka, who referred to the adverse balance of payments on tourist account which is almost certain to appear in our international accounts this year. He asked whether there was any hope for the future. We are continuing in our efforts to increase our income from tourist spendings in Canada and we have every hope of achieving the target that I have taken over from the preceding government of $1 billion in 1967. I have also been looking at the question of how much help we might be able to give to encourage travel within Canada by Canadians. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka will realize if he has looked at the figures carefully, the reason for the adverse balance is not because there has been any failure in our earnings on tourist account but because the great prosperity of the Canadian people has induced them to travel abroad in greater numbers. Therefore we will do what we can as a Canadian government to assist the provincial governments and the Canadian tourist association to encourage travel within Canada, in this way helping to reduce this adverse balance.

One minor point, Mr. Chairman. May I make a suggestion to the minister regarding all these comments he has on points raised by hon. members. Perhaps he could put some of his very excellent staff to work in merely dropping a note to hon. members. This has been done by some of his colleagues and predecessors in office and is very effective. I do not think hon. members appreciate just being ignored.
I thank the hon. gentleman very much for his suggestion and I shall be very happy to follow it.
