Harold Wilson, who advocated in his statement, as far as I can understand the press report, the extension of the powers of the international monetary fund to the point where it could create credit in much the same way a national central bank could do so, as a method of solving the question of international liquidity? As far as I can understand, Mr. Wilson was advocating something in the nature of a proposal that is usually associated with one of the professors in British Columbia, Robert Triffin. I wonder whether the minister took note of that statement, and could he indicate what the Cana-

Supply-Finance
dian government's position would be if such a proposal were formally advanced?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I promised my hon. friend, the member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands, that during my consideration of the estimates I would expand on some of the questions he asked earlier about the differences between the reported views of the minister of finance of France and the Triffin plan, and the proposals that were made in discussions that took place at Tokyo.
The major proposal before the board of governors of the international monetary fund at its annual meeting in Tokyo, as the house will be aware from my statement of September 14, was that there would be a general increase in the quotas. That is an increase in the contributions and drawing rights of all members of the fund. The specific figure mentioned by various governors for this general increase was 25 per cent.
As I indicated in my report to the house, and as I said in my speech to the governors at Tokyo, it seems clear to us that the time has come for another general increase in fund quotas. Moreover we considered that an increase larger than 25 per cent could be justified. That is certainly the Canadian view.
The French minister of finance, on the other hand, stated quite explicitly that the 25 per cent increase in quotas did not seem to his government to respond to an evident and urgent need, and that they did not consider the increase of international liquidities to be the main target of the studies which had been undertaken. In my reply to the hon. member for Chicoutimi on September 29, I intended to make clear this distinction between our view and that of the French finance minister.
Turning now to a question raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, I believe there may be some similarities between the ideas expressed by the French minister and the Triffin plan. In his statement to the governors, the minister of finance of France envisaged a system based in the first instance, and as is the present one, on gold, but supplemented as necessary by other "sources for supplying owned resources." The minister was extremely cautious in speaking about these other sources and the extent to which they would be used to create additional reserves. For instance, he pointed out that, "as there is always temptation to accumulate an over supply of world liquidities, cautious regulations would be required in order to assess the need for such a creation and to adjust its amount". He added that "if the need were to arise for an increase in

the amount of owned reserves, there should be a concerted and limited recourse to additional fiduciary means". These remarks by the minister suggest that he does not consider that there is at present a shortage of liquidity and that he did not put forward his proposal as a means for increasing reserves at least in the immediate future.
Professor Triffin in his plan suggested that an institution such as the international monetary fund should be empowered to increase the total of international liquidity by creating deposits based either on loans or investments. He recognized, of course, that the power to create additional liquidity should be limited, but thought that the best way to handle the problem might be to limit the increase to a total amount which would, together with increases in the world stock of monetary gold, raise total world reserves by 3 per cent to 5 per cent per year. This suggestion contrasts sharply with the more cautious approach suggested by the minister of finance of France.
The minister did not mention whether he had seen the report from London of the British prime minister's proposal, which seems to go a bit farther than this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not seen the report but I will be interested in looking it up, and I must say that a more expansive approach would be sympathetically received in these quarters.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the Minister of Finance a question which I asked the Secretary of State some days ago, but did not get any reply. I brought up the fact that we have an economic council which reports to the Secretary of State, and in addition we have the Department of Trade and Commerce which is very important in economic matters, and also the Department of Finance, the Department of Industry and the Department of Labour, all dealing in the main in economic questions. The question that many of us have tended to come up with in the past is, how do all these economic ministries of the government, one might say, dovetail? It is not so much a question of who is the senior minister or who is the central person or which is the pivotal office in all of these economic arrangements. It is not a case of probing for cabinet secrets with regard to what may be a private cabinet committee. It is just a question of where

the prime responsibility lies, the central portfolio in all these economic affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will do my best to answer that question. In government nowadays I think that the various phases of activity in the economic sphere are so all pervasive that appropriately they must be divided between different ministers. I do not think it is any secret that in the present government there is a cabinet committee on finance of which I as Minister of Finance am the chairman. In the last analysis it is the Prime Minister who must accept the responsibility for coordinating the views of different ministers, but to a considerable extent this is decentralized through this particular cabinet committee. We have frequent meetings and we discuss the different views of the various ministers to whom my hon. member referred, and other ministers. I am inclined to think that this approach has been quite effective.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN STERLING SUPPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN STERLING SUPPORT
speechtext: I wish to announce Canadian participation in a new credit arrangement to provide massive support for sterling. The purpose of this is to enable Britain to meet speculative selling of the pound. Under the new arrangement 11 countries consisting of Austria, Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, The Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States and the bank of international settlements have provided credit facilities totalling $3 billion. The Bank of Canada's share of this total is $200 million. These credit facilities are separate from the $1 billion stand-by arrangement which Britain already has with the international monetary fund. A drawing under this stand-by is expected to take place shortly. This will be used in part to pay off presently outstanding short term credits from central banks which was arranged last September.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN STERLING SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the statement made by the Minister of Finance, I believe that it would be appropriate for us to make some comments, and it would be in order to ask the minister why the Bank of Canada is entitled to lend $200 million to assist another country-$200 million as a loan to England- whereas the Minister of Finance always told us that the Bank of Canada could not lend money to provinces, municipalities or school boards.
Then our school boards, our municipalities and our provinces will borrow from England and the United States the money which the Bank of Canada loaned to England-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN STERLING SUPPORT
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN STERLING SUPPORT
speechtext:
You will agree with me that it amounts to a complete about-face in the present government's monetary policy.


The government has always maintained that the Bank of Canada could not lend money, and here we find that it made a loan, not to Canadians, but to foreigners.
I wonder if, after making such a statement, the Minister of Finance does not fear the resentment of the Canadian people, who have to borrow money abroad, at a high interest rate, while the Bank of Canada, on the minister's advice, is making a loan to Britain practically interest free.
There is surely something wrong there and, in my opinion, the Minister of Finance should start by telling us what rate of interest is to be charged. While he specified the amount of the loan, he made no mention of the interest rate, and we should be told about that.
Second, is this a new Bank of Canada policy? And under that new policy, will the Bank of Canada now grant loans to provincial governments, municipalities and school boards?
It is all very well to loan money to England but let us start with our own people who need loans, that is the provincial governments.
One knows that the province of Quebec had to borrow $100 million from British Columbia. Why did that province not get the chance to borrow that amount from the Bank of Canada? I feel it would be more normal if the Bank of Canada, rather than another province, were to loan money to the province of Quebec.
Further, Saskatchewan borrowed money from Alberta.
That statement takes us by surprise because it goes against what the Minister of Finance told us previously and it contradicts his previous monetary policy.
We hope the minister will at least tell us what interest rate the Bank of Canada will charge to Great Britain and that he will say whether or not he is willing to let the Bank of Canada lend to public bodies in this country.
In my opinion the statement is most important, because it proves what we have always claimed that the Bank of Canada is in a position to lend money. However, it should stop lending to save foreigners and lend once in a while to help out the Canadian people.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN STERLING SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the sapient comments of the hon. member for Lapointe I think most informed members of the house

will be very glad to hear that the Canadian government has taken the necessary action in the international monetary field to deal with the straits in which our friends in Great Britain find themselves today. However, I think the very situation we have had to move to correct necessitates a far reaching review of the whole international monetary system and indicates the necessity for taking much bolder action in regard to the solution of these problems than has been taken so far.
I hope the Canadian government, at this particular juncture in history when we have to take this action, will press for much more forward looking policies in this field.

subtopic: BANK OF CANADA CREDIT ADVANCES TO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
1. The conditions governing loans and advances which the Bank of Canada may make to the government of Canada or to the government of any province are set forth in section 18 (1) (i) and (i) of the Bank of Canada Act:
[The Bank of Canada may]
"18(1X1) make loans or advances for periods not exceeding six months to the government

Questions
of Canada or the government of any province on the pledge or hypothecation of readily marketable securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province;

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The hon. member raising these innuendos must make a charge and have the courage to stand behind them, or any further remarks on the same point are out of order.

maintopic: STUDENT LOANS-DESIGNATION OF CREDIT UNIONS TO OPERATE AS BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have never seen hon. members opposite so jumpy as they appear to be today, and I have never seen so many red herrings dragged across the trail. They keep asking the hon. member for Yukon how he got access to a report of the R.C.M.P. What they should really be asking is how a report like this was apparently kept under wraps so that members of the government did not have access to it, and the Prime Minister apparently was not aware of its contents, despite the fact that senior civil servants and a parliamentary secretary were named in it. That is what they should be asking themselves.
The first point I want to make is that I do not propose to be a bomb proof shelter for the government. Members of the government have said several times today that I asked for a judicial inquiry, that they are complying with that request and everybody should be happy. This is true; I did ask for a judicial inquiry because I do not think parliament is the place to try a case, and I think that condemnation by declamation is always a dangerous business.
I am anxious to see this judicial inquiry, and I welcome the fact that the government is prepared to have it, but I raise two points. The first is that I feel very strongly the government should have waited until these justice estimates were disposed of, because there may be other matters that ought to come before this inquiry. We as members of the House of Commons have a right to know a great deal more, not about this particular case so much as about the procedures that were followed by the Department of Justice in handling it.
There is information which I would like to have about this matter, but if I may judge from the statement of the Acting Prime Minister this afternoon, this order in council is to be used as a muzzle, to muzzle parliament and keep us from asking questions and getting information. I am not talking about any of

the people implicated; I am talking about the procedures of government.
For instance, I would like to know what was the date upon which the counsel in Montreal is alleged to have been offered a bribe. I would like to know the date when he reported this fact to the R.C.M.P. I would like to know something about the reason for the gap between those dates. I would like to know something about what happened between the period September 18 up to the present time.
An hon. member across the way says we want to have the trial here. I am not proposing a trial. I am not proposing to try the people who are implicated, but I am proposing to ask whether or not the Department of Justice carries out the administration of justice in a proper manner.
I would like to know why this whole thing came up to the Minister of Justice in the first place. I have a suspicion that if I had a complaint laid against me back in Burnaby the chances are that the R.C.M.P. would take it to the crown prosecutor for the area and he would decide whether or not he had a prima facie case to lay a charge against me. I doubt very much if it would be sent up to the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. and he and the Minister of Justice would have a secret conclave to see whether or not they would prosecute.
Are there two sets of laws? Does the process of the administration of justice travel one route when one group of people are involved and a different route when an ordinary group of citizens are involved, those who are not within the hierarchy of the Liberal party? That is the kind of question I want to see dealt with, and I think this order in council should have been held up until after the estimates of the Department of Justice were passed. For instance, one of the reasons is that I understand, if I recall correctly, the hon. member for Yukon had moved what is virtually a motion of no confidence in the Minister of Justice. The only way in which members can decide whether or not to support such a motion is by giving the Minister of Justice every opportunity to discuss fully his handling of the matter. For this reason I do not believe the committee of the whole when it is discussing the estimates of the department should be precluded in any way from discussing this question-not the persons involved; that aspect will be dealt with by the commission, but the whole procedure of the administration
Supply-Justice
of justice in this country and whether it has been carried out in a fitting and proper manner.
The second proviso I put when asking for a judicial inquiry was that it should have the widest possible terms of reference. And this is what the Prime Minister promised as recorded at page 10427 of Hansard. My question was:
May I ask the Prime Minister if he is prepared to see that in the order in council containing the terms of reference there is provision for an investigation into the propriety of the procedure followed by the Department of Justice following the reception of the R.C.M.P. report on September 18.
To which the Prime Minister replied-I will read the latter part of his answer:
The evidence that has been referred to will be before the commission. Any other evidence bearing on what was mentioned and alleged yesterday will be before the commissioner. I am perfectly certain that the commissioner will undoubtedly, in considering the evidence, inquire into the propriety of any action which has been taken.
And, as reported on the next page, when I asked the Prime Minister again whether he would undertake to widen the terms of reference, the right hon. gentleman said:
I believe the terms of reference are wide enough to deal with the matter referred to by my hon. friend but of course there is no desire on the part of the government to hold back anything from this inquiry. We want to make this inquiry both full and fair and I will look at the terms of reference with that in mind.
Well, let us consider these terms of reference. Both the Minister of Justice and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have told us they are in the widest possible terms. As the Prime Minister said, there is to be a judicial inquiry. The recommendation is that a commissioner be appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act-
-to inquire fully into allegations about any improper inducements having been offered to or improper pressures having been brought to bear on counsel acting upon an application for the extradition of one Lucien Rivard and all the relevant circumstances connected therewith-
May I pause here to point out that so far this has to do only with improper inducements offered to counsel or improper pressure on counsel. Now, may I go on:
-and in particular but without limiting the generality of the foregoing to consider fully the reports submitted to the Minister of Justice by the R.C.M.P. and the evidence laid before him in connection therewith and any further evidence elicited by or laid before the commissioner-
Let me pause at this point. The commissioner may look at any information contained

Supply-Justice
in the R.C.M.P. report or at any other information laid before him as a commissioner. It goes on:
-to consider such other matters as may appear to the commissioner to be relevant, and-
Here is the real power which is given to the commission:
-to report whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant any prosecution for offences that may be involved.
I submit there is nothing in these terms of reference which specifically authorizes the commissioner to look into the propriety of the procedures which were followed so as to ascertain whether or not the department behaved properly in not taking action on the basis of the report it had received; whether the minister was derelict in his duty in not notifying the ministers whose staffs were involved; or the Prime Minister, whose parliamentary secretary was mentioned in the report. There is no specific authority given to the commissioner to do this, though this is exactly what we asked for. There is nothing here to follow up the suggestion made yesterday by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, I believe, that the commissioner be allowed to look into the operations of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration inasmuch as they might be affected by the fact that one who had been employed there for a considerable period of time was mentioned in the report.
What did the Prime Minister say about this yesterday? On page 10429 of Hansard, the following exchange took place:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question I should like to direct to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister include in the terms of reference of this judicial inquiry, authority for the judge or commissioner to thoroughly examine the affairs of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration during the employment of Mr. Raymond Denis, in view of the fact that Mr. Denis served in that office for a rather lengthy period of time?

Mr. Speaker, there is now a commissioner inquiring into certain aspects of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration:	I
refer to Mr. Sedgwick. The particular man in question who worked in the department of immigration most certainly will be under investigation by the commissioner.
Today, when my hon. friend from Greenwood asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration whether Mr. Sedgwick was indeed a commissioner and whether he had any authority to investigate the activities of Mr. Denis, the minister had to admit, of course, that he was not a commissioner; that he was brought in as an adviser to advise on the overhaul of the immigration regulations. He

was never a commissioner. There has been an attempt to evade the question completely. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration told us today that Mr. Justice Dorion, the commissioner, would be able to look into this matter. I ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration where under these terms of reference Mr. Justice Dorion has any authority whatever to look into the activities of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration or into the activities of Mr. Raymond Denis during the period when he held high office in that department.
This whole attempt to evade questions and sweep these things under the rug arouses suspicions in my mind which were not there when this business began. Criticism was directed toward the hon. member for Yukon. Members opposite said: Produce charges. But if he had not pursued the matter the other day and if I had not asked the minister whether an R.C.M.P. report was in his possession regarding the allegations of Mr. Pierre Lamontagne, this house and the country would still be in complete ignorance of what has transpired.
It is all very well to say: "Make charges". Members of parliament do not have investigative facilities or powers. We have to rely on the good sense and devotion to duty of the Department of Justice. But, so far, everything we have been able to gather we have had to dig up; we have had to dig it up in spite of every conceivable kind of evasion. Today a minister stands up and tells us: "My department will be investigated by Mr. Justice Dorion." I say an examination of these terms of reference completely refutes that statement. Mr. Justice Dorion will have no power other than the power to look into the allegations about improper inducement and improper practices, to look at the material contained in the R.C.M.P. report, and to consider any subsequent material, and to report whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant prosecution for any offence which may be involved. That is all.
I will not be satisfied until there is placed in the terms of reference a specific instruction to the chief justice to ascertain whether or not the due processes of law were followed and the proper practices respected with reference to the handling of this whole case. I would think that for the sake of the government itself it would have made these terms as wide and sweeping as possible so as to remove any shadow of doubt that may linger in any person's mind to the effect that there

is something amiss in the higher echelons of government administration.

No, Mr. Chairman, I do not have that fear, because I am not asking that a great net be cast to deal with every insinuation or innuendo that may be tossed out. I am asking that in addition to these narrow, specific terms of reference which will cover the allegations about improper inducements and improper pressure and will look into the contents of the R.C.M.P. report, there be an investigation into departmental administration. That is not going to deal with innocent persons; that is going to deal with ministers and senior civil servants and the people who are responsible for administering departments, and whether or not they have discharged their duties with propriety, uprightness and proper dispatch. That is all I am asking. That need not bring in any innocent persons.
I just want to close, Mr. Chairman, by saying that I hope that even though the order in council has been passed-and I have the uneasy feeling that it was passed in some unseemly haste in order to, if possible, curtail any further discussion on this matter- the government will give some consideration to widening the terms of reference as to the propriety of the procedures that have been followed, and also with reference to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, particularly during the period that one of the gentlemen under discussion was employed in that department. As far as I am concerned, I get no pleasure whatsoever in pointing any 20220-667

finger at any person, and least of all people who cannot defend themselves.
I have been, until this matter came to the fore, scrupulously careful not to mention names, although I was in possession of these names when I raised this matter on the orders of the day on Monday. But as a member of this house I have a responsibility, as has every other member, to make sure that the due processes of law are carried through and that when the police report regarding allegations made and complaints submitted concerning certain people in high places, that there shall be no suspicion whatsoever that those persons are being protected and that the charges are being swept under the rug; because it seems to me that any minister of the crown who gets an R.C.M.P. report in which a reputable legal counsel alleges that he was offered a bribe and was subjected to intimidation must know that the person who makes those allegations must have very serious reason for doing so. He had nothing to gain personally by making the allegations, except to protect his good name, and he must have known that this would involve him in publicity and investigation.
Therefore it is a serious matter and I am not convinced that proper attention was given to it and that the proper haste was shown in prosecuting the matter in the manner in which it should have been prosecuted. It is an old saying, Mr. Chairman, and it is still true, that not only must justice be done, but it must appear to be done. For that reason the government would be well advised to widen these terms of reference in order that we may have a full and uninhibited investigation into this whole affair.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
Let me read the reply I made. My hon. friend wrote to me under today's date, as Acting Prime Minister:
Dear Mr. Martin:
During the debate on the estimates yesterday Mr. Douglas, the leader of the New Democratic party, expressed the view that the terms of order in council P.C. 1964-1819 were unduly restrictive and in fact would confine the commissioner to the allegations relating to the inducements offered or pressures to be put upon counsel acting on behalf of Rivard.
I have accordingly redrafted the order in council in such a way as to clarify beyond doubt two further matters:
1. That the commissioner should inquire and report on the way in which the allegations when brought to the attention of the R.C.M.P. and the Minister of Justice were dealt with:
Inquiries of the Ministry
2. That the commissioner should inquire into and report on the activities in the Department of Citizenship and Xmmigraton of Mr. Raymond Denis.
You will recall that the-
I take it that when my hon. friend was asking me a question a few moments ago he was not referring to the person that we are talking about in this letter, Mr. Denis. The question my hon. friend put a few moments ago, I take it, did not have reference to Mr. Denis:
You will recall that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration indicated that this latter matter would be within the purview of the inquiry, but I see nothing in the terms of reference as presently drafted which would permit this.
It is our belief with these expanded terms of reference a full and adequate inquiry would be possible and that no suspicion could arise that there was any intent or desire on the part of the government to limit the inquiry unduly.
And there is no intention on the part of the government to limit the inquiry. Now here is my answer of November 26:
Dear Mr. Brewin:
I have carefully considered your letter expressing the view that the terms of the order in council P.C. 1964-1819 are unduly restrictive and suggesting two amendments thereto.
Your first suggestion is "that the commissioner should inquire and report on the way in which the allegations when brought to the attention of the R.C.M.P. and the Minister of Justice were dealt with". The incorporation of this suggestion in the order in council would be a specific direction to a commissioner who is not a member of parliament to pass a judgment upon a minister of the crown whose responsibility under our system of government is to the House of Commons. After careful consideration, therefore, we felt that we should ask the commissioner to inquire into all the facts and all the relevant circumstances connected therewith and to consider such other matters as may appear to the commissioner to be relevant, to present a report upon these facts and his conclusions to the government and to leave to parliament the responsibility of deciding, as is its right and duty, whether the Minister of Justice had acted reasonably in the matter.
We cannot think that adding to the terms of reference "and into the manner in which the R.C.M.P. and any officer thereof and the Department of Justice and the minister thereof dealt with the said allegations when brought to their attention" would in any way increase the scope of the inquiry, and we would feel that the exclusion of a specific direction to the commissioner to report "whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant any prosecution for offences which may be involved" would be to ignore the original allegations made in the House of Commons respecting the Minister of Justice.
Your second suggestion "that the commissioner should inquire into and report on the activities... of Mr. Raymond Denis" brings in a matter that is not connected in any way with the allegations that have been made.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
I can assure you-

Inquiries of the Ministry
This is the real point, and I am sure my hon. friend, as a devoted upholder of civil rights, will subscribe to this.
-that if any member of the House of Commons, or anyone else, is willing to take the responsibility of making any specific charge of wrongdoing against Mr. Denis, the government will not hesitate to have such charge inquired into fully, but we do not feel that we should set aside the ordinary rules for the protection of the civil rights of an individual and authorize any general inquisition into his conduct when no specific charges or even allegations have been made respecting it, apart, of course, from the one matter which is specifically referred to in the order in council.
And I would add in a parenthesis of my own "based on a charge that was made". The letter continues:
It is our opinion that the order in council is drawn broadly enough to enable the commissioner to inquire and report fully upon all the circumstances relating to the only allegations which have been made in this matter.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In view of the importance of the whole question the Chair has been as lenient as possible, but I would call two citations to the attention of hon. members. The first is a ruling of Mr. Speaker Michener which is to be found in the Journals of the House of Commons, Canada, 1959, at page 583, and the second is a statement I made myself on October 30, 1964, following along the same line as Mr. Speaker Michener, to the effect that if a charge is to be made against a member in the house, a member should take his own responsibility, should stand in his place and make that charge rather than by making miscellaneous remarks which tend to inculpate an hon. member. It is the only fair and proper way or, putting it in another way, in the words of Mr. Speaker Michener at page 584:
In my view, simple Justice requires that no hon. member should have to submit to investigation of his conduct by the house or a committee until he has been charged with an offence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. subtopic: SHIPS LAID UP THROUGH LACK OF TECHNICAL PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report appearing in this morning's Globe and Mail is essentially correct. The action taken does not reflect an over-all shortage of men in the Royal Canadian Navy but rather the lack of sufficient numbers of personnel in certain skilled trades resulting from the introduction into service of new ships and new equipment in ships already built which would require both a higher level of skill in tradesmen and more of them.
This problem has been building up over a period of several years, and a solution would be to increase the number of personnel signing on for re-engagement. Some success has been achieved in this area but not sufficient to fill the gap, and with the requirement for crews for H.M.C.S. Annapolis and Ottawa plus the fact that H.M.C.S. Bonaventure has completed a minor refit, action was taken to tie up six older ships in order to release necessary manpower.
These ships, which are about 20 years old and nearing the end of their usefulness, are nevertheless being maintained in a constant state of operational readiness, and should an emergency arise the crews would be immediately augmented with trained personnel now employed in naval training schools ashore.
We realize that this is by no means a satisfactory state of affairs, and every effort is being made to retain in the navy the necessary number of highly skilled tradesmen. Inquiries of the Ministry is being given serious consideration within the department.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: LONGUEUIL, QUE.-DISPOSAL OF JACQUES CARTIER RESERVE PROPERTY
speechtext:
On Friday last the hon. member for Bow River made an inquiry concerning the sale of some 20 acres of land in the city of Longueuil and suggested I had been dealing with an individual instead of the city.
The lands concerned have been under the administration of my department for an extended period, but were reserved for use by national defence since 1939. In 1960 the municipal officials made application to purchase the property through their member of parliament, Hon. Pierre Sevigny, who was then associate minister of national defence. The military authorities finally agreed to relinquish their interest in the lands, subject to certain conditions, on the express understanding that they would be made available to the national harbours board and the municipality, in that order.
Pursuant to established policy, various agencies were contacted to determine if there were any continuing federal, provincial or municipal requirements for portions of the site, and the public works department selected about 100,000 square feet for an unemployment insurance commission office. The national
Inquiries of the Ministry harbours board waived all further interest in the property, and the only outstanding application was the one filed by the city of Longueuil, formerly the town of Montreal South. In accordance with the principles which were later advocated by the royal commission on government organization, my department undertook to fulfil the commitments made to the civic administrators by national defence in 1960.
However, in view of the fact that the lands were to be used for commercial development, rather than public purposes such as parks, etc., no special concessions were made, and the sale price was established on the basis of recommendations by several accredited appraisers of the soldier settlement and Veterans' Land Act administration. Two offers were rejected because the bids from the city were not commensurate with our equity in the lands, until the municipal council finally agreed to pay the full appraised value of $870,000, which was arrived at by an exhaustive analysis of sales of comparable lots in Longueuil over an extended period. This transaction was formally authorized by order in council P.C. 1964-406, of the 19th March, 1964, and, as soon as a resurvey of our property is completed the sale will be finalized.
Our negotiations have been carried out direct with the municipal council and the city manager and, if successful, it is our intention to convey title in fee simple to the city of Longueuil. Once the lands have been alienated from the crown, resale will be subject to the discretion of the elected representatives of Longueuil and we will have no jurisdiction whatsoever. Neither I nor any officer of my department has been contacted by Mr. Jean-Paul Auclair, as mentioned by the member for Bow River, and it is apparent that any interest which he might wish to acquire must be secured from the city of Longueuil.

Mr. Chairman, even though I have no personal knowledge of this thing

and did not have the opportunity to consult a thick file on the matter we have now been discussing for a week, I feel that the announcement of a judicial inquiry would have been welcomed if the terms of reference had been adequate.
In appointing Hon. Frederic Dorion, the chief justice of the Quebec superior court, to preside over the inquiry, I think the government made a very good choice. Because of his reputation, the appointment of Mr. Justice Dorion will surely be well received and guarantee that this inquiry will be conducted conscientiously and honestly.
However, Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at the terms of reference that have been laid down and under which the inquiry will be held.
A summary of those terms of reference is found in the last three lines of the order in council setting up a commission of inquiry which read as follows:
-to report whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant any prosecution for offences that may be involved.
Well, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) stated many times that sufficient evidence was lacking until now. The inquiring commissioner will therefore have to decide, in other words, whether or not the minister was right in stating that sufficient evidence was lacking. What will then be the minister's role in that connection? As I said the other day, the officials of the Department of Justice will try to prove that there was not enough evidence.
Then, the Minister of Justice puts himself in an extremely weak position because he takes it upon himself to prove that there is not sufficient evidence, whereas he should try to supply sufficient evidence, if possible. But, as he assumes the position that he was right, that there is a lack of evidence, he, therefore, sides with those who might be implicated, if there was sufficient evidence.
Mr. Chairman, you will admit that such an attitude is not normal, that it even means depriving justice of the impartiality which it should have. Under the circumstances, the crown attorney, and the officials of the Department of Justice take it upon themselves to defend those who might be implicated, whereas the opposite should be the case.
Mr. Chairman, we do not want to lay charges. However, some have been laid, explanations have been asked for, and there has been a request that the terms of reference of this commission should be broad

enough to allow a full study of the facts in this affair.
For instance, two days ago, the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Rouleau) resigned as parliamentary secretary. We would not have asked him to resign, since he is innocent until he is proved guilty and since to this date, no charge has been laid against him. What amazes me most in this matter is that his resignation was accepted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). If the Prime Minister had trusted his parliamentary secretary, if he had been convinced that he had nothing to do with that matter, it was his responsibility to turn down his resignation. That is how we would have conceived the role of a leader who has confidence in his parliamentary secretary. But his resignation was accepted. On the other hand, why such haste in resigning?
What amazes me also in this matter is that everything is connected with fairly serious problems. All this is related to an investigation on narcotics smuggling and all those things are brought together.
At the same time, the same individuals on the Liberal side can all be suspected, because it was suggested that six hon. members from the city of Montreal had received $1,000 cheques from Hal Banks, another tie with the criminals and the acts of violence in the Montreal region. But when the 22 hon. members from the island of Montreal are placed under suspicion, we do not approve of such an attitude. Why not name the individuals who are said to have received cheques in an attempt to clear up the situation for the 16 other members? We are told that six of them are supposed to have received cheques, but no names are given and then 22 hon. members are suspected.
We find that it is always the group of hon. members from the island of Montreal who are implicated in such things. Why is it always the same group who get cheques and payments? And, at a certain time you do some people favours contrary to the administration of justice; perhaps too many Montreal members are exerting undue pressure on officials of the Department of Justice in order to allow favours to some of their friends or to people who have rendered them certain services.
When a Liberal member or candidate receives $1,000 from an individual such as Hal Banks, toward his election, that person surely has a claim on him for having paid him that amount and when we find, later on, one year later, that this same Hal Banks gets

Mr. Chairman, just before six o'clock I was saying that in this debate I hoped to be able to muster all the reasonableness and charity that I had, but I must say that having mustered all the reasonableness and charity available to me I find there is only one way in which I can describe the terms of reference and the unwillingness of the government to change the terms of reference in this matter, and that is that they

appear to me to be a studied effort at evasion. The terms of reference as originally drawn were so narrow that they could only invite one conclusion, that conclusion being that the government indeed must have something to hide. I cannot understand any other reason why they would refuse the reasonable request that I am going to describe in a minute to clarify the terms of reference, and make them broad enough to have a full and adequate inquiry.
Again, why does the government seek to hide something? What do they fear? Do they fear a full and adequate inquiry? What is the reason for their fear? I think that is something that this house has to be concerned with and must look into very carefully. As long ago as October 7 the hon. member for Yukon introduced a motion in the debate on item 1 of these estimates to reduce this particular item to $1 and, as I understand it, Mr. Chairman, this is equivalent to a motion of nonconfidence in the minister. I want to explain tonight why we feel obliged, reluctantly obliged I may say, to support that motion.
If the government had been willing to accept a broadening of the terms of reference so that the commission of inquiry could include in its inquiry the basic question, which is the manner in which the Minister of Justice, having been informed of the allegation of attempted bribery, from that point on discharged his duty as Minister of Justice, my observations this evening might have been different. That is the matter that should be inquired into and if it had been included in the terms of reference we would have been very glad in this debate to say that it would be premature for us to come to any conclusions on that particular matter. We would not have attempted to prejudge the decision of the commissioner. We would have waited until the evidence was produced before him and we had had the benefit of his findings in this matter.
But I say to the committee, Mr. Chairman, that it is abundantly clear on any fair reading of the terms of reference that the commissioner is precluded from looking into that basic matter. The terms of reference have been read before and I do not intend to go into them in detail. I simply wish to remind the house that there is only one matter of substance referred to in these terms of reference and that is the allegation about improper inducements offered to and improper pressures brought to bear upon counsel. The one matter of substance that is included in these
Supply-Justice
terms of reference is whether counsel, Mr. Lamontagne, I take it, was in fact offered improper inducements or had improper pressures brought to bear upon him. All the other words that follow from there on are just words to bring in other matters relative thereto, and so on and so forth. They are all connected with this one narrow aspect of whether in fact these improper inducements were offered, and at the end the commissioner is asked to report on one thing and one thing only, whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant a prosecution for offences that may be involved. All the rest is words, Mr. Chairman, and there is no other instruction to the commissioner whatsoever.
When we saw this we were disturbed because of the allegations that have been made. We had hoped that they might have been adequately answered and we felt that although no one in this house and no one anywhere else so far as I know had ever accused the minister or ever will, I hope, of any participation in wrongdoing, nevertheless, despite the fact that no one suggests wrongdoing or any suspicion of wrongdoing on the part of the minister, the Minister of Justice requires more than being above suspicion in that way. His judgment and his ability to deal with matters of this sort are in question and that matter is not within the terms of the inquiry at all. That was made clear by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam when he invited an extension of the terms of reference.

speechtext:
I have not the slightest doubt that the Minister of Justice, in making that statement, is speaking with the greatest of good faith. However, he is a good enough lawyer to know very well that when a matter of this sort comes before the commissioner the judge will decide how the terms of reference are to be interpreted. If the terms of reference are in themselves too narrow to permit the inquiry about which I am speaking, then it does not matter how much the minister says in Hansard: The judge will say, "I am bound by the terms of the order in council".
I point out to the Minister of Justice, the Acting Prime Minister and the other members of the government, that when I wrote to the Acting Prime Minister this morning I suggested that this matter be put beyond any doubt. I said that this should be added to the terms of reference, that the commissioner should inquire into and report upon the way in which the allegations, when brought to the attention of the R.C.M.P. and the Minister of Justice, were dealt with. I still say that it is not too late now. We do not want the minister, who I am sure would like to see the thing fully investigated, to make a statement; we want to see the terms of reference broadened so that when the chief justice comes to deal with the matter he will have terms of reference that will enable him to inquire into this matter, which I say is at the root of the confidence of the Canadian people in the administration of justice under the minister.
I know that the Acting Prime Minister wrote me a letter and made a proposition in his letter in regard to this, with which I intend to deal. I will come to that in a minute. This is only one aspect of the terms of reference. The other aspect that I asked should be included beyond any peradventure was that the commissioner should be given the power to inquire into and report on the activities in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration of Mr. Raymond Denis. I say that if these matters were included so that there could be no doubt the inquiry

would encompass them, then we would be happier and prepared to say that the matter is being looked into fully and adequately, so that we would not be required to censure the Minister of Justice at this time. We would wait to see what the inquiry brought out.
The minister cannot get away from the letter written in black and white and read this morning by the Acting Prime Minister, because it very clearly turns down the suggestion for broadening the terms of this inquiry. Indeed, he used this argument. He said that the incorporation of the suggestion-that is the suggestion that the commissioner should inquire into and report upon the way these allegations were dealt with by the Minister of Justice-would be a specific direction to the commissioner, who is not a member of parliament, to pass judgment upon a minister of the crown whose responsibility, under our system of government, is to the House of Commons. I believe that this sentence contains a dangerous and nonsensical doctrine. Certainly the house should be the final judge of this matter. However, there have been innumerable examples in Canada, Britain and the provinces- I cannot mention them all at the moment- in which the conduct of a minister has been inquired into. I, myself, was counsel on the royal commission on crime in Ontario when the conduct of the attorney general was one of the main subjects of inquiry. To suggest that the commissioner cannot be given that authority to deal with the conduct of a minister of the crown in this case is nonsense. As I said, we are not imputing misconduct in the sense of any participation in wrongdoing. What we are imputing is inadequacy of judgment, the sort of judgment that is required from a person holding the high office the Minister of Justice holds. This excuse, therefore, offered by the Acting Prime Minister as the reason that they will not expand the inquiry is without substance, without meaning, and so far as I can see can only be taken as evidence of a desire to limit the terms of the inquiry unduly and prevent a full inquiry being held.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what about the second aspect of the inquiry, the second item that should be dealt with? There has been clear and undisputed evidence about a person holding a confidential position of executive assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. This credible evidence may turn out to be wrong, but it was given by a man of reputation and substance. This is evidence to the effect that there was a bribe offered by people who were said to have

participated in a narcotics ring through a person holding the position of executive assistant. We say that if that very sensitive position of executive assistant to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is occupied by a man who is found to be intermediary of a narcotics ring, then it is time the whole activities of that particular gentleman in the department were looked into. This is a department where desperate people may be ready to do anything to get into this country. I do not have to bring forward any smear because it has been admitted by the minister himself.
Let us see what the government's attitude toward this matter is. On Tuesday the hon. member for Grey-Bruce got up and said that the inquiry should include these matters. The right hon. Prime Minister answered him in this way saying that Mr. Sedgwick is a commissioner and Mr. Sedgwick is going to look into this matter. This was on Monday. On Wednesday I asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because I knew that was not Mr. Sedgwick's function and he was not going to inquire into the matter, another question. Perhaps the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration had forgotten to tell the Prime Minister what Mr. Sedgwick was doing. The Prime Minister was clearly mistaken. What does the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration say? I will read what he said as reported on page 10517 of Hansard: He was asked by myself about this misunderstanding by the Prime Minister, and he replied:
Mr. Speaker, the setting up of a special inquiry commission under Chief Justice Dorion, as decided by the cabinet, leads us to hope that all the aspects of the problem raised in the house, where the name of Mr. Raymond Denis was involved, will be considered and therefore there is no reason now to believe that Mr. Sedgwick would have to conduct an investigation with regard to Mr. Denis' activities since they will be covered by that inquiry.
So on Wednesday the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration tells us that Chief Justice Dorion is going to look into this matter. What do we find on Thursday, when we point out as I did in my letter to the Acting Prime Minister that this matter was in no way covered in the terms of reference. We find out on Thursday that it is not within his terms of reference at all. Anybody who is interested in the details should read Hansard to see what the minister said in that letter. On Monday it was Sedgwick; on Wednesday, it was the chief justice; and on Thursday no one at all is going to look into this, although

the matter we believe is serious enough that the people of Canada have a right to know the answer. So long as the government continues to insist on its unwillingness to broaden the terms of reference, so long will suspicion be created that they are trying to hide something they do not want the people of Canada to know.
I have said, and I am quite serious in this, that if the terms of inquiry were broadened adequately we would be very glad to have to deal on these estimates with a motion which is the equivalent of a motion of censure on the Minister of Justice. But we are not permitted to take that course. As the Acting Prime Minister has said, that is for the house, and we are now faced with the painful task of deciding whether we should or should not vote confidence in the administration of the Minister of Justice.
I say reluctantly, and I speak for the other members of my party in this matter, that we have come to the conclusion that we have no choice, in the absence of proper terms of reference, but to vote in favour of that particular motion. I said reluctantly, and I mean reluctantly because so far as I am concerned-I cannot speak for everybody here-I have appreciated the fairness and courtesy of the minister. I know of no other member of the government front bench who is more highly regarded, but this is not a matter of personal friendship and good will. This is a matter of adequacy of performance of the vital, important functions of the Minister of Justice.
Before I go on to deal with our conclusions on this matter in detail may I be permitted to say something by way of background. Not only have members of the opposition created an undocumented fiction in this accusation; they have also been able, under the rules of parliamentary immunity, to give this fiction the widest possible publicity.
The immunity of parliamentarians from suits for damage is a necessary democratic safeguard; but its use, in instances of this kind, is being pushed too far.
Members of parliament must be protected in their right, even their duty to speak forthrightly and fearlessly about the behaviour and policies of their colleagues. But when they use this right merely to smear an opponent and thus to destroy him in public life, they are grossly misusing their high privilege.
It is not too much to demand that legislators and parliamentarians use their immunity as a democratic tool rather than a political weapon. It is not too much to expect them to conduct themselves as decently in the House of Commons as they must conduct themselves in open society.

They rather decided to stick to low class discussion which the Canadian people from coast to coast condemn as being incompatible with the almost sacred character that should be reserved to the parliament of the nation.
Consequently, I hope that this fratricidal struggle will be brought to an end, because it could unfortunately degenerate into a national genocide for us in Quebec, leaving it to Hon. Let the unbounded ambition of some yield to moderation. Let the thirst for publicity be quenched by more evident sincerity in parliamentary work. Let the petty politicians try and become politicians worthy of that name and the Canadian parliament will remove the blot on its escutcheon due to the happenings of these troubled days.

This week we have been treated to an example of negligence in high places, I think unexcelled in recent Canadian history, largely brought about because of a conspiracy of silence from the Minister of Justice. The risks this hon. gentleman was prepared to take in September would make the most daring and avid speculator catch his breath. He has hazarded himself and his career. He hazarded, of course, his Prime Minister by withholding vital information from him. He hazarded his party and his government; and he hazarded something he had no right to do-the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the integrity of the whole Department of Justice.
This minister was one who was known as being a devoted public servant before he entered political life, but he has turned his back on the very department and officials with whom he once served and with whom, I would have thought, he would have shared a common loyalty and a common trust. By his failure to share this burden with others
Supply-Justice
he surely has compounded the problem and compounded that which faces all of us when we try to make a judgment about this affair. As a matter of fact I think his omission to tell the Prime Minister is one of the most incredible omissions imaginable and really stretches the bounds of our belief to the very limit.
The Minister of Justice, the Prime Minister and the government, who now scramble behind a narrowly drafted order in council, must share responsibility for any danger done to the reputations of others. The minister must have realized the contents of the R.C.M.P. file could not have been kept from public scrutiny. The minister had many avenues open to him which would have provided a thorough investigation of the charges, but he chose to cover up, thus vastly compounding the hurt to those allegedly involved.
I think we are entitled to some explanations. What explanation could the minister give, for instance, for the failure to inform his Prime Minister of this police report? What excuse could the minister possibly provide us with for his neglect in asking that the contents of the file be examined by independent minds? What reason lies behind the minister's refusal to permit the commission to examine the procedure or the obvious lack of procedure followed by the department in pursuing this squalid affair? What other telephone calls were made to other people during this interesting year? What excuse is forthcoming for any executive assistant, or parliamentary secretary for that matter, communicating with a lawyer engaged in a court appearance? What excuse can the Prime Minister of Canada have for preferring the clear reaches of the west to the place where his duty lies, namely this House of Commons? What is more important this week but for the Prime Minister and the government to take every necessary step to restore the shattered confidence of the people of Canada in the government, and the manner in which they conduct the public business? What is the explanation for the Prime Minister's utter lack of control of members of his cabinet? What is the explanation for the lack of frankness and loyalty of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration?

NATIONAL DEFENCE-SHIPS LAID UP THROUGH LACK OF TECHNICAL PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to use my full seven minutes on this subject. I asked the Minister of National Defence a supplementary question, following upon a series of questions, concerning the matter of housing for armed forces personnel in the Halifax area and elsewhere where our forces are stationed. The minister had said that one of the problems in keeping trained personnel in the navy with the necessary skills to man all of our ships was that there was a certain amount of dissatisfaction with the housing that has been provided for naval personnel.

My question was whether the minister would take immediate steps to initiate a program of housing for naval and other military personnel under which such housing would be intermingled with civilian housing wherever military personnel are stationed. If this were done the result would be that when military personnel came home from work at the end of the day they would come in contact with civilians with other interests living on each side of them. In this way I felt that military personnel would be more a part of the community and would be happier if they were living a normal type of life. A person who happens to be in one line of work does not want to live in close proximity with people who are all doing the same type of work. You will have a far better opportunity to enjoy an ordinary healthy type of community life if you have a bank clerk living on one side of you and a dentist living on the other side, and so on and so forth. It is the variety of interests of your neighbours that makes community life worth while.
I want to compliment the minister and the associate minister on the many changes they have made since this administration came into office. Never before has the Department of National Defence had such expert direction as it has had during that period of time. I suggest that the department should continue its worthwhile improvements in order to provide for our greater security and that the lot of the men and women of the armed forces can be improved by following the policy suggested in my question.
The department should establish such a policy with regard to housing even if the acquiring of land under such a plan may occasionally result in greater cost. Even if it costs a little more, let us remember that the men and women in the armed forces provide security for our country and it is worthwhile to see to it they are well treated. We have to overcome the problem of too many of these skilled people who have been trained at the taxpayers' expense wanting to leave the services prematurely. I hope the minister will look deeply into this matter and will be able to do something about it in the near future.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
As has been stated in the course of the discussion on the estimates of the Minister of Justice, the government is most anxious to have an inquiry which would be comprehensive. We have been giving consideration to suggestions which have been made on this side and on all sides of the house.
Our view was that the original terms of reference were sufficiently broad and comprehensive to take into account everything which could reasonably be considered relevant to the allegations which have been made. However, it is apparent there are some concerns on the part of some members. It is the desire of the government that the inquiry

Administration of Justice should not only be comprehensive but that reasonable and serious concerns that it has all the necessary powers to be so, should be satisfied.
In an endeavour to meet these points while at the same time avoiding certain of the problems which were mentioned in my letter of yesterday to the hon. member for Greenwood, the government has decided on amendments to order in council P.C. 1964/1819 of November 25, 1964. These are set out in an amending order which was passed this morning, copies of which I now table and copies of which, in English and French, I send to the leaders of parties opposite.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext: And read into the record.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
And which I will read. I think with these changes there can remain no reasonable doubt whatever that the inquiry will be comprehensive.
It will be recalled, with regard to one of the amendments to the order, that the Minister of Justice himself rose last night and said that in relation to the correctness of the position he had taken in the matter he would see to it that the commissioner examined that feature. This voluntary statement made by the minister is now incorporated in the language used to provide authority to the commissioner to deal with this very point. I will read the whole of the order in council:
The committee of the privy council on the recommendation of the Prime Minister advise that order in council P.C. 1964-1819 of 25th November, 1964, be amended by deleting, in the first paragraph thereof, all words commencing with the words "to inquire fully'', and substituting therefor the following:
"to inquire fully into allegations about any improper inducements having been offered to or improper pressures having been brought to bear on counsel acting upon an application for the extradition of one Lucien Rivard and all the relevant circumstances connected therewith, including the manner in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and any officer thereof and the Department of Justice and the Minister of Justice dealt with the allegations when they were brought to their attention, and in particular but without limiting the generality of the foregoing to consider fully the reports submitted to the Minister of Justice by the R.C.M.P. and the evidence laid before him in connection therewith and any further evidence elicited by or laid before the commissioner, and, if he considers that there is prima facie evidence of an offence in relation to the activities as an employee of the government or an officer of a department of any person involved in the allegations, to consider such other matters as may appear to the commissioner to be relevant, and to report fully thereon".

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION

Mr. Speaker, in view
of the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Acting Prime Minister, I can only say that this has been a strange story of denial and then retreat. To begin with, the government said it would set up an inquiry that would sit in camera, and had to back down in that regard. Then for a couple of days it was argued by the government, and it was their contention, that the terms of reference in the order in council, hastily constructed in the light of all the political considerations connected with this matter, were sufficiently wide. All of us said they were not; the government said they were. The Acting Prime Minister even wrote a letter in that connection.
Finally today we have the government, having passed one order in council, now amending it having learned that the New Democratic party were going to vote nonconfidence. This government, fearing for itself, has retreated even in the face of what it has done. While it represents, apparently, an agreement between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the Minister of Justice who met together, I doubt whether it goes far enough. But it does indicate the fact that this government knows it has been and is in difficulties.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since this matter was first brought to the attention of the house by a question asked on Monday by the leader of this party our position as a party has been very clear. It was stated explicitly last evening by the hon. member for Greenwood. It has been our view throughout that the matters that have been brought to light should be fully investigated. We felt that the order in council was not drawn in terms sufficiently wide to make possible that full investigation. Yesterday the hon. member for Greenwood, on behalf of this party, put in a letter to the Acting Prime Minister the three points concerning which we thought there should be an amendment of the order in council.
First, it was our belief that provision should explicitly be made for an inquiry into the manner in which the Department of Justice and the Minister of Justice dealt with the allegations when they were brought to their

attention. In the second place, we stated the view that the order in council should provide for an investigation into the allegations made against persons in the employ of the government. In the third place, we asserted that the power of the commissioner to report should be wider. We were disturbed and concerned that the order in council in its original wording seemed to us, at any rate, to limit that power to report to one question and one question only.
We have, as I say, made this clear in statements on the floor of the house. There is nothing to hide when I say we have made this clear in conversations we have had with various ministers of the government. I note that the revised order in council which the Acting Prime Minister has now laid on the table of the house meets the three points the hon. member for Greenwood indicated in his letter. From a quick reading it strikes me that it has met his first point by using verbatim the words proposed by the hon. member for Greenwood, and it has met the other two points in spirit.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we stand by the decision taken on our behalf last night by the hon. member for Greenwood. He stated quite clearly that if the government did not widen the terms of reference we would have no option but to support the amendment of non-confidence that is before the committee of supply. On the other hand, if the terms of reference were widened we would not prejudge the inquiry of the commissioner. In that circumstance we would not vote in a manner to prejudge that inquiry.
The debate this week, Mr. Speaker, need not have taken all this time. The Minister of Justice on Monday last could have answered the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam by saying that he would have a full investigation. However, since he did not do that, this week has shown the value of parliament and the value of constructive criticism, as a result of which these changes have been made. In the light of these changes we feel the house should not prejudge the action of the commissioner to be appointed under this investigation, and therefore that the non-confidence amendment should now be voted down.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the government has acted wisely in yielding to the pressure that has been brought as a result of the debate which has taken place during the last few days regarding widening the terms of reference of the judicial inquiry. Last night the hon.
Administration of Justice member for Sherbrooke, speaking in the debate, made our position very clear when he said that providing the terms of reference of the commission could be extended to encompass all the actions taken within the Department of Justice, we would be prepared to support the estimates of that department.
This revision of the action taken by the privy council has met these requirements. There has been considerable debate as to whether the Department of Citizenship and Immigration should also be included, but I believe that the revision now made, which definitely allows for an investigation of the conduct of an employee of the government or of an officer or employee of the department involved in the allegations which have been made, providing there is prima facie evidence, covers this point as well.
I agree it is rather unfortunate that the Minister of Justice did not agree to this action earlier in the week, in which case much of the time which has been consumed in bitter debate would have been saved. It is imperative at this stage that the government clean its stable. The integrity of the Minister of Justice and his own sense of fairness have not previously been called into question, but now that he has left himself open to the charges which have been made, whether his conduct be the result of an error or mistake in judgment it has become essential that these terms of reference be broadened as they have.
Public opinion is very important at this stage, because not only are the government and the Minister of Justice involved in this matter, but parliament itself. I am very concerned that the image of parliament and the image of we who constitute this House of Commons be not brought into further disrepute as far as public opinion is concerned. To prejudge this whole situation without the fullest possible inquiry into it would likewise be unfair.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of the broadened terms of reference of the judicial inquiry, we in this party give our support and will also assist in the passage of the estimates of the Department of Justice as quickly as possible.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TERMS OF REFERENCE TO INQUIRY COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words in order to state our position in this house concerning this matter.
Yesterday we had decided to vote against the government because, like the other groups of the opposition, we wanted to know the

Administration of Justice truth about this affair. I believe that we would have been blamed by the public had we not participated in forcing the government to broaden the terms of reference of this inquiry.
This morning we learned from the Minister of Justice that after the decision made had been reconsidered, the order in council regarding the creation of that commission was amended so as to clarify this situation.
We are happy to have at last a commission of inquiry which has the necessary powers to reveal everything possible concerning this affair. That is what we were asking for: that all facts be revealed and that justice be made to prevail.
Therefore, we can no longer blame the government if the terms of reference are not sufficiently broad to look further into that affair. However, I regret that we lost two or three days during which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) was quite busy. This is the first time that he presented his department's estimates, and we regret that things have turned out as they did, but we could not do otherwise because we have trust in Canadian justice.
In view of what went on during the last few days, we could not do otherwise, because we wanted to see Canadian justice prevail and retain its integrity, as has always been the case.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: PROTECTION OF HUNTING RIGHTS GRANTED BY TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the orders of the day on November 12 the hon. member for Lisgar asked for assurance that the hunting rights granted to the Indian people by treaty would be protected.
The hunting and fishing rights of Indians under the various treaties is a most complicated subject and has given rise to a number of closely related questions in the house. The first was asked on May 31, 1963, by the hon. member for Skeena following the announcement of the judgment of Chief Justice McRuer of the Ontario supreme court in the Calvin William George case, which involved the application of the Migratory Birds Convention Act on an Indian reserve in Ontario. In reply the Prime Minister indicated that he would be pleased to communicate the decision to other federal and provincial administrations, as well as to do what he could to ensure that the royal proclamation of 1763, and its provisions for the Indian people, would be maintained.
Immediately thereafter we learned that the McRuer judgment was being appealed. As yet no decision has been handed down, and it would therefore be inappropriate for the Prime Minister to circulate for administrative action information on a case which is still before the courts.
Another case which recently received much publicity involved Michael Sikyea, an Indian of the Northwest Territories, who on appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada was convicted of unlawfully killing a duck out of season, contrary to the Migratory Birds Convention Act regulations. There have been other sim-


ilar cases, and I might mention that of Rufus Prince and Robert Myron, involving an infraction of the Manitoba game act, which in December, 1963 resulted in a supreme court decision in favour of the Indians.
These cases are all part of a process to determine the precise quality of the Indian rights under the treaties which must be maintained. Although not a party to the litigation, my department has taken an active and conclusive part on behalf of the Indians and has paid the costs of counsel so that the legal position of a substantial number of Indians in relation to a particular law or treaty, or within a particular region of Canada, could be clarified.
The supreme court judgment in the Sikyea case provides for the first time the precise relationship between the terms of the Indian treaties in the Northwest Territories and the Migratory Birds Convention Act. Other departments of government are involved, and when their views have been obtained the whole question will be considered in detail to determine the most appropriate course of action which might be taken by the government.
