It is like a lot of the allegations which are made; the less information the house has the better. I can understand perfectly why the Minister of Justice feels that this information should not be given the house. Naturally he will be a little embarrassed at revealing to the House of Commons how many of his colleagues he has more confidence in than he has in his own Prime Minister. He does not want to tell us-although he has had to reveal that he did not dare tell the Prime Minister-how many other cabinet ministers, colleagues of his, he had sufficient confidence in that he went to them and discussed the matter with them to see what was in the best interests of the government and of his party. I do not care whether he tells this house or does not; the significance of that action and of his failure to tell his Prime Minister can lead us to no other conclusion but that he had not enough confidence in the Prime Minister to tell him.
I got the impression from the way the secretary of state and the Minister of Transport jumped into the discussion from almost the first day that they were acting like two ministers who had been fully apprised of the situation and had been warned that it was coming up. I would not be surprised if the Minister of Justice had found it politic to take advice of the real front bench politi-

cians of the party. I think it is a shame that he probably took the advice of the politicians rather than the advice of someone would expect to be more interested in the proper administration of justice than in pure politics.
I wanted to comment briefly, Mr. Chairman, on a point which was brought out by the Minister of Justice and reiterated by the hon. member for Verdun and other hon. members opposite. I am sure no member of this house will quarrel very violently with the proposition that it is most unfortunate to have the name of a person smeared by allegations unless or until that person is facing a trial. However, I would ask hon. members opposite to consider what happens to the average citizen who is suspected of a crime, and an investigation by the police follows. Let us consider the amount of consideration given to the average citizen who does not have as his friend or employer the Minister of Justice. Across the length and breadth of the country thousands of criminal charges are laid every day and good citizens are hauled into court for the first time. When I say "good citizens" they are citizens with no previous record who so far as their friends and neighbours are concerned enjoy a spotless reputation. Many charges against citizens brought to court for the first time go no further than the preliminary hearing, after which the case is dropped. Some are arrested, their names appear in the paper, but the matter does not even get to the preliminary hearing stage before the case against them is dropped.
I suggest to the minister, who shed crocodile tears over the slurring of the reputations of the two gentlemen involved here, that it seems to me he has gone just a bit too far in his solicitude. His most prominent duty is to make sure that justice is done. Certainly the most solemn duty he has is to make sure that the appearance of justice shall not be tarnished. It must be obvious to all that there is such a thing as fair and equal treatment to all citizens, not just fair treatment to the friends of the minister.
This is a point which I think has not been mentioned enough in this house but which has been beaten to death on the Liberal side of the house, namely what is fair to those two people. Certainly if a cabinet minister is fair and impartial he must expect that judges, on whose activity he must keep an eye, must be fair and impartial as well. But he knows from his own experience in court that practising lawers of many year's experience who are appointed to the bench do not automatically acquire an ability for impartiality. This is

something which is built up over the years. How the Minister of Justice can stand in his place and eloquently state that he had to be fair to that one citizen, just as though he were a practising lawyer in court talking of his client, when his own duty, which should be uppermost in his mind, is to watch for any weakness in his own character which would not permit him to be impartial when he is closely touched by the affair is beyond me. Certainly he has enough experience to recognize this.

The answer is obvious. Not having seen the report and not knowing the evidence I would be silly to try to suggest what charges should be laid in view of the way the minister has handled the case. I am not saying that charges should in fact have been laid at all. I do not know. Maybe they should, maybe they should not. But what is obvious is that we do know the manner in which the matter was handled. We do know the duty of the Minister of Justice. I was explaining to this committee what the Minister of Justice should know, when it comes to a question of judgment, that the degree of impartiality required in a court of law is something which judges usually acquire only after long practice, and I sometimes think some of them do not acquire much of it even after many years. The minister should know that this is a great weakness. It is a human frailty of most of us, no matter how honest we may be, that we are simply incapable of coming to a really impartial decision, especially when it concerns the welfare of someone we know, someone for whom we may feel great pity, as obviously does the Minister of Justice to the gentlemen involved here.
I simply want to re-emphasize to this committee the unfitness for office of a minister of justice who puts his duty to his friends, his personal loyalty to them, first; who is unaware of that natural disability which we all have, that incapability of being completely im-

Supply-Justice
partial, and who should have known that he could not make a proper judgment.
He failed to report to his Prime Minister, in whom he should have great confidence, so that he might have obtained proper advice as to how to handle the situation. I suggest the fault lies in this complete failure on his part to do his duty to his department and to the administration of justice in this country. That is his first and predominant duty and he must sacrifice all else in order to carry out that duty. If he is not willing to do so-and he has shown by his attitude in this house during the past several days that he is unwilling-or has not realized his shortcomings, he should not occupy the position he now occupies, because he is not mentally suited for it. I say that without in any way impugning the honesty of the gentleman. I believe he is completely honest but suffers from a very high degree of stupidity.
In spite of all the comments and facts which have come to light, the minister still fails to show any recognition of the attitude that must be adopted by a minister of justice. I am not sure whether other members of this house become as inflamed as I do about this kind of situation, but I have observed many court cases in which a policeman has failed to do his duty, the crown prosecutor has failed to do his duty, and lawyers have been very harshly treated for making an honest but stupid mistake. In those circumstances a lawyer is likely to be suspended or disbarred. Certainly when we observe this obvious example of stupidity on the part of one so close to the seats of the mighty, one who should not only show but should exert the highest standards possible, it is unacceptable to the point that I would be surprised by any hon. member in this house who would seriously disagree with the comments I have made.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks about this subject under discussion, and in view of the fact that I have not been in the house during the last four days but have been in the far north, I may have some detachment that others, who have participated in the debate during the last week, may not have.
There is one issue which has not been discussed that I should like to raise seriously for consideration by the minister. That issue is whether people who aspire to and achieve high public office have a responsibility at all times to not only level with the public but give the appearance at all times of being completely and scrupulously honest. When a report falls into the hands not only of members of the treasury benches but of any member of parliament which suggests some impropriety, it can only be dealt with satisfactorily in the minds of Canadian people by an open and thorough study.
That has not taken place in respect of the case now under consideration. It is obvious from reading the debates which took place last week, which I might say have been very stormy, that the resignation of the parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister only came about after the facts were smoked out into the open by the hon. member for Yukon. The hon. member was not named by the member for Yukon, but it was only until after several days of suggestions that others in positions of influence had been involved that his admission was forthcoming.
While all of us are happy today that the terms of reference of the judicial inquiry have been expanded so that all aspects of the case can be looked into and, hopefully, cleared up, I am wondering whether any other parliamentary assistant should make a statement

During the last few days the house has been interested in the developments that have taken place, and I think the country will watch very closely the attitudes that have been taken toward some of these things. However, Mr. Chairman, I am sure in calling the justice estimates when we did we did not expect they were going to last this long. When the house leader made the arrangement for the limitation of debate on the estimates we did not consider we were going to be taking this length of time on them. I should like to say that I personally think we owe a vote of some type to the hon. member for Yukon for bringing these matters to the attention of this house. Personally I feel quite sad that it had to be done in this way; however, I know of no other way of doing this. I have seen this done a number of times since I have been here, and I know of no other way in which this type of matter can be raised.
I feel it is very foolish for some hon. members on the other side to say the things they have said. I suggest also that it is unfair if the opposition continues to rag the government after a judicial inquiry has been

achieved, because I am sure it will get to the bottom of the matter with which hon. members have been concerned. Personally I have been hoping we would come to a consideration of penitentiaries, because I should like to change the subject for a moment, through I know this is not nearly as important in gaining headlines as is the case when people are being tried.
However, those who have been tried and found guilty are asking for a hearing in this place. I think it is necessary for someone to speak about some of the abuses that take place in our penal system. I would be very optimistic if I thought I was capable of changing the attitude of parliament, of the press and the public into one which would give assistance to some of those on behalf of whom I wish to make representations.
I should like to refer briefly to the riot that took place in St. Vincent de Paul. I have discussed this with many guards, as have people on a number of television programs, with a number of prisoners and some others who are connected with prisons and have been connected with them from a time prior to this riot. I want to be very fair. There is a new warden at this penitentiary, a warden who was not responsible for the riots. In my opinion he has gone a long way toward correcting some of the abuses that took place in that prison. The Minister of Justice is going to have to consider some of the results that have accrued from that riot and their effects upon individuals.
I believe this Minister of Justice is fair and reasonable, but that he is not fairly well attuned to the political climate that we have in parliament. This may be the result of his civil service background. I am sure I could have been of some assistance to him if I had been sitting behind him during the last two or three days. I do believe he is honest and that he is going to do something about penal reform. Anyone who read the statement he made, but which got lost in all this other confusion and court procedure we have been engaging in, must have seen in it a great response to the requirements which have been indicated by all the organizations interested in penal reform.

Then I shall be pleased to continue, because I have an amendment to move. Recently we received a delegation which discussed many aspects of prison reform. Its members were interested in many of the things I have been advocating for years, such as conjugal visits to prisoners and better rehabilitation before a prisoner is released. We also had a visit from a person recently released from St. Vincent de Paul, who told us of conditions there which I believe make it the duty of any member of parliament, aware of them, to investigate the problem. We went to St. Vincent de Paul in company with this gentleman, and none of the things he told us were incorrect. He may have exaggerated a bit. Many hon. members may have seen him on television and, like many other persons, he has a propensity to exaggerate. The penitentiary staff gave us every cooperation, and we were able to ascertain many of the things which the minister himself must have learned, as revealed by his statement.
I am still of the opinion that there should be only one committee established. I do not want to be a member of a committee which is going to visit Stony Mountain and all the other penitentiaries merely to look at their physical aspects. I feel that unless one has an inside line into a prison nothing will be

Supply-J ustice
seen that could not be seen on an ordinary visiting day. A prison is a big institution and many things go on in it. I do not believe anyone would hide anything from such a committee, but I do not believe everything would be shown. Therefore such trips around the country would be without much purpose.
However, I believe every member of parliament should be pledged to the reform of our penal system, should be interested in sentencing, pre-sentencing, trial procedures and equality of sentences for similar offences. This is why we ask the minister to establish only one committee, and if he likes to put representatives from other associations on it we would be pleased to have them.
Dealing with the riot in Montreal, I have before me a copy of a sessional paper which indicates some of the conclusions reached as a result of the inquiry. One of these points to the fact that there was maladministration at St. Vincent de Paul. I have not yet heard whether this committee has reported to the minister, and I would like to know whether he has received the report on maladministration.
I have talked to many guards who confirm that prior to the riot the warden at St. Vincent de Paul had got to the stage where he met every morning with two homosexual inmates, who did not live in the prison proper but slept in the administration offices. The guards have admitted they were not able to see the warden; that they would lay charges against prisoners but would then find the warden would call in his special informants, two homosexuals who slept in the administration offices, and get his information from them with the result that conditions in the prison deteriorated.
I am sure the second report must indicate that the maladministration was the total responsibility of the warden in charge of the penitentiary at that time. Where is this warden today? He has been promoted. He was a flop as a warden, but now he is the information officer of the department. So far as I am concerned, before these estimates are passed that man's salary must be deducted from them because I have tried him and found him guilty of gross maladministration, and so far as I am concerned under the circumstances I am not in agreement with paying his salary. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare disagrees, then I can go into this case and explain many more things. All I am asking now is that the minister tell us whether he has received the report of the commission

which dealt with maladministration at that institution.
I have here a letter from a prisoner which I would like to read to the committee. He is a man who was accused of manslaughter. You may remember the case. His wife and he rented a canoe at the dock below the parliament buildings and went out into the bay. A pleasure boat went by and the canoe was upset. The man swam ashore; the woman was drowned; he was charged with manslaughter and sentenced to five or six years at St. Vincent de Paul. I have a thick file of the evidence in his case. It is in French and I have not yet been able to get the Secretary of State's department to translate it so I do not know much about the case, but in his letter to me he talks about the riot at the prison. I should point out that French is his principal language but he wrote this letter in English because he knows I and my colleague do not understand that language. His letter reads:
Mr. Frank Howard and Arnold Peters.
Dear Sirs:
The great sense of justice that was emitted by you, while visiting St. Vincent de Paul, has force me to write and relate to you the unbelievable events which took place in June 1962. Your visit has shown that there still are some human beings in society that are trying to end the suffering of their human brothers.
The following story, incredible as it may seem, is the truth.
The 21st of June 1962, I was brought out of my cell 2-V-16 by guards Lafranee and Leroux, who told me then that I was wanted in the nerve centre of the penitentiary. My hands were handcuffed behind my back and we started to go toward the dome. While walking, they punched me behind the neck without provocation.
I said to them: It is not a big score hitting a man who is tied up.
As I was a big man weighing about 190 pounds and practicing weight lifting, Lafrance said to me: "It is you, Nick the he-man? Wait a minute bastard, I will fix you up". We passed through the dome going to the hospital. After arriving they pushed me down the stairs, kicked me, then dragged me in the "hole".
"Holes" are segregated cells which are closed off; there are no beds and people have to lie on the floor.
After arriving there we went in a small room where I was frisked, undressed. After this, wearing only underwear I was put in a cell-No. 6- where a dozen human monsters were waiting for me. Their names are: Lafrance, Edouard Pepin, Lagueux, Leroux, Martel, Tellier, Fortin, Lang-lois, Lacombe, Lemay, Prevost, Cousineau.
Lafrance encircled my neck, Leroux paralysed my arms, then they asked me: Who was the bastard wearing the white T-shirt? I said: Nobody wearing a white T-shirt was with me June 17. One said: We will refresh your memory you no good dog." Another said: "Guard Proulx

told us that you were the leader of the riot and his assailant". "Confronted with him would you deny this?" I answered "Yes" Suddenly Pepin and Martel started to hit me, which awakened the sadistical tendencies of the others. "Result?" I was brutally kicked, hit with fists, black jacks; I fell on the wooden bed, kicked over and over in the face, head, ribs and before falling unconscious kicked in the genital parts. I awakened the next morning feeling pain all over, dazed, bloody. The floor was covered with my human waste. Suddenly I remembered the reception I had the previous day. I concluded that being kicked so many times in the belly, my bowels had agitated and this was the result. My head was cut and bruised, the rest of my body as blue as a navy uniform. My genital parts were swollen the size of a football and multicoloured. An excruciating pain stopped me from walking. That was the way I was treated (disgusting, is it not?) I managed to fix a bandage for my cut head by tearing my underwear. A while later, I heard a commotion. Painfully I went to the door which had a little porthole in the centre that served to keep vigil on prisoners. Suddenly, I heard a guard screaming excitedly, "Here comes Gunn, here comes Gunn" by the porthole, I saw Pepin and Lafrance followed by guard Proulx who was dressed in civilian clothes, dragging Alvin Gunn.
They threw him in cell No. 5 beside me, and followed him in. A few minutes later, I heard meanings and noise coming from the cell. It sounded like punches, kicks, black jack hits. It continued for about 15 minutes. Suddenly, I heard a voice (which sounded like Lafrance) say get the stretcher he's unconscious. I thought he was dead. They probably took him to the hospital. A while later my door was opened. I said to myself maybe Gunn is dead, and they are coming to murder me. Proulx, nicknamed "Killer", came forward with Lapointe (keeper of the hole), Lafrance, Lemay, Pepin, Martel, Lagueux, Leroux, Tellier, Lacombe, Langlois and Fortin. Lafrance said to me: "Will you deny that you are his assaulter and the leader of the riot?" Killer Proulx is here now." I said: Yes I deny it! I pursued by saying: even though I am hurt, you won't force me to accuse myself; I have enough courage left in me to fight you one by one! I talked that way then because, I thought I would die anyway. Finally I said: I'd rather die than talk with you. Immediately, I was hit over the head with a contendent object-
I believe he means a blackjack.
-blood streamed down my neck, guard Proulx punched me in the face. I was slugged over the head with black jacks, kicked by the others. I fell on the floor. While I was in a state of semiconsciousness, I saw Pepin, Lafrance and Proulx looking at me with the most heinous looks I have ever saw. My indignation then knew no bounds, how can sadistical treatments like these be still happening? Were we in a Monte Cristo jail era? It did not end there. Pepin kept on kicking me, until an unknown guard dragged him away from me. Then I fell unconscious once more to wake up a while later seeing by the half open door of my cell, Lecorre, Dr. Lefebvre and Nurse Hudon staring at me without doing anything, even if I was hurt. To be brief, they have participated by failing to do their duties and stop the carnage. This proved that they cannot be given important duties. After my door was locked I heard screams from the other inmates who were getting beaten up. A nurse came in and bandaged my head. I think it was Paulin. Pain stopped me from eating, my head was full of
Supply-Justice
lumps, my genital parts hurt so much I had to hold them when I walked. A few days later Lecorre came, he looked at me and went away. They changed me from cell No. 6 to No. 5 where A1 Gunn had been beaten. The cell had been washed, but blood spots were still visible. I thought he was dead. Myself the only thing that saved me was my strong constitution. Today my reflexes have diminished; I don't think I would be able to bear what I have endured in the hole. I am physically and morally affected. Three weeks later I was taken out for a shower-
Note that. It was not until three weeks later that he was taken out for a shower.
-my bandage was stuck to my wounds. I had to use soap to unstick it and it was very painful. A spot about 3 inches by 2 inches in the back of my head was free of hairs. Then "coco" Paul-Emile Demers No. 6201 saw me and said: "Nick, what have they done to you? You are in bad shape, Look in the mirror".
I did not look because I knew I was cut all over. Demers himself had been beaten and was blue all over his body from the punishment he suffered. I asked for the nurse who came and bandaged my head. A few days later they took me out for a 15 minute exercise.
This is almost a month later.
The other inmates hardly could recognize me. While in the hole we were served meals without soup, tea, dessert and this for over a month. What a treatment after being nearly killed. We were transferred in segregation C-B-l and while there A1 Gunn complained to Lecorre about the soup and finally we started to get it at every meal. Everything was done and is still being done to break my spirit where I am confined since July 1962.
He is confined in segregation. He is in that cell 23J hours a day as punishment for a riot which took place 2-| years ago.
The ignominies that the inmates have suffered and are still suffering to this day must be uncovered for the sake of our sanity. This contemptible institution is directed in an idiotic manner. The only action they take is revenge. When after being provoked for years an inmate looses his nerves and gives a well deserved punch in the kisser to a sadistical guard the newspaper try to get the poor guy's head. But does the newspaper print the infamies that are committed here? No, even though they are aware of them.
Now you are asking yourselves after reading this story: How come this happened to him if he is innocent? Here is the answer.
The day of the riot, guards were all excited and they were shooting at anybody. I asked guard Proulx politely to tell the guard over the carpenter shop to cease fire as innocent inmates were getting shot at without provocation.
I have discussed this with several of the guards and I understand Nicholas did not do this as gently as he indicated. But this is one of the things he did; he tried to get them to stop shooting. This is one of the ways in which he participated in the riot.

Supply-Justice
A while later after guys were getting shot I asked the same question of Lecorre. Is it a sin to ask for the cessation of a massacre? Results? They had to find a scapegoat and I was chosen. For this I was given 14 additional long years. If I had been guilty I would have taken my medicine. All this because a ridiculous penitentiary had concluded (framed) that I was a rioter.
Dishonest guards have committed perjury-
I stop there, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that many of these guards did commit perjury.
-some of them were fired from this institution.
I would point out that some have been charged and have been let out of the service; others have quit. I go on with this letter;
The yard is about 16 acres in size, full of buildings. The day of the riot a dense black smoke was covering the yard. How can a man, in these conditions, see convicts about 300 feet away; a bunch of them with blue sweaters, pick one out of them and say he was a rioter? Well maybe they are lynx! That is it! I have lost great confidence the way justice is carried out there, even though I am a person of good will. My parents have suffered very much, the day I was sentenced.
I am innocent, and once for all a royal inquiry should be made about my trial, a revision of it for the sake of justice. I do not want a conditional release-
You should note this, Mr. Chairman.
I do not want a conditional release, which would be an affirmation of guilt. What I want is a full pardon or at least a retrial.
We want in this institution, rehabilitation facilities, work, occupation of some kind. We are fed up with being locked up to vegetate with moral turpitude for years. For Christ sake, will some people of good will do something? Will it change? I sincerely hope it will for the sake of us.
St. Vincent de Paul is a public disgrace, and presently it only breeds psychopathy, insanity, hate. I end this letter by asking justice for me and all the others in here. Also hope you will do something to ameliorate the fate of hundreds of human beings.
In you we trust to accomplish the impossible.
Thank you very much.
I could also read a letter written to the commissioner of penitentiaries. This is the problem; I do not know whether there was an answer to this letter that was written to Mr. MacLeod, the commissioner of penitentiaries, because I do not have access to all this information. But I believe this is a great deal of the problem in St. Vincent de Paul. The prisoner never knows whether his letter has been answered; he never knows whether his request goes anywhere; he is completely isolated from the warden. When I went to Kingston penitentiary I found that the warden knew the prisoners by name. I was surprised to find out that in St. Vincent de Paul the last time the prisoners had seen the warden was when he was in there after the riot. I
also found out they have not had any connection with him other than when he made his Christmas broadcast last year. They do not know whether the warden is a good guy or not. They think he stopped the beatings about six months after the riot took place, but they do not really know. The previous warden is a disgrace to the prison service and it is a damned shame that we still have him and are paying him $14,000 a year. I suggest that before these estimates are passed his salary should be deducted from them.
I should like to continue with Gaston Nicholas' case. This case has been reported widely in the newspapers, and I think at the request of the commissioner of penitentiaries Mr. Nicholas has been moved to Kingston penitentiary. I thank the commissioner for having done this. I would also suggest this is not really enough, because I have talked to many people in similar circumstances in St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, people who were connected with the riot. I am told there has been consideration by commissions that have sat and dealt with this matter, but it was indicated to me that those trials were a mockery of justice.
Alvin Gunn, O'Brien and Melangon were indicated as the leaders in the riot. Only twice in the evidence regarding the riot is there any evidence that Gaston Nicholas was involved, and then only in a very minor manner. Gaston Nicholas went before a court in Montreal and was sentenced to 14 years imprisonment for his participation. He was charged with causing public mischief. Public mischief; and he got 14 years. Is that fair? Mr. Alvin Gunn, who admits himself that he was a leader-he said he was pushed into it, but admits he was a leader of the riot- says that Nicholas was not one of the leaders. He went before the new attorney general of the province of Quebec, Mr. Wagner, who was the judge in his case. Mr. Wagner heard witnesses on both sides. He heard in particular from a chaplain. I asked the chaplain why he did not testify in the other cases, and he said "My effectiveness was only good in one case and I had more personal knowledge about this case. I picked that case to testify about".
Mr. Wagner when hearing this case heard evidence that Alvin Gunn had been beaten almost to death. He lay in hospital for four days and was not expected to recover. What did the penitentiary do about it? Did they send a doctor on the first day to see him? Did they send a doctor on the second day? The third day was St. Jean Baptiste day so they

did not send any doctor then, either. It was four days before a doctor saw this prisoner. When the present attorney general of Quebec, the judge in this case, heard the evidence he sentenced Mr. Gunn to one day's imprisonment, to run consecutively. You can look at the return made in this house on November 16 and you will find the offences listed there. Mr. Melangon-I do not know him; I have not met him-got two years on the first and second charges and three years on the third.
Another man who has always been mentioned is O'Brien. There was not sufficient evidence to convict him and he was acquitted. He was acquitted on the evidence of some of the prisoners who received very severe sentences. Five years went to the other leader of the riot, the sentence being consecutive to the sentence imposed by Judge Provost. Each of these sentencing judges passed different sentences. I do not know what the defence was. I know these people do not have any money. I do not know whether defending lawyers are provided in Montreal. I understand that some of them see a defending lawyer only half an hour before their trial commences.
There was a great deal of evidence that the penitentiary staff would not allow lawyers to come in, and that these men were discouraged from having lawyers. But this man received a sentence of 14 years imprisonment. The appeal period has gone by and I know that justice cannot be served now. I do not know whether the minister has the right to ask for a new trial; I do not know whether it would serve any purpose. But we had better ask ourselves one thing. What the hell are we doing with these prisoners? Do we want to rehabilitate them or do we want to punish them? If you wanted to punish Gaston Nicholas, why didn't you put one more guard in there and kill him, instead of beating him half to death?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON ATLANTIC DEVELOPMENT BOARD
speechtext:
This man's nerves are bad; his mental condition is not good. He says himself that he is mentally upset. The staff are accusing him of inciting this riot. He was segregated for 23 months in a cell and was not in contact with any other prisoner, had no job and received no exercise except for this half an hour; and they do not get even this amount of exercise every day. We treat these men as animals. We treat Gaston Nicholas as an animal because he participated in a riot. His participation was grabbing the warden and telling him "For God's sake don't shoot my friends who are lying on their
Supply-Justice
bellies on the ground". Don't forget, Mr. Chairman, that the smoke was down almost to the ground, and also that the army was in there, the federal police were there, and all the guards. Most of them have never fired a gun in their lives.
The minister will have to do something about this, because the situation is a disgrace. I do not blame him for it, but in all honesty he must do something about it. These men got rid of $2 million worth of property. Guards should be well enough trained to see that property is not destroyed. We do not want homosexuals sitting in an office with the warden drinking coffee every morning. That is not the way to run a prison. Why should this man be promoted to this position? This is not a Sunday school outing. What is an information officer for the penitentiaries branch anyway? Is this a $14,000 a year job which some clerk did before? We should not put him in a soft job to keep him out of trouble.
I know the minister has considered this problem, and I appreciate that he has given the penitentiaries more consideration than they have had for many years. He is, in my opinion, energetic and is making decisions in light of the over-all problem. But as long as the back door to a prison exists there will be no more beatings in St. Vincent de Paul, because I am sure they will get news of any beatings straight to parliament. So it will not happen again. They will carry the blackjack for self defence from now on.
I know the minister will correct some of these problems, but I should like to know what will happen to the people who took part in the riot and to the general inmate population of the prison. I do not suggest you should let all prisoners out for exercise every Sunday, but there must be enough guards provided to let one half out one day and the other half out another day. When there was a riot at Dorchester we did not cut off for three years the privileges of all the prisoners, many of whom had nothing to do with the riot. I am sure this was not done at Stony Mountain and at all the others. There have been riots at Kingston. Kingston has been burned on a number of occasions, but not all the prisoners were penalized. In my opinion this hits at the whole idea of reform.

speechtext:
I do not wish to say much more, Mr. Chairman. In St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary there is still a terrific fear on the part of the guards. This arises from their lack of training, which is being corrected with the building of a training centre, but it is my suggestion that some of the guards at Kingston be transferred to St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary and some of the guards at St. Vincent de Paul be transferred to Kingston on a temporary basis. I have been in Kingston penitentiary, and I found a much better morale among the guards there than at Montreal. I found this was mainly because the guards at Montreal have not had the opportunity for training as have the guards in the other institutions. I know the minister has this matter under consideration and will consider it. I think the chief warden at St.

Vincent de Paul is to be complimented on the fact that he has been able to eliminate most of these abuses.
I might mention that under the former warden it was possible for a homosexual to be moved into a cell next to his friend; this was always arranged for with the guards. Perhaps there is nothing wrong with this, because I do know some of the problems connected with homosexuality. I do not know what you can do about it in prison. The prisoners themselves say that this affects 60 per cent of the prison population and affects the guards too, though not all according to Mr. Gunn. But it is a factor which has to be considered, and the guards should be sent to a proper training centre where competent people will be able to train the staff.
The penitentiaries are also plagued by a lack of psychiatrists. For example, the psychiatrist in charge of Kingston penitentiary said something which surprised me, and that was that we have such better success in curing psychiatric patients in the penitentiary at Kingston that we sometimes send other patients there too. This psychiatrist to whom I talked indicated that they were able to keep them within the confines of the prison because of the better environment, which I think is the word he used.
What do they do with these patients at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, Mr. Chairman? They put them in a dungeon in the basement, a rat infested place where no person could ever be treated. There is only a part time psychiatrist, and all he seems to do is give them pills. When the goof ball rumble commenced they said it was due to the psychiatric patients. Half of the prisoners convicted as leaders were doped up with goof balls.
Although the psychiatric aspect is very important there is no excuse for it. I say to Mr. MacLeod, the commissioner, that there is no excuse for not immediately evolving some system whereby the complaint of an inmate is referred to some designated person who will be able to give a reply the following day. I found when at St. Vincent de Paul that the morale of the guards was much higher four years ago under the former warden who has now retired, whose name was Lacourt or something like that. He used to see all the inmates who had complaints. I do not say that all complaints should be handled in this way because probably the warden would have more to do than that, but the prisoners should be able to go to somebody.

Let us suppose, Mr. Chairman, that you are a prisoner in jail. A prisoner may receive a letter indicating that his wife has decided to leave him and live with the next door neighbour because he is not there. The prisoner immediately wants someone with whom he can consult, someone who will not only make an effort to do something in the prison but will, if possible, contact the John Howard society, the Elizabeth Fry society or other agencies including the Salvation Army, so they may visit his home and talk to his wife because he is not allowed to do. I think a prisoner has a right to expect that this will be done on his behalf. They should not be thrown in a dungeon to which the key is thrown away.
Mr. Chairman, I have a letter here and a reply from the deputy warden, in his own handwriting, which contains a picture of Gaston Nicholas' little girl. This picture was sent to him and is of his six year old daughter dressed in a confirmation dress. He wanted to have possession of this picture in his cell, but he was not permitted to do so. There are stooges today who carry the keys to the locks on their cells at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. Those individuals have their cell walls covered with pin-up girls. I see the commissioner shaking his head, but he was with me when I visited those cells and knows that that is the situation. Why should we allow this situation to exist, yet not allow a prisoner such as Nicholas to have this picture of his little girl in her confirmation dress? I think that is a reasonable request on the part of any prisoner.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to belabour the point, but there seem to be discriminatory practices in various penitentiaries. I believe this situation has existed for a long period of time. I know what Mr. MacLeod said in this letter, and that he was influential in having this prisoner transferred to another penitentiary. I am sure that through investigation he would find that this man is not a vicious or antagonistic prisoner. While he is very highly strung, he is serving whatever sentence has been imposed upon him. He has now served one year of the new 14 year sentence, and I think some consideration should be given to him.
If the minister is not interested in the individual prisoners themselves and their representations, all his highfalutin' statements about changes to be made at the higher echelon level will be to no avail. These prisoners must feel that the minister is their
Supply-Justice
friend and that justice is being and will be done. They must also be convinced that the officials believe they are not fair game for anyone just because they have been convicted of an offence. We must convince them that they cannot be punished in any other way or in addition to the sentences imposed by the courts for the offences of which they have been convicted. When one looks down the rows of segregation cells he will find that individuals have been kept there in some cases for 23 months, not even knowing when they were going to get out. That is not fair and just treatment but a form of punishment worse, in my opinion, than corporal punishment. The lash is used at the Kingston penitentiary, and if by using the lash there they have done away with the practice of segregating prisoners one might even consider that a less barbaric form of penal reform.
Mr. Chairman, I will conclude my remarks by suggesting that anyone who has listened to the story told by Gaston Nicholas will realize that he is not an unreasonable prisoner but an individual who feels he has been taken advantage of, that justice has not been done and that he is being punished to a greater degree than the punishment imposed on him by the court for the offence he committed.
It is my understanding that the original court case involved grave doubts as to whether he was guilty of manslaughter. As I remember the circumstances, some evidence about an insurance policy came to light several weeks after the death had been certified as accidental drowning, at which time the case was reopened. There was considerable doubt about the innocence or guilt of this man at his first trial, and if by some strange quirk of justice he is innocent, one can imagine the agitation of his mind at times when he is unfairly treated, to say nothing of the fact that he is serving a lifetime sentence for something that he at least claims he did not do.

National capital commission-
60. Operation and maintenance, general administration and interest charges on outstanding loans that were made for the purpose of acquiring property in the national capital region, $5,420,000.

I am interested particularly in a decision that is being made, and which is before the house, in relation to moving the railway station. I am curious about whether or not if we defeat this bill, the capital commission will still be empowered to go ahead and move the station. I should like to know if we have the right to instruct the national capital commission as to the wishes of parliament.
I do not want to belabour the point, but in my opinion, this should be the last time the national capital commission estimates are brought before parliament in this way. I believe the commission itself should appear before a committee of the house so that hon. members could be acquainted with what the commission is doing and the commission could

receive some direction from members of parliament. I believe that when the former government was in office they decided to divest the prime minister of this responsibility and put it under the ministry of public works. I believe the capital commission should be in the same category as Canadian National Railways and some of these other large government operations and should, therefore, come before parliament in one way or another for direction.
I believe there are many members in this house who believe a commuter station should be constructed, not necessarily anything like we have down here now, in the centre of the city. In this way Montreal and Ottawa could be connected by means of a rapid transit service. This commuter service could utilize a two track road through a tunnel from the area where the proposed station is to be erected. I understand the whole area is going to be covered over, anyway.
We had a discussion yesterday, Mr. Chairman, in which we were told of plans to build a 500 bed hotel near the Chateau Laurier- at least, they are going to offer the property for this purpose. For what purpose are you going to build a hotel if you are not going to make any arrangements to get the passengers down town? I do not believe we have thought this plan through. I understand that Mr. Greber came over from France and drew up a plan. It has been changed a number of times. I do not say that parliament changed it, but it has been changed as a result of Ottawa politics, the mayor and her council. I do not believe parliament has been able to really consider this matter. I think it is the responsibility of the commission to give some consideration to the wishes of members of parliament.
I have never been happy with the Expo '67 coat of arms. Parliament said that they thought it was nuts, but that decision was overruled. Perhaps if we had considered this matter a little earlier the directors might have given more consideration to our wishes. However, we are not too late to give consideration to this station. I understand they are going to have a depot for express at Alta Vista road on Industrial avenue. However, we are not too late for the station. The cloverleaf is not built at Alta Vista. The trains cross the road there and stop traffic every morning as I come in. There is an open crossing there which is going to be eliminated when the cloverleaf is completed. If they are going to construct a four lane highway along the canal, as has been indicated, you will have a four
Supply-Public Works lane highway leading nowhere. We are going to get rid of the railroad bridge, as I understand it. While I am not objecting to the four lane highway, it seems to me that much more consideration could be given to a small two track roadway coming in from the marshalling yard at Walkley road or Industrial avenue.
I have no objection to the erection of a small station out there to serve that end of the city as well. It seems to me a survey was conducted which indicated that about 75 per cent of the passengers coming into the station were businessmen who were going down town. There are not many people coming to visit other people in Ottawa. It is true that we have government buildings now at Confederation heights as a result of some crazy deal to spread them all over the landscape. They should be concentrated near the parliament buildings so that members of parliament could walk over and have investigations made into matters which interest them.
If we had not agreed to this silly business of cutting off debate tonight I would not be prepared to pass the national capital commission estimates. I do not believe there has been any study made of this plan. I do not believe it is too late to do so now. I do not want to be obnoxious and hold up the minister's estimates, but I think we should have some assurance that the national capital commission is not going to get itself into a mess. If the members from the other parts of Canada are not going to support a national capital commission, you are not going to have one. It certainly is not going to be run the way it is. The Minister of Public Works is going to be responsible for the parkways, and so on, rather than the capital commission, and that may be the way to do it because we can question him. We have the commission in an exalted position where we have not been able to talk to them. The first time I had the opportunity of talking to them was in the railway committee room.
This is the first time I have heard anything about this plan or had any opportunity of discussing this plan since 1957 when I first came here. I understand it was discussed in 1956, but since I have been here it has not been discussed. I do not believe we should say it is too late to change it, because we never had a chance to change it or to say anything about it.

The points raised by the hon. member are not only interesting, but I can say they are well taken. We are dealing

Supply-Public Works here with a portion of the over-all Greber plan, a plan which has been reviewed by Parkins and Associates. I may say to the hon. member that so far I have received many suggestions, many of them coming from this side of the house, which have had to do with expropriation by the N.C.C. and other matters such as the relocation of the railway lines and the tearing down of the old union station.
It would not be easy for me to go into the very technical details of this over-all plan, but since the plan was made some 15 years ago I think it would be a good thing to have it reviewed by a committee. I have previously said so, and I believe it would give all hon. members an opportunity to become more acquainted with the plan and to express their own ideas. If some members are not satisfied with the expropriations by the N.C.C. they would have an opportunity to say so.
I would bring the N.C.C. experts with me and, if it could be arranged with the house leader, I would be most happy to arrange for a committee and have my officials present at it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay passage of the national capital commission estimates we are considering at present.
We had a plan prepared by Mr. Greber who came to Ottawa and I know that, since then, implementation of the plan has started on the Ontario side, but the Quebec side has been completely overlooked. In fact, the Greber plan has been shelved because it provided for two stations, one in the western area, in Ottawa and the other in the eastern area, in Hull.
I asked officials of the national capital commission what would be done on the Hull side and I was told: "We are going to repair the station we have there".
Mr. Chairman, that station is nothing more than a shed which cannot be repaired. A new station is a necessity in Hull. It would permit us to enjoy more rapid service between Montreal and Ottawa, through Hull, as the distance is 20 miles shorter.
But no one seems to worry about Hull. It is remembered when time comes to build a road to the Gatineau hills, because the scenery is beautiful; other than that, the national capital commission forgets all about Hull.
I maintain that this situation should be remedied, with regard to the attitude not only of the N.C.C. but of all the departments, for the city of Hull is an integral part of the na-

tional capital. It seems that Hull is ignored, and this is where I start to revolt.
It seems that we must always bow and abide by the decisions of the national capital commission. I am tired with this state of affairs, and I do not intend to accept it in the future. The national capital commission will have to grant Hull the services which we can see from the parliament buildings, and also those from the inside, which we cannot see.
All kinds of works are undertaken in Ottawa. Contributions are granted toward the construction of the queensway, the sewer and water systems, but when we ask assistance for the city of Hull, no financial means or time are available.
I would ask that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) intervene with the national capital commission so it changes its attitude toward the city of Hull.
Hull is part and parcel of the national capital and it should enjoy the same services as the city of Ottawa, on a smaller scale, I admit, but it should still be considered as an important thing, and I am tired of the unfortunate attitude taken by the commissioners.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that when the mayors sat on the commission, things went differently because they stood up for their municipality. But since the mayors were eliminated, decisions are reached without our being told about them. I ask the minister to urge the authorities of the national capital commission to open their eyes, their ears and their hearts, to look on the other side of the river where something important is going on, is developing and wants to become an important part of the national capital.

Mr. Chairman, we are all aware of the value of the tourist dollar which comes into Canada each year. The city of Ottawa is quite conscious of the large number of tourists visiting it each summer, and in Ottawa there are certain places of interest which tourists like to see. One of the most attractive is the parliament buildings, and tourists also are great patrons of sightseeing trips by bus through the city.
A friend of mine who often drives one of the O.T.C. sightseeing buses tells me that in summertime, travelling along Sussex street, when the bus stops outside 24 Sussex drive it is almost impossible to see the residence of the Prime Minister behind the trees and shrubbery when they are in full foliage. The

same is true of the residence of the Governor General. It cannot be seen from Sussex street, but if a little pruning were done a wonderful view of the residence could be obtained from McKay street.
I ask the minister to place this suggestion before the N.C.C. as it would please a lot of tourists if they could see these two points of interest.
