I appreciate very much the opportunity of making a short statement. It is not too short but it should not last many minutes. It is an attempt to summarize the activities of the Speaker's establishment or department during the past year. I am sure that this statement-and I have copies of it for all hon. members-will prove to be of interest, and if I might have the consent of hon. members-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are going to read your speech, are you, Mr. Speaker?
This is an occasion which arises once a year. If the house will give me a little indulgence-it is my only opportunity-
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I think it might be of some assistance to the committee if I were to make a brief statement at this time.
Someone once observed that the real difference between the Speaker and his fellow members is that he never says anything which does not need to be said. Whether that be so or not, I do think that this is one occasion on which a Speaker is bound by the responsibility of his office to speak and to give an accounting of his stewardship.
In a very real sense, the Speaker's estimates are of more direct interest and concern to the members of the house than those of any department of government. Included in the amount which parliament is asked to vote under the legislation item are all the funds necessary for the payment of the staff, the maintenance of services and facilities, the
Supply-Legislation
printing of Hansard and other parliamentary papers, the work of committees, and all the other complex activities that are part and parcel of the operation of a modern democratic parliament.
In Canada today the nation's business has become big business. And it seems to me that the time has come to bring a business approach to its operation.
The Speaker's establishment-totalling some
1,000	persons and with a budget this year of nearly $10 million-is the equivalent of a fairly sizeable business operation. It is, of course, very different in many respects from any other business or government organization-and not the least of these is the fact that it has not one but 265 bosses.
This has been, shall we say, an "interesting" year for the Speaker in this very interesting house. I shall not comment on the Speaker's experiences in the Chair-interesting or otherwise-as these are a matter of record.
Suffice it to say that this has been the longest session on record-both as to the number of sittings and as to uninterrupted continuity. Questions on the order paper are nearing the 2,500 mark; Hansard exceeds 10,500 pages; and on December 1, the House of Commons will have completed more than 200 sitting days.
A Speaker in this country must not only be bilingual; he must be ambidextrous as well. He has on the one hand his responsibilities in the chamber; on the other hand, he has to assume the ministerial responsibility for the administration of all staff and services of the house.
In these brief remarks, I should like to deal first with developments related to the chamber itself and then to comment on some of the administrative and related questions.

As hon. members will know, we have had during this session a very active special committee on procedure and organization of which I have the honour to be chairman. This committee was appointed on the motion of the right honourable the Prime Minister and with the unqualified support of the leader of the official opposition and the leaders of all other parties in the house. Its appointed task was to help improve the efficiency of our operations, in short, to suggest any changes or reforms that would strengthen parliament and make it more effective.
I think the committee has many positive- if unspectacular-achievements to its credit, and that it continues to make steady prog-

When the Speaker's supplementary estimates were under consideration last April, the 
hon. member for Lapointe spoke of certain difficulties in respect to the French edition of the debates of the house. He referred to the fact that the French Hansard was often late in delivery. He also made the suggestion that some means be found whereby the pagination of the French version would be the same as that of the English edition.
I am very pleased to report that both of these problems are solved-or on their way to solution.
Late Delivery of French "Hansard"
A number of changes have been made in the Hansard format, type-styles and editorial practices which have all but eliminated the problem of late Hansard. Implementation of other proposals is pending or under study to effect further improvements in this important area. Corresponding improvements in the translation, printing, and publication of committee proceedings are also under review.
Uniform Pagination of English and French
"Hansard"
Experimentation began in April of this year, commencing with Fridays, and by June 19, these experiments had been extended to each sitting day of the week. Since then, the pagination differential between the two editions has remained almost constant. It should be possible, if we start at the beginning of the next session, to maintain uniform pagination between the two editions.
Entirely English and French versions of
"Hansard"
Since September 1963, Hansard has been printed entirely in English in the same manner as the French edition. An average saving of $400 for each sitting day has been possible through this change.
Order Paper
Hon. members will have noticed, I am sure, the improvements made in the order paper during this session, on the recommendation of the special committee on procedure and organization. In June 1964, the content and format of the order paper were changed on a trial basis for the present session with a view to providing
1)	a weekly projection of the order of business day by day of the house;
2)	a complete list of all house business under each heading of the order paper;
3)	permanent numbers for government orders; and
4)	a disposition list of finished government business or of business otherwise disposed of.

From the comment which I have heard, the changes in the order paper seem to be welcome improvements and I expect that they will become a permanent feature.
I may say that the committee on procedure and organization-through a subcommittee under the chairmanship of the former Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton West-is now working on a number of additional suggestions for the further improvement of Hansard and other parliamentary papers.
Division Time Shortened in the House
A modified division list has been devised which has shortened the length of time formerly required to call and record divisions in the house by as much as 35 per cent.
Physical Services
An effort is also being made to improve the physical services directly related to the chamber of the house and its committees.
Simultaneous Interpretation
On the recommendation of the special committee on procedure and organization, simultaneous interpretation facilities are being extended to all galleries of the house so that visitors from all parts of Canada will be able to follow the debates regardless of which of the official languages is being spoken.
This work is already in progress together with the repair, refinishing and reupholstering of gallery seats.
Electronic Recording in Committees
We are also, on the recommendation of that committee, experimenting with the use of electronic recording of debates in committees.
Trials with electronic recording apparatus in selected committee rooms started at the end of May and have been successfully extended to provide a complete recording service of all committee proceedings in rooms equipped with suitable sound pick-up amplification apparatus. In actual practice, the French portions of these recordings are being transcribed for use in the printed proceedings of committees. In this way, the problem of French reporting services in committees has been solved. The trials will be continued and extended to those committee rooms not having any sound pick-up or amplification apparatus.
Renovation of the Chamber
We have been informed by senior officials of the Department of Public Works that major renovation and repair work is necessary, both in the chamber itself and elsewhere throughout this building. The work in the chamber is
Supply-Legislation
extensive, involving stone work, glazing, lighting, seating and other general repairs or replacements.
The house will be glad to know that arrangements have been worked out to have this project-involving about nine months' work-scheduled during recesses and in such a manner as to have the chamber completely refurbished in time for the centennial year of 1967.
Renovation of the Centre Block
The work elsewhere in the building will involve, among other things, complete rewiring, extensive plumbing and the installation of air conditioning throughout the building. There is also work to be done in the library, the hall of honour and the restaurant. This extensive work would involve major disruption and disorder in the building if it were intended to have it completed by 1967.
It has therefore been decided to postpone this major work until 1968 when it can be carried out most efficiently and with the least inconvenience to members.
This decision does not mean that normal maintenance and repair work will come to a standstill for the next three years; nor would it preclude new major work that could be carried out in the interval without serious disruption or inconvenience to members.

Let me turn now to administration. Reorganization
The most notable event on the administrative side has been a thorough organization study of the structure of the staff and services of the house. This study revealed that the Clerk, who has extremely heavy burdens of responsibility at the table, has to spend a disproportionately large amount of his time dealing with administrative and personnel problems large and small.
The result has been a complete reorganization, carried out in June of this year, to-provide sufficient senior staff to relieve the Clerk of administrative routine and to pursue problems to a solution. A director of administration has been provided as well as a director of legislative services.
These two men, together with the Sergeant-at-Arms, as director of building services, form a three-man staff board to which all questions respecting establishment and personnel are now referred, whatever the source of the questions or whatever the branch involved.

Supply-Legislation
Hon. members may be interested in learning that the new staff board held its first meeting ,on August 31, and has met nine times to date.
Salary Revisions
Following the salary revisions for group B employees in the civil service last August, all employees of the house in comparable occupations also received pay adjustments. By and large, the amounts of revision authorized for our employees were the same as those granted civil servants in the same salary groups. None of our employees got less; a few, however, received more.
This is as it should be, for members are entitled to the very best of service and this can only be provided by competent staff. To retain our present staff and to attract our fair share of good candidates in the future, salaries and working conditions should be as good as they possibly can be. In these respects the House of Commons should lead and not follow.
Classification Study
Altogether apart from the general salary revisions, a complete classification study of all positions on the staff of the house is now under way. This will result in further salary adjustments where warranted.
Sessional Employees
I should point out that almost half of the staff of the house is composed of so-called "sessionals". I am sure that all members will welcome the action taken by the commissioners of internal economy in September, on my recommendation, to grant sessional employees benefits which they had never previously enjoyed.
In the past, sessional employees have not been eligible to accumulate vacation leave, regardless of their length of service. This anomalous situation has been corrected and sessional employees may now earn vacation leave on the basis of 1J days for each complete month of service, for a total of 15 working days per year.
The new benefits for sessional employees is only one item in a series of new measures- some already approved and some still under study by the staff board-to improve working conditions for the staff of the house.
Changes in Vacation Leave Benefits for Continuous Employees
Regulations governing the granting of vacation leave to continuous employees were also

amended in September. The restriction against the granting of leave while the house is sitting has been removed. Employees are also granted one extra week annually after 25 years of service. Furthermore, compensation for work done on a day that is not normally a day of work is on a day for day basis and is no longer included in the over-all vacation leave provisions.

Provision has now been made, for the first time, for a formal grievance procedure which will provide for consideration of grievances by:
(1)	the immediate supervisor of the aggrieved employee and, failing satisfaction, by
(2)	the director concerned, and failing satisfaction, by
(3)	the staff board and, failing satisfaction, by
(4)	the Clerk of the House of Commons, all with pre-determined time periods for each step in the procedure. It is hoped that this will eliminate the presentation of grievances direct to the Speaker or to individual members of parliament.

With guidance and advice from the joint committee on the restaurant and under the capable and energetic leadership of the hon. member for Winnipeg South, steps are being taken to improve further the services provided to members by the restaurant, cafeteria and the coffee shop.
The manager, maitre d'hotel and chef recently underwent a most valuable two-week internship in one of Canada's leading hotels. They have returned with a great many useful suggestions which are now in process of implementation.
Working conditions of the restaurant and cafeteria staffs-to which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and other hon. members have referred-are also being studied with a view to improvement. For example, plans have been approved for alterations and renovations to the staff washrooms which will be carried out on the very first occasion when the house recesses for a sufficiently long period to permit the work to be done.

Space in the centre and west blocks for the essential needs of parliament continues to be an extremely difficult problem. Every effort is being made to accommodate the

requirements of party leaders, ministers, members and staff as equitably as possible. We are also trying to discourage the use of accommodation on parliament hill for nonparliamentary purposes.
The long term solution, of course, will require additional space and this will probably have to await the availability of the east block for parliamentary use.
As part of the accommodation problem, there is the difficult and long-standing question of the parliamentary press gallery. Conditions in the space occupied by members of the gallery are entirely unsatisfactory and represent a very serious fire hazard. The dominion fire commissioner has been insistent that the corridor adjoining the office space must be cleared just as soon as possible.
I am concerned, not only with the overcrowding, the unattractive appearance and the serious fire hazard, but with the fact that gallery members are not accommodated in the manner that senior newspapermen reporting the parliament of Canada should be. I am most anxious to find a solution that will provide to members of the gallery adequate, attractive and efficient accommodation free from the hazard of fire. In this connection, I have made a specific proposal to the executive of the gallery and it is now under consideration.

Tourists
The activities of our parliament, and in particular of this house, are probably attracting greater public attention than at any previous time in Canadian history; this may be an understatement. This is a development to be encouraged, for parliament is the central hub of our public life and should be the embodiment of our dignity as a nation and a people.
I am able to report that a record number of people visited parliament hill during the past tourist season, and that visitors from other countries no less than Canadians themselves have been showing an unprecedented interest in our parliamentary buildings, our traditions, our history, and our proceedings.
To date this year, more than 660,000 persons have visited the building-an increase of 100,000 over last year's total. In the peak months of July and August we had nearly
300,000	visitors-296,880, in fact-and on the long week end in May there was a three day total of 33,221. The record for a single day was on Sunday, May 17-during the tulip 20220-672
Supply-Legislation
festival-when no less than 15,600 persons visited the building.
Student Guides
Many of these visitors were conducted around the parliamentary buildings by the special student guides who were appointed for the summer to augment the regular protective staff. These students-many bilingual and drawn from a dozen Canadian universities-performed their duties with outstanding success, and I should like to take this opportunity of commending them for their excellent work.
I may say that student guides were appointed on the recommendation of the heads of their respective universities.
So successful was this experiment that I plan to have the program expanded next year. I hope that in time we will be able to draw students from all the universities of Canada and build up a corps d'honneur of parliamentary guides. In bringing these young people together, and in bringing them into contact with the public, we can promote better understanding, the exchange of ideas, and a greater awareness of our common heritage as Canadians.
New Seating Plans
The recruitment of these guides has done much to promote the public relations of parliament. However, this is an area in which much more needs to be done. One of the best ways of doing this is through the provision of attractive informational material.
The new coloured seating plan folder, which was produced on the initiative of the special committee on procedure and organization, is a first step in that direction.
The new seating plan has now been in circulation for five months and has been very well received. A copy is automatically given to every visitor to the building. Members may like to be reminded that they are entitled to receive on request to the Sergeant-at-Arms up to 1,000 copies each year free of charge for distribution to their constituents.
The importance of good public relations was brought home to me very forcibly during my visits to London and Washington last January, where I found a wide range of high quality material, including books, brochures and postcards, available for purchase by the public. This surely is the way to bring home to the people the significance of parliament and the representative system. It is not commercialization; it is education for citizenship.

Supply-Legislation Publications Sales Desk
With this end in view, we plan to establish within the building a sales desk where suitable material on parliament can be sold at reasonable cost to the public by the queen's printer. It will be of dignified design and located in the short corridor on the west side of the hall of honour leading into the reading room. Here we hope to make available postcards and slides, of which a wide and impressive range can be produced from the excellent photographs available; published works relating to parliament; appropriate material already available through the queen's publisher; and booklets especially commissioned on behalf of this house.
I propose to take a special responsibility for the last-mentioned category, and to make every effort to ensure that the quality of their writing and presentation is of the very highest standard.
Christmas Cards
Members will be aware that this year, for the first time, a special parliamentary Christmas card-in six different designs-is available for their use at the very economical price of four cents a card, excluding the envelope. Its sale is being restricted to members and the senior officers of the house. Like the seating plan, it was initiated by the procedure and organization committee, and the bulk of the work involved was very capably undertaken by the hon. member for Northumberland.
I understand that orders for the Christmas cards have reached the impressive total of
120,000	to date.
May I congratulate the hon. member for Northumberland and her colleagues on the committee for the excellent taste shown in the selection of photographs.

One of the matters to which my colleague, the Speaker in the other place, and I have given a good deal of thought during the past year is the provision of improved research facilities for hon. senators and members. Let me add at once that we are fully conscious of the excellent services provided to both houses by the library of parliament and its staff. Within its sphere of operation the library is a model of efficiency and conscientious dedication, but no library can provide individual research service to 265 members and 102 senators.
In order to determine whether the high quality service of the library might be still

further improved, a complete study of its organization-similar to that carried out for the House of Commons staff services-is now under way. In the meantime there is the evident need for a research staff.
It is a truism to say that the responsibilities of members increase with every passing year. The demands upon their time and their commitments in a multitude of spheres make for a very full and busy life. They are expected to be well-informed on all matters concerning the public interest, but this is easier to expect than to achieve.
The fact is that few of us can hope for an extensive knowledge of matters outside the areas of our own interests and we must rely on other sources of information. In these days the affairs of government extend into almost every area of human activity, and there is no limit to the range of subjects on which members are likely to require information.
It seems to me that the answer to the problem is to have trained research workers available to do this essential work on behalf of members. Such people would be able to undertake tasks which the present library staff, because of the pressure of their own work, are unable to do.
Those members who have visited the library of congress in Washington will no doubt be familiar with the legislative reference service which operates there, and of which our United States colleagues are so justly proud. While I do not envisage so ambitious a scheme for the Canadian parliament at this early stage, I certainly believe that steps should be taken which might lead eventually to the development of such a service.
To that end, I hope that next year will see the establishment of a small research unit under the jurisdiction of the library, and that it will provide the nucleus for something more ambitious in the future. By the way, it is planned to start with about five research officers.

The work of the various interparliamentary associations has grown tremendously and the importance of these associations will continue to increase. Two of the associations-the NATO parliamentary association and the commonwealth parliamentary association-have just concluded most successful annual conferences in Paris, and Kingston, Jamaica, respectively. Hon members all know how important the NATO association is to Canada as

an inter-parliamentary link-particularly at this time-and I need not dwell on this.
I do want to say a special word about the commonwealth parliamentary association- one of our most important activities in this field. As hon. members will recall, the commonwealth prime ministers, at their conference last July, collectively emphasized the importance of the work of this association, as did the Prime Minister of Canada in his statement of July 17 last to the house, following that conference.
Within the past year, important steps have been taken to strengthen the work of these various interparliamentary groups and other delegations. We now have a room especially designed for the reception of distinguished visitors and its formal opening will take place in the very near future. I may say it is hoped to dedicate this room when Prime Minister Wilson comes to Ottawa. We have also appointed a full-time officer to act as co-ordinating secretary for the various parliamentary associations and he is now fully occupied in planning for the next meeting of the Can-ada-U.S. interparliamentary group, to take place in Canada next February, and for the 54th conference of the interparliamentary union which will bring some 600 delegates from up to 75 nations to Canada next September.
Planning has also been commenced for the important month-long general conference of the commonwealth parliamentary association which will take place in Canada during 1967.
While much of the staff work can be done by the co-ordinating secretary and other officers of the house who have worked with these associations, it will be the contribution in time and energy-and ideas-from hon. senators and members that will make these conferences a success and a credit to Canada.
These, then, are some of the highlights of the past year covered by the funds provided in the Speaker's estimates which, I hope, will commend themselves to the committee.
I would not wish to conclude this brief review without a special word of appreciation to the Clerk, the parliamentary librarian, the Sergeant-at-Arms and all the officers and employees of the house for their loyal and effective service. May I mention in particular the Clerk, Mr. Raymond, who under very difficult circumstances in this longest of all sessions in Canada's history, has been my constant adviser. I should also like to express my appreciation to my colleagues on the special committee on procedure and organiza-20220-672J
Supply-Secretary of State tion, especially to Mr. Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of Committees, and to all members of this house for their confidence and good will.
Item agreed to.

SECRETARY OF STATE Atlantic development board-
20. Administration and operation. $508,300.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether I am in order in asking this particular question of the minister, and I intended to ask it this morning when reference to the subject was made by the hon. member for Northumberland, but when the Atlantic development board amendments were passed by this government the minister indicated that the $100 million made available would only be a floor. Does that mean there will be further funds available to the premier and government of Newfoundland for the development of the Hamilton falls project?

There have been no funds made available for the Hamilton falls project out of the moneys of the Atlantic development board. I think what the hon. member has in mind is the grant toward the development of the Baie D'Espoir project in Newfoundland. I do not think it would ever be contemplated that the Atlantic development board with its scope could have any relationship to such a large project as the Hamilton falls project.

I am completely satisfied with the answer given by the minister, but what I had in mind was the transmission lines which will in all likelihood go through the maritime provinces. Will funds be made available as assistance to this particular development?

I cannot imagine, sir, that if a project of that magnitude should come before parliament in any way it would be done through the Atlantic development board. Of course there is other legislation under the minister of northern affairs through which aid for transmission lines is given. This whole matter is hypothetical. I hope it does come about, as I know the hon. gentleman also hopes, but it is still in the planning stage and until it gets beyond that stage it would be premature for me to attempt to suggest how it will be done.

Supply-Secretary of State

The minister suggests that this is still in the planning stage. Is that statement in any way in support of the statement made by Mr. Lesage last evening to the effect that what Premier Smallwood has said is not true, but a false statement?
I do not think that has anything even remotely to do with my estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question that does have a great deal to do with the minister's estimates. I am wondering whether the minister can, with his: usual precise brevity, indicate just what is in prospect for the province of Prince Edward Island under the Atlantic development board projects. I am confident there is more than one project in prospect covered by the $100 million. Has the minister any report to make about discussions that may have been taking place by the Prince Edward Island people and others, so as to give us a clear picture of what lies ahead for our province?

As the hon. gentleman is aware, the biggest project in prospect at this time for Prince Edward Island is covered by a grant for the laying of a power cable across Northumberland strait which will involve the expenditure of an amount in the neighbourhood of $6 million to $7 million. Speaking from recollection, but I think I am right, the province has indicated that in principle it is favourable toward this project. I hope that the discussion going beyond the principal stage will advance as rapidly as possible, because all the information available to me leads me to believe that if this power project were carried out there would be a substantial reduction in the cost of power to users, and particularly industrial users in Prince Edward Island, and that is of course of real interest to the Atlantic development board in its efforts toward developing the economy.

Mr. Chairman, I assume that the experts on the Atlantic development board have considered the comparative costs of transmittal on the causeway if it should be erected. Do I understand also from what the minister has said that the discussions of principle have been final and have now reached the stage of working toward something concrete? May we in fact count this as one of the things in which the Atlantic development board is going forward?

It would be very wrong for me to speak for the government of the province of Prince Edward Island, but I am bound to say that I have had nothing but the most amicable relations with all the ministers of that government with whom I have had any contact. I had a conversation with the acting premier, Mr. Matheson and with Mr. Rossiter, the minister of industry-
I may not have his precise title correct, and I apologize for not having all these things at my fingertips-last Saturday morning regarding certain projects. Considering that we are not of the same political complexion, I do not think we could have had more friendly relations than have existed between me and the ministers of the government of Prince Edward Island.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to prolong our consideration, but the amicability of the ministers of Prince Edward Island, or of the people there, is not in question. Is this project one which is definitely slated or slotted for Prince Edward Island?

The Atlantic development board has recommended it strongly, and it has been accepted in principle by the government of Canada. I do not think there will be any delay beyond the point when the government of Prince Edward Island, or a company in Prince Edward Island designated by the government, is ready to receive the power. After all, the government of Prince Edward Island or a power company will be the recipients of the power. I am sure the hon. member will realize that it would be impertinent on my part to try to intervene in any way in provincial consideration of this matter.

Mr. Chairman, can the minister tell me whether negotiations are now under way with the authorities of the city of Quebec, in order to deviate, as was asked many times, toward Charlesbourg, the railway line which now crosses the northeastern part of the city.

speechtext: Order, please. I do not think the subject referred to by the hon. member has anything to do with vote No. 20. Perhaps the minister has some information for the hon. member for Quebec West.

Civil aviation-
35. Administration, operation and maintenance including the administration of the Aeronautics Act and regulations issued thereunder, $38,008,600.

I have one point I should like to take up again with the Minister of Transport. It is something I have raised with his predecessors and something I have raised with his officials. I believe our international airports are highly deficient in one aspect. It is a small thing, but if there is anything that is cold it is the welcome we give to those landing in Canada at international airports. There is not one blessed sign that says, in French or English and it should be in both languages,

Supp ly-T ransport
"welcome to Canada". We have directions in three languages to the comfort station, but that is something that is already provided on the aircraft. There have been suggestions in the past that this sort of thing should be done by local chambers of commerce. Well, I disagree. I do not believe local chambers of commerce have any business being at our international airports with signs saying "welcome to Canada".
These vast termini that we have now have all the room in the world in which to put up a suitable sign. We see them in other countries, and it gives you a feeling of welcome. You know, there is a difference between certain modes of transportation, a difference between private and public, but the one that is going to succeed is the one that welcomes you on board. I say to the minister that if the Department of Transport wishes to put these huge buildings to some greater use, then let us see what we can do. I think with a few thousands of dollars spent across the country, perhaps at half the cost of one of those very controversial murals or pieces of sculpture that we have at these terminals, we could erect these welcome signs and make Canadians and strangers alike coming here feel welcome.

I am going to do something I do not believe I should do, but happily I have no officials in front of me. I am going to say that if I can warm the cold heart of the President of the Privy Council I will do what the hon. gentleman has suggested.

I should like to add to what the hon. member for Edmonton West had to say. I have returned recently from the commonwealth parliamentary association conference. I was speaking with members who had travelled practically all over the world. They rather embarrassed me by saying that the terminal in New York, I imagine it was at Kennedy airport, operated by Air Canada had the poorest service, was the most rundown airport and most in need of repainting, of any airport they had seen in their travels. I merely pass this on to the minister.
I will pass it on to where it may do some good.

I have one other point in this regard. Has the minister made any provision to establish a medical review board, similar to that operated in the United States, whereby a pilot who has had his licence cancelled as a result of some physical ailment, and has recovered, may apply to have the licence

renewed? Have we made any progress in this regard?
I understand some progress is being made. I have not got the details in front of me but I will give the hon. gentleman the information.

When I was minister of transport, unfortunately I could not warm the heart of our treasury board. I could not get it warm enough to get any favourable decision on rolling sidewalks at Montreal airport. I know this would be a very popular move if it could be done. It is a splendid airport, but unfortunately it is a tremendous walk for older people, children and tired passengers from the plane to the terminal. I should like to ask the minister if he has had any more success with his treasury board than I had with mine in this regard?
Mr. Chairman, I will do my best.

It had been my intention originally to make a half hour speech on this one subject. However, in view of the circumstances I will reduce it to a question. I have been in continuous and close contact for over one year now with the pilots and private owners of aircraft in Vancouver and British Columbia in attempting to get some study of their problems. There is one other point which is a carryover from the previous discussion. What steps have been taken to work out safety measures with the respective authorities, whether they are hydro commissions or private power companies, in these mountainous areas of Alberta and British Columbia where we have transmission lines going through the valleys and presenting tremendous hazards to low flying aircraft doing charter work as they move along these mountain valleys? pilots of low flying aircraft. What progress has been made in this regard?

Would the minister write me a letter?
Yes.

I do not want to encroach on the territory of the charming and attractive member for Westmorland but I would like to point out that a great many Prince Edward Islanders spend a lot of time at Moncton waiting for planes and trains. I hope the minister, in his mood of benevolent exertion, will look into the situation. I believe the C.N.R. has somewhat fouled up its Ocean Limited schedule and, willy-nilly, is pushing more passengers on to Air Canada. Moncton is still the hub of the maritimes, and though the minister has paid tribute to us as a genial people, we do not like standing up for hours on end.

The hon. member said too inadequate. I hope the facilities will not be inadequate at all. The hon. member for Cumberland raised the same question the other day and I may tell my hon. friend we are making a very careful examination of this point.

I should like to make a plea on behalf of the flying clubs in Canada. Practically every modern country in the world had a surplus of pilots in the past, but the first generation of bush pilots have now reached the age of retirement and most pilots who earned their wings during the war are, like the rest of us, getting older. We have somewhat neglected our flying clubs and the great training work they did in the past which helped keep public interest alive in aviation and assisted us to supply pilots to practically every air line in the world.
We have the best pilots in the world and this is a reputation we should maintain. I hope the minister will study the matter to see if he can financially help the flying clubs of Canada which at present are all operating in difficult financial circumstances and are all making great sacrifices.

I believe this is the general vote relating to the national harbours board. I understand that the delegation which recently came to Ottawa representing the Hudson Bay route association met with officials of the national harbours board to discuss the question of further dredging at the harbour of Churchill. It is my understanding the delegates were told that the board considered the dredging program which has gone on for the past few years to be complete and that no further dredging was being considered next summer.
Nevertheless it is my understanding from the authorities at Churchill that there is still a certain amount of dredging to be done. So there is a conflict of opinion. Mr. Chairman, for a few moments I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) to the disastrous situation in which the Chicoutimi harbour now finds itself.
As you know, the Saguenay river has but two ocean ports, that of Port Alfred, fortunately operated by a private industry, Alcan, which makes it quite important, and that of Chicoutimi, which is completely neglected and in a deplorable condition. The amount spent by the Department of Transport on the improvement and maintenance of those facilities is extremely low, if not non-existent.
I wish to bring to the minister's attention the fact that this year operations in the port of Chicoutimi are showing a substantial growth and, in my opinion, the minister should

give favourable consideration to all representations made in the past by the Chicoutimi authorities, whether to the present government or the previous one. Important improvements are necessary at the port of Chicoutimi to facilitate transshipment of goods as well as its warehousing facilities.
I suggest that this is a very important point and that the Minister of Transport should give a little more attention to the port of Chicoutimi.

I am trying, whenever I can get a little spare time, to visit each of the national harbours and I am very anxious to visit Chicoutimi myself. I intend to do so at the first opportunity. I will discuss the whole matter with the harbours board as soon as I can get a little time in a place other than this.

The information I have is that those persons who wanted to make representations are sending a delegation to Ottawa for the purpose.

I hope we shall find a solution to this problem quite soon.
May I ask the minister whether we can expect not only a solution but thorough explanation of the results of the negotiations and any quid pro quo which may have been necessary?

105. Operating deficit and capital requirements of canals and works entrusted to the St. Lawrence seaway authority with the approval of the governor in council, and to authorize, notwithstanding the Financial Administration Act or any other act, the disbursement by the authority of revenues derived from the operation and management of such canals and works, $2,838,000.

I should like to hear from the minister when he intends to make a full statement to the house and to the country with regard to the operations of the seaway. There are a number of outstanding problems. There is the matter of the tolls on the Welland canal. There is a sort of suspension in mid-air. There is also the question of the long range prospects of the seaway-whether its operations are likely to be financially successful. The record indicates there is some doubt about this. In view of the fact that the cost to the country of this project amounted

Supply-Transport
to some $350 million, I think we should hear progress reports from time to time. I can readily understand that in the early stages there might have been some difficulty about this; the operation was still shaking down; the wheels were probably not running as smoothly as they might. But the seaway has now been in operation for five years and I think it is time we had a full and comprehensive report, together with a forecast. After all, when the minister was on this side of the house he was a great one when it came to calling for these forecasts. I now ask him to follow the old adage "Physician, heal thyself", in this regard.

I am sure you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that there is no more important subject than the St. Lawrence seaway authority and I will seek the first opportunity, when we have a little time available in the house, to make a statement of the kind suggested.
Meanwhile I should like to say that the traffic has increased enormously this year. I only wish we could cope with it and get it moved, particularly through the Welland canal, a little faster-though this year we have made great progress in that direction as well.

Perhaps I may add to the imposing catalogue which the hon. member for Edmonton West mentioned a few moments ago. I am sure that the minister, with his new found interest in Newfoundland and elsewhere, will consider too that it is incumbent upon him to resist all those who in this age would move in the direction of trying to create of the St. Lawrence seaway an all-season route, because this would be a disastrous thing to very important parts of the country, namely the winter ports, the aspect of which was one of the great things which the maritimes brought into confederation. Often one hears the siren sounds of those who would advocate a different course. I am not going to speak any longer on this matter, Mr. Chairman, because I know that the minister's heart is in confederation and he knows this sort of thing would be most inappropriate.
Item agreed to.

Yes, a real horse trader. He has classified this to the extent that he cannot understand why he should have to sit in the back benches with this class of member with whom he is associated. Nobody argues with the fact that labour leaders are entitled to make contributions to campaign funds, but I would remind that hon. member and all hon. members on the other side of the house that to accept contributions from someone of the calibre of Hal Banks, especially while he was 20220-673J

In reconsidering it they certainly should not take exception, as the member for Halifax did, to their own Prime Minister; because the Prime Minister indicated-I am not saying that he in any way came out completely and said there were these contributions-that there have been such contributions; and at the same time the Prime Minister indicated that he would not accept contributions from a man such as Hal Banks. Yet the member for Halifax rose in the house and defended the idea of accepting such contributions.
In accepting contributions from a labour leader of that calibre, who was at that time under investigation by a royal commission, these members, if they examine their conscience, will know very well-I refer to the contributions that were accepted, for there has been no indication that there were not and we have the word of the Prime Minister that there were-that they did wrong. The hon. member has said that they did not in any way commit themselves. Any member of parliament who accepts a contribution by way of cash, cheque or otherwise, is certainly putting himself in a compromising position. It is my experience and the experience of other men here that in your campaigns you have somebody to look after such things as that, and any member of parliament who at any time has permitted such payments to cross his hands is making a very, very bad mistake.
Do you know of any?
The member for Leeds asks whether I know of any.
Make a charge.

The member for Leeds is coming up with the same old "make a charge" business. I say to the member for Leeds, if you have a question to ask me about whether I know of anybody or not, you would be well advised to speak to your Prime Minister, who indicated on television that there is reason to believe such payments were made, not to the Liberal party but to Liberal members.
That is not true.

You will have your chance to get up and say whether or not it is true. If you did not follow the remarks of your own Prime Minister on T.V., at least you can get the transcript of what he had to say. At the same time the Prime Minister indicated that he would never place himself

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the member for Cape Breton South is certainly misrepresenting very badly anything that I said in this house, and I do not think that is proper. I do not believe the member for Bow River needs anyone to defend him, but the member for Cape Breton South is so sensitive to criticism, as displayed by the manner in which he carries on his political campaigns with his fists-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is no question of privilege in what the hon. member for Halifax is now saying. Certainly what he has been saying up to this point indicates only that he disagrees with what has been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and that is no reason for raising a question of privilege at this time.

Mr. Chairman, realizing how pressed we are for time this afternoon I intend to go no further than to stuff down the hon. member's throat what he said. He said I have misrepresented the facts. I would call your attention to the last column on page 10405, where the hon. member for Halifax is reported as saying this:
The trained seals opposite had nothing to say during those six years on this subject.
Hon. members opposite used to be referred to as the Pearson team. If this sort of thing continues-and in all likelihood it will catch on-it is more likely to be called the Pearson gang. The hon. member for Halifax had this to say:
Not one backbencher had anything to say about Hal Banks.
I say this is complete disregard for the truth.
When I came here in 1957 I was aware of the fact that representations about this had been made. I see the hon. member for Kootenay West present in the committee, and he has indicated to the house in the last month or so that he, along with other members of parliament, had been making rep-

resentations on this matter as early as 1956. So that again I say that the hon. member for Halifax with complete ignorance showed utter disregard for the truth of this matter.

I rise on a question of privilege. I would point out that as reported at page 10405 of Hansard I had started to say that not one backbencher had had anything to say about Hal Banks, but at that point in his usual manner the hon. member interrupted me. I then completed what I had started to say when I next had the opportunity, and as reported on the following page I said they did nothing about Hal Banks and said nothing that was constructive and produced results. That is what I intended to say had I not been interrupted by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
The hon. member has also misrepresented the situation regarding the time of the alleged contributions. There was no royal commission under way at the time of the alleged contributions, which was during the 1962 campaign. It was only after that. The hon. member also said I suggested that it was all right for contribution to be made by labour leaders direct to members. I never said that or never intended to say such a thing. Naturally I meant contributions made in the usual manner to the campaign funds of a candidate.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has just made an interesting observation. He said there was no royal commission set up at the time of the alleged contributions, and then he referred to the date of the contributions, 1962. That is rather ambiguous, because I am led to believe that there were actual contributions, and that has now been admitted.
Alleged.

I said alleged. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I call your attention to the fact that although I referred to page 10405 of Hansard there were a number of remarks made after the hon. member for Halifax made his statement, and I would respectfully ask the Chair to rule on his question of privilege, as it did on mine last Monday.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member will admit to the Chair that he had completed his remarks. The hon. member for Halifax had the right to rise. Whether he prefaced his remarks with the statement that he was raising a question of privilege is rather immaterial. He has the right to speak and he took his right to speak.

I might say that if I were requested to rule I would recognize that there was no question of privilege here but simply a rectification of what the hon. member considers were inaccurate statements made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
Mr. Chairman, you used the phrase "inaccurate statements" made by me. I am sure the Chair did not intend that.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one question to put to the Minister of Justice. Even if some members on the other side of the house seem a bit surprised, I am not going to let it distract me.
Since 1958, it has been decided that a penitentiary would be built in the municipality of St. Pie de Bagot. To this end, four plots of land were bought at a cost of $83,000; work has been performed by various experts at a cost of over $20,000. In addition, the cost of plans prepared by an architect for the institution in question amounted to $50,000. As you can see, at least $150,000 in taxpayers' money has been spent.
According to the statements made by the Minister of Justice, conditions at the present time in penitentiaries are said to be unsanitary, and living conditions almost indescribable. But, owing to the political partisanship of the predecessor of the present Minister of Justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the construction of the penitentiary at St. Pie was immediately cancelled after the 1963 election.
I do not hesitate to say, Mr. Chairman, that this was a measure of reprisals against the riding of St. Hyaeinthe-Bagot which had elected a Conservative member of parliament.
I want to ask the minister what he will do with the lands which were bought, because the farmers who owned those lands left them and also removed the buildings which were on them.
I would also ask the minister to tell us why the construction of that institution in the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot was cancelled, if not through reprisals because its population elected a Conservative to the House of Commons-
The reasons have been given ten times already. That will be the eleventh time.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Public Works interrupts while remaining in his seat but he does not have the courage of

getting up to tell the house why the project has been cancelled. The Minister of Public Works is unable to deny categorically that this change was motivated by political considerations on the part of the former minister who was known throughout Canada as the minister of injustice.
You are unable to do so.
Order.

Mr. Chairman, naturally I did not intend to participate in the debate on these estimates. However, since the hon. member has challenged me to give the reasons why the construction of a maximum security penitentiary at St. Pie de Bagot has been cancelled, I feel I have to state those reasons.
I told him a while ago, and I repeat it, that those reasons were given to him at least ten times. First of all by the previous minister of justice, Mr. Chevrier; then I myself gave him an answer once or twice on the orders of the day and, if my memory serves me right, the present Minister of Justice also gave him a reply.
We are the owners of the land that we bought and we keep it. We have already told the hon. member that it is quite possible that we may use that land to build a federal building.
We are now considering such a possibility but I would not want him to take my remarks as a certainty. However, such a thing is under consideration.
In the second place, it was said a number of times following the whole revision of the penitentiary program, that such a penitentiary should not be located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, but rather on the north shore, and that is the only reason why the penitentiary would be built at Ste. Anne des Plaines. Such a decision was taken and we must carry it out, whether it pleases the hon, member or not.
As far as the retaliation referred to by the hon. member, we would not like to give the hon. member more weight than he carries.
We will rely on the voters of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot county.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Public Works has just shown his ignorance in this matter.
He is talking about a maximum security penitentiary, while the decision was that a minimum security penitentiary would be built at St. Pie in the county of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot.

That does not matter.

Now, Mr. Chairman-
Him again.

I will point out to the hon. member for Lotbiniere that he can resume his seat to make the remarks which he did not have the gumption to make otherwise.
There you see how inaccurate the Minister of Public Works can be. He does not know what he is talking about. When he rises to make statements in connection with matters he knows nothing about, when he says he will let the voters of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot county decide the fate of the one who now has the floor, I extend to him an invitation to come to my county. The former minister of justice came twice to my county and each time my majority increased by 1,000 votes. When the incompetent who interrupted a moment ago comes into my county, my majority will increase not only by 1,000 but by 2,000 votes.

Mr. Chairman, we have witnessed during the past 18 months a series of crises in which the government of this country has found itself. Almost every week something new is divulged that is of the greatest significance to the nation as a whole, and of the greatest concern to the people of this nation, relating to the manner in which this country is being run. Certainly what has transpired this week gives no one any justification for the feeling of security as to the manner in which justice is being administered. This week we have witnessed perhaps the greatest crisis that this government has had to face, yet we have been denied the presence in this chamber of the leader of this government, the Prime Minister of this country. We have not had an opportunity to ask him the questions which are foremost in the minds not only of us but of all the people of Canada, in relation to his obligations to this nation and to the administration of justice in this nation.
It is indeed very significant that the Toronto Globe and Mail on Thursday of this week had as its lead editorial one which stated that his place was in Ottawa. I am going to place this editorial on record because it is the type of editorial which indicates the degree of concern shown by responsible people in this country toward the attitude of the Prime Minister, as evidenced by his complete disregard for his responsibilities as the leader of this nation.
The editorial reads as follows:
Events of the last 48 hours In Ottawa have both bewildered Canadians and given them cause for deep concern. A judicial inquiry has been ordered into the involvement in a narcotics extradition case of two executive assistants to cabinet ministers and a member of parliament who was parliamentary secretary to Prime Minister Lester Pearson.
It is true that the shadows will not be lifted until this judicial inquiry has sat and sifted the whole of the evidence and made its report. But it is equally obvious that the existence of the inquiry will not dispel the interest of the opposition parties in related issues, or prevent them from calling into question the integrity of men in the government and their servants.
Mr. Pearson has left the House of Commons and gone to fulfil a prearranged schedule of engagements in Saskatchewan, leaving the nation in the hands of external affairs minister Paul Martin, justice minister Guy Favreau and an aroused opposition. He may have felt that by so doing he would communicate a feeling of confidence to the people. But in these troubled days the presence of the Prime Minister, not only in the house but in his party caucus, would be a reassurance to Canadians. Mr. Pearson should come home.
Mr. Chairman, if the Prime Minister left this house at the time he did with the intention of keeping pre-arranged meetings on matters of great significance to the future of this nation, I am certain no member of parliament or citizen of Canada would argue about the merits of his doing so. However from what I have read in the newspapers, both since and prior to his departure, I have gained the impression conveyed by these stories that the Prime Minister was going to western Canada to feel the pulse of the people of that part of this nation, with the possibility in mind of calling a general election, and to determine how the funds are flowing. I imagine that many sources of funds have dried up in the past week and that the Prime Minister will have to stay there for some time in an attempt to sink some new wells to replace the dry holes he has drilled this week.
Mr. Chairman, we have a Prime Minister who can be compared to the famous Roman emperor Nero who fiddled while Rome burned. The Prime Minister is out west endeavouring to find oil somewhere to salve his conscience and the conscience of his supporters because of the manner in which justice is being administered at the present time. He could have come back to this house today, giving the opportunity to members to pose questions which, because of the growing concern across this country, should be answered. Since I have been in this House of Commons no government has been under such an aura of suspicion as now exists because of the way justice is

being administered. I think all members of the house feel it was the duty of the Prime Minister to be in his seat. Certainly, from the look of things, Canadians do not have to worry about the government calling any elections for some time to come. Certainly the Prime Minister will find other times when he will see more enthusiasm in the greetings of his supporters than at the present time. Canadians are shocked. They are bewildered. They do not really believe such a thing could have happened in this nation. They hope for, and fear, the results of this inquiry, and certainly all members as well are fearful of the results.
I say that a great deal more in the way of information should have been forthcoming from the government and would have been forthcoming if the Prime Minister had remained in this house and answered questions honestly and emphatically, in the way he should have answered them with regard to this situation. The fact that the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister found it necessary to resign his position because of his involvement in this affair, and the fact that at the same time the Prime Minister would feel he could get up and walk out to go on a barnstorming tour for political funds, is just unbelievable and beyond the comprehension of most Canadian people. I say that the Prime Minister's position has reached a new low in this nation as a result of the action he has taken this week in leaving the House of Commons in the atmosphere in which we find it at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to place our position on the record with regard to the amendment before embarking on further remarks. The amendment was introduced last October 7, and will be found on page 8849 of Hansard. I believe it would be worth while for me to read my remarks immediately preceding the presentation of that amendment into today's Hansard. I quote:
The S.I.U. do not provide these facilities for nothing. Because of the manner in which the government has failed to act on this matter; because the minister has shown a singular lack of understanding of the function with which he is charged in carrying out the responsibilities of his office; because of the degree to which the law, good order and justice in this country have been dragged in the mire by the inaction of the minister and of the government as a whole, it is both my belief and the belief of a good many of us on this side that the minister is no longer fit to hold the portfolio of Minister of Justice. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South:
That vote No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Justice be reduced by the sum of $16,999.

That will leave by way of salary for the minister $1 per annum.
Question.

I hear hon. members calling for "question", and I will be brief, I can assure them, if I may speak without interruption. These remarks are as applicable now, indeed the more so. I believe the minister is unfit to hold his portfolio. He has shown deplorable conduct in the handling of matters to which I referred in this house last Monday and during subsequent days of this week. The minister has shown a singular lack of common sense, of good judgment, indeed a singular lack in my view-perhaps after I have completed my remarks, in the view of others-of a knowledge of the law applicable in the circumstances which were brought before him on August 14. There was a particular course he should have followed on August 14 which he did not follow and which has not yet been discussed in the house. I intend to raise it this afternoon.
One point should be raised before I proceed. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona was speaking this afternoon and the minister replied in French. I have since that time been supplied with a copy of the translation of the phrases which he used. I do not vouch for its accuracy, but if it is accurate then it raises some question in my mind and in the minds of others. The minister, I believe, in reply to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, said this in French:
"As soon as the final report-not the final but the last report available in the files was received, I made him-
Referring to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
"-aware of it and together we discussed this affair. We took together a decision relative to his executive assistant. So far as the other question, that is the legal procedure, is concerned, naturally I took it myself."
Now, that is the English translation I have of the minister's words. If it is accurate I feel it again shows a deplorable lack of good sense, of good judgment and a departure from what the responsibility of the minister was. In the light of the circumstances, he should not have taken it upon himself to make any decision with regard to this matter with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. The first course to follow, I do not want to belabour the point, was to have referred the whole matter to the independent scrutiny of and to have obtained the opinion of the law

Supply-Justice
officers of his own department. But it raises this question, if the translation is accurate, what decision was taken by the two ministers? What decision was taken by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will allow me to interrupt I must say in all fairness to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that, so far as he was concerned, the only matter with which he dealt in relation to the report was a matter of internal administration, and his relationships with those of his department with his own executive assistant. So far as the question of deciding whether or not to lay an information on the state of the evidence available at the time, I must take full responsibility therefor. Of course, it was not the duty of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to take any decision in this respect. He did not, and that is why I made this distinction this morning.

What is the final report the minister had reference to in his reply to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, the final report which he discussed with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration? Yet he has been referring throughout to an open file. I think the minister has some explanations to go into in this regard. These and other questions, of course, occur to all.
Throughout, Mr. Chairman, this has been an extremely serious matter. Since I raised it on November 23 I have tried to be meticulously and scrupulously certain of every fact which I have placed before the committee. None of these facts has been denied by the minister. I want to be meticulously and scrupulously certain not only of the facts but I want to continue to be sure that the manner of stating those facts leaves no room whatever for any misunderstanding or misinterpretation.
I am sure there are a lot of questions occurring, not only to members of the treasury benches but to all members of the house with regard to how I came into possesion of the information which I have disclosed, the information I have. I have seen many people and I have been outside Ottawa in search of this information. I want to assure all members of the house that I have no knowledge of any matters relating to this affair that are not in the police report.
I want to say that I have done nothing unlawful in any of my activities in connection with the obtaining of the information which I have obtained.
We will find out.
I want also to tell the house that I have shared with no one the whole of the knowledge that I have.
I thought there was no secrecy in your party.

In reply to the hon. member who so flippantly interjected, I am sure all members will admit quickly that the information which I have carried about with me was weighty material to say the least. I wanted no one to share the responsibility, and I mean of the whole of the information which I did carry, and which I still carry and intend to do so unless by lawful requirement I am required to disclose it.
I have a high regard for all judicial bodies, judicial bodies which I feel were thwarted in this case, and no one will find me reluctant to comply with the letter of the law in this or any other matter. But I want to say immediately I consider the content of the material I have of such an explosive nature that I did not want to share that responsibility with anyone else.
Not even your leader?
I have told hon. members that I have shared the knowledge with no one and it was in consideration of others that I did that.
Would the hon. member allow a question at this point?
Yes.

In view of the emphasis the hon. member has now placed repetitively-I think four times in the last five minutes-in view of the weight of burden he has been carrying, the knowledge which he has not yet disclosed, is it the hon. member's intention to share this weight of knowledge and facts with the royal commissioner who has been appointed to investigate all phases of this matter?

I suggest to the hon. member for Vancouver East that he read carefully my remarks in Hansard and he will find that I answered that question just a moment or two ago. And again I am being extremely careful of what I say in the house and I want to be meticulous in that regard.
Oh, oh.

I would suggest to hon. members opposite who moan and groan that they should do the same.
I want to say a word too, before leaving the matter, about Mr. Lamontagne, the counsel

lor the United States government who was acting, and is still acting in this matter, the matter ol Rivard, that I feel words are not adequate to express my admiration for this-
Oh, oh.
Again I hear flippant grunts over on the other side.
Where do they come from? Identify them.

Mr. Lamontagne, I might add, is a loyal-and I use the present tense-loyal member of the Liberal party. I cannot find adequate words to express my admiration for the integrity, the professional integrity of this young member of the bar.
It is extremely refreshing to me to find someone of his calibre who is able to resist not only the oilers and pressures which were brought to bear prior to last Monday on him with respect to this matter, but subsequently as well, and when I say subsequently I mean the barrage of questions which must have been directed at him by members of the press and by others.
I think one of the hon. members on my left referred to the harassment and embarrassment that he has subjected himself to by reason of his confirmation, in substance, of what I placed on the record on the 23rd of this month. It took courage, it took integrity, and this young gentleman had both in good measure.
I want now to deal for a moment with the law, law of which the minister should be aware, law which he should have followed with respect to this case and law of which I can only assume he must be unaware. I am going to read to him first a very short paragraph from volume 8 of "Halsbury's Laws of England", the most recent edition, the third edition, at page 12 under the heading ''Obstructing officers of the court":
Contempt by obstructing an officer of the court is punished, not for the purpose of vindicating the dignity of the court or the person of the officer, but to prevent undue interference with the administration of justice.
I want now to refer him to the most recent case of which I am aware, dealing with matters of this nature, to be found in volume 40, 1963, of the "Criminal Reports". It is a case coming from the minister's own province, a case decided on June 5, 1963. It is in the Quebec court of queen's bench, the appeal side, and three eminent judges, Mr. Justice Bissonette, Mr. Justice Owen and Mr. Justice Rivard sat on the matter. It is entitled "Sommer v. the Queen."
Supply-J ustice
Briefly the facts in that case as stated by Mr. Justice Owen are these, and they are relevant so I put them on the record:
This is an appeal from a conviction for contempt of court. While a judge exercising criminal jurisdiction was conductng the hearing on a writ of habeas corpus, the object of which was to obtain the release of one Ripple from a mental institution, the appellant wrote letters attacking the presiding judge and the courts. The letters were produced and, on a verbal motion by the attorney for the mental institution, a rule nisi was issued by the presiding judge. This rule was served upon the appellant who was thereby ordered to appear at a fixed time before the presiding judge to show cause why he should not be held in contempt of court and sentenced accordingly. The appellant appeared as ordered, was interrogated under oath by the presiding judge, was convicted summarily, and was sentenced immediately to three months in prison.
I draw the procedure to the attention of the minister, if he is not aware of it; that procedure being summary procedure, procedure under which no information is necessary to be laid and which allows a judge to require the presence of a person accused in circumstances such as these, summoning him immediately before the court and interrogating him under oath and immediately thereafter giving a decision as to whether or not there has been contempt. By way of explanation I think I should put on record that this procedure is a rare one. It is set up for the purpose of protecting the integrity of the courts, to prevent any undue interference with the administration of justice. As reported at page 429 of the case I have cited, Mr. Justice Owen, in the course of his judgment, used the following words:
But when we consider the process of summary punishment for contempt, the position is different. Here the power to award punishment is inherent in the court, as already stated: not in the judge and jury, but in the court itself, and being so inherent, it has to be adequate to meet the conditions which call for its exercise. Thus, it is conceded that the person charged not only does not have the right to put forward the testimony of witnesses on his behalf, but is even exposed to have to answer interrogatories. Neither has he the right to a trial by jury.
It is an extraordinary power, but it is me which is necessary, as I have said to protect the courts from undue influence or interference in matters affecting the administration of justice. The point I am making is that in this case, as was quite proper, the Quebec attorney general brought the matter to the attention of the judge concerned at the moment the offence was committed. The judge dealt with it summarily and immediately passed sentence. The report I read from was

Supply-Justice
the report of the appeal court where the decision of the judge in the lower court was upheld.
Excepting as to sentence.

Excepting as to sentence.
The minister has by now, I am sure, no longer any doubts as to the suggestion I have been implying thus far. I intend to make it clear, now, by asking him this question. He is an eminent member of the Quebec bar and, as such, he is an officer of the Quebec court. Why did he not bring this matter immediately to the attention of the judge? Why did he not at least bring the matter to the attention of the provincial attorney general of Quebec and let him deal with it as he dealt with the matter in the case I have cited? The very least the minister should have done was to have informed the Quebec attorney general fully as to the situation. I repeat, he should have been fully informed. I might also add that the minister will also find a reference in the report I have read to the effect that if an accused person is a lawyer he loses his status as counsel when he appears before the judge under an order compelling him to appear in circumstances of this sort. So he is not treated as a lawyer at all, and all the privileges which counsel usually have in the courts are lost to him.
The remaining question with which I intend to deal concerns the terms of reference of the order in council. Now these have been finally defined.-I assume this is the case-I have made up my mind to allow the judicial inquiry to take its course without hindrance from myself-
Bully for you.
If hon. members will allow me to complete my words without interrupting-*
Will you assist?

I will assist the judicial inquiry in every way I can. I did not mean to be presumptuous by my previous statement and if hon. members opposite had allowed me to complete it they would not have found it so. I intend to be of every assistance to the judicial inquiry if I am called before it. I also wish to say with respect to the inquiry that if I were to deal any further with the questions which have been referred to the inquiry then, certainly, I would have grave doubts as to whether I would be doing the proper thing. Having those doubts, I have resolved them in favour of

silence in the house and I will follow that course now.
I am sure this matter will be dealt with fully by the judicial inquiry and I am just as certain that all the details will be before that inquiry as soon as it sits. I am sure all such witnesses will be called before it as are necessary to fulfil the terms of reference contained in the order in council and I am sure the first thing the judge will call for will be the police report in order to familiarize himself fully with the details it contains, because that report is the source from which he will derive the most useful information upon which to base his decision as to which witnesses should be called and which information he should seek in order to fulfil his function as the commissioner appointed under the order in council.
Having said these things, I believe I have covered those aspects with which I intended to deal this afternoon. I regret, as many other members have so expressed themselves, the conditions and the circumstances which made it necessary to reveal and expose this whole situation to the committee but I feel, without intending any injustice to the officials involved in the R.C.M.P. and in the department, that had I not brought these matters to the committee's attention they would in all probability not have seen the light of day.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I believe I have already made myself clear with respect to discussing the facts surrounding this affair. There has been a very real suspicion raised in my mind. I do not intend to do the hon. member any injustice, nor do I wish to imply or leave anything by innuendo because of the question that I am about to put to him, which is this, that some of the things he said last night, particularly the reference to "20 days", leads me to believe that he may well either have seen the police report himself or have had passed on to him information from it.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Chairman, I still have not had an answer to my question. I am just wondering-
