speechtext: Order. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to be quite brief in this matter and refer to only two of the points made by the hon. member for Yukon in the speech he has just completed. The first of these-and I hope the hon. member will correct me if I in any way inadvertently misrepresent what he said -is that he indicated to the committee that he was in exclusive possession of all the information he has laid before the house during the present week. The deduction is my own; I do not think the hon. member said that. I think he implied that he had

arrived at his own conclusion that there was at least a prima facie case established, from the material he had in his hands, that criminal offences had occurred, and he has taxed the minister very much for failing to take action both in his public capacity and in his private capacity as a member of the Quebec bar or the bar of any province of Canada. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quote as follows:
The power to prosecute may be abused in ways which have nothing to say to the procuring of evidence and the procedure at the trial. If it is important that the accused should be protected while he is a prisoner, it is also of importance-. (a) that the executive should not be free to prosecute or refrain from prosecuting in order to serve its political ends, and (b) that prosecutions which are vexatious or without evidence capable of supporting them or against the public interest, should be stopped as early as possible. If it is wrong that accused persons should be unfairly treated in connection with their trial, it is also wrong that those against whom no proper case can be made should be subjected to the distress and expense which a prosecution may entail.
It is in the discharge of what are now the firmly established traditions and functions of his office that the attorney general protects the subject from both these dangers.
Further, at page 33 of the same lecture it is said:
The considerations which weigh with the attorney general in deciding whether or not to prosecute go beyond the existence of evidence proving the commission of the offence in question. He must also regard wider issues, such as the effect of a prosecution on the public interest and any special circumstances which may have a bearing on the justice or rightness of a decision one way or the other. In all this he must exercise his own judgment and his own discretion-
I emphasize that:
-but he is entitled to inform himself of the relevant facts and probable consequences and, in doing so, to seek from his ministerial colleagues such help as they can give him. This sort of consultation may sound a delicate business, but once the underlying rule is accepted, the line separating the functions of the consulting ministers can be easily drawn and maintained in the right place. Mr. Attorney, for example, should never ask or be told whether or not he should prosecute. But he can ask and be told with perfect propriety what effect a prosecution would have on the common weal.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, are we not now arguing something that is going to be taken up before a commission?

When I replied to the question, the case was being appealed. After August, or rather after September, two investigations were held in this matter because two persons were involved.
The inquiry was held before an investigating commissioner appointed by the R.C.M.P. commissioner, and he was chosen at Edmonton to preside over this case in Montreal. The investigation was held and two reports were submitted-one for each inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a question of privilege, this is about the seventh time this has been untruly stated. I never said that. The right hon. gentleman was not there to look at the program. Canada is not a concept in the air. Canada is a collective identify of all those who fulfil this everyday living of the Canadian fact.

Nothing at all, except that the parliament of Canada shall decide. I notice that the other day Mr. Levesque received the approval of one of the ministers of this government, I think it was the Secretary of State, who said he "stands for great things". Mr. Chairman, he stands for an associate state and a nation within a nation, something this confederation cannot accept and which would not permit the continuance in the next hundred years of this country in all its strength and its power.
Would the right hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question?
Oh, absolutely.
Is the right hon. gentleman now admitting that the power of delegation which he recommended two years ago showed so little foresight that it would make it possible to have an associate state?
I have mentioned that there was delegation. But there has been change.
Oh, oh.
There is nobody more helpful than the Minister of Transport, because he just blindly gets up and blurts something out; he has no idea what the answer will be. He is a wonderful fellow.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I can tell the right hon. gentleman that I know there would be no direct and honest answer to that question.

I know the care that the hon. gentleman always exercises in what he says. I am not going to deal with it today, but I will have the opportunity soon of quoting some of his remarks regarding some hon. members of this house, and I am sure he will be ashamed that he ever made the statements.
Supply-Justice
Oh, oh.
Does the minister ask what they were?
No.
Oh, no, he does not.
I am not interested in any Pickersgill regurgitations.

I recall that on March 28, 1963, in Sudbury he spoke of the hon. member for Red Deer, the leader of the Social Credit party, and said, "He has got nothing. He is the most pathetic creature I have ever seen in parliament in my days. He has nothing but a Pepsodent smile and is able to comb his hair". That is what he said about one whom today he draws to his bossom in political embrace. I could go on, Mr. Chairman, but that is just one sterling example of the changed attitude of the hon. gentleman between March, 1963 and November, 1964.
I say this, Mr. Chairman, that in so far as this formula is concerned, we want it examined. We want to know from the government what we have not been able to secure information on, namely, do they intend to take the British North America Act as it now is, bring it before parliament and re-enact it as a Canadian statute? Do they intend to give us the opportunity to deal with it section by section? What is the plan the government has in this regard-for I warn the government now that in so far as any agreement is concerned respecting repatriation, this parliament is going to have the right to give it the fullest consideration.
I do not know why the minister has been so evasive in this regard. He has been asked several times, "What is your plan? What do you intend to do? Do you intend to bring the act as a whole before parliament?" I ask him now, let us know. I know he has been very busy in recent days, weeks and months; but this is something regarding which Canadians have a right to know the course of action being followed. We want to know whether in the amendment of the constitution we are to be assured by the government that this nation shall be preserved on the basis of the principles of an equal partnership between the English and the French, at the same time with equality for all Canadians over and above the constitutional rights. I ask the minister, what is the plan?

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister, who has been dealing with this matter in the house, if my memory serves me correctly, stated some days ago to the house

Supply-National Defence that the final plans with regard to the manner in which the matter of the constitutional amendments would be brought into the house would not be announced until such time as the agreement of the provinces to the formula had been obtained.

Has not the government of Canada any plan? Why should parliament be kept in the dark? Mr. Chairman, there are two matters I would like to raise with the minister at this time. I spoke on this item initially but there are two matters I wish to bring to his attention. First of all, yesterday the minister answered in sort of a discursive fashion questions relating to the state of the navy in Halifax concerning six ships which had been laid up under skeleton crews because of the lack of skilled technicians. Then we find further disclosures have been made to the effect that the net loss to the navy of trained personnel is about 75 men a month, and there have been examples of people leaving the navy in such large numbers that almost

the whole, if not the whole, of a class of trainees left on graduation or did not sign on for a further term of service.
There is something radically wrong within the service if this is the condition that exists. I am making these remarks because of my sincere worry and concern for the navy, because the Department of National Defence should be taking care to provide training for its men. They have devoted a tremendous amount of money to bringing forward these trained men, and yet we see them disappearing from the service. The minister himself will agree that there must be something wrong with a state of affairs that produces this result. These men are going out into industry. Certainly there will be a certain amount of wastage, and this applies to the air force and to the army; but to the extent that it applies at the moment to the navy there must be something radically wrong. It certainly is not only limited to questions of pay allowances; there must be some worry on the part of these men about their future in the service. I have had this opinion expressed to me by men who left the air force this year. They were offered extensions of commission and they said, "Not on your life"; there was too much uncertainty to induce them to remain in the service. These are men with relatively few years in the service; they are young men who have been trained at a cost of thousands of dollars. Yet they have not confidence enough in the service to remain in it. There is something fundamentally wrong when numbers of men leave the service, be it the army, the air force or the navy.
I have one particular question in this connection. We would like to hear a fuller explanation from the minister than was given in the question period yesterday, and we want more than what seemed to be a script of apology that was given by some correspondent, on behalf of the navy, last night over the news system.
The second point I make is on behalf of the hon. member for Oxford, and it is a matter into which I should like the minister to inquire because something is fundamentally wrong. I should like to refer to question 1,745 and parliamentary return No. 2,572, dealing with four questions asked by the hon. member for Oxford concerning a certain Department of National Defence vehicle bearing Ontario licence plate number 27120F and its performance between the hours of 10.30 a.m. and 11.30 a.m. on Monday, August 17, 1964. The hon. member for Oxford asked what the vehicle was doing at

those times, under whose charge it was, and so on. The answer to the second of his questions was:
This vehicle was assigned to and under the control of a member of the privy council office, assigned as office manager in the secretariat of the third commonwealth education conference at the time in question.
The answer to the third question was as follows:
Two assignments were carried out during the hours of 10.30 a.m. and 11.30 a.m.-
Then (a) is not pertinent because it concerns a trip to the queen's printer in Hull. The answer continues:
(b) The driver, accompanied by a messenger, proceeded to a local business establishment to obtain supplies for the commonwealth education conference.
This is the official reply given to the hon. member for Oxford. He cannot be here today but he tells me that he was an eye witness and saw this vehicle at 11.15 a.m. outside the national Liberal headquarters on Cooper street, and certain personnel were removing boxes and parcels of papers or documents, in any event stationery of some kind-pamphlets or something of that nature. These documents were loaded into this army vehicle at precisely 11.15 a.m. I am wondering whether the euphemistic phrase "a local business establishment" has been substituted for the exact establishment. It would be interesting to know why this vehicle which was assigned to an officer in the privy council office would call at the national Liberal headquarters to take documents from that location to whatever destination they were taken.
I would ask the minister to look into this matter very carefully because I do not think we can stand army vehicles being used for the transportation of party literature or documents from any location at all. I do not think the minister would tolerate this if he knew about it, and I should like him to look into it.

Mr. Chairman, on the first question raised, as I said yesterday there are many factors in respect to re-engagement rates and I believe it is the case that they are not satisfactory. One of the factors, probably the most important factor of all, is the question of opportunities in the civilian economy. It just happens that there are many opportunities at very good salaries and wages for highly trained technical personnel, and consequently when terms of re-engagement are considered and opportunities are available in private life which pay more money with
Supply-National Defence equal security it is not unnatural that a number of people take advantage of the situation and go to other employment. So that you will find if you plot re-engagement rates over a long period of time that there is a direct correlation here, and probably the most important factor is the opportunities existing in the civilian economy. Particularly does this apply to technical personnel-electricians, electronic engineers, and so on-who are in most short supply.
There are also other factors affecting the situation. It is difficult to gauge the proportion of one factor to another because it is a subjective analysis, but certainly in the Halifax area housing is an important consideration and has been for a number of years. There is inadequate housing for naval personnel, particularly at rates that ratings can afford. Consequently this has a direct bearing on any decision they might make to go into civilian employment as against remaining in the Royal Canadian Navy. I have no doubt that the reorganization which is taking place is another factor, and this is inevitable. We have made no attempt to hide the fact that in a major reorganization of the kind now in process you cannot avoid some dislocation and uncertainty. I think this is regrettable but it is the fact; you cannot achieve what we are trying to achieve without there being an element of uncertainty, at least for a period of time.
Having said that I again reassure the hon. gentleman and the committee that every effort will be made to overcome as many factors as can be overcome. The shipbuilding program, which may have some bearing on the sense of insecurity which members of the navy may feel, will be announced as soon as we can get governmental approval.
Will it be destroyers?

The type will be announced in due course. The housing situation is being reviewed at the moment to see whether something can be done in that area. I am sure that the civilian employment situation is something which hon. members will applaud -the fact there are opportunities available in the civilian economy. But this means that we have to compete with and offer more than those opportunities.
With respect to the question of uncertainty we will make every effort to end this uncertainty, or as much of it as we can, as early as we can; it is a matter under active study. I agree with my hon. friend this is a matter of concern, but I say again it is not a new

Supply-National Defence problem. However, it is one we must face, and every reasonable step will be taken to overcome the shortage.
In respect to those particular ships which have been put in alongside, this is not a matter of too great importance, because as my hon. friend knows they do not add very much to our operational capability. They are old and long in the tooth. But that does not mean that we must not take every step to see there are crews available for our first line fighting ships in the future.
With respect to the second point raised, about the car, I am as surprised as is the hon. gentleman. I can assure him that if his allegation is true, and I certainly do not doubt the word of an hon. member, I not only do not condone it but I will issue instructions that it must not happen again. I was informed that this car was under the control of the privy council office. I think it is one permanently assigned to that office. I am afraid I cannot give any more satisfactory explanation than that at the present time, but I will undertake to look into this question and if any instruction is necessary I will see it is given.

Mr. Chairman, there are a considerable number of matters I should have liked to go into in detail, but in the very few minutes remaining it is obviously impossible to do so. Therefore I will briefly touch on two or three.
The minister has just told us something about the difficulties involved in maintaining a sufficient number of technical personnel as far as the navy is concerned. During the past year or so I have expressed concern on a number of occasions about what has been an apparent decline in the efficiency and effectiveness of our naval forces. Again only yesterday an announcement was made that six more naval vessels are being tied up at Halifax because of an inability to man them with technical personnel. I think this is conclusive proof of the extremely serious decline which has taken place in our naval strength and effectiveness.
Only a little more than two years ago, at the time of the Cuban crisis, all six of those vessels now tied up were at sea, plus nine other vessels which have since been taken out of commission. Those vessels were all crewed at that time with sufficient technical and other personnel to enable them to carry out their jobs. The minister is shaking his head, indicating that is not the case. I was the minister at the time and received good


reports about all of these ships. I am willing to admit that there has always been some shortage of technical personnel, but we had a sufficient number of men to man those ships and enable them to carry out their tasks effectively. I do not think there is a senior officer now in the navy who will say anything else.
In two years time we find that over 16 ships, which were manned two years ago, at sea and prepared to do whatever was required in the event the Cuban crisis developed as it was feared it would at one time, cannot now be manned and are being tied up. The excuses given by the minister as to the difficulty involved in maintaining a sufficient number of personnel are inadequate. They are excuses which will not hold water.
The basic reason for this drop in the number of technical personnel, and I think the minister is aware of this, is the decline in morale in the navy resulting from the discouraging things this government has done. One of the most important of those discouragements is the cancellation of the shipbuilding program and the failure, at least to this date, on the part of the government to replace that program. The minister has spoken of a shipbuilding program, but he has been speaking along those lines for several months, and nothing has come of it. If the minister does have a shipbuilding program in mind, the time is long overdue for an announcement so that the program can get under way. After a decision has been made it will take four or five years to put the ships into operation at sea. The time lag in this regard is already serious, but the excuses given by the minister relating to the lack of technical personnel are inadequate.
The housing problem, to which he referred, is no worse now than it was two, three or four years ago, and in fact I suspect it is better now than it was at that time. The opportunities for employment in civilian occupations has been a factor in this regard throughout the time period I mentioned. No real change has taken place in that regard. The real change which has taken place is the result of what the government has done or failed to do. This has been discouraging to naval personnel and has broken down their morale, causing the personnel to feel that there is little use in continuing in the navy because there will likely be no future for them, and that they had better get out while the getting is good. That is exactly what has been happening.

I want to make one last plea to the minister to make some changes in the announced plan as far as reserve forces are concerned, and to continue to maintain some of the squadrons and companies in rural areas, which have throughout our history been among the best sources for militia men. It is essential that these units continue in operation in those areas, and I might mention particularly the Hastings-Prince Edward regiment, whose outside companies are disappearing, and the New Brunswick Hussars, which was the best armoured militia regiment for a number of years. I doubt very much whether any money will be saved by doing away with these detached companies and squadrons, and I make one last plea to the minister to reconsider some of these cuts, and to maintain some of these rural units and companies.
One other matter I should like to deal with relates to a return which I received, dated October 28. My question had been on the order paper for some three months, and was related to the number of officers of the rank of commodore and above in the navy, and officers with similar ranks in other forces that have ceased to be members of the permanent force, or have been given notice that they would be retired, or who have sent in their resignations. In each case I asked for the name of the officer, the appointment held and, where applicable, the number of years and months the officer would have to serve until normal retirement age. In each case I asked that an indication be given as to whether the officer retired on reaching normal retirement age, whether the officer put in a resignation on his own volition, or whether he was asked to retire.
I must complain bitterly about the return I received in this regard, Mr. Chairman, because it is a false return. The retirement age of a lieutenant colonel is laid down as 51 years of age; of a full colonel, 53 years of age; of a brigadier and major general, 55 years of age. However in this return, and I am not going to take the time to read it all, the majority of officers retired below the full age of 55; yet under the heading "Remarks" appears the notation that they were normal retirements. One air commodore retired at age 53, which is two years earlier than normal retirement age. Yet under the remarks appears the notation that this is a normal retirement and there was no length of time left until normal retirement age, and no extra payment made. There is no indication as to whether this was a voluntary retirement or whether the officer was asked to retire.
Supply-National Defence
Another air commodore, who was chief of telecommunications, retired at age 53, and in this case the notation is that it was a normal retirement.
Another air commodore retired at age 51, four years before normal retirement age, and the notation in this case is that it was a normal retirement. He was the deputy commander 29 region NORAD.
Another air commodore retired at age 52, and the notation is that this was a normal retirement. I have just given a few examples to indicate that this is not a correct return. If the officers had retired at normal retirement age, they would have retired at age 55, and if they retired younger than that, there should have been some notation as to the number of years still to be served until normal retirement age, and whether the officers retired voluntarily or as the result of a request. I object strenuously to this kind of incorrect information being provided to members of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether I may be permitted to answer that allegation at once. First of all, may I just say one further word in respect of naval technical personnel. For some time, when the hon. member was minister and since then, ships have been manned by taking naval technical personnel off ships, as soon as they tie up for refitting, and putting them into another crew on a ship on its way out to sea. This has created a serious condition of overwork for naval technical personnel. It has contributed also to a considerable decline in morale amongst them.
Now, the new cyclical use of ships crews eliminates that practice. This will improve morale, but at the same time it means that we do not overwork the technical personnel to the extent that they have been overworked in the past. Consequently more technical personnel are required in order to keep the ships operating. I think my hon. friend will appreciate this.
In respect of his allegation that the information contained in the return is incorrect or false, this is not right and I deny both allegations. The information given was correct. The question asked for information as to the names of all officers of brigadier or equivalent rank who, since January 1, 1964, have ceased to be members of the permanent force or have been given notice that they would be retired or have sent in their resignations. In each case, the name of the officer was asked for, the appointment held by him, his age and where applicable the number of

Supply-National Defence years and months to go to normal retirement age. Information was asked also as to whether each officer retired on reaching normal retirement age, put in his resignation of his own volition or was asked to retire.
In answer to this question, information was given as to name, rank, age, appointment, length of time to normal retirement and remarks, that is normal retirement by notice of voluntary retirement. The age given was the age of the officer at the time the return was prepared. The length of time to normal retirement age was interpreted as the time to go between actual retirement date and the date at which the officer would reach compulsory retirement age.
An example given by the hon. gentleman, I do not think he named him, was that of Air Commodore Timmerman. He will reach compulsory retirement age on February 12, 1966. He will start his retirement leave on August 19, 1965. He was informed to this effect on June 1, 1964. It is normal practice in the Royal Canadian Air Force to notify, whenever possible, all officers from 12 to 14 months prior to the date of terminal leave.
The other relevant point is that air commodores on the general list of air crew are retired at the age of 53, whereas air commodores and brigadiers on the other lists are retired at the age of 55. This rule has been in effect for a number of years. I can give the hon. gentleman, if he wishes, the names of four air commodores who were retired at the age of 53 when he was a minister. I do not know if he wants me to put those names on the record or just to send them to him. In February, 1961; in January, 1962; in May, 1961, and in February 1962, four air commodores of the pilot branch were retired at the age of 53. They, too, would have been given notice many months in advance when they were 52 or 51, depending on the length of notice the Royal Canadian Air Force had given them. This return, therefore, is correct in that detail. It is not misleading and there was no attempt whatever, nor was there in fact, any misrepresentation with regard to it.

Mr. Chairman, I do not accept that explanation as being correct in these cases. As I say, the normal retirement age is 55 for all these people, and to say that a man is given notice when he is going to be retired after six months leave and then take this case which was mentioned at age 51 and try to have it appear as a normal retirement, I do not believe stands up. I asked for the ages of these people. I think it is quite clear that the age that was required

was the age when the man retired. To put another interpretation upon it is to try to twist the sense of the question and twist the information which was required, out of context. In my view, this is an incorrect return.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with the question of the Canadian militia. I will try to be brief. It is only because of the pressure of time that the minister is fortunate enough to escape a thorough discussion of his estimates which should normally take about three days. We have had just one day on them. I had hoped that the militia alone would have been the subject of a full discussion because it is an important branch of the service in Canada. I expected there would be some criticism of the minister's action with regard to the Canadian militia. The hon. member for Calgary North, when he was speaking, expressed the hope the minister would take another look at what he is doing to the reserve forces of Canada.
I do not expect the minister will take another look. In the over a year and a half that we have been dealing with him, I do not know of any suggestion from our side of the house which he has adopted. He has obstinately refused to change his position. This is most unfortunate. There is some value in getting advice from all sides of this house. I suggest that the minister should review his action with regard to the militia, but I hold out no hope to militiamen across this country, as I have told several of them, that he will do that. His record with regard to the militia is not good, nor is the record of the party he represents. I speak from the experience of 15 years of service in the militia. I know what I am talking about in this regard.
I know how desperately the militia, in the interwar years, was in need of assistance and how niggardly was the response to that need, particularly in the years 1935 onward when it was obvious to everybody who had any sense at all that we were facing an outbreak of war. I am surprised that the minister has dealt with the Canadian militia so carelessly. When we were dealing with the estimates before, I mentioned that the minister had said not one word about the Canadian militia. It was a subject uppermost in the minds of the members of this house, and uppermost in the minds of the militia across Canada. There was not a word, not even a word of thanks to the regiments that were being disbanded. I think that this is not right.
Surely, the government of this country has a duty to people who will give militia serv-

ice. It is not an easy service. People have to sign on in the full knowledge that, having signed on for service in the militia or in any reserve unit in this country, they are obligated to go wherever trouble occurs, to stand up and be counted or be shot at. It is a serious decision that men make when they enter the militia of this country. It is not just a casual occupation. It is not a social club, as I have been told by some people. I have never known that in all the years I served in the militia. There was not one word of thanks from this government to regiments that are being disbanded. Almost worse than that, there has been a massive silence across this country with regard to these changes in the militia; there has been indifference and apathy.
I have been shocked at the response in Canada to the changes made in the militia regiments, the changes that will occur in cities and towns because of the disbandment of regiments. Even those people who do such a good job from day to day disseminating news and editorial comment have published nothing in their papers but obituary notices concerning regiments being disbanded. In the newspapers and magazines I have not seen any series of articles dealing with the importance of the militia to Canada and the history of the militia. The history of the Canadian militia extends over three and a half centuries. It is an honourable one which should be known to everybody, and as Canada is approaching the 20 million population figure the militia, rather than being reduced in size should be enlarged to give young people an opportunity to serve their country.
The minister is wiping out the Winnipeg Grenadiers and the Victoria Rifles, two regiments about whom the conscience of Canada should be bothered. These were the two that went to Hong Kong on that forlorn expedi-dition that was so disastrous, and now they are being wiped out, 25 years later. If there are any two regiments that should be maintained these are they, at least so far as the present generation is concerned. Do we owe a debt of gratitude to these regiments? I say we do, and that they should be maintained in the order of battle.
By question and short answer we have dealt with the Irish Fusiliers and the Irish Rifles. It is most unfortunate that the minister has taken such a stubborn stand with regard to these two important units in the militia, with such great tradition behind them. Indeed I am surprised that the people in the cities where they are located have not impressed upon the government the mistake that 20220-674
Supply-National Defence is being made. The minister is also wiping out the Princess Louise Dragoon Guards of Ottawa, a regiment that has 92 years history behind it. I do not name all of those which are being disbanded but I say the minister is giving the militia disgraceful treatment.
He and his advisers do not appreciate the work of the militia. I wonder if he and his advisers served in the militia and put in those evening drill periods, those week ends, and summer camps year after year. Militiamen do this, though there are things of greater interest to them that they might be doing.
One recommendation of the Suttie commission that I hope will be followed deals with a publicity operation with regard to the militia, to let the people of the country know the service being rendered by thousands of young men. This has been one of the serious weaknesses in the militia. Even at this time of crisis to the militia its officers and men are prohibited from publicly stating their case. They are under military orders, and so it is left to the civilians to protest the mistake. The officers and men cannot do that. They are dependant upon their outside supporters within communities, and that is why I am now speaking on behalf of the militia.
I shall not take up any more time of the committee except to refer it, and the newspapers of the country, to a book published a few years ago by the Macmillan Company, "Canada's Soldiers 1604-1954," written by George F. G. Stanley of the Royal Military College of Canada. It gives the story of Canada's soldiers right from the beginning of the country, and deals with the importance of the militia. I conclude by reading the last paragraph in the book in which is expressed very ably the debt that we owe to Canada's militia:
For three centuries and a half Canadians have borne arms. Essentially a civilian people, an unmilitary people, they have, through historical necessity, fought to preserve their freedom and their identity. No men have fought better: no men have as quickly discarded the skills of war to return to the farms and factories of peace. During their 300 years and more, Canadian soldiers have tramped over the white snows of Canada, the quiet countryside of England, the rugged mountains of Italy, and the muddy polders of Holland; they have battled the Indians, the British, the Americans, within and on the frontiers of their own country; they have fought the Germans and Italians in Europe, and the Japanese in Asia; they have left their dead behind them from the Arctic to the Mediterranean. Canada's soldiers! They are the farmers, the traders, the mechanics, the labourers, the doctors, lawyers, and teachers of peacetime. Very few of them have ever been professional soldiers.
But, militiaman and regular, they have carried the torch of Canada's military tradition. A brave buckskin, the white, the red and the khaki

Supply-National Defence
tunics. Their deeds are our history; their names are forgotten, but their achievements are commemorated in the very existence of Canada as a nation. This military story of Canada is a bold and mighty thing, and yet it is a bald tale and unadorned, a tale of those simple virtues of courage, endurance and self-sacrifice which war, for all its horrors and wanton destruction, seems to evoke in men inspired by a common sense of purpose. Perhaps out of this comradeship of arms, this memory of heroic past, will some day come that sense of inward unity which is born of perils shared and victories won.

I would like to congratulate the hon. members for Calgary North and Winnipeg South Centre on coming to the aid of the militia. It seems ironic that at this season, long dedicated to remembrance of the fallen, and indeed within a few days of the date solemn to their memory, which we celebrated at our cenotaphs, that one should be obliged to speak in defence of the traditions for which these men stood, and for the facilities and system that made their service possible. I believe it is an accurate statement now, as it has been for many years past, that Canada's defence is based on this hypothesis: a small but intensively trained regular army acting as an instructional cadre to the citizen-soldiers who form a well-trained and competent militia, which is brought quickly to full strength and training in time of war.
Modern weapons and their technology have complicated the soldiers' equipment and drills, but surely the will and the skill to defend is still the most important defence and deterrent the nation possesses. How can we foster these talents without a continuous attention to and emphasis upon the proper training of our youth within their various localities and in conjunction with home and school, as a healthy and normal activity?
Surely all will agree that for many years past our local militia units and the armouries in which they train have amply illustrated and stood for that will and that skill. Indeed they have been our only means of translating the nation's determination to action in the hard shock of war. Now I am given to understand that in my own constituency two militia units, those at Picton and at Napanee, are to be disbanded and if I interpret the verdict correctly their respective armouries are to be disposed of, with the likelihood that these valuable buildings will be torn down and sold to the highest bidders. I think they are worthy of a better fate than that. These units, their influence and their quarters, are simply to disappear. Is that true, Mr. Chairman?
It is well recognized that military reorganization is necessary from time to time, that

some units must merge with others or that units must change from one corps to another and be designated to other tasks. No one would dispute this. There would be no serious disruption if this were the case. What has caused the storm of protest is the appalling news that not only are the units to be disbanded but that the very armouries are to go as well. I have received 150 letters from the riding of Prince Edward-Lennox protesting against this measure taken by the present government-150 letters from ordinary people across the riding whose sons, yes and whose daughters, have made use of the training afforded by these two installations for the past 50 years in Picton and Napanee. The tragic news is not only that the units are to be disbanded but that the armouries are to go as well.
I wonder whether the full implications of this policy are really understood by all members of this committee-whether they can really appreciate what this will mean to small communities where communal activity of many kinds, civilian as well as military, centers around these noble and historic buildings? In cities, where a number of military formations exist, each with a headquarters to house it, an armoury might be removed without greatly disturbing the over-all efficiency of training and the life of the society, but to a small and largely rural community it is a disaster of no small proportions. The fact is that the rural communities contribute the greatest military potential per capita of any part of the country. Though people fail to realize it, no matter what condition may exist, and no matter what the reasons behind the decision may have been, if these armouries are destroyed, military training and all that it means is forever destroyed with them. I say to the minister: if he destroys the volunteer will to defend this country he will have to establish another system in its place in case of emergency, possibly conscription; and hon. members know how distasteful conscription is to certain parts of this country. He would do better to maintain the militia force, which has been of such value to this country in the past. If the armouries are destroyed, military training and all it means is forever gone. It is a dead issue and it cannot be revived.
The most serious aspect of this is the fact that the tradition of voluntary military service vanishes with it. Let there be no mistake: The voluntary participation by our young men in military service-the characteristic feature of Canadian defence-starts first in

these small towns, in these armouries across the land. If this spirit does not start with the volunteers it will not exist on the day war is declared. What will happen to these young men who are now engaged in military training, if present plans are carried out? On my last visit as a spectator on training night at Napanee armoury I counted a total of 34 young men of all ranks on parade. That was on November 5, one of the last drills being held by the 47th medium battery artillery R.C.A., Napanee. I submit that 34 men out to drill on a mid-week evening represents a very good turnout for a town of that size.

subtopic: SIR WINSTON CHURCHILL
SIR WINSTON CHURCHILL
subsubtopic: TRIBUTES ON NINETIETH BIRTHDAY ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Today, as the world knows, a remarkable man has reached a remarkable age. Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill is celebrating his ninetieth birthday anniversary. Just four months ago today, on July 30, we paid tribute to Sir Winston Churchill on the occasion of his retirement from parliament. At that time the right hon. Prime Minister, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and the leaders or spokesmen of the other parties in this house acknowledged our "unbounded admiration and gratitude for Sir Winston's services to freedom and to free men everywhere".
In pursuance of a motion agreed to unanimously by the house I transmitted these tributes to the right hon. gentleman. Hon. members will be interested in the acknowledgement which I received in Sir Winston Churchill's own hand, and which I am sure they would want me to read into the record:
28, Hyde Park Gate, London, S.W. 7 8 November, 1964.
Dear Mr. Speaker,
I am indeed obliged to you for your letter of October 19. I have read with the utmost pleasure the motion passed in the House of Commons and the speeches which accompanied it. I am deeply honoured that this moving and eloquent tribute should have been paid to me by Canadians, whose country I hold in such deep affection and high esteem. I shall always remember your kindness to me.
Yours very sincerely, Winston S. Churchill.
I am sure that today all members of this house would again want their affectionate good wishes to go forth to him whom historians may well call "the greatest Englishman of the century". I therefore propose sending the following message to Sir Winston on behalf of this house:
It is my privilege to assure you, sir, of the undiminished gratitude, affection and admiration in which you are held by all Canadians as you begin your tenth decade of "days memorable in the history of our race". We fervently wish for you
and Lady Churchill many more years of strength, of good health and of happiness in your retirement. From all our hearts and with one voice we say, "Happy birthday."

subtopic: SIR WINSTON CHURCHILL

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the words you have uttered pay fitting and eloquent tribute to the greatest man of our time on reaching his ninetieth birthday, a stage which not many of us are likely to achieve. I think your tribute represents the feeling of us all. He is indeed a man of our century, this terrible twentieth century. He is a man of parliament. He is the man who led the struggle for freedom, and his name will live forever in the hearts of all free men.
Therefore I should like to move, seconded -if I may do so, Mr. Speaker-by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition:
That the message proposed by Mr. Speaker be sent by him on behalf of all members of this house to Sir Winston Churchill.
Righf Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I join with the Prime Minister in this motion. Indeed, one of the fondest recollections I have of the period during which I was prime minister was to have the opportunity, on every occasion that I was in the United Kingdom, to meet and talk with Sir Winston. I was greatly impressed this morning as I listened on the radio by what happened yesterday in front of his home at Hyde Park Corner. Hundreds were gathered there and they were asking that he come outside. Finally he stepped up to the window. Then his wife went outside and said "I am saving him for tomorrow".
That, Mr. Speaker, has been his life history. One follows him in India, the Sudan, during the days of the first great war and throughout the years; often in defeat, always defiant. His record, as the Prime Minister has said and as you, Mr. Speaker, so very eloquently stated, makes him a great citizen, an immortal figure in the present century. We see him now at 90 years of age able to look back on several lifetimes, measuring time on the basis of achievement.
Great author, orator, parliamentarian, artist, historian, only once did he turn to poetry. There is only one couplet in his name:

Tributes to Sir Winston Churchill No more let us alter, or falter, or palter,
From Malta to Yalta,
From Yalta to Malta.
That epitomises his life story. He never paltered; sometimes he did alter his viewpoint with the passing years, but at no time did he falter. I think of one instance which took place in London, I think in 1959, during the occasion of a prime ministers' conference. Prime Minister Harold MacMillan gave a dinner at Downing street to my wife and me. She sat at the table between Mr. Macmillan and Sir Winston, and I sat across the table and some distance down. Beside me sat Mrs. Neville Chamberlain, the widow of the prime minister of the United Kingdom whose place Mr. Churchill, as he then was, took in May of 1940. During the course of the conversation I said "Is it not wonderful that he has lived this long full of alertness, never losing that sense of good humour so necessary to those who are in public life. He is enjoying himself tonight". Her answer was "You know, we would not be here if it was not for him". That to me represents the relationship in public life and in national affairs that gives substance to British parliamentary life.
I join with the Prime Minister in the motion he has moved. This house will never forget that day in December of 1941 when he stood where the Clerk of this house sits and used those words that had greater influence on this nation than any words ever expressed in describing the dark days of June, 1940. He said a French spokesman had stated that the generals believed it would just be a matter of three weeks before the neck of England would be stretched like that of a chicken. Sir Winston then said "Some chicken, some neck." Those are words never to be forgotten.
We salute him today, and in honouring him we honour the parliamentary system to which he gave so much and to which, as a House of Commons man, he devoted his life and his talents.

We are also well aware of numerous occasions when the house has changed its order of business, and frequently has reverted to motions for some special announcement or motion to be put before the house by the government. speechtext:
['I was about to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not of English ancestry but rather my grandfather on my father's side came from the highlands of northern Scotland, and on my mother's side my great grandfather was Pennsylvania Dutch of loyal united empire loyalist stock. I was very proud today when the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) directed our attention to the fact that this is St. Andrew's day.
As I say, great disunity has been created in this country since the flag debate was first introduced in the House of Commons. We have had riots in various parts of Canada. We have seen flags burned. We have had an increase in the separatist movement in the province of Quebec. We have seen our armouries raided and robbed. Yes, Mr. Speaker, murders were even committed while this was being done.
When I spoke on my own flag resolution I stated that I was expressing my own personal opinions as well as the opinions expressed in approximately 90 per cent of the letters and telegrams I had received up until that time. That was last June 1, Mr. Speaker, and previous to that date I had received nearly 150 signed letters and telegrams all asking me to support the retention of the Canadian ensign as Canada's national flag. This figure has now mounted to 611. Since June 1 I have received many letters supporting my stand on the ensign but since that date I have received only three letters supporting some other design than the ensign.
In all fairness to those who are writing me in support of the ensign and to those supporting some other design I propose to put on the record some comments from each side. Before doing so I may say that some time ago I received a clipping from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal, being an article written by Jean Sweet. The article is entitled "In My Opinion", and in my opinion it exemplifies the feelings, I am sure, of many millions of Canadians. I am going to quote from the article. This lady says:
Normally, like most peaceful citizens, I'm a coward about public issues. But I think the time
has come to stand up and be counted on this flag matter.
Most people who ever saw a tree know that big trees rise from big firm roots. If you trim away the roots you weaken the tree. If too much root is removed you have nothing. The tree-that grew slowly over many decades-weakens, falls and decays.
Loyalties grow the same way, putting down roots in friendly soil. Without loyalities, even misplaced loyalities, man is nothing but a drifting derelict.
Millions of Canadians grew up as I did in the friendly soil of a Canada we learned from earliest years to respect and view with immense pride. We were taught not to brag loudly and constantly about our land, but instead to know what we had and to feel secure in its tenets.
Above all our flag has symbolized this land. It has grown with us. From pre-school age we loved the simple but intricately planned design of the union jack, so carefully integrating the major elements of Great Britain. We were proud when we saw the Canadian coat of arms in the fly of the beautiful flag. We sang songs to it. It meant our land.
Through school days I have no recollection of any "Quebec question". I remember Montreal as a fascinating place I longed to see where, right in our Canada, two languages were spoken and peoples from many other lands settled and lived.
Above all, as a child I watched the proud Van Doos march through the streets of our town, where they trained, headed by the tall lean figure of Colonel Vanier (I didn't know his name then, not until I met him as our Governor General). From that time I "saw" those proud French speaking troops "fighting for our flag" as news of their exploits trickled home. When we sang "We'll never let the old flag fall'' the Van Doos were in the picture, dying in France for that flag.
Well, as far as I am concerned no one man, no one group of troublemakers, can tell me "here is your new flag". This is a matter of roots, Canadian roots. If my flag can be readily discarded, so can my country and any other belief I ever held in it. It is disturbing and makes me wonder: what next?
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.']

I shall endeavour to maintain that attitude in the few brief remarks which I have to make on this occasion. The resolution setting up this committee was moved in the House of Commons on Thursday, September 10, and in order that the record may be kept straight I would like to read that motion

again. On the motion of Mr. Favreau, seconded by Mr. Churchill, it was resolved:
That a special committee of this house consisting of 15 members, to be designated later by the house, be appointed to consider and report upon the flag question; that the said committee be empowered to report from time to time and that its final report be submitted not later than six weeks from the date of its first sitting; and that the appointment of this committee, its power to report and the capacity of this house to act upon the report be not restricted by any motions now on the order paper.
On September 15 this house appointed to the committee 15 members. Those members were: the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Cadieux); the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman); the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Dube); the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming); the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz); the hon. member for Megan-tic (Mr. Langlois); the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard); the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso); the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson); the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith); the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh); the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tis-dale (Mr. Rapp); the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard); the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) and myself. This committee held its first meeting on Thursday, September 17, and in pursuance of the resolution passed in this house it was therefore bound to report not later than Thursday, October 29.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a comment regarding the work of the members of this committee. In the years I have been in the House of Commons I, like other members of the house, have had the opportunity of being a member of various house committees. I would like to say to the house now that I have never had the opportunity of being a member of a committee that was so diligent in pursuing the task that had been given to them. For a very large number of the meetings 100 per cent of the members were present. The opinions expressed were strongly expressed; I believe that they were sincerely held. I say to the house now-and I do this on my own initiative-that I would like to commend the members of the committee for the excellent work which they did over a period of time when the meetings were many and the work rather concentrated.

Following the organizational meeting on September 17, 45 meetings were
Canadian Flag
held. During those 45 meetings 12 witnesses were heard. They came before the committee with the understanding that their remarks would be considered in camera, but I would like to say now-and I know I am speaking for the members of the committee when I say this-how grateful we all are for the contribution which they made to the committee itself. They gave us a great deal of information on Canadian history, heraldry, protocol and flag design; and for the contribution which they made to the work of the committee I am very grateful.
During the deliberations of this committee approximately 2,000 new designs were examined, as well as designs which had been presented to the house on previous occasions. I would also like to thank those who were sufficiently interested in a Canadian flag to submit designs to the committee. All the designs submitted had a great deal of merit, and as the selection process continued it became more and more difficult for the committee to pick the design which it favoured most.
I would like to say a word regarding the method of selection. The flags presented to the committee were divided into three groups; those which had for their main part three maple leaves, those which had one maple leaf, and those which had the union jack or the fleur-de-lis or both. There was then a process of selection, and the committee was finally able to reach the point where there were five flags in each of these groups. From there on the process of selection was carried on by secret ballot. Finally the committee was able to get down to one flag in each of these groups.
Your Honour will recall that on November 18 the house passed a motion proposed by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton ordering that there be laid before the house copies of the final flag designs in categories (a), (b) and (c) as voted upon by this committee. For the convenience in debate of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, other members of the flag committee and members of the house in general, I should like now, with the unanimous consent of the house, to table photographic copies of these final flag designs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to say that I appreciate the words of the hon. member for Hum-ber-St. George's concerning the attendance of members of the committee and, as he put it, the sincerity of the members of the committee. I think there was an awful lot of hard work done. I in turn, Mr. Speaker, should like to congratulate our chairman on the fact that he handled a very difficult committee in a very competent manner. I do not often go on record as congratulating a member of the government or a member of the government party, but I must say that he did keep us

under control with a kindly but firm approach throughout. During six weeks of very concentrated sittings, and facing a deadline, all of that time tension was increasing and nerves did become frayed; and the chairman deserves full credit, Mr. Speaker, for a job well done.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as a member of that committee I feel it is my duty to say a few words at this time. As the chairman mentioned, our first meeting was held on September 17 last. It was not held in camera; it was an organization meeting at which we elected a chairman, a vice chairman, and so on. At the second meeting, which was the first in camera and which was held on the afternoon of Monday, September 21, we discussed, first of all, our general approach to this question with which we were faced. I agree with the chairman that it was probably the best attended committee which has ever sat in this building. There was frequently 100 per cent attendance of that committee from that date on.
At that first meeting held in camera I was encouraged by the way various members sitting on the committee from both sides of the house appeared to be approaching our very difficult objective. There were several who spoke of compromise, mentioning retaining something of the past and suggesting something of what might be considered the new. I have to say, Mr. Speaker, that I was doomed to disappointment.
The chairman has read out certain terms of the report of the committee, and I should like to read at this time the first four paragraphs:
1.	Pursuant to its order of reference of September 10, 1964, your committee had before it, for consideration and report, the flag question.
2.	On September 15, 1964, the House of Commons designated 15 members of the committee:-
The chairman has mentioned the names and I do not want to repeat them.
3.	A subcommittee on agenda and procedure was appointed. The members were-
And so on.
4.	Your committee held 45 sittings in camera-
I would emphasize those words "in camera".
-and heard 12 witnesses in the fields of history,
heraldry, protocol, art and design. The members of the committee express their gratitude to these witnesses for their efforts in providing detailed information and also to the nearly 2,000 Canadians who submitted flag designs and suggestions.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, with the chairman's words of appreciation to the witnesses who came before us and to those who presented designs for our consideration.

10S81
Now I should like to refer back to those words "in camera". First of all I should like to refer to some newspaper articles and quotations therein. I do not have them all by any means, but I should like to point out that to me there has been some inconsistency regarding the real meaning of the words "in camera" and the apparent interpretation given them by certain people.
The first reference I would make concerns a picture of the hon. member for Leeds which appeared in a newspaper under date of September 23, 1964. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the committee had been meeting since September 15. This picture depicting the hon. member for Leeds appeared in La Voix de L'Est, Granby, Quebec, under date September 23, and pictured him holding what at that time had been thought and claimed by the government to be their flag. That was the three maple leaves flag with the blue bars at the end. I do not know when the picture was taken, but it was published in this newspaper on September 23, 1964.
I pass now to an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on October 5, 1964 headed "Judy regrets harsh things said about proposed flag". This article is datelined Gander, Newfoundland, and goes on as follows:
Health minister Judy LaMarsh said Saturday the new flag under study in committee at Ottawa may "never recover from some of the outrageous things said about it".
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether this was the tip-off that the government members were going to switch their allegiance from the three maple leaves flag to the one which is now described in the report, and were actually instructed to do so. I would point out that in the first interview which the chairman had with the press-perhaps it was his first press release after the committee's first meeting-the chairman suggested, I believe, that it would be appreciated if there was no pressure put on the members of the committee to reveal what was going on in camera, and I think pretty generally this request was observed by the press, at least up to a certain point.
At this stage I began to wonder how these news items concerning conjecture about what was going on in the committee became published. I have before me a copy of the Toronto Daily Star of Monday, October 19, and I should like to refer to an article written by Mr. William MacEachern in which he said the following:
Canadian Flag
Indeed, there is some question whether it will be able to make a report at all, unanimous or otherwise, by the Oct. 29 deadline set out in its terms of reference.
Conservative members are already pressing for an extension of the deadline but Liberal members are opposed.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer again to an earlier stage of the committee's meetings, and say without equivocation that at a very early stage of those meetings there were many members who indicated that if we were faced with a deadline and there appeared to be a possibility of coming up with something, we might ask for an extension of the six weeks time limit. That was our aim throughout the hearings from the first day we sat. However, this thought was expressed by more than just Conservative members, as I said, at an early stage of our meetings.
I should like to quote one other excerpt from this article, as follows:
According to one committee member "the Tory position hasn't changed one iota from the stand opposition leader John Diefenbaker took when he spoke on the flag question in the Commons in 1945.
I should like to know who that committee member is, because this article very definitely states "According to one committee member". I guarantee that he was not a member of our party, because our members had the sensitivity to appreciate what the words "in camera" meant. Apparently others did not so appreciate them.
The next article I wish to quote from appeared in the Peterborough Examiner of October 19, under the heading "Top Secret Lid Taken Off... Students get 'inside information' on Flag". I think I will read a portion of this very interesting article, as follows:
The meetings of the Commons flag committee in Ottawa have been labelled "top secret" and the committee room is strictly "out of bounds" to outsiders.
But a group of Crestwood secondary school students broke the barriers Friday and gathered an impressive array of previously hushed facts.
They were the first outsiders to gain entry to the room.
They learned the original backdrop of the Pearson flag may be rejected, and they saw a banner which could possibly be Canada's future flag.
They were told Canada now stands where the United States stood more than 100 years ago before its civil war and that Canadians may be on the threshold of a similar conflict.
The 37 students from grade 10 travelled to Ottawa with Stuart Howard, head of the history department.
Their tour of the flag committee quarters was arranged by Richard Honey (M.P., Durham) and Fred Stenson (M.P., Peterborough).

Canadian Flag
I am informed that Mr. Stenson had nothing whatever to do with arranging this visit to the flag committee. The article then continues:
John Matheson (M.P., Leeds), committee member, and Prime Minister Pearson's personal adviser on the flag issue, greeted the students and spoke to them on the issue.
"There were flags everywhere in that room," said Mr. Howard.
Mr. Howard described the physical appearance of the room with flags draped all around. Then the article states:
Mr. Matheson emphasized to the students the continual reappearance of the three maple leaves on the flags being submitted by the public, and mentioned their prominence in past Canadian flags and badges.
"He seemed convinced the national flag would include the three maple leaves," said Mr. Howard, "but he was not so sure of the background.
"He also said the sea to sea motif on the Pearson banner may be seriously altered."
Mr. Howard said the M.P. questioned the importance of the sea to sea idea, saying that about 50 countries used the format and "maybe some other aspect of our history should be used."
Mr. Matheson said wavy royal blue bars at the top and bottom of the banner-an idea submitted by the group of seven painter A. Y. Jackson-is getting considerable attention.
He then pointed at a group of flags resting at one end of the room and said they were getting the most serious attention from the committee.
Resting prominently in the centre of these was a large white banner with three red leaves in the centre.
"The leaves were the same as the Pearson leaves," said Mr. Howard, "only they were more upright and closer together.
"Below that was this same flag inset on the traditional military service flag in place of the union .jack."
Mr. Howard said several flags displaying the fleur-de-lis were to be seen.
Mr. Matheson told the students of a recent committee meeting when Dr. A. R. M. Lower, professor emeritus of history at Queen's University, addressed it and said Canada now stands where the United States stood just before the civil war.
I think I should point out at this stage that each witness who appeared before that committee was assured that none of the evidence given would be published but that it would remain completely private so they could be free to speak as they saw fit. This fact was impressed upon the witnesses so we could, as I am sure we did, receive from them their honest and candid opinions. This article is a good example of the information that has leaked out.
Again quoting from this article, and this is Mr. Matheson speaking:
"He said the flag is symbolic of the tensions in certain parts of Canada between the races," Mr. Howard said, "and in his opinion there could be civil war here unless the differences are settled."
Mr. Speaker, what kind of scare statements are those being made by a member of parliament, and a member of this committee, to
[Mr. Monteith.l
students of this country, particularly when one remembers that the meetings of the committee were held in camera?
I should now like to quote from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on October 20, under the heading "A. Y. Jackson's Flag Favoured". This article is written by Ken Kelly of the Canadian Press and states in part:
Famed artist A. Y. Jackson's flag design is reliably reported to be the choice of a majority of members of the Commons flag committee.
Informants say the committee probably will split 9-5 to recommend to the Commons that the 82 year old Canadian painter's maple leaf flag design become Canada's flag and that the Canadian red ensign be used to mark Canada's commonwealth connection.
Reliable sources say the Jackson design has the support of Liberal, New Democratic, Social Credit and Creditist M.P.'s so far.
The five Progressive Conservatives still haven't committed themselves and one source says they aren't expected to back the majority choice. Conservative committee members, many of whose colleagues in the Commons favour the Canadian red ensign as the Canadian flag, were reported to have proposed several designs to the committee. .. .It is anticipated that at least one effort will be made to get committee support for a request that the committee's deadline be extended.
Here again I ask, Mr. Speaker, who was this reliable source? I guarantee it was not a member of the Conservative party. I can only suggest that whoever gave this information to Mr. Kelly was certainly misleading him. Whether he was purposely misleading him or otherwise I would not know, but at any rate it is obvious that Mr. Kelly has been led down the garden path. I feel that this deliberate attempt to mislead the public must certainly have caused great discomfiture to that famed artist, Mr. A. Y. Jackson.
Then I come to October 23 and another article by Ken Kelly of the Canadian Press which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen. I will only read some excerpts.
Most of the Liberals on the committee are insisting on a design containing three maple leaves. They do not want the union jack in any form. The majority of the Conservatives, on the other hand, are said to be insisting that the jack be present in some form and that the maple leaf theme be confined to any number of maple leaves except three.
Here again, Mr. Speaker, I point out that somebody has talked, but certainly not a member of the Conservative party. There is another article to which I should like to refer which appeared on October 24 under the byline of Mr. Douglas Fisher, M.P. I am going to read the following paragraph to which I should like to make particular reference:
Some suspect that the leader of the official opposition has been privy to every move of the

committee and has been piping advice through several of the Conservatives.

I continue:
This suspicion is the explanation for the retreat to the Gatineau this week end, or so the story goes.
I cannot speak too strongly about this article. First of all I should like to point out that so far as the report we are now discussing is concerned, all votes had been taken prior to the so-called retreat to the Gatineau. I cannot speak too strongly against the words of the hon. member for Port Arthur and the innuendo to be found in this paragraph. He is implying that the leader of our party was in continuous contact with and was piping instructions to the Conservative members of the committee. I can say without any qualification that no member of the committee discussed this matter at all with the Leader of the Opposition until after the votes had been taken. Never at any time until the final vote had been taken did any member do so, nor was there any effort whatsoever on behalf of the Leader of the Opposition to pipe information to the committee members. I cannot say the same for the government members.
As hon. members know, the committee report was presented to the house on October 29, the last day on which it could be presented. I come now to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of that date, which is quite interesting. Incidentally, as you will remember, Mr. Speaker, the newspaper containing the article appeared on the streets of Ottawa some 45 minutes before the House of Commons sat. This is but another example of the Liberal party's contempt for parliament. Other speakers will no doubt refer to this article as the debate continues, but I should like to refer to one or two paragraphs of the article which was written by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman). He wrote:
Here is the inside story which I am now free to tell provided I do not attribute votes or statements to individuals on the committee or reveal the confidential testimony of witnesses.
He denies the right of the hon. member for Leeds to reveal the testimony of witnesses, but the hon. member for Leeds did not show that integrity. I have read what he said as quoted in the Peterborough Examiner. There are many other excerpts well worth mentioning. I am not going to go into the article in detail at the moment, but here is another excerpt:
Canadian Flag
In the fourth week we were beginning to know what prices would be put on concessions.
I should like to know just what is meant by that statement "what prices would be put on concessions". Here is another paragraph:
Tension mounted as the day drew near. There was much lobbying from room to room and whispering in the comer. Frequent skirmishes broke out in committee sittings.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra was running around lobbying from room to room, although it would seem he admits he was. He says he visited other members. I accept the fact that he undoubtedly did do a lot of lobbying but certainly no lobbying was done by the Conservative members on the committee. This gives an indication of the mood and thinking of the Liberal members throughout the sittings of the committee. We recall that the newspaper appeared on the streets 45 minutes before the committee report was presented to the house, and to me this is a complete abdication of responsibility to the House of Commons.
I have only one more reference, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is worth noting. I have here the Brockville Recorder and Times of November 2 last which contains a quite interesting article under the headline "Tory Strategy Backfired On Flag Says Matheson". I assume that throughout the hon. member for Leeds endeavoured to give his home town paper a sort of inside story as to what went on, but I should like to quote one or two excerpts from this article to show how ridiculous and how completely wrong the hon. member for Leeds was. He makes this statement:
It was at this point they-
Meaning the Conservative party members on the committee-
-were given full reign to set the rules.
This is utter rot and the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) knows it. We never had any kind of control over setting the rules. I agree some of our suggestions were accepted. Some of the suggestions of other members of the committee were accepted. But when the hon. member makes a statement like-
It was at this point they were given full reign to set the rules-
-this is simply atrocious. I quote further from the article:
At this point, Mr. Matheson said, the Conservatives almost turned white in consternation since they had voted in violation of Mr. Diefen-baker's instructions to make sure there were no unanimous votes.

Canadian Flag
I go back to what I said earlier. Never at any time, until after the final vote had been taken, had there been any contact with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on any matters concerning the flag committee proceedings. That is correct, and you know it.

You may get up and ask any question you like afterwards. Just sit down for the moment. Mr. Speaker, this is simply not true.
I think I should also put on the record one or two other statements made by the hon. member for Leeds in his article. There was a reference to the behaviour of the Conservative members of the committee. I presume he thought it was humour. I do not propose to quote it because I feel that does not deserve any notice whatsoever. I am sure he will understand what I am talking about. The article continues:
Mr. Matheson said he is happy with the committee's choice, although he had hoped for the three leaf design.
How ridiculous can you get. Here he is trying to indicate to his home town paper that he was standing behind his original choice, he who is presumed to have advised the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on this three maple leaf choice. Mr. Speaker, he did not vote for it. That is obvious, but here he is trying to leave the impression in his home town that he had been standing behind his original choice. I quote further:
"It's a beautiful flag," he added, saying all the talk about it looking like the Peruvian flag was not correct.
This is in reference to the design reported by the committee on October 29. I leave it to your judgment Mr. Speaker, as to whether or not this flag looks like the Peruvian flag. I suggest that the citizenry as a whole examine it and it will be very obvious to them whether the flag chosen looks like the Peruvian flag. I simply repeat that the condition to which government members have brought this flag question is a shameful mess. To Conservative members this was an in camera committee. To at least one or more other members it was not.
I now quote from paragraph six of the committee report:
Elimination by an agreed procedure left only one design in each category. A vote for the retention of each finalist was then taken with the following results:
A-The three maple leaf design was retained by a vote of eight to six (8 to 6);

B-The single maple leaf design was retained by a vote of thirteen to one (13 to 1);
C-The design containing the union jack and/or the fleur-de-lis was rejected by a vote of nine to five (9 to 5).
I would like to inform the house that when we were defeated in our desire to retain the red ensign, something which had taken place earlier, we wanted to find out whether the government and other members of the committee were taking an uncompromising stand. We showed our desire for a compromise in a design which was produced for the committee, containing the union jack and fleur-de-lis, but we just could not get any support for any flag with the union jack on it.
