speechtext:
On August 24 last I spoke during the flag debate and dealt at some length with my feelings on the issue. I do not propose to go into more detail in that regard today. I also dealt at some length with the reason that I believed in a matter so personal, so close to one's heart, there should be an opportunity for every citizen to express his or her preference through means of a plebiscite. I believe the majority of Canadians wish to have this opportunity, something which has been strongly borne out by opinion polls across the country.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp):
That the sixth report of the special committee be not now adopted but that it be referred back to the committee with instructions to strike out paragraph seven of the said report and substitute therefor the following:
"However, as the final vote of the committee did not reveal a sufficient degree of unanimity for the proposed design for a national flag for Canada, your committee therefore recommends that the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to conduct a plebiscite to be held at the next general election in order that the Canadian people may be given their rightful opportunity to declare their choice concerning a national flag".
And that the committee for such purpose be revived.
I close simply by reminding the house of the Prime Minister's rather delayed expression to the effect that on anything concerning the flag there is to be a free vote.

speechtext:
The objection is on several grounds. The first has to do with the right to refer the report back to the committee. Such a right does not exist because the committee is a special committee, not a standing committee; it is a special committee whose final report has been made.
In support of this position I would refer Your Honour to citation 286 on page 236 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, where it is stated;
A select special committee ceases to exist on the moment its final report is presented to the house. The report cannot afterwards be sent back to the committee with instructions to amend it in any particular. If further proceedings are desired it is necessary to revive the committee.
That is the first ground of objection. There is a further ground of objection which is even more fundamental, and it is this. It will be recalled that the committee was set up after several weeks of debate on this flag question and it will be noted on reading the motion to set it up that the terms of reference were very special; this is not only called a special committee but it is, in fact, special by its very nature. The reason is easily understood by anyone who bears in mind the history of the flag question in the House of Commons this session. The motion will be found in Votes and Proceedings No. 145 of September 10 and it reads as follows:
Canadian Flag
That a special committee of this house, consisting of 15 members, to be designated later by the house, be appointed to consider and report upon the flag question; that the said committee be empowered to report from time to time and that its final report be submitted not later than six weeks from the date of its first sitting; and that the appointment of this committee, its power to report and the capacity of this house to act upon the report be not restricted by any motions now on the order paper.
The point I wish to make in this connection is the following one: Even if it were generally in order to refer a report back to a special committee this would not be sufficient in this particular case. The committee, in its present form, could not be revived by implication or even by a motion, as is sought to be done. What is involved here is the whole charter of the committee, its whole constitution, its whole character. This will be well understood if hon. members would bear in mind its history. It was to report back to the house within six weeks after its first meeting, and its first meeting was held some time in September-I forget the exact date. So even the implied revival of the committee is not effective. Sending back what is sought to be sent back to it for further consideration cannot be effective; it would be a mere nullity because the committee, by its own constitution, does not have the authority or the power to carry out the function which this proposal seeks to refer to it, because of the limitation of time in its constitution.
The authority for a special committee is very limited. It has only the authority given to it by the house. Perhaps I could read an excerpt from Redlich, page 196:
It remains, finally, to explain the legal relation of a committee to the house as a whole. The main principle to be attended to is that a committee only exists, and only has power to act, so far as expressly directed by the order of the house which brings it into being. This order of reference is a firm bond, subjecting the committee to the will of the house; the reference is always treated with exactness and must be strictly interpreted. A select committee therefore always acts under a special, not a general, authority.
The point I wish to make is that there can be no authority in the committee to do what is sought by the motion for reference back. If the constitution of the committee is to be changed, that of course will require a substantive motion which must be dealt with in the ordinary way. Notice must be given and it must be treated as any substantive motion is treated.
Those are the main grounds of objection. The last, I submit, is not open to any argument at all because of the nature of the instructions the hon. member has sought to

Canadian Flag
transmit. The first hinges on the fact that the committee is a special committee only, and the cases applicable to standing committees do not apply to it.

I have only a few remarks to make relative to the points of order raised by the President of the Privy Council on behalf of the government.
The hon. gentleman said the committee must be revived. Well, the amendment itself provides for the revival of the committee, if the minister insists that this should be a condition. If he would read the amendment he would see that the house, in adopting the amendment, would revive the committee if such a course were necessary for the particular purpose of the motion. So this condition has been provided for; even the citations and the precedents relating to this direction for revival have been met.
I turn now to the other point the minister raised. He seemed to think that because the committee had presented its final report it had, ipso facto, died in the literal sense and could not therefore be revived. But I would point out that we are considering not the final report of the committee but merely the sixth report. In logic, if on the presentation of the sixth report the committee were deemed to have come to an end, how could it present its seventh report? The seventh report is a matter of record on the order paper. I would say, therefore, that in so far as consideration of the sixth report was concerned we are not dealing with the final report of the committee and, therefore, for the purpose of the discussion of the sixth report, the committee has not come to an end.
What we have before us is in essence an interim report. Therefore, the argument that having prepared its final report the committee has died does not wholly apply. Certainly the discussion of interim reports, if such reports were delayed or adjourned until the presentation of what might be a final report, could not be curtailed by using this device as a tool to prevent any discussion of any report of a special committee-not a select committee but a special committee- by merely delaying, on the initiative of the government, discussion of any interim report until what is deemed to be a final report has been presented. Nor has there ever been such a rule, because it would serve to stifle any discussion or any amendment of any report of a special committee. My third point is that any references the minister has made
[Mr. Mcllraith.l
that have applied to select committees certainly do not apply to special committees, because there is a clearcut distinction between the two.
I would put it to the minister once again that his arguments against this amendment have been countered, first by the fact that the amendment provides for a revival of the committee for a specific purpose; second, that we are considering an interim report and not a final report; and third, that this is a special committee and not a select committee. For those reasons I put it to you, Mr. Speaker -there may be other reasons which other hon. members of the house may advance for Your Honour's consideration-that the amendment is in order for discussion at this time.

Mr. Speaker, there is just one consideration which I would like to bring to your attention and one respect in which this particular special committee is different from, I believe, any other special committee that has been set up by this house. It is different, for instance,, from the special customs committee of 1926. It is different in that the order setting up this committee established a particular time limit within which the committee had to work. It was a decision of this house that this special committee should do its work within six weeks, and then it finished.
If it is now considered in order to move an amendment which in its terms revives this committee, we are then reversing by an amendment an order of the house which established a committee for six weeks. We would be restoring a committee without any time limit at all; it could go on indefinitely, because there is nothing in the amendment, presumably, which would prevent that. If it can go on indefinitely, it is entirely in opposition to the original motion which said the committee must end its work in six weeks. I know that arguments can be made for and against reviving by amendment special or select committees; we could argue that matter for a long time. But I do not know of any case, because I do not believe there is any case, where a committee was set up for six weeks to do a job and then an amendment of this type was accepted; because this amendment, if carried, would restore that committee for an indefinite period of time, thereby contradicting the order of the house that it be set up for six weeks.

Hon. members opposite now want to prevent an amendment being moved. Let me place before you, Mr. Speaker, examples of what has happened in this connection in the

past. A special committee of parliament was set up in 1926 for the purpose of looking into a certain alleged wrongdoing on the part of a minister of the crown, Hon. George Boivin, and also certain administrative officials. A motion was made to confirm the report of the special committee which was set up. This matter is referred to in the Journals of the House of Commons for 1926. When the matter came before the house the motion moved by Mr. Mercier (St. Henri) was that the third and final report of the special committee appointed to investigate the administration of the department of customs and excise be concurred in. Then Mr. Stevens moved an amendment to the motion in the following terms:
That the report be not now adopted, but that it be referred back to the special committee with instructions to add thereto as sub-clauses to paragraph six:-
And so as to make the record clear I will read the amendment-
The evidence further discloses that ministerial action has been influenced by the improper pressure of political associates and friends of the minister, or acting minister administering the department, resulting in the suspension and in some instances the abandonment of prosecutions against those charged with violation of the statutes, and in the loss of revenue to the country. Moreover successful appeals have been made to the minister and acting minister administering the department to improperly interfere with the course of justice between the conviction of the offenders and the execution of judgment thereon.
That was after conviction. There was no question of interference by ministers in 1926 or prior thereto. In those days there were only a couple of executive assistants. I think there were one or two parliamentary assistants at the time; in any event there were in 1919.
The Prime Minister and the government had knowledge for some considerable time of the rapid degeneration of the department of customs and excise, and their failure to take prompt and effective remedial action is wholly indefensible. The conduct of the present minister of the department, the Honourable George H. Boivin, in the case of Moses Aziz is utterly unjustifiable.
Your committee deplores the practice, as revealed by the evidence, of certain men influential in public life to direct appeals to the minister to relax and depart from the proper administration of his department for reasons of political expediency.
If there is any likeness between this situation and subsequent events it is merely coincidental that I am raising this particular matter.
Your committee is of the opinion that this practice is detrimental to the best interests of the country and prejudicial to the administration of the department.

Then there is added the following paragraph, which is also included in the amendment moved today by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith):
And that the committee for such purpose be revived.
Now that amendment, Mr. Speaker, to which I have referred is to all intents and purposes the same as the one now presented and put before Your Honour.
Then Mr. Woodsworth, the leader of the labour party at that time, seconded by Mr. Heaps, moved in amendment to that amendment the following:
That all the words after the word "instructions" in the third line of the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:-
"1. To add to clause 4 the following: Since the enquiry indicates that the smuggling evils are so extensive and their ramifications so far reaching that only a portion of the illegal practices have been brought to light, your committee recommends the appointment of a judicial commission with full powers to continue and complete investigating the administration of the department of customs and excise and to prosecute all offenders.
2. That the following be added to clause 6: Your committee deplores the common practice as revealed by the evidence, of members of parliament and others of appealing to the minister to relax the regulations of the department for personal advantage or political expediency.
Then there were added two further paragraphs in the subamendment, and then again the words:
And that the committee for such purposes be revived.

Mr. Meighen-

On Mr. Mercier's motion for concurrence in the final report of the special committee appointed to investigate the customs and excise department, Mr. Stevens moved that said report be referred back-
And so on.

I really did not feel the inclusion of the maple leaf design was very difficult to arrive at, and in this connection I point out the committee had before it literally thousands of designs from Canadians from coast to coast. I believe I can safely say that a ratio of five to one contained the maple leaf and that, therefore, in the minds of a good many Canadians there is absolutely no question of what constitutes the symbol of Canada, that the symbol is the maple leaf, and as such it is included in the recommended design.
I am aware that some members of the committee felt very strongly that a flag ought to contain the union jack and the fleur-de-lis. That is a view we listened to with the greatest of respect and we explored every possible argument pro and con. I respect that view, but in the end most of us came to the conclusion that by putting emblems such as that on our national flag we would be merely giving ourselves a perpetual reminder of the things that divide us, and that it would be preferable to have a distinctive flag that says just one

thing, Canada-not French Canada, not English Canada, not ethnic Canada, but Canada.
As I have said, I respect the views of those others; I only regret that I do not share them.
The main thing about the whole question is that it must be decided. Ever since the debate took place in the house I am sure many hon. members have visited their constituencies and have had an opportunity to get around to various parts of the country. Without exception I think almost everyone with whom I have spoken, no matter what their view, whether they wished the red ensign or a new flag, with unanimous voice said that they hoped at least parliament would make a decision.
The one thing which it seems to me is significant about the committee report, and which lends great weight to its recommendation, is that if anything can be said it is that this is a parliamentary flag. This is not the flag of any particular party. It is not the flag of any particular individual. It is the best consensus that we were able to get from the members of all the parties represented on the committee. I know it was not unanimous, and all of us regret that. But as I said in the beginning, we respected each other's views and we agreed that if necessary we would disagree in good faith. I think it is fair to say, however, that this design does command support among all parties in the house. I realize a good many members of the official opposition are perhaps not prepared to support it. But there is support for this design within their party, as there is in all quarters of the house. If anything, this flag is the flag chosen by the parliament of Canada and by nobody else.
I could go on at great length but I do not think it is important that I do so. Many of us feel the whole matter of the flag has detracted from this present parliament. If we had been able to spend as much time and energy discussing other matters such as automation, education and important problems of this nature, the present parliament might have been more distinguished in its accomplishments. At the same time we realize that these events are not within our control. The Prime Minister chose to have a decision reached on the subject at this time. Nobody is quarrelling with his prerogative. Many of us thought it was not an opportune time to raise this question, but at least the Prime Minister had the courage to deal with a subject which has been a most contentious one in Canada for very many years.

I was all the more happy because I realized the importance of the work this committee would be called upon to perform, taking into consideration all the difficulties it would have to face.
If we recall the numerous discussions which occurred and the various opinions which were expressed during this debate which preceded the creation of that committee, we know that it was not without apprehension that the 15 members gathered to study this matter and endeavoured to reach a solution in order to present unanimously, if at all possible, a design to the house.
Mr. Speaker, the members of the committee dedicated themselves to this task for more than six weeks and some 45 meetings averaging two hours each.
For my part I think I went through a wonderful human experience, because it is certainly a great experience, a difficult but most rewarding one, for 15 men to be confined to a room, sitting in camera for such a long time to discuss but one subject.
What made for an interesting discussion was the fact that each member of the committee expressed his views in all candour. And here I should like to express my appreciation to each and every one of them for the manner in which they acted. I feel it is most unfortunate that we could not reach the complete agreement which would have resulted in a unanimous report, but I do not believe that any member acted in bad faith in not making this possible.
They all expressed their views verbally or by their vote. They were free to do so, since it was their duty, and I respect everyone's opinion.
Mr. Speaker, we are called upon today to approve a report submitted by the committee.
I should like, however, to remind the house that when this debate opened last June

the members of our party stated their position quite clearly, namely that every one of us was free to decide, according to his conscience, the position he intended to take in this connection.
Today, this report must be concurred in. I must say that this position still holds and that all our members are still free to approve or reject the committee's report.
However, may I assure the house that the committee's report will have a more than substantial support from the members of our party; I believe that the work of the committee deserves our appreciation inasmuch as the report which has been tabled is well thought out, is the result of work which, in my opinion, could not have been accomplished better.
Since the beginning of the debate today, we have heard various points of view expressed and I should like to comment on them a little.
I do not think that at this point we stand to gain anything whatsoever by referring this matter again to the committee. After six weeks of work the committee has made its decision known and I cannot imagine that by taking up the matter again it can in any way arrive at another decision.

Now, if I may, I should like to say a few words to my friends in the Conservative party. I should like, also, to make a sincere appeal to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). Although I have been in this house for only two and a half years I can remember many occasions on which the right hon. gentleman correctly and strongly stated that, provided sufficient time is allocated for members to express their views on a subject, good democratic government must be assured by permitting the voice of the majority in the house to decide. This is my interpretation of words used by the right hon. gentleman on many occasions.
In my own opinion-and I think this is also the opinion of the majority of Canadians-this house has been afforded plenty of opportunity in the past to discuss this issue
Canadian Flag
and it is time for us to decide by voting on this question. I recognize that all hon. members have the right to express their views one way or another, but I do not think Canadians will condemn them in any way if they put an end to this debate and vote according to their consciences. If members find themselves opposed to the design put forward I think it is their duty to vote against it. But I do not think they have the right to prevent the majority of the members of this house from deciding. It is time we brought this debate to an end and allowed the majority of members to declare their position on the question by their votes. The people of this country have entrusted us with responsibility and we should discharge our responsibility by voting upon this subject. If we are wrong, I am quite sure that Canadians will judge us in the next election. Those who have not expressed the wish of their constituents will be defeated and others will take their places.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is high time for us Canadians to adopt a distinctive flag. If you consider the international situation today, which is getting more and more troubled, it becomes increasingly necessary for Canada to fully establish its identity and to let people see clearly that it is independent from any other nation. I think that by deciding today to give ourselves a distinctive Canadian flag, which will have nothing in common with the emblems of our mother country or the other countries which dominated us in the past, we are taking a step which the whole population has long awaited.
I am sure that in a few years those who will come after us will be grateful to us for making that decision which is a very difficult one, I will admit, and which might bring criticism to several of us, but we are here to face such criticism and to assume our responsibilities.
If we are in this house it is because we have been sent here to make decisions. Today, we have the opportunity to make a decision which, above any other, is of great significance. In my opinion, this decision should be made by a vote according to our conscience so that in Canada, at the beginning of 1965, we could fly a flag which would be a Canadian flag, in short, the flag of the whole Canadian people.
There have been criticisms on the choice of the design. If someone in Canada could suggest to us a symbol more representative

Canadian Flag
of Canada than the maple leaf, I would ask him to rise and suggest it. Up to now we have been unable to find one more representative of Canada. The maple leaf is typical of Canada. Even if that maple leaf cannot be found in every little part of Canada, it must be agreed that, at the present time, this symbol is still the most popular in Canada and does not appear on the flag of any other country.
In my opinion we must all unite in a gesture of Canadian solidarity in an effort to build a strong and united country. Let us prove to all our Canadian citizens that when important matters are at stake we must set aside some particular and partisan interests for the general interest of the country. I believe that today we have the opportunity of doing so.
Finally, I ask all members of the house to set aside their petty grievances, their petty private interests in order to grant our country a truly distinctive flag. I only wish that this flag should receive the unanimous approval of the members of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. This is not the first time I have spoken on the matter of a Canadian flag. On May 28, 1963, I took the opportunity to speak on the Canadian flag, the red ensign. I spoke at that time with some emotion because I listed all the matters that I thought should be considered when dealing with the Canadian flag. I said the red ensign was the first free flag I had lived under, and I hoped my family would continue to enjoy living under this free flag. The second time I spoke on the question of a Canadian flag was during this debate.
Mr. Speaker, it was an honour for me to be a member of the flag committee. Reference was made to the fact that the chairman of our committee handled the committee's business very effectively, and I give him full credit for that. But at the same time I must say it was a strange committee. It was a committee in camera, but if any one of our members missed something the day before, he could read it next morning in the newspaper. I went into this committee as a red ensign man. I still respect the red ensign as a Canadian flag. However, at the same time I went into the committee with the understanding and conviction that if the committee could decide on a flag that was acceptable to all people in Canada, I was

ready for a compromise. But I was not ready for a compromise between the three maple leaf flag and the one maple leaf flag; I was ready for a compromise which would incorporate the past history of Canada, as set out in the flag I now hold in my hand, incorporating the union jack and the fleur-de-lis.
When I look at the United States flag I see that it is a flag which does justice to their past history; the 13 stripes on that flag represent the 13 colonies that were instrumental in bringing about the United States. I thought a compromise flag should do justice to our past, too. What is wrong with having a flag with the union jack in it? What is wrong with having a fleur-de-lis also in that flag? Some members of the committee and others said this had no connection with France; but the fleur-de-lis is the Quebec flag.

subtopic: CANADIAN FLAG
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, somebody said, "So what?" What right have we to pass up our history? Not very long ago three students from the University of Ottawa came here to discuss this matter with me; they wanted to know if I, as a member of the flag committee, could give them some information on it. When I showed them this compromise flag they said, "Why do not the people of Canada better understand what a compromise flag means?" It is exactly the same as the one maple leaf flag approved by the committee, except that it incorporates these two symbols, the union jack and the fleur-de-lis. I am sure if the people of the country were given the chance to vote on these flags by way of a plebiscite- that is, the flag approved by the committee, the red ensign and the compromise flag- we could then say proudly that the people had made their choice.
What right, Mr. Speaker, has this government to make the decision? It is not a government elected with an over-all majority. They have no mandate to bring in such legislation. This government was appointed by the governor general and that is the reason they are in power. Therefore, for that reason more than anything else I think the people of Canada should be given the right and the privilege to decide the flag issue. Only 71 or 72 per cent of the committee voted in favour of the recommended flag, about 28 per cent of the committee members opposing it. Most of them opposed it because it was not a compromise flag.

I should also like to point out that the motion for a plebiscite was voted down nine to five. The second motion, which was for the adoption of only one national flag, was carried 14 to 0. However, after two or three weeks of debate we discovered there was going to be a second flag. I brought this matter to the attention of the chairman of the committee and to the attention of every other member of the committee, because all of our discussions from the first day onward were based on the understanding that there would be only one national flag. Then to our surprise in the last week again the question came up: What about a second flag? As a minority group in the committee we had no choice. We abstained from voting because all during the committee proceedings we had understood we were only dealing with one national flag.
The second point I should like to raise at this time concerns some of our discussions. We had heraldry experts in attendance who gave us some very valuable information. We thought the maple leaf design was good because it had the maple leaf as our national emblem; therefore the maple leaf on a white square was adopted because it was a Canadian symbol. Since the union jack and the fleur-de-lis were not in the corner of this flag it meant they were nothing more than emblems.
After my second speech in the flag debate I received thousands of letters from my constituents-and I mean thousands-all of them asking me to support the red ensign. After the first vote was taken in the special committee and the Canadian red ensign was voted down ten to four, it was apparent to many people in Canada that there should be a compromise flag. It was also apparent that the people would be willing to accept it. Therefore, why do the people not get the chance to vote on the proposed flag by way of a plebiscite? In such event justice would be done to everybody. Instead of splitting the people and disuniting them on the flag question the correct thing to do is to hold a plebiscite and the people will be pleased to accept the result. This plebiscite could be held at the time of the next election; it does not require special action.
Again I return to the proceedings of the committee. Thousands of flags were presented for the consideration of the committee. Finally we arrived at the point where we had the original three maple leaf flag with the blue bars at the end, then the flag with a maple leaf on a white square with two red bars at the end, and then the same flag with
Canadian Flag
the other two symbols to which I have referred. They were the last three flags on which the committee voted. By way of the elimination process, which I thought was a very good way, we arrived at a final design. To start with we eliminated by a show of hands various choices until there were four or five flags left in each group. One group represented flags with three maple leaves, some with blue bars and some with no bars. The second group consisted of one maple leaf designs. The third group comprised flags of compromise design. One was a red ensign with the fleur-de-lis superimposed on it. Another had a maple leaf in the centre, another had it on the side, and there was also the fleur-de-lis with the red ensign superimposed on it.
This matter, Mr. Speaker, is of great importance to the people of Canada today. We have been debating the flag issue for some time and the people want an answer. They know parliament is not able to come to a decision which would be adopted by the people of Canada, so for that reason I urge the house to give serious consideration to holding a plebiscite. Thousands of our people have fought in two wars. Many of the people who came to this country looked upon the Canadian flag as the flag under which freedom is the order of the day, under which there is no persecution and there is freedom of speech, freedom to speak one's own language, although the law decrees there are only two official languages, English and French. If you were to ask many of these people of ethnic origin what the Canadian flag means to them, they would point out that one reason so many of them came to Canada and are still coming to Canada is because the Canadian flag stands for democratic freedom. Indeed if we dispose of or do away with the Canadian flag, generations will pass before people will accept another flag as the flag of Canada. Although the committee did not come to a unanimous decision, I had the impression that the members of the committee commenced their meetings with the idea of deciding on a Canadian flag. As the days passed we in this group found ourselves isolated, not because we were the members who stood for the red ensign, but because we were the members who wanted a compromise embodying the symbols of the founding races. I still feel the committee might have decided to recommend the adoption of a compromise flag. Had we done so, I am sure we might have avoided dividing the nation, as it is now divided as the result of doing away

Canadian Flag
with the red ensign, while at the same time using some of the familiar symbols on a flag as recommended to the committee.

maintopic: MR. NASSERDEN-"HANSARD" REPORT OF SUPPLY COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: CANADIAN FLAG
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the moment for a final decision on a national flag for Canada draws near we are sensible of the trust imposed on every member of parliament to act wisely for all Canadians alive and unborn. If ever there was a time when we should discipline our tongues and elevate ourselves to the dignity of sane and disinterested patriots, this is it. Each of us in this chamber I know loves Canada with a poignancy that is too real to express-our "quiet lakes reflecting the glory of the sky and the shadows of the upland forest; the wide firmament flooded with crimson sunset; the long haggard hills formless and low; the desolate mountains"-places like Heart's Delight, Val d'Or, Red Deer, Nakusp. What flag is worthy of such a land?
Speaking for myself I have come out of the flag committee, after its six weeks sitting with nothing but respect and, I must say, affection and regard for every other member of that committee. I stand earnestly in support of the recommendation of this committee that the national flag of Canada be a red flag of the proportions two by length and one by width, containing in its centre a white square, the width of the flag, bearing a single red maple or, in heraldic terms, described as gules on a Canadian pale argent a maple leaf of the first.
I would remind members of this house that this is the third time a flag committee has been designated in the Commons of Canada. If members care to refer to Hansard of June 17, 1925, page 4364, they will find that a question was raised by Mr. T. Church in which he asked Right Hon. Mackenzie King who was asking for such a Canadian flag and for such a change, and why. The prime minister reported that he had set up an advisory committee consisting of G. J. Desbarats, Esq., C.M.G., deputy minister of national defence; Thomas Mulvey, Esq., B.A., K.C., under secretary of state; A. G. Doughty, Esq., C.M.G., LL.D., dominion archivist, Commodore Walter Hose, C.B.E., A.D.C., director of the naval service; Major General H.A. Panet, C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., adjutant general, and Group Captain J. S. Scott, M.C., A.F.C., A.D.C., acting director of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
It is 1 think to be deplored that as a result of very strong objection taken in respect of the composition of that committee, not-
[Mr. Rapp.)
withstanding the fact that two of them were on the original arms committee appointed by Sir Robert Borden, it was dissolved without action taken.
You will then recall, Mr. Speaker, that on November 6, 1945, as reported in Hansard, the prime minister appointed a committee to consider and report upon a suitable design. So in fact when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) on September 10, 1964 reported to the house the establishment of a special committee on the subject of a Canadian flag, this was the third time this sovereign nation had made an attempt to establish a banner denoting its sovereignty.
This is a subject not of recent date or of recent concern to Canadians, but is something that goes back a long while. I have before me an article written by John S. Ewart, K.C., in 1907 which appeared in a Canadian magazine. I should like to read two brief extracts from this article. Mr. Ewart said:
A flag should denote correctly the sovereignty which it represents.
The second extract is:
Canada's self-respect requires that her acknowledged right of independent self-government, her accession to national rank, and her admission to a footing of equality with the United Kingdom itself, should not only be amply recognized at imperial conferences, but should be evidenced by her flag-by the flag of the Dominion of Canada.
Weeks ago, sir, it was drawn to my attention as a result of our trip to the archives, that the "Royal Reader" of Nova Scotia, a pleasant book for junior scholars, published by the T. Eaton Company Limited of Toronto, and Winnipeg, for 11 cents, portrayed a flag flying over a maple tree with these words: "The union jack our emblem dear guards our maple tree." What we seek now is a change in emphasis. The revered old union jack remains undifferenced and unaltered and will remain as a precious kindly memory of our inheritance, while this sovereign nation now flies its own device and colours in the position of precedence and honour. In October, 1923, in Montreal, David Lloyd George spoke of Canada's contribution in the first world war in these terms: "The maple leaf was embroidered forever on the silken folds of the banner of human history." It is about time, sir, that we recognized this fact at home.
One of the books we discovered at the archives was a little book entitled "The Story of the Union Jack", written by Barlow Cumberland, and in it is "A plea for the maple leaf". Incidentally this article was written in 1897 and Mr. Cumberland stated:

Flags are signals to be used for conveying Information to persons at a distance; their details should therefore, be simple in form and be displayed in simple colours.
The maple tree is found in luxuriance in every province of the dominion.
He then stated as we have already heard during our earlier flag debate, that this maple leaf was an emblem of the festival of St. Jean Baptiste, in French Canada, in 1836. He pointed out that the maple leaf was on the colours of the Royal Canadians, the 100th regiment, raised in Canada in 1865, and that it is still worn as the regimental badge of their successors, the Royal Leinster regiment. It is on the northwest medal of 1885, and on the uniform and accoutrement of the Canadian infantry and of the Northwest Mounted Police.
Mr. Cumberland also points out that it has revelled in poetry and prose; is the theme of the songs of our children, and that the stirring strains of "The Maple Leaf" form an accompaniment to our British national anthem.
Everywhere throughout the world the maple leaf has won recognition as the emblem of Canadians, and may well be displayed upon their flag. So, at any rate says Mr. Cumberland. This story was written many years before Canada achieved the dignity of arms.
The committee has recommended to parliament a flag of classic simplicity, consisting only of national colours. I must say that I agree with every word I heard the hon. member for Danforth utter in respect to the heraldic proprieties. This recommended flag consists only of Canada's national colours as provided in the proclamation to which my friend referred, of November 21, 1921. Displayed in the crest is a lion holding in its right paw a red maple leaf.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, during his quite scholarly address of some weeks ago referred to some of Canada's heraldic traditions and devices. Actually since 1868 the maple leaf, in one form or another, has by overwhelming consensus been accepted as emblematic of Canada. The flag colours, that is, the combination of white and red, may be found in the Fenian service ribbon, which was for the period 1866-70 which also covered the Riel rebellion, the Royal Military college flag, the Canada medal ribbon and finally in the Canadian decoration.
This flag sends one message-"Canada". It is in good heraldic taste. The committee's unanimous choice is immediately distinguishable from every other flag in the world and it is conspicuously Canadian in character. From the first day this flag flies it will be recognized 20220-677
Canadian Flag
I know, as being the flag of this country. It will look striking whenever occasion calls for it to be flown or draped alongside the union jack.
It might interest hon. members to know that the Royal Military college was founded in the year 1876 and since its founding the colours of the college have always been red and white as evidenced by their uniforms. This was, of course, the college of the nation. The original uniform was a red tunic, white trousers and white belt. That hat was a black shako, with white plume and red tip. The sash, which was worn in the wintertime, was red and white striped. In the late thirties, the library was destroyed by fire, but from ex-cadets we know that the R.M.C. flag of red, white and red was flown certainly in 1916 and again in 1918, and many of us on the defence committee have seen it since then. I remember studying it for some time during the past summer.
Now, sir, we find opposition to this maple leaf emblem. I refer to the Montreal Star of Tuesday, September 15, 1964. You will note that the committee was appointed on September 10, 1964. The heading of the article is: "Maple Leaf Out-Diefenbaker; Says Emblem Has No Place On New Flag". The article reads in part as follows;
Mr. Diefenbaker, "taken aback" by this statement-
The reference is to a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
-took to the air waves last night to suggest that the maple leaf had no place in any Canadian flag...
"Now I have no objection to a maple leaf," Mr. Diefenbaker said. "I don't criticize it as a symbol of the country-but can you tell me any country in the world that ever put a symbol on its flag?"
I have been challenged in the house not only today but on previous occasions with regard to a change in my position. I will not deny, sir, that for quite a time I had hoped that Canada's flag would carry the royal badge of three red maple leaves on a white field. There has been a good deal of research into this matter, and it was indicated that Her Majesty, on August 15, 1962, entirely on her own initiative had caused to be created by the College of Arms a banner as Queen of Canada. This was our Queen's personal tribute to this honoured realm, her gift to Canada, the first of the nations of the commonwealth beyond the seas.
This flag when designed was sent by Sir Anthony Wagner, Garter King of Arms, to Canada for approval in 1962 and it was approved by the then prime minister himself, now Leader of the Opposition. Recently we

Canadian Flag
have had occasion to examine this banner carried by our Queen on her B.O.A.C. and Air Canada aircraft, on H.M.S. Britannia, over her several dwelling places in Charlottetown, Quebec and Ottawa, and at every saluting stand where she has presided. I believed that after the royal visit to Canada the significance of the three red leaves on white would be understood by all. Yet on Wednesday, October 28, the evening before the flag committee tabled its report, the Leader of the Opposition referred contemptuously on national television to the "troika flag" introduced in the government resolution.
I had felt, and was confirmed in this belief by some of the best heraldic authorities we were able to consult, that we should follow the example set by Her Majesty in 1962 when she created her Royal flag from the ensigns armorial. Certainly since October 8, 1957, when Hon. Ellen Fairclough issued a news release with respect to the arms of Canada, there was no questioning the fact that our colours were white and red and that our national emblem was three red maple leaves on a white field.
I would also point out to hon. members that on November 21, 1962, the government then headed by the present Leader of the Opposition caused a communication to be sent to the College of Arms through government house advising as follows:
Needless to say the emblems of particular interest to the government of Canada are those granted In the royal proclamation of November 21, 1921, including "three maple leaves conjoined on one stem proper".
Sir, I thought they meant that. I thought the Conservative party was quite serious in believing that this was the national emblem because on the day that their government was defeated, February 5, 1963, they submitted in written form an answer to my question No. 1,449. The first part of the question was:
Does Canada have national colours and, if so, what are these colours?
The answer was:
Yes, white and red.
The second part of the question was:
Does Canada have a national emblem and, if so, what is the emblem?
This was the answer:
Yes, three maple leaves conjoined on one stem.
I thought it was fair and reasonable to suppose this was not the "Pearsbn pennant" or "troika pennant" but was the royal badge. I am simply putting this on the record be-
[Mr. Matheson.l
cause I do not want any vilification of this national emblem to detract in any way from the very fine work that has been done by our armed services for something like 40 years in bringing their badges and many of their devices into harmony with our ensigns armorial. But I must agree with the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) that while we must regard a flag as being in the area of heraldry, there is a licence and a freedom to deal with such devices and generally speaking a lot more freedom than there would be in the case of a shield or crest. The flag that has been recommended to the house is a strong and very impressive flag. We have been satisfied that it will meet the heraldic requirements of the most exacting experts in the world.
I know it is regarded that those of us on the government side have changed our position in voting for this proposed flag. By what he said the Leader of the Opposition would have preferred to see us locked tightly to a particular design. Thus he would have been able to gain disagreement in the committee which might have frustrated the choosing of a national flag for decades to come. Quite frankly, sir, in spite of strong feelings on this matter we felt this was a matter of great national importance. I went to the committee with a strong personal preference, as I have said, that the device accepted by the Queen should be recognized as the official emblem of the nation, but with the resolve that my personal preference would not impede the creative work of our committee. I prayed that I might forget my own heraldic notions and views and think only of Canada and her welfare.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, reference was made before the dinner hour by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) to certain items that appeared in the press, and I think I would be doing him a discourtesy if I did not refer to them. He mentioned the fact that a picture appeared in the publication La Voix de I'Est. I never saw this paper but I can assure the hon. gentleman that the picture to which he referred was taken some several days before the creation of the flag committee.

He also referred to press comment in the Recorder and Times but I can assure him I never made a speech on this subject. I did have private conversations with a good friend of mine who is the editor of that paper, and who questioned me with respect to the final report of the flag committee which he had read as it appeared in Hansard. I must confess I did not appreciate that this would be the subject of a press report. This was, of course, my indiscretion. Perhaps in my remarks I was a little undiplomatic but at least I am sure that what I did say I said honestly.
With respect to the visit of the grade ten children from the Peterborough school, it is true that at the request of certain members of the house, and I include among those the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Honey), the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Stenson), and the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb), all of whom were present, a number of children were in our flag committee room; but this was by no means the first such visit. I think the hon. member for Perth will remember that several groups were admitted, and that they moved around and examined suggested designs shown on the walls. On that occasion I did give each of the children a copy of a rather outdated address I made in the house on June 17, 1964, which may perhaps explain some of the press comments in that regard. However, I do not think I disclosed anything which was secret in character, but if I did I pray the hon. member's forgiveness.
I assure him that to the best of my recollection I did not have any conversations with members of the press, in relation to the flag, during the period we sat as a flag committee, nor indeed with my leader, directly or indirectly. I can assure him of that fact.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), whom I never had occasion to really know before sitting on the flag committee with him, and where I must confess I learned to respect and admire him very much, has referred to the fact that a new flag for Canada should contain in it the symbols of our national origins. I respect his view, just as I sincerely respect the view of anybody who would like to see the Canadian red ensign in its present form continue to fly as the flag of Canada. I am sure there is not anybody on this side of the house who does not love this old flag and feel deeply with respect to what it has meant in our past.

speechtext:
I am sorry I was not able to hear that remark, but I shall be happy to answer questions at the conclusion of my comments. But directing myself very briefly to the matter raised by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale I think I should read to him a letter which was drawn to my attention, a letter written to several papers in Canada by Lewis Grant McNab who served as an artillery counter-battery officer in world war I. He lives at 4250 Sherbrooke street west, apartment 18, Montreal, Quebec and under date of September 11, 1964 he wrote this letter:
Dear Sir:
On a recent trip overseas, there was an Anglican clergyman on my continental bus tour. He has a parish just outside London. It is what is known as a royal living, the property belonging to the crown. As such this reverend gentleman has enjoyed close contact with the royal family over a period of years.
I was talking to him about the current flag controversy in Canada and he told me something which I thought was very interesting. He said that King George V felt very strongly that the commonwealth nations should have a flag of their own which did not embody the union jack, and that if they wished to fly the union jack, they could do so under their own flag.
I took the trouble to telephone Mr. McNab about this, and I may point out he is well known in certain military circles.
I should now like to read from a letter written to me by J. R. B. Walker, a very distinguished scholar enjoying the appointment of Lancaster and Registrar, I believe since 1953, at the College of Arms, Queen Victoria street, London E. C. 4. His letter is dated May 27, 1964, and reads:
As the union jack symbolizes the union of England, Scotland and Ireland I would have thought it would be rather illogical to incorporate it in the heraldry of any other country; but the sovereign can do anything she pleases, and if she decided that the union jack was to be incorporated in the national symbol of any country in the commonwealth other than Great Britain, her decision would, of course, be perfectly valid.
My hon. friend from Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale, as do I, believes in this exciting development of the commonwealth, and in fairness I think he will recognize that India, Pakistan, Ceylon, Rhodesia and Nyasaland, Ghana, Malaya, Cyprus, Nigeria, Tanganyika, Sierra Leone, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Uganda and Malta have all followed the guidance of the College of Arms. Very recently Rouge Dragon, Dr. Conrad Swan, who was in Canada for a few days, informed me that nearly every new nation in the commonwealth has taken instruction from the old College of Arms with respect to national flags,

Canadian Flag
and that the style and pattern of incorporating the union jack in them is no longer followed.
A friend of mine has just passed me an article which appeared in the Daily Gleaner of Tuesday November 17, which shows a plaque recently unveiled in Jamaica. The inscription on the plaque reads:
On this spot was erected the flag staff from which was lowered the union jack and on which was hoisted the flag of Jamaica to mark the beginning of the independence of Jamaica at midnight 5th-6th August 1962.
Here also was sworn in the first native governor general of Jamaica, Sir Clifford Campbell G.C. M.G., at 8.50 p.m. on Saturday 1st December 1962. This plaque was presented by Herbert G. Macdonald, O.B.E., J.P.
We must recognize that we are living in a new and changing commonwealth of nations, where new things are expected of us if we are to play the type of leadership role that as Canadians we are expected to play.
Certain comments were made by earlier speakers with respect to the flag of Peru and I feel these must be answered. I feel Strongly about this. I referred a few moments before the six o'clock recess to the fact that the Leader of the Opposition had referred to the three leaf flag containing the royal badge as "a troika flag". On the same occasion, on television, in an interview with Mr. Geoffrey Scott over C.B.C.-T.V. on October 28, the night before our flag committee was called upon to present its report, the right hon. gentleman was asked: "Would this be acceptable to you as a national flag?" Mr. Scott was referring to the flag which is now the subject of discussion. The Leader of the Opposition replied: "Certainly we couldn't accept that type of flag". Later on in the program he added: "Not this Christmas- or any other Christmas". His words were:
All I have to say about that, aside altogether from the fact that it shows nothing of our heritage, is that it would be far from being distinctive. As a matter of fact, it would be the Peruvian flag... If we ever get that flag, we would have the Peruvians saluting it anyway.
As I say, I feel strongly about this because only a few hours before the right hon. gentleman taped that broadcast for national television I had produced to the flag committee the admiralty book Flags of All Nations, volume 1, which sets out the national flag and ensign of Peru, the merchant flag and the jack. Not one member of that committee took exception on the grounds that our recommendation was not clearly distinguishable both in its proportions and in its general appearance from the Peruvian
[Mr. Matheson.l
flag. The comment made by the right hon. gentleman is therefore in my opinion, completely unfair.
This has been a difficult time for some of us on the government side. If it is felt that we have acted sometimes in a discourteous manner, believe me we have been under tension, too. I do not want the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) to feel he is the only person who has at times felt trapped. Listening to the attacks made on us with respect to what we thought was an honest effort to find a good flag, one recommended by the highest authorities, listening to it being assailed as a "Pearson pennant" and a troika, we have been disposed to shout at the Leader of the Opposition as Churchill did over the B.B.C. on one historic occasion when his foes across the channel were harassing England with bombs: "You do your worst and we will do our best."
We sought to find an acceptable flag design on the basis of the royal badge. That would not do. On the flag committee we struggled hard to find a strong and distinctive flag which represented a fresh approach. For a moment, indeed, we achieved unanimity- and then we discovered that the Leader of the Opposition was even more contemptuous and scathing than he had been before. I think it is quite impossible to please this angry man. I say to him, in the language of Tom Jones:	"I am very sorry, sir, for your
unhappiness. Whatever is the occasion of it?"
We have tried to do our best. The original design, I must say, meant a great deal to me. However, I can tell the house with complete conviction that I love this new design.

I believe that increasingly this country will be playing a larger role in certain international areas of responsibility. Those of us who have been active in the defence committee and who have taken part in the defence debates can, I am sure, be satisfied that the reorientation of our defence activities is in the direction of peace keeping. It has been manifest from the time of Suez to the present day that it is not helpful for us to continue flying a flag which is a colonial ensign or which appears to some to have that connotation.
In bringing my remarks to a close I should like to refer to an address delivered in England on June 2, 1941 by the grand old man we all honour today, we think of him almost as one of our own. Mr. Winston Churchill, speaking to Canada on June 2, 1941 used these words:
X speak to you this afternoon from No. 10 Downing street, here in the capital and the governing centre of this battered but indomitable city and island. Our people have been through much in the last few months. They have learned much-and some things they will never forget. But above all they have learned their own strength... no one doubts that we can or that we shall see it through: and that when at length we march again into the light of happier and easier days, Canada will play her just part in laying the foundations of a wider and a better world.
This is not the kind of country that is only for us Scots. Of course we are happy to celebrate St. Andrew's day today, and we will never forget the rock from which we were hewn or the pit from which we were digged. And he shewed me a pure river of water clear as crystal... and on either side of the river was there the tree of life... and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy tonight to follow the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), mostly because I always feel that if you follow a strong speaker nobody will pay any attention; and certainly I believe that the best chance I may have of getting some attention from the house or indeed from the country is the fact that we have just listened to a speech which contains all the pious platitudes and all those symptoms of that lack of sincerity which have characterized the Liberal party since the question of the changing of our national flag has come into prominence.
Certainly I listened with rapt attention, as so many did, when the hon. member said, "I love this flag". It seems to me there is a line somewhere, "How constant is thy love?" Some of us heard the hon. member on another occasion and have reason to suspect that there was a first love of his when it came to the flag design, which was the three maple leaves. In fact I do not know whether he now claims that he was dishonestly given the credit or discredit for its sponsorship; but he has been blamed by most of us for being very prominent in trying to foist that design on the nation. Certainly he gave every indication that he loves that flag. It is not just those few words of his that characterize his attitude, and indeed the attitude of his colleagues on the Liberal benches, to this question of changing our national flag. In this at least he has been constant in that he is most inconstant, and so is the Liberal party.
I had hoped tonight, Mr. Speaker, to start out by expressing a little admiration at least for the many hours of hard work that the

Canadian Flag
members of the flag committee of this house have put in. Certainly I am sure that no matter how much members of this house have been maligned by the press from time to time because they fail to understand that committee work keeps people out of the chamber, or that other duties keep people out of the chamber, those of us in the house have some appreciation of the amount of effort that has been expended by this committee and how much extra work was undertaken by those members who sat morning, noon and night some days in order to carry out this task. I feel I would not be completely honest if I did not add that I think their burden was unnecessarily onerous because of the insistence on a time limit. Certainly the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), in his few remarks this afternoon on the point of order as to the amendment proposed, put everything in its proper perspective and revealed to us all exactly why the time limit was so important. I think the Prime Minister has revealed to this house and to the country that as far as he was concerned the work of that committee was little more than a sham. He had introduced this most controversial subject in the worst and most political way possible and he expected the committee would bring in something that would allow the government to get rid of its embarrassment as quickly as possible, and therefore the time element was the only point that mattered at all.
I suggest that all of us who are genuinely interested in the question of a flag, those of us who have some understanding of the number of people in this country who recognize the importance of tampering with our symbols in this political, halfhearted or lighthearted way, are bound to take cognizance of that fact. Therefore I have to say that, while I believe the members of that committee have certainly deserved the thanks of this house for the number of hours expended and the way in which they applied themselves to their task, it has been obvious from the outset and it is even most obvious today that the government of this country has done everything it can to make their work meaningless. I suggest that from the outset, from the way in which the Prime Minister set the stage, it was a little unreasonable and really we were asking a little too much to think that the members of that committee would have attacked their task in other than a lighthearted manner.
Consider for a moment how this flag debate started, with the Prime Minister proclaiming

to the country loud and long and in the most partisan way that he was going to shove his design down the throat of parliament and give the people of Canada his design for a flag, in place of the red ensign which has been Canada's flag for the last 100 years. I suggest that the tremendous struggle that was necessary to get him to concede this much at least, namely that it should go to a committee, had become so partisan, so violent and stretched out so long that no member of that committee could have undertaken the task without a feeling of frustration; and if not frustration, at least considerable cynicism. I suggest that this degree of cynicism made itself evident as the work of the committee progressed and we saw leaks to the press from time to time; reporters reporting what was going on in a committee which was sitting in camera. I do not care how vehement members may get about a flag or how many may feel it could not matter less, but surely members of this house should feel that no member should sit in this house who cannot be called an honourable lady or gentleman. Certainly the word of a committee that it is in camera is a binding oath that should be as sacred to the members of that committee as any oath could be.
I suggest that only the worst possible foundation for starting a committee, the worst possible approach and the most cynical attitude toward it on the part of some members can account for the most shameful course of conduct on the part of those who wanted to enhance their own reputations by ruining their own good name. Any member of that committee who is accused of deviating in the slightest manner from his duty to keep those proceedings secret should, I think, be most indignant if he is accused unjustly, and most guilty if there is any falling away from his duty at all. I think there should be on the part of those who have been mentioned a very spirited effort in their own defence. Here I must pay special attention to the hon. member for Leeds who has just finished speaking.
I did not try to be complimentary to him when I started, and I repeat my original assertion that I have never heard anything so ridiculous in my life as his statement that he loves this flag. His whole speech as far as I am concerned consisted of platitudes, trite sayings and red herrings.
I was in this house this afternoon when the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) listed what I thought was a most damning indictment against the hon. member for Leeds. He gave chapter and verse the statements which

that member had given to the press, and I heard hardly a word from the hon. member for Leeds in his own defence. Certainly I want to say on my own behalf as far as I am concerned my view of the meaning of an in camera meeting, and the duty it lays on each and every member of a committee which holds a meeting in camera to keep silent their proceedings, is a much higher duty than apparently the hon. member understands.
1 am not going to be any more charitable to the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman). I know that members on both sides of the house-although those on the Liberal side who were disgusted by him are likely to be quiet and not say anything in this chamber-were disgusted, indeed shocked, by the performance of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra in his attempt to gain for himself all the publicity and glory he could from anything which came out of that committee meeting. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman), who is now known as "Mr. Leakman", certainly received his share of publicity, but I suggest that a member of this house who should have some regard for the duty he owes that committee and the equality that the members of the committee were supposed to share one with another, should at least have the decency to wait till the committee's report was made public to the house before making press statements.
I do not mind revealing, Mr. Speaker, that some time after this occurred I had a conversation with one member of the committee who was very incensed, not only at the fact that this had occurred, but because he felt that what had been said was so wide of the truth in so many respects that he wondered whether we had been released from our obligation to keep silent, and he wondered whether we could not get up and publicly set the record straight. I advised him that I thought that just because there might be sinners on the other side of the house was no reason to emulate them on our side. I am afraid that is a little different from the attitude taken by the Liberals, who whenever they are found at fault ask: And what did you do? This might be a good time to remind government supporters that if some of the sins they commit bear any resemblance to the sins of their previous government, the people of Canada will chastise them as they did the previous government during the last two election campaigns; and I hope hon. members opposite will be prepared to pay the price of
Canadian Flag
their sins instead of sitting in this house and talking to us as though this would absolve them from guilt.
I cannot to this day understand why a time limit should have been set on the proceedings of the committee. The only conclusion I can come to-and I have given it lots of thought- is that the political gain which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) hopes to achieve by presenting a flag to the country within the time he dictated was most important to him. Members of the house might have gained a ray of hope at the start when the Prime Minister, who had introduced the flag in a most political manner, announced there would be a free vote. We thought for a while that perhaps he was going to give us some inkling of the importance of a flag; that perhaps it was a little more important than just another political issue and a political gain of the moment. Then he explained what he meant by a free vote, and indeed we found he had become a real Liberal propagandist.
Then when the committee was appointed we thought that perhaps one thing had impressed him, and that was that we on this side were sincere in this flag debate on the question how this should be handled. We had thought that even if the government were successful in ramming down the throat of parliament a flag which most of us did not like, passing an act of parliament is not the same thing as a new flag which the people would welcome and accept, and we had thought that at last our long battle to persuade him to send the question to a committee might have left some impression on him. We hoped he would think there was much good in a committee discussing the question and that the people of Canada might have some feeling of satisfaction from the fact that this flag issue had at last been handled in a way which would satisfy the dissident groups in as much as there had been a fair hearing in an unpolitical manner and in a way which reflected the concern for Canada over this issue. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the attitude displayed by some of the members of that committee regarding their duty to be silent certainly shook the confidence of most of us in our sincerity adequately to consider the feelings of the various segments of the population and the various opinions they held.
I must say that no more concrete proof of the sincerity of the government backbenchers on that committee is necessary than that contained in the report presented to us for concurrence today. Those of us who were in the house earlier heard the Minister of Transport

Canadian Flag
(Mr. Pickersgill) ask one question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to this effect: How about the question of reviving an issue which has already been decided in this session?

speechtext:
Yes, that is it, reversing. The Minister of Transport, in his argument about the question whether the amendment was in order, said that if we were now to send it back to a committee before the house had decided there should be a time limit, we in this house would be reversing a question which had already been decided. My argument to that was that I thought the house can send back to a committee something the committee has already decided, and 1 said that had been established many times.
If you look at the committee report in which we are asked to concur, Mr. Speaker, you will find that the first question settled by that committee is whether there should be one flag or two. With regard to that, Mr. Speaker, you find unanimous agreement. This committee which we fought so hard to get established, and which we hoped might do so much to at least give the appearance to the people of Canada that the question was going to be handled in a responsible manner by members of parliament, who would be guided by their conscience as Canadians with a true understanding of the meaning of symbols, instead of simply acting as politicians following the party line, voted unanimously that there should be only one flag. I would have thought-I still hope there may be a chance of this-that the Minister of Transport, since he is so familiar with the rules, would side with me when I say that for the committee to bring up the same point later on which it had earlier unanimously disposed of and finished with is clearly contrary to the rules. For them later on to attempt to revive it by bringing in a partisan vote with a different decision than originally arrived at is also clearly contrary to the rules. It is not only contrary to the rules but is an affront to the integrity of the members of that committee. To suggest that all the members of that committee were free to vote independently from any political control by the Liberal party is an insult to the intelligence of hon. members. I suggest that such a thing could not have taken place, as it did, without some direction from the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, I observe that I am touching upon the sensibilities of the Liberal backbenchers, and I suppose I have been a little

naive in complaining about the lack of integrity on the part of the Liberal members of this special committee on the flag. Perhaps I am being naive in suggesting that this subject is of such importance to the people of Canada, and so sacred to all those who believe as I do in this country, that it should have been treated as something other than a political football. I am not unhappy in many ways about the amount of adverse publicity the press has given members on this side of the house because of the weeks and weeks of fighting we have done to get the flag resolution sent to a committee, but I cannot understand the political legerdemain by which the Liberals have convinced most of the people in this country that it is the Conservative members who are wasting the time of the country by debating the flag issue, when all the time these things are controlled by an absent Liberal party. I do think it is rubbing salt into a raw wound for that same Liberal party now to expect the people of this country to be gullible enough to stand for this sort of contempt of the rules of this house.
We have witnessed in this house day in and day out Liberal contempt for parliament, and this has been apparent ever since the Liberal government was elected, as evidenced by the government's refusal to answer questions, and in their attitude when they have been caught in errors. Certainly what took place last week was a striking example of this attitude. We witnessed the actions of a minister of justice who obviously did not have any idea or concept of his duties.
When the Prime Minister of this country spends his time out west, as he did last week, instead of being here to answer to parliament for the actions of this wayward ministers, surely that is a manifestation of this contemptible attitude. The Prime Minister decided to go on a campaign junket out in the west, which is an effrontery to this country. He talked about now being the time when we need unity in Canada. Surely that is too much for the long suffering people of this country to put up with. How phony can one get in talking about unity? The Prime Minister speaks about unifying the nation and starts out by introducing this flag issue in a political way, making sure that the country is divided. He has taken every step possible to make sure that whatever else happens the reputation of parliament is ruined, and then has the temerity to suggest that the criticism of this house shall be lessened.

He established a committee composed of a bunch of members who find little difficulty in acting with this obvious contempt for the rules of parliament. This is an indication to this nation that their obedience to the whim of the Liberal party is more important than their duty as members of a committee. How then can the Prime Minister have the effrontery to talk about unity in this country, in view of the manner in which he has handled this debate, which has done more to cause disunity than the actions of all people in the last quarter of a century?
I am glad to see the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Forgie) sitting in his place this evening. He is an old friend of mine and I say to him, as an old friend, that there is one thing I have always known about him. That is, he is a good Liberal, and a good Liberal is one who never allows logic or common sense to bother him.

I happen to know a few of the members on the Liberal side of this house quite well, and I am happy to say that there are some members over there for whom I have a great deal of respect. I have managed to
