speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If I wandered astray, it was because I was considering the report of the committee and the fact that at least at first appearance that committee has blatantly violated the fundamental rules of this house.
I pointed out that the house could refer this subject back to the committee for reconsideration, but certainly it is obvious even to those on the Liberal back benches, who find it painful even to consider the obvious, that for a committee to make one decision and then a completely different decision in the next moment is a very shameful course of conduct, and they cannot even plead ignorance. We all realize that that is the kind of excuse they have been making for so much of the time on that side of the house. I suggest to them if they cannot understand these few remarks, they should remember, with some chagrin, the amendment to the labour code which included November 11 as a holiday, at which time the government was defeated in the committee of the whole, and then consider that all that party had to do on that occasion was bring the subject up again the next day when they had a majority and reverse the decision.
That is what the flag committee did. I suggest that the Liberal members of that committee had to report to the Prime Minister

Canadian Flag
on progress every day. All members of the committee, not just the Liberals or the Conservatives but every member of the flag committee, were unanimous that there should only be one flag. That matter was settled and disposed of, and there is only one explanation for its coming up again. The Liberal members of the committee got their orders from the Prime Minister that this would not do. Joey would have somebody's neck; and so the matter had to be opened up again. That is why the question was brought up again.
I would be happy to hear any logical explanation from any Liberal member of that committee. I must say that they were pretty prompt in speaking to the press while the committee was sitting. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra was a little too quick in getting his story before the public before the house received the report of the committee. What is stopping these hon. members now from getting up and giving us a logical explanation of why they should trample on so obvious a rule of the house?
I hope to say a few words about the design of a flag generally. I want to come back to the remarks of the hon. member for Leeds. He spent a great deal of time telling us what this flag meant in heraldry, the importance of the three maple leaves, and so on. His arguments can be disposed of very simply. As far as I and my constituents are concerned heraldry does not mean one tenth as much as pleasing design. It does not mean one hundredth as much as whether or not the flag stands for something.
The flag that has been presented by the committee, thanks to the efforts of the Prime Minister and the government and those willing co-assassins of Canadian democracy who have supported them, stands for pure political propaganda. It stands for the ability of the Liberal party to prove once again that they can sell a lie to the public faster than the public can catch up to them.
The hon. member referred to a dozen African countries. He did not mention countries like Australia and New Zealand which like Canada have a long, proud history and tradition of established democracy, countries which have a flag that means something to their people because they have a history of which they are not ashamed. I must say I cannot understand Liberal members not having the intestinal fortitude to stand up and tell the house what is meant by a compromise by the Liberal party on a flag. While most of

us in the opposition felt that the red ensign was good enough we were ready to compromise. I think the general feeling on this side of the house was that we wanted a flag which would retain some symbol of our history and heritage to show that we are not ashamed of a flag that has flown over this country for 100 years and to show that Canada has 100 years of history of which we are proud.
The difficulty was that on the Liberal side compromise meant only one thing. No flag should fly over Canada which has on it any symbol denoting anything of our history and heritage. That is all. Anything else would pass. Then member after member would get up, like the hon. member for Leeds, and say, "I truly love this flag". I bet you that if it had been a plain, dirty handkerchief he would have been able to say the same thing, so long as it did not have any suggestion of anything indicating our history, our heritage and our traditions. All I can say is that the new flag brought in by the committee stands for the Liberal party.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) when he says it is being brought in by parliament and not by any one person. That is nonsense. I think he is being very naive when he does not concede that it is being brought in by the political power of the Liberal party exercised on the members of that committee. Oh, I admit they were given a little discretion: As long as you have a maple leaf on it, it does not matter. That is what I like, a party that really stands for something. Political opportunism is what the Liberal party stands for and that is what this flag stands for.
I hope that those on the other side who feel I am wasting my time and that the voters of the country are going to say I am wasting the time of the house, because we all know that public opinion says this matter should be wrapped up quickly, are feeling really happy and secure now. I have never seen more typical examples of leadership than those Liberals show who watch to see which way the flock is running, and then run a little faster in order to catch up. As far as I am concerned the duty of members of this house is to try to deal with the business of the house as their consciences dictate, and we can see from the erratic behaviour of those on the other side of the house that they have been trying to do this. But having no consciences they have been wandering willy-nilly wherever political opportunism leads, and I hope they are happy.

maintopic: MR. NASSERDEN-"HANSARD" REPORT OF SUPPLY COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: CANADIAN FLAG
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the time has come to give Canada a distinctive flag, symbol of unity and pride, and I would even say of paternity and sovereignty for Canadians.
This motion concerns the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag proclaiming the sovereignty of our country.
Canada, through its history, has experienced a constant constitutional evolution. It has now become a sovereign state within the commonwealth and the nations. A state is sovereign when it holds supreme soreveign authority at home and when it is submitted to no other country at the international level. Sovereign does not mean independent or absolute, because all nations must submit to public international law.
We can assert with pride that our country enjoys today the eight main characteristics of a sovereign state: the right to legislate, the right to give our legislation extraterritoriality, the right to diplomatic representation abroad, the right to have Canadian courts of last instance, the right to declare peace, war or neutrality, the right to amend our constitution according to our desire and our own decisions, the right to negotiate and to sign ourselves our own treaties, and finally, the recognition of our sovereignty by the other nations of the world.
Several factors and developments have made possible the achievement of such a maturity, but the most outstanding was the Statute of Westminister passed on December 11, 1931, which gave our country its sovereignty and independence within the commonwealth.
There is more than the possession of Canadian sovereignty which is talked about so much in this house, within the United Nations, within NATO and almost everywhere in the world; this real sovereignty must express itself through outward signs which proclaim our distinctive Canadian personality.
Our national impulse for a distinctive character does not in any way hurt our relations with the other members of the commonwealth, with which we are united through a common allegiance to the British crown.
That is the spirit behind a project which promotes the existence of a Canadian sovereignty which can express itself through external signs: a distinctive national flag, a distinctive national anthem and a national day celebrating Canadian sovereignty.
Therefore, the thing is to adopt a distinctive flag, one which would be characteristic of
Canadian Flag
our country, both a flag and an anthem completely different from those of other countries and which would bear our colours and show our national aspirations as truly Canadian and distinctive.
We, Creditistes, had adopted a distinctive flag, we had advocated a diagonal one. We felt that because of its simplicity, it should have been accepted, but such was not the case. The members of this house decided otherwise.
We spent almost three weeks dealing with the flag and then a committee was set up which discussed the matter for six weeks. That committee has brought us its report. Now, since we did not come here merely to indulge in petty politics, but to do things, and because the time has come to give Canada a distinctive flag, we accept the report of the committee. We are pleased to approve it, because the old parties have been calling for the adoption of a flag for such a long time. In fact, they have been doing so for 25 years, but the Canadians have never had a distinctive flag. They are still waiting for it and since we are here to take a stand and act, we are ready to vote in favour of a distinctive flag which will do credit to all Canadians and the entire community.
It is not the first time that such a matter is raised in Canadian politics; in the past, some governments, some associations, certain members of parliament and a great number of Canadians have raised that important issue without avail.
When we consider the origin and background of flags, we note that the union jack has become the national emblem of Great Britain under a royal proclamation of January 1, 1801. We note that the red ensign, authorized in England by Queen Anne in 1707 and by Queen Victoria in 1864, is, under section 72 of the merchant and shipping act of 1894 the proper flag of all ships belonging to British citizens.
If Canadians are really to express their new Canadian citizenship, which they have possessed since January 1, 1947, and a really distinctive patriotism, those two flags no longer suit their legitimate aspirations.
Besides, the order in council of September 5, 1945 clearly indicates that the red ensign will be flown until parliament decides otherwise. The order in council thus recognizes a temporary situation which we must now rectify and define by a specific action, namely by finally adopting a distinctive national flag for this Canada of ours.

Canadian Flag
Since the last war, public opinion in Canada has constantly evolved in this field and has reached an unequivocal degree of maturity.
Why has the time come to make this decision? It is because our country, Canada, a sovereign state, needs external signs to demonstrate this legal and progressive sovereignty.
If our country has developed to the extent that everyone acknowledges its obvious maturity, we must show this emancipation by means of a truly national and essentially distinctive flag. The pride and the future of our country, and the acknowledgment of our final liberation are at stake.
Most Canadians in this North American country ardently wish to live, not for the mother countries of their remote ancestors, but for the land that feeds them and will feed their sons and daughters, for the land where they will draw their last breath.
Only a really distinctive Canadian national flag will strengthen convictions which presided over confederation in 1867, only a really distinctive Canadian national flag will give concrete form to our common aspirations, our parliamentary and individual liberties, our mutual understanding and our Canadian patriotism.
Mr. Speaker, if the Canadian people as a whole need such a flag, if the Canadian people as a whole insist on it with the support of the political parties, if the whole world recognizes that Canada has reached its maturity and has a distinctive personality, what are we, members of the House of Commons, waiting for to take the necessary step?
I hope this motion will be enthusiastically received and that the house will soon give it by a positive vote.
If we adopt a distinctive Canadian flag, we should also proclaim a distinctive national anthem, for we could not very well look at our distinctive Canadian flag and, at the same time, sing the national anthem of another country. Let us not make such a blunder, which would be absolutely intolerable and ridiculous.
Since a parliamentary committee selected a flag, the government should see to it that a national anthem is adopted at the same time as a national flag. The vote should be taken at the same time on the flag and on the anthem, and one should be just as national and distinctive as the other.
Both our Conservative and Liberal governments have long postponed the granting of a [Mr. Latullppe.l
distinctive national flag to Canada. It is their business. We are anxious to have a distinctive national flag but we can wait. For us in Quebec, there are more urgent things to settle in our relations between the provinces and the federal government. But in all these other fields, we do not wish that cultural and intellectual matters be always settled by dint of numbers, nine against one. This is too unfair, too unequal, too despotic. We ask all nationalities making up Canada to try to understand us on a human basis, on an essential basis instead of considering us always by different standards.
We are then ripe for a truly national flag. The failures and the errors of the past are over. Let us face the future and let us consider ourselves as one people made up of human beings having the same essential needs; indeed, there are now 19,300,000 Canadian citizens and in 1967, when we celebrate the centennial of the confederation there will be 20,000,000.
These 19,300,000 human beings have rights recognized in our Canadian statutes. For instance, there is the famous Canadian Bill of Rights passed on August 10, 1960, which states that:
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God., the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions.
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion, or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely
(a) the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person... freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and association, freedom of the press:
Mr. Speaker, that proves that we can do something which is national in scope, something which is truly Canadian, in the realm of the intellect, of the mind, of intelligence. I understand that it is harder and it takes longer to achieve unity when you have ten provinces instead of one and 28 nationalities instead of one, but why do we not follow that example in essential and humanitarian fields.
The drafting of the Canadian Bill of Rights required several weeks, several months and, indeed, several years of parliamentary work; it cost a great deal of money, of effort, of energy and of enthusiasm, but in the end every member of parliament voted for this humanitarian legislation, and the whole Canadian people rejoiced on August 10, 1960, when the bill was given royal assent.

And that was a document strictly Canadian in scope, in dimension, which contained not a single word likely to show our subservience to any other people in the whole world.
Did you give any thought to this initial action finally taken by the Canadian parliament, without feeling obliged to ask permission from any other country, without feeling obliged to repatriate or amend the constitution?
This is proof, Mr. Speaker, proof that we can do the same thing here through our own powers, in this house of representatives of the people, the whole Canadian people, all the people from one coast to the other, and from the North pole to the U.S. border.
But, once more, by a national initiative, like choosing a distinctive flag, each section must recognize the fact that while claiming rights for itself, at the same time it assumes the duty to respect those same rights towards other sections.
Do you admit that? This is what we have to consider before going any further in the life of the whole people whom we want to be Canadian, just plain Canadian and not French Canadian, English Canadian, Scottish Canadian, Irish Canadian, Italian Canadian or German Canadian, no more than American Canadian.
Just Canadian, Mr. Speaker; Canadian on Canadian soil, with a Canadian flag, that is what I am, that is what I want, that is what I hope to see in the near future, for me, my children, my friends, for you, for all of us here in this house, in this parliament, in this government, in this- whole country, this Canada, this Canada of ours.
Canada's history is but beginning. The history of confederation is but 100 years old. The past is gone. The past saw joy, it saw grief, it was borne with its faults, its glories; now we see where we stand and look towards the future.
Let us cease to dwell on the differences, and learn to love one another better by looking at such things as we have in common, common essence, Canadian essence, human essence, both human and divine, the ultimate principle of our unity, of our vitality, of our universality.
Because if we are proud enough some day to fly a truly Canadian flag within the limits of our territory, let it be known that we shall also have to be proud enough to fly it throughout the whole world as a really distinctive Canadian flag.
Such a flag will date, we hope, from 1964 or 1967 but let it be, if possible, really Ca-
Canadian Flag
nadian, a true sign and symbol that will rally the minds and actions of the various nationalities making up the Canadian people on Canadian soil.
We will thus be able to sing before that Canadian flag the Canadian national anthem; "O Canada".

maintopic: MR. NASSERDEN-"HANSARD" REPORT OF SUPPLY COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: CANADIAN FLAG
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
To use an
expression employed by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), I was one of that bunch of cynical members who participated in the work of the flag committee. So were five Conservative members whom I did not know very well before we began our discussions and whom I have come to respect very much for the way in which they did their work, and also for the sincerity they showed throughout the sittings of that committee.
I wish to take this opportunity tonight to report to you, sir, that this committee was one of the best of any I have known. Every member participating in its discussions was in earnest, trying very hard and very honestly to find and reach a reasonable compromise on this difficult question of a national flag for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that at the beginning of the discussions, I was faced, like most members of this committee, with an issue that seemed terribly difficult. We had the opportunity during our meetings to listen to experts in the fields of heraldry, history, protocol, and so on, who briefed us, as fully as possible, on the purely technical aspects of this matter.
I think I should say the committee's members reached a decision through a logical process which could not lead them to any other choice than the one which they eventually reached by a majority vote.
First of all, we recognized there are traditions in Canada even if, among the public and the members of the House of Commons they appeared to be ignored. There exists a tradition in Canada, as far as our country's symbol is concerned.
Here, may I underline this-I said it often during the meetings of the committee as the hon. members who sat on that committee may recall-that when we are faced with the question of adopting a national flag, we cannot think of incorporating in such an emblem every glorious event in our history. We must reach as technical and as simple a definition as possible of what a flag should be.

Canadian Flag
A flag is a signal, a message aimed at identifying the bearer, and there is no question of recalling the historical background or trying to encumber such a flag with all kinds of signs recalling the history of the country it seeks to identify.
Such a flag must be readily identified. Consequently, it should be simple. Moreover, it should bear a familiar symbol. During these numerous meetings, several precedents in the history of Lower Canada as well as of Upper Canada were recalled indicating that, spontaneously, in both Canadas, the Canadian people when they wished to identify themselves always showed a maple leaf.
It is the reason why the first inevitable conclusion reached by the members of the committee-and I might even say by the hon. Conservative members who were on the committee-was that the emblem of Canada was the maple leaf.
Somewhat later, we tackled the problem from a rather more legal point of view, shall we say. Then, I remember, I very candidly remarked to my Tory friends that they had themselves made to the solution of this problem an exceptional contribution and that, for one, I was shocked to find that now that we must reach a decision ratifying what tradition had already decreed, they repudiated it.
As a matter of fact, a cursory look at history, as regards this question of a Canadian flag, will show, following consideration of this matter by the committee, that the army has more than 400 military badges bearing the maple leaf and that a Conservative government asked His Majesty the King, in 1921, to proclaim what was to be the emblem of Canada. At that time in the coat of arms of Canada, that emblem was selected, and it was three maple leaves on a single stem.
At first discussion arose as to the colour of those maple leaves. Then, in 1957, again under a government headed by a Conservative prime minister, the colour of those leaves was changed from green to red. And more recently, in 1962, the government under the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), once again suggested that the Queen herself incorporate in her personal flag, as the Queen of Canada, the three red maple leaves on a single stem.
Therefore, I repeat this question to my Conservative friends. Why do you disavow that important contribution you made in our efforts to choose a distinctive emblem for Canada?

We therefore established in the first place that Canada's emblem should be the maple leaf. We established that because it is an emblem that Canadians chose spontaneously, as I said, and also because it is an emblem known everywhere.
I recall that during our discussions, when we heard, as we heard them so often in the house, that easy oratory recalling that Canadian soldiers had died fighting for the red ensign, we asked one of our own people who was on the battle front during the last war whether that was the actual truth. He admitted not only the fact that, in contemporary times, armies do not fly any flag in battle but also that even the officers take their badges off, so that nothing may identify the brigade or division in the line. And we also heard the testimony of a person who recently visited the cemeteries of Canadian soldiers abroad. This person told us that on every white cross which marked the tomb of a dead soldier, there was a maple leaf showing that this soldier was a Canadian.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that through logic we had arrived at the choice we are submitting tonight. The same applied as concerns the colours of the flag. Once more, we inspired ourselves from the proclamation which, in 1921, established the colours of Canada.
I know that this afternoon a member who supported this motion of the flag committee was asked what part of the proclamation stated that white and red were the Canadian colours. It is to be found not in the proclamation itself but in the interpretation of Canada's coat of arms.
That is why we asked experts in heraldry to tell us, laymen, what interpretation should be given to the coat of arms. It is also through logic that we have been able to determine the importance of this historical souvenir, the genealogy mentioned by our friends opposite. It is in the Canadian coat of arms that we have found the answer.
If you examine them closely, you will see that they include the lion of the Plantagenets, the lion of Scotland, the harp of Ireland and the fleur-de-lis of France when it was ruled by the monarchy. That is Canada's ancestry. The Canadian emblem, the three maple leaves on a single stem, hold the position of honour, under the shield. As far as the national colours are concerned, they are represented by the red and white mantle at the top of the coat of arms.

Technically we must therefore observe the implicit instructions given to Canadians by the royal College of Arms which had been asked to decide what should be our national colours, and our distinctive emblem.
Mr. Speaker, as far as compromise is concerned, the hon. members on the other side must accept the idea that the representatives of the Liberal party have compromised as much as possible. Indeed, we arrived at the flag committee with an emblem which we felt was already accepted by the population, three red maple leaves and two blue stripes. We came out of the committee with a flag bearing a single maple leaf and two red bands instead of blue. It seems to me it is difficult to ask for more from the representatives of a political party.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) asked the following question:

What is wrong with the union jack and the fleur-de-lis? There is nothing wrong with the union jack and the fleur-de-lis except that neither is the Canadian flag. The union jack is a foreign flag: it is the flag of England. The fleur-de-lis represents royal France. These flags do not and cannot represent Canada. This was our argument all along, Mr. Speaker.
I hope that hon. members on the other side of the house are not going to pursue this line of trying to discredit the committee. Some of their own members were members of the committee and they were eager to succeed, as was every one of us. I hope they will not try to infer that there was as much cynicism as we are told there was, its having been said that we were a bunch of cynical members. We were no bunch of anything. We were very eager to find common ground for understanding, and I believe we found it. At one time, irrespective of anything which can be said on the other side, there was actually unanimity that there be one national flag only for Canada.
I also hope, Mr. Speaker, that all of the members of that committee who will participate in this debate will be accurate and honest. When we refer to one of the motions voted on in the committee, the motion for only one flag, we omit a very important word. We voted first for one national flag; and then we voted separately for a flag which would indicate our participation in the commonwealth. These are two different questions. We accepted the fact that the flag we were going to choose was going to be submitted as the Canadian
Canadian Flag
emblem, and for that purpose only and exclusively. Therefore I think that in all these discussions we must be strictly honest, as were all the members of the committee when we were discussing this matter.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry to have to differ from my friend the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), who sat next to me during all the meetings of the committee. I found him a very nice gentleman, but I am surprised and shocked to a certain extent to hear him suggest that there were instructions to the Liberal members given by the government. I can say most emphatically that I talked not once during all those sittings with any member of the cabinet, especially with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson): I did meet the Prime Minister many times in the elevator but I did not talk to him except to say good morning, especially in view of the situation I understood we were in. Some members in our party know that even the most innocuous question was left unanswered by members of the committee. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope-I do not want to delay the house-that this committee's recommendation will be carried and considered in the light in which it is offered. I believe the committee did its duty, and I do not think it becoming of any hon. member of this house, especially those who were not members of the committee and who therefore must not of necessity be informed about what went on, to discredit the committee and the members of it who participated so honestly. It is very unbecoming to be submitted to the kind of speech that one hon. member made tonight.
I have nothing more to add, Mr. Speaker. From the way things look I am confident that the committee's recommendation will receive from the house, if a vote is permitted as quickly as possible, an astounding majority; I venture to predict that, Mr. Speaker. If hon. members on the other side are so eager to have the question settled let the matter come to a vote. That is the easy solution. At the suggestion of hon. members opposite we consented to form a committee. This committee held extended sittings; everyone admits that. We have studied the question as objectively as possible. We could not come to complete agreement, and that is unfortunate. We tried very hard to reach full agreement; but we did present a majority report, supported by an important majority.
When hon. members talk of a plebiscite, if they do not accept a majority of ten to four what kind of majority would they ask from

Canadian Flag
a plebiscite? If hon. gentlemen opposite are not satisfied with 72 per cent, what are they going to request from a plebiscite? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this question has been aired long enough and that we should now proceed with the practical side of the question, which is to vote on this matter.

maintopic: MR. NASSERDEN-"HANSARD" REPORT OF SUPPLY COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: CANADIAN FLAG
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking this first opportunity of speaking on the flag issue, as I did not avail myself of an opportunity to do so when it was before the house earlier. There will be some who will say I have already spoken during this debate, and in one sense that is true, as on February 18 I placed a resolution on the order paper asking the government to consider immediately the introduction of legislation which would acknowledge the Canadian red ensign as Canada's distinctive national flag, as endorsed by the Canadian Legion and the I.O.D.E. I had an opportunity to debate this resolution on June 1, but of course you realize that a member is limited to 20 minutes on the debate of a private member's resolution. Therefore at this time I wish to put forward some other thoughts I have had about this subject. These are thoughts I have collected during many interviews in past weeks with my own constituents, as well as ideas resulting from correspondence I have received, not only from the people in my riding of Elgin but from all across Canada.
During two week ends I had the opportunity of being present at quite large nonpolitical gatherings, and I was amazed by the number of individuals who voluntarily expressed their opinions to me about the flag issue. As a result of these conversations I can only come to the following conclusions. The majority of the people in my area prefer the retention of the red ensign as Canada's distinctive flag. Those individuals who feel that now is the time for a new design were not happy with the three red maple leaf design. They are still not happy with the committee's proposed flag with the one maple leaf and the red borders. The third conclusion I came to was that they were discouraged and disgusted with the present parliament, and that the government should get off its high horse and finish the legislative program now on the order paper before bringing the flag issue back into the House of Commons. I might point out that a great portion of the legislative program on the order paper has been on the order paper for several months without members of parliament having the opportunity of discussing it.

The first group of individuals with whom I had the opportunity of discussing this issue was made up of 300 people representing municipal and county councils who had gathered together to pay honour to a retiring clerk-treasurer who had served in that capacity for 25 years. These people are retired or serving representatives of municipalities, and have done so faithfully for many years. On two week ends I had an opportunity of visiting different rural fairs, where one has wonderful opportunities of meeting a crosssection of the public and obtaining knowledge as to the feeling of those people about an issue such as the flag issue. I also attended a Labour day celebration last September which brought together people from all walks of life, and again I was afforded the opportunity of taking part in discussions on the flag situation.
At this stage of the debate we are supposed to be discussing an amendment to the committee report, and this ties in with the unity of Canada through a plebiscite, asking that a ballot be taken at the next general election. I hope that this ballot will be taken but that the results will not be related to any specific region. I think that is how it should be carried out, because we know, as a result of various polls that have been conducted, that certain sections of Canada are strongly in favour of the retention of the red ensign, while other areas are predominantly in favour of a new design.
There was a time when I thought the Ottawa area was predominantly in favour of the three maple leaf flag. Last summer we observed a great deal of ballyhoo about the three maple leaf pennant which was being flown on car radio aerials throughout the city. Some people are still flying these pennants from their aerials. I am pleased that the new proposal has changed that design, because I am sure we can all recall having seen some of these pennants that were flown for two or three months and remember that they turned a dirty grey, with the blue colour having faded, and with frayed edges. In fact, I saw one one morning not long ago that was so anaemic in appearance I stopped and asked myself: Is this the design if passed by parliament to which we would pledge our allegiance and the allegiance of future generations? I think we must still ask ourselves this question in relation to the new proposed design.
I recall the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), in speaking to this house, drawing to our attention the fact that

the three maple leaf design had been devaluated in one joke shop in the city from 98 cents, which was the retail cost when it first became available, to 19 cents. I am pleased that we are not now witnessing the same type of pennant, with the single maple leaf design, being flown in the same manner, but I do wonder why the Prime Minister has not proposed that a flag with the one maple leaf design, having red bars, be flown on a mast on parliament hill so that members could view it, as he did in respect of his own design.
One morning last week I was listening to a local radio station which each morning conducts a survey about various topics. The listening audience is invited to call the radio station and discuss the topic of the day. The morning I was listening the topic was the design of the flag expected to be presented to the House of Commons on the following day. I was surprised to learn that of ten or 12 telephone calls, only one approved the suggested design.
The same individual wondered why the present leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, when he was the prime minister, did not bring in a measure to make the Canadian red ensign, with or without changes, Canada's flag by act of parliament. One could also go back in history and ask why Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, when he was prime minister, did not make the ensign official by an act of parliament, or bring forth a new design. We know that he took the initial step, by order in council, to make the ensign the official flag to be flown on all government buildings at home and abroad. We could also ask why Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, when he was prime minister, did not make the ensign the official flag by an act of parliament, or bring forward a new design.
I believe the three prime ministers I have referred to were aware of the danger of creating more disunity across this country by presenting a flag that would not be acceptable to a large majority of Canadians.
We of the Conservative party have endeavoured to place before parliament the reasons the present design is not acceptable to a large percentage of Canadians. We will continue to place these reasons before parliament. We have offered time and time again suggestions as to how the government should proceed to regain that lost unity which is evident across Canada, and which has resulted over the flag design proposal.
Canadian Flag
I wish to give two examples, Mr. Speaker, of how the flag question has created disunity and has divided our populace into two camps. A few weeks ago I had lunch with a resident of Ottawa who related to me an incident that happened to him last summer. During the hot days of July he had left his car parked with the windows open and some person had placed on the inside of his windshield a small Canadian ensign sticker reading "This is Canada's flag, let's keep it flying". As he related the story to me, this could have been on his windshield several days before it was brought to his attention by his young son. He did not tell me whether or not he was an ensign supporter but did say as far as he was concerned the sticker was doing no harm to him or anyone else until several days later when he went to unlock his car to drive home and noticed a young man standing by the car with an object in his hand. This man swore at him and told him to remove the ensign or he would smash his windshield to pieces. Naturally his reply was, "In the first place I didn't put it there and, in the second place, if you attempt to remove it by force there will be more than a broken windshield. It will be your head."
Several months ago, after I had placed my own flag resolution on the order paper, I recall receiving a picture postcard from the city of Toronto which was unsigned, the picture being of the Prince of Wales gates at the eastern entrance to the Canadian national exhibition grounds. The picture showed some 21 red ensigns flying over the top of the entrance and through each ensign there was a big black cross. On the back of the card were the words: "You Englishmen, there will be blood spilled over your ensign if you don't get rid of it".
We saw blood spilled several weeks ago during the flag debate, and spilled right here on the green carpet of this very chamber.

speechtext:
I was about to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am not of English ancestry but rather my grandfather on my father's side came from the highlands of northern Scotland, and on my mother's side my great grandfather was Pennsylvania Dutch of loyal united empire loyalist stock. I was very proud today when the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) directed our attention to the fact that this is St. Andrew's day.
As I say, great disunity has been created in this country since the flag debate was first introduced in the House of Commons. We have had riots in various parts of Canada. We have seen flags burned. We have had an increase in the separatist movement in the province of Quebec. We have seen our armouries raided and robbed. Yes, Mr. Speaker, murders were even committed while this was being done.
When I spoke on my own flag resolution I stated that I was expressing my own personal opinions as well as the opinions expressed in approximately 90 per cent of the letters and telegrams I had received up until that time. That was last June 1, Mr. Speaker, and previous to that date I had received nearly 150 signed letters and telegrams all asking me to support the retention of the Canadian ensign as Canada's national flag. This figure has now mounted to 611. Since June 1 I have received many letters supporting my stand on the ensign but since that date I have received only three letters supporting some other design than the ensign.
In all fairness to those who are writing me in support of the ensign and to those supporting some other design I propose to put on the record some comments from each side. Before doing so I may say that some time ago I received a clipping from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal, being an article written by Jean Sweet. The article is entitled "In My Opinion", and in my opinion it exemplifies the feelings, I am sure, of many millions of Canadians. I am going to quote from the article. This lady says:
Normally, like most peaceful citizens, I'm a coward about public issues. But I think the time
has come to stand up and be counted on this flag matter.
Most people who ever saw a tree know that big trees rise from big firm roots. If you trim away the roots you weaken the tree. If too much root is removed you have nothing. The tree-that grew slowly over many decades-weakens, falls and decays.
Loyalties grow the same way, putting down roots in friendly soil. Without loyalities, even misplaced loyalities, man is nothing but a drifting derelict.
Millions of Canadians grew up as I did in the friendly soil of a Canada we learned from earliest years to respect and view with immense pride. We were taught not to brag loudly and constantly about our land, but instead to know what we had and to feel secure in its tenets.
Above all our flag has symbolized this land. It has grown with us. From pre-school age we loved the simple but intricately planned design of the union jack, so carefully integrating the major elements of Great Britain. We were proud when we saw the Canadian coat of arms in the fly of the beautiful flag. We sang songs to it. It meant our land.
Through school days I have no recollection of any "Quebec question". I remember Montreal as a fascinating place I longed to see where, right in our Canada, two languages were spoken and peoples from many other lands settled and lived.
Above all, as a child I watched the proud Van Doos march through the streets of our town, where they trained, headed by the tall lean figure of Colonel Vanier (I didn't know his name then, not until I met him as our Governor General). From that time I "saw" those proud French speaking troops "fighting for our flag" as news of their exploits trickled home. When we sang "We'll never let the old flag fall'' the Van Doos were in the picture, dying in France for that flag.
Well, as far as I am concerned no one man, no one group of troublemakers, can tell me "here is your new flag". This is a matter of roots, Canadian roots. If my flag can be readily discarded, so can my country and any other belief I ever held in it. It is disturbing and makes me wonder: what next?
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard the words of the Prime Minister, but I think there are large gaps in what has been proposed. For instance, this proposition does not deal with statements made on motions by ministers. It does not mention other matters. For example, it does not deal with written or oral questions, on Mondays and Wednesdays, together with notices of motions for production of papers. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the whole of our routine business prior to the calling of orders of the day has to be considered.
This question was raised yesterday as a matter of interest to all hon. members of the house, because it is not only the members on this side of the house who are interested in these proceedings but also hon. members on the other side of the house. For instance, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) obviously would have some questions to ask at this time, as would the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan); and there are also other points.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that he reconsider his position and make a definitive statement, after negotiation dealing with routine proceedings. The urgent business of the house as detailed by the Prime Minister a month ago has been dealt with, with the exception of the present matter and another matter under the Minister of Labour, which it has been the government's choice to defer. I suggest that the advancing of the hours of sitting is quite extraneous to our routine procedure. What is the pressure? I see a shrug of the shoulders and a snicker on the part of the Prime Minister, but what is the pressure in the government's eyes on the basis of the government's announced business?
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister reconsider his position and that he deal with motions; that he deal with notices of motions for the production of papers; that

Flag Debate-Suggested Procedure Change he deal with other routine matters. The government may wish to bring forward some bills; I am sure some of the Prime Minister's colleagues have some interesting matters to disclose to the house. There are a number of matters. subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, November 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Batten that the sixth report of the special committee on a Canadian flag presented to the house on Thursday, October 29, 1964, be now concurred in, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Perhaps this decision will have a slight dampening effect on some of the high spirits which marked the start of our sitting this afternoon.
The house will recall that yesterday the hon. member for Humber-St. George's, in his capacity as chairman of the special committee on the flag question, moved concurrence in the sixth report of that committee. The hon. member for Perth, who was also a member of the committee, proposed an amendment to the motion for concurrence that seeks to refer the report back to the committee with instructions to strike out paragraph 7 and substitute something else in its place. On the proposed amendment a point of order was raised by the President of the Privy Council.
It is for the Chair to determine whether the point of order raised by the government house leader is well taken or whether the amendment of the hon. member for Perth should be admitted for debate and decision.
I have had the advantage of hearing the views of several hon. members, which have been most helpful to me in reaching a decision. In addition to the house leader I have heard arguments by the two senior officers of the house themselves, the right hon. Prime
Canadian Flag
Minister and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. I have also had the benefit of the views expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who is the house leader of the official opposition and who seconded the motion setting up the flag committee. It has been helpful as well to have had expressions of opinion from the former Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton West, and from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who is an acknowledged authority on the rules. There were also brief but valuable contributions to the discussion by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency and the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona.
I have considered the point of order with care in an effort to reach a decision that takes account of the various arguments that have been advanced, and a decision that is in accordance with the practice and precedents in this country and in the British house whose practice, under our standing order No. 1, must be followed in cases not provided for in our own rules. In reaching my decision I have tried to take into account a number of factors which I will enumerate as briefly as possible.
1.	We are here dealing with an unusua. matter, namely the establishment of a national flag.
2.	It is a matter with a very considerable emotional impact for every one of us.
3.	The motion to commit the flag question to the special committee was moved by a member of the government, seconded by the house leader of the official opposition and passed unanimously.
4.	As the Prime Minister has said, there has already been a very extended debate on the flag question in the house itself, with 165 speeches over a 23 day period.
5.	In that debate the Chair has shown considerable leniency and has not enforced the rules of relevancy and repetition with rigidity.
6.	The committee has also considered the question fully and has held no less than 45 meetings.
7.	It is the duty of the Chair to see that the rights of members on all sides are fully protected so there will be freedom of discussion and the right of expression will not in any way, be stifled. Parliament is not a court but a forum.
8.	The right of freedom of expression, however, should not imperil the right of decision.

Canadian Flag
I have also tried to take account of some of the unusual features of this particular committee, as follows:
1.	It was a special committee.
2.	It was charged with the task of considering a specific but most encompassing question.
3.	It was asked to make a final report.
4.	It was given a particular time limit in which to complete its work.
5.	Its appointment, its power to report and the capacity of the house to act on the report are not restricted by any motion on the order paper on September 10, 1964.
I have also been conscious of certain factors relating to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Perth which I shall enumerate:
1.	It relates to the question of a national plebiscite.
2.	The question of a national plebiscite has already been discussed and voted on in the committee; in fact the first vote taken in the committee was on the question of a national plebiscite, and it was rejected 9 to 5.
3.	As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has pointed out, however, Bourinot's fourth edition, at page 479, makes it clear that a committee may reconsider and even reverse a previous decision.
4.	A vote was taken in the house itself on the question of a plebiscite on the 1st September 1964, as recorded on page 660 of Votes and Proceedings for that date.
5.	That vote, however, was on a subamendment which dealt with details as to what questions should be included in a plebiscite but not with the basic question of whether or not a plebiscite should be held.
6.	The basic question of whether or not a national plebiscite should be held, which is the subject of the amendment of the hon. member for Perth, has not as yet been decided by the house.
It will be apparent to all that these various factors which I have just listed, some of which are in direct contradiction with others, make the matter a difficult one for the Chair. We have heard it suggested that the flag committee no longer exists because it was a special committee set up for a fixed period of six weeks and a final report has been made. We have also heard that the matter before the house, however, does not relate to the final report of that committee but to its sixth report. We have been reminded, as well, that committees receive their authority from the house itself and that the authority of the house overrides that of any committee.

In order to reach some kind of reasoned judgment I have looked at all the factors in the situation. First let us look at our general practice with regard to the recommittal of a report.
1.	In General, Recommittal of a Report
It seems that it has been our constant practice that when the motion to concur is proposed, the report of a select committee may be referred back to the committee for further consideration or with instructions to amend it in any respect.
(a)	Bourinot's fourth edition, at page 479, states in part as follows:
A report may be referred back to a committee for further consideration, or with instructions giving them power to amend the same in any respect. In this way a committee may regularly reconsider and even reverse a decision it has previously arrived at.
(b)	Citation 322 of Beauchesne's fourth edition reads in part as follows:
When the motion to concur is proposed the report may be referred back to the committee for further consideration or with instruction to amend it in any respect.
(c)	Paragraph (4) of citation 325 of the same edition of Beauchesne states:
When a motion is made for concurrence in a select committee report, it is competent for the house to adopt it, reject it, refer it back to the committee or decide that consideration of the report will take place "this day six months".
(d)	Moreover, the precedents recorded in our Journals establish that when it is intended to refer back the report to a select committee on the motion for concurrence, the procedure has been to do so by amendment to such motion, and therefore without notice. With the time at my disposal I have failed to find during the last 45 years any instance in contradiction of that contention.
Now let us consider the recommittal of the final report of a special committee.
2.	Recommittal of the Final Report of a Special Committee
It has been suggested that a special committee ceases to exist when its final report is presented to the house and that such a report cannot be referred back to the committee unless the committee is revived.
(a)	In support of that view, citation 286 of Beauchesne's fourth edition states as follows:
It Is important that the motion for the appointment of the committee should state whether the committee shall report from time to time, for if it should report once without having been given such power, it will be defunct but may be revived. Special authorization should also be given to sending for persons, papers and records.

A select special committee ceases to exist on the moment its final report is presented to the house. The report cannot afterwards be sent back to the committee with instruction to amend it in any particular. If further proceedings are desired it is necessary to revive the committee.
(b)	W. F. Dawson, in his book "Procedure in the Canadian House of Commons", expresses a view similar to that set forth in the second paragraph of citation 286, when he states at page 206:
It is possible for the house, on the rare occasions when it does debate a committee report, to move to accept it, reject it, hoist it, or refer it back to the committee with the power to amend, except of course in the case of special committees, which have to be reconstituted by the house before their reports can be referred back.
Mr. Dawson refers to no authority to substantiate his statement. It is likely that since he was the assistant chief of our English Journals branch from 1955 to 1958, and published his book in 1962, he made such a statement having in mind citation 286 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which also appears verbatim in citation 555 of the third edition by the said author.
(c)	In support of paragraph (2) of citation 286 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, the author gives as his authority May's thirteenth edition, page 486, and he refers to a procedure in the British house that is indicated as 105 C.J. 201.
Upon examination, the supporting refer-rences invoked by Beauchesne to substantiate the second paragraph of citation 286 are not very convincing and do not seem to corroborate the broad statement made by the author. The pertinent reference at page 486 of May's thirteenth edition is as follows:
If a committee, at the conclusion of their inquiry, make a final report to the house, the sittings of the committee are assumed to have been closed; and if further proceedings were desired it would be necessary to revive the committee.
However, in reading the footnotes below this statement, which are purported to be the supporting authority therefor, it would appear that these references are not related to the question of referring back a report but deal rather with cases where it was intended to commit a new matter to select committees which had concluded their work.
One of these footnotes also makes mention of a ruling of the Speaker in the British house in 1893 to the effect that a motion to commit a bill to a select committee on another bill was out of order as the committee, having reported the bill committed to it, had ceased to exist.
Canadian Flag
The other footnote on page 486 of May's thirteenth edition is the very same reference as the one given as additional supporting authority in citation 286 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, and deals with a procedure in the British house in 1850 which seems on all fours with that of 1893 referred to earlier.
There can be no quarrel with citation 286 in this regard and, in similar circumstances, those precedents probably would be valid in our house. However, other circumstances now prevail.
3.	Our Practice
If citation 286 is to be interpreted as meaning that, with the presentation of its final report, a special committee ceases to exist to the extent that it has to be reconstituted, or that it has to be revived by a special motion before that report can be referred back to it, with instructions to amend, it is my view that such interpretation does not seem consistent with our practice.
A review of the comparatively few precedents which we have in this regard would indicate that in no case was a special procedure involved which would provide for the revival of the committee when referring a report back for consideration or with instructions.
What are the precedents?
(a)	On April 14, 1919 (cf. Journals, p. 171) a special committee concerning the abolition of titles was appointed without any mention that the committee would report from time to time, and that committee was not so empowered at a later date. On the motion for concurrence in the committee's report, as will be seen at pages 293-4 of the Journals for May 22, 1919, an amendment was moved purporting to amend the report itself. Mr. Speaker Rhodes then stated in part:
When a motion is made for the adoption of the report of a committee, it is competent for the house to adopt it, to reject it, or to refer it back to the committee with or without instructions. Or, a motion may be made for the six months' hoist. I do not think it competent to move to amend the report of a committee.
The amendment was thereupon withdrawn and another amendment was moved to the effect of referring back the report to the committee with instructions to amend it in certain particulars.
(b)	In 1926, when an amendment was proposed to the motion to concur in the final report of a special committee on the administration of the department of customs and excise, a sentence to the following effect was

Canadian Flag
appended to the amendment, and to the subamendment, namely:
"and that the committee for such purpose be revived".
I would direct attention to the Journals for June 22 and 23, 1926, at pages 461-2 and 464-5.
Since this is the only occasion on which such a phrase was employed, and as the authority for its use is itself in question, it is suggested that the omission of that or a similar phrase would provide meagre ground for ruling a proposed amendment out of order. In any case, the amendment of the hon. member for Perth does contain the phrase "and that the committee for such purpose be revived".
(c)	On May 30, 1928, as recorded at page 476 of the Journals, a motion was made to refer back the third and final report of the standing committee on industrial and international relations with instructions to amend it in certain particulars. A point of order was then raised to the effect that the committee, having made its final report, had ceased to exist so far as the reference was concerned, and therefore no other reference with respect to the subject matter first referred could be made.
Although in this instance the house was dealing with the report of a standing and not a special committee, it is relevant to mention here the following statement which is part of the ruling made by Mr. Speaker Lemieux at that time, as recorded at page 3563 of Hansard for May 30, 1928:
So that the practice in the Canadian parliament does not prevent a report, even if it is a final report, of either a special or, better still, a standing committee, being referred back to be amended.
(d)	There are other instances to be found in our records to the effect that although the word "final" did not appear in a special committee report, we may assume that it was the final report, and where amendments to refer the report back to the committee with instructions were moved on the motion for concurrence. In that regard I refer to pages 754-5 of the Journals for June 26, 1948, where two amendments were proposed to motions to concur in a report of the special committee on prices. While both these amendments were ruled out of order for various reasons, no question was raised with respect to the validity of referring the said report back to the committee.

4.	Conflict between Citation 286 and the Formula in Beauchesne's 4th Edition
Much has been said about Beauchesne's citation 286, which states in effect that a special committee ceases to exist once its final report has been presented to the house. However, there is a fundamental contradiction between the terms of this citation and formula No. 95, which is to be found at page 397 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. That formula reads as follows:
The question being proposed "That the final report of the select standing (or special) committee on	 be now concurred in,"
Mr	moves in amendment
thereto, seconded by Mr	 "That the said
report be not now concurred in but that it be recommitted to the select standing (or special)
committee on	 with instruction that they
have power to amend the same so as to recommend that	".
It will be seen that in this formula provision is made for recommitting a final report of a special committee with instructions by way of an amendment, and no reference is made to the revival of the committee.
5.	Unprovided Cases
Let us now consider unprovided cases. It must be borne in mind that if the procedure now under review is at all to be considered as an unprovided case, under the terms of our standing order 1 recourse must be made to May's sixteenth edition wherein it is stated at page 642 that when a report is recommitted the select committee with all its powers is thereby revived.
6.	The Present Instance
What of the present instance? It has been suggested that the case of the special committee on the flag question is different from others, more particularly in that:
1. The resolution appointing such committee has fixed a limitation on the life of the committee in establishing that its final report was to be submitted to the house not later than six weeks from the date of its first sitting and that the referral back of either the sixth or the seventh report to such committee, after the time limitation provided in the resolution for its existence, goes beyond the decision taken by the house. It may also be said that the committee should again be empowered or reconstituted by a substantive motion after notice. Obviously at this stage of the session, when members' notices of motions have disappeared from the order paper, private members would be precluded from moving such a motion.

2. On the other hand, argument was made that what was before the house was not a final report of the flag committee but only an interim or sixth report.
It is my view that if paragraph 2 of Beau-chesne's citation 286 were to be interpreted as meaning that with the presentation of its final report a special committee ceases to exist to the extent that it has to be reconstituted, or that it has to be revived by a special motion after notice before that report can be referred back to it, with instructions to amend, it is reasonable to say that the committee having ceased to exist on the presentation of the seventh and final report, which was tabled at the same time as the sixth, paragraph 2 of the citation should apply to the sixth report as well. But as I have already indicated this is not, in my view, a valid interpretation of the citation.
I am also of the opinion that the resolution appointing the committee should be considered in the light of the surrounding circumstances at the time it was adopted. If we do so, we see that at that time there was before the house the motion appearing under government orders, No. 44(A), an amendment moved thereto and a subamendment. There was also government order No. 44(B). Both these were suspended by agreement. It has been argued that it is unlikely that these two orders will again come before the house. In that case it would be reasonable to assume that the practical effect of refusing amendments to refer back either of these reports to the committee, with or without instructions, would be tantamount to preventing any decision of the house on the particulars mentioned in such amendments or on any other particulars connected with the subject matter of the question. In other words, to all intents and purposes it would have the effect of limiting the house to accepting or refusing the decision of the committee, and nothing more.
I have examined Hansard and have been unable to come to the conclusion-unless a very narrow interpretation, which would seem to me arbitrary, is given to what was said in the house with regard to this committee-that there was any intention unanimously expressed or any final agreement that the normal procedure should not be followed when the house would be acting upon the reports of the committee.
7.	Conclusion
In conclusion I may say that if we look at all the special circumstances surrounding the complex and what seems to be unique problem confronting us, I think, rightly or
Canadian Flag
wrongly, that to a great extent the problem goes beyond the mere strict and rigid technical and procedural sphere and that, for a large part, the answer is to be found in asking ourselves what is fair and equitable, having regard among other things to the surrounding circumstances, the commitments or agreements made, and also having regard to the desirability of not depriving members of certain basic rights through technicalities, real, doubtful or fictitious.
After careful consideration of all the factors involved I can come to no other conclusion but that in the present circumstances the point of order cannot be entertained. It is my intention to put the amendment before the house.

Many, many thanks for your kind letter of June 5 with which you enclosed copy of Hansard for June 1 which I eagerly perused. I am sure I speak for

all members of the Royal Canadian Legion and other loyal Canadians when I say our most grateful and sincere thanks to you and your fellow members of the House of Commons for the tremendous effort you are making in an eifort to keep our flag -the Canadian red ensign-flying. We had a wonderful convention and I feel sure millions of Canadians now realize that we do have a truly distinctive Canadian flag and whoever heard of the red ensign causing disunity?
I was on T.V. C.B.C. and this was one of the points I stressed.
I should like to put on record some feelings of another of my correspondents, who says:
Regarding the flag issue, my husband and I hold this opinion.
A spokesman for the French Canadians who are a minority group, says that any flag incorporating the union jack is totally unacceptable to them. What about the majority group of Canadians in every other province who would consider any flag not incorporating the union jack entirely unacceptable to them? Must we accept a minority rule?
Again I wish to quote from other correspondence.
On a point of order, I should like to know how relevant these letters are to the amendment put forward.

I believe the amendment refers to a plebiscite, and I am endeavouring to present this correspondence to show why the people desire a plebiscite. I will not read all this correspondence, but another letter I have received says this:
We have been and are permitted to fly in this fair country at the present time a flag known far and wide as the red ensign. It contains the union jack, which is truly a known and honoured emblem all over the world. Also on the same flag is the Canadian coat of arms, which is truly Canadian, and while the union jack makes the flag part of the British commonwealth of nations, the Canadian coat of arms identifies this as a Canadian flag.
The right and justice this flag symbolizes has been fought for by men of our country. This flag was here before a lot of people who are now citizens came here or were born here. If they do not like it they are free to go somewhere else, where there is one they do like. So let's keep what we have, while we have something to be proud of, instead of a few dried up maple leaves, or something else to satisfy Quebec and a few others.
What has that to do with the plebiscite?

I am endeavouring to point out that the flag question is creating disunity. It is pitting one part of Canada against another part. I am showing the feelings of the people in other parts of the country who live outside the province of Quebec. This correspondent continues:
When the time comes to vote on this flag issue how many members will be coerced into voting for a new flag fearing that if this issue is defeated the Pearson government will call an election. I hope that you will use your vote and influence to retain our present flag, the red ensign.

Then I received a photograph from Winnipeg showing the citizenship court in session in that city. It depicts a swearing in ceremony for new Canadians which was held on March 4, 1964. In the background on the wall are two red ensigns in the form of a V. At the top of the V is the Canadian coat of arms. Below that picture is Her Majesty the Queen. This is a matter which is again creating disunity in Canada.
