Dear Sir:
I am respectfully drawing to your attention the following resolution:
Whereas local 97, Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers, St. Thomas, Ontario, do hereby support with strong intent the Canadian red ensign as the national flag of the Dominion of Canada and that no other design or proposed design will be acceptable as a national flag by this local.
This resolution was passed unanimously at a meeting of this local this 13th day of May, 1964.
This letter was signed by the president and secretary.
A few weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, when the representatives of the commonwealth countries were meeting in the west block, we had an opportunity to view the flags of each one of those nations. I viewed them on many occasions and was quite interested to note, as I am sure other hon. members of the House of Commons noted, that six of the commonwealth countries have incorporated in their flag the union jack. I refer to the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Northern Rhodesia and Southern Rhodesia. One day when I was standing outside the west block a tourist came along, and I asked this party to pick out the flag he liked best. I do not know where he came from and I did not ask him. I do not know whether he was from the United States or Canada, but he picked out our present ensign.
Having put forward these views, to satisfy my hon. friends across the other side I will quote from a few letters written by some who desire a flag other than the red ensign. I am sure members will not call me to order 20220-678i
Canadian Flag
when I mention these letters. Here is one which says, in part:
Our country is today facing trying times due to fanatic separatists in Quebec who are the first to benefit by the stubborn insistence of these England-lovers to keep the union jack on our flag. A truly Canadian emblem such as the maple leaf should be the only emblem on our banner and should create greater unity throughout Canada and would serve to abolish the hyphenated Canadian-ism we now have. We should all be proud to consider ourselves as Canadians first and if we must still fly the union jack we could do so as a commonwealth banner. I cannot understand how anyone who claims to be a Canadian could be satisfied with anything less than a truly distinctive Canadian flag without any foreign symbol whether it be British or French or that of any other country. ...
We have a wonderful country here so let us all unite behind a symbol of which we can all be proud and love no matter what our racial origin was. Let us all be Canadians first and put Canada ahead of Britain, France, or any other country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The amendment before the house is to refer the report back to the committee for the discussion of a very definite question, the holding of a plebiscite.
The hon. member who has the floor at present is discussing just about anything except the amendment. In view of the very wise remarks you made a moment ago to point out that the debate is restricted to the amendment, I suggest that the hon. member should come back to the amendment or, still better, since the amendment was moved by his own party, that we should take the vote immediately.
At any rate, I feel that the hon. member's remarks are not relevant to the matter under consideration, since he is now reading letters he received. We all got letters about the flag but if we all started reading them, there would be no end to this discussion.
Consequently, I would ask you to call the hon. member to order so that the debate may be concluded as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, it seems rather strange that the hon. member for Lapointe should claim that the remarks of the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain) are not relevant, while almost everytime he speaks during a discussion, the hon. member for Lapointe is the first to make statements which are out of order as regards the rule of relevancy.
There seems to be a rule for the hon. member and another rule for the rest of the house. This is not the first time that he rises on a point of order; whether it comes from the

Canadian Flag
opposition side or from the government benches, if something does not please him the hon. member always takes exception, but when he is called to order, he claims that he is being throttled. Let him bridle his tongue instead of rising on points of order.

Order, please. I do not think I need any more instruction on this point, but I should like to refer hon. members to Beau-chesne's fourth edition, citation 119 (3), which reads as follows:
Relevancy Is not easy to define. A wrong comprehension of it may have a serious effect on the freedom of speech. Members are often deprived of their right to speak on the pretext that their remarks are irrelevant when as a matter of fact they refer to matters perhaps remote but yet related, even indirectly, to the question under debate. In borderline cases the member should be given the benefit of the doubt. A great deal of latitude must be allowed in the House of Commons which is a forum where every phase of public affairs can be discussed and every member has the right to be heard, even if in doing so he sometimes disregards the rigidity of procedure.
I hope the hon. member for Elgin, having heard the discussion, will do his best to speak to the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, in pointing out the attitudes taken in correspondence I have received I was endeavouring to put before this house the divergence of public opinion, in a fair manner to each side of the question about the flag and a plebiscite. I read some comments from correspondence from individuals who prefer retention of the red ensign, and some from correspondence from individuals who prefer the other design.
Oh, oh.

If the hon. member for Lapointe does not wish to hear these expressions of opinion it must be because they irritate him. I suggest that otherwise he would not rise on points of order.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to be fair to both expressions of opinion in the correspondence I have received. I do not want to draw attention to one other telegram I have received in favour of the retention of the red ensign, but I should like to draw attention to a telegram I received which endorses a new flag. This telegram is from the international association of machinists, local 1975, St. Thomas, Ontario, which reads:
Members of international association of machinists local 1975 St. Thomas Ontario endorse the idea of a new distinctive flag for Canada.
Yesterday we were informed by the chairman and other members of the flag committee

about the diligence of hon. members in attending committee meetings, which sometimes occurred as often as three times in one day. It is gratifying to know that this committee on most occasions had 100 per cent attendance. I might say that I wish other committees of this house had as good attendance at their meetings and did not have to wait for such long periods of time before getting a quorum. I will not refer to the specific committee, as I think hon. members know which one it is. I do wish to congratulate the flag committee for its long hours of devoted work in an endeavour to bring back a report which would be acceptable to parliament.
The flag question has been before parliament for many months, probably for so many that at this time I should review the whole situation so hon. members will appreciate how it developed.
The first indication we had of the new flag was on May 14, when the Prime Minister invited reporters to his home-I assume that was at 24 Sussex street-and informed them that the government intended to proceed with new flag legislation. On that occasion he displayed several designs that were being considered, and mentioned that the government would stand or fall on the issue.
Three days later the Prime Minister went to Winnipeg to address the Royal Canadian Legion, dominion command, at which time he said he believed most seriously at this time that we should have a distinctive Canadian flag incorporating the maple leaf design. The next day he showed a few designs to a press conference. The next day, on May 19, it was reported that the government was considering designs, and on May 21 that the government had reached a decision, but that decision was not revealed. On May 27 the design with the three red maple leaves on a white background with blue bars at each end was made public.
I wonder why the Prime Minister brought in that type of design; because on looking through the parliamentary guide I noticed the Prime Minister was born on April 23, which is St. George's day. I would have expected the Prime Minister, in recognition of his birthday, to suggest a design that at least had some religious crosses on it.
It is the opinion of the majority of the general public on the question of the flag that it has been badly mismanaged by the Prime Minister and the government from the start. First we were asked to accept one design

or there would be a general election. The Prime Minister had his sights set on the unfurling of a flag of this design by July 1 of this year. When that situation did not materialize his sights were set on a second goal, which was to have Her Majesty unfurl the flag while visiting Canada, and I expect she would have unfurled it while in Quebec city. The second goal being unattainable, the Prime Minister has moved on to his third goal, which is to have a flag by Christmas.
I say this whole situation has been badly mismanaged, because parliament was asked to make a decision on only one design, a design personally selected by the Prime Minister. At least three designs should have been submitted to parliament for a decision by parliament. Parliament was asked to make a hurried decision, not as to the choice of a design, but to accept one which was the personal choice of one man.
We hope that on July 1, 1967, Canada will celebrate its 100th anniversary as a united nation. Would it not be fitting and proper to have as one of our major centennial objectives a flag design accepted by parliament or by the majority of Canadians, through a plebiscite later approved by parliament, to be unfurled on July 1, 1967?
Again I must commend the committee for their long hours of objective work carried out in their effort to honestly narrow the field of designs from thousands down to two or three. That committee has reported, but we are still faced with the dilemma of accepting or rejecting one design and one design only. The committee's report would be more acceptable to me if it had given parliament the opportunity through a free and unbiased vote to choose between the one maple leaf design, or a design with the union jack in the upper left hand corner and a fleur-de-lis in the right hand corner of equal proportions. If parliament is not to be given the opportunity of deciding between those two designs there is no other alternative but to let the people of Canada decide between these designs through a plebiscite.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
You may with his permission.
Go ahead.

Thank you. Would the hon. member tell me whether the Canadian Legion at their convention in Winnipeg unfurled or displayed the red ensign for the first time, and

whether previous to that time the Legion at all their conventions flew or displayed only the union jack?

Mr. Speaker, by Your Honour's ruling it may be that this question will be referred back to the committee, possibly on the ground, sir, that the people of Canada have a firmer grasp of reality than the members of this house, which may be so and may not; but it did seem to me that some comments on the questions of reality and symbols might perhaps be in order this afternoon.
When I was a very small boy, Mr. Speaker, if you can cast your mind back to that very remote period of history, someone put in my hands a little book of tales of an instructive, elevating and edifying nature. I presume the idea was to improve my moral character. There may be some question whether or not the effort was successful, but I will not press that point. However, some of what I read has remained with me.
There is one particular story which has remained in my mind and even to this day I can see the illustration that accompanied the story. It was a story which illustrated the stupidity of a dog. The dog was depicted as standing on a low footbridge over a stream. It had just dropped a bone from its jaws in an ill advised attempt to snatch at the more enticing looking bone which was reflected in the water below. Of course the idea of this cautionary tale was to impress on the infant mind the folly of throwing away the substance for the shadow. I would not go so far as to say that the effect of this cautionary tale was very great on my subsequent behaviour; nevertheless this story has come back into my mind as I have listened to the flag debate in the house.
I have noted that we have here the question of symbols and reality. Symbols, of course, are very important to us. We could not live without them. We could not live without the symbols we see on every printed page. We could not live without the symbols we make in sounds with our mouths. But because symbols are so important to us there is a very

Canadian Flag
common human tendency to confuse the symbol with the reality. In fact I think one could go further and say that periodically this tendency to confuse symbol with reality has created many, if not most, of the woes that mankind has brought on itself.
We have only to recall the quite violent and bloody schismatic troubles that arose in the early Christian church over the question of whether the divine blessing should be invoked by the priest raising in benediction two fingers or three fingers. In this case, of course, symbol had not only been mistaken for reality but actually had replaced reality in the minds of those pious people, and with great piety and vigour they proceeded to express their own choice among symbols, leaving reality to fend for itself.
This would lead me to suppose, Mr. Speaker, that as a general rule those with the slenderest grasp on reality are those who are most likely to be concerned with symbols. I have had this confirmed by the correspondence I have had on the flag. I have noted that my correspondents can roughly be divided into two categories, those who take a fervid and emotional approach and those who take a cool and objective approach, and I hasten to add that representatives of each variety can be found supporting each contention on the two sides of this quarrel.
But this leads me to suggest that here we are confusing symbol with reality in a very dangerous way. In my correspondence the cool and objective ones appear to take the position that the symbol itself is of no consequence. They are much more concerned with the reality that lies behind it, and they have become quite impatient with their representatives because they are so concerned with the symbol that they have had no time to get to work building the reality.
There is, of course, one all-important fact about symbols, and this is what concerns those who take the cool and objective approach; namely, that the symbol should be accepted by everyone to represent the same thing. We have achieved that in our language. We do not quite agree over the shape of the letters that are printed on paper, but we have all agreed that these letters, whether we like the shape of them or not, whether we think they are aesthetic or not, represent particular sounds and that a combination of those letters represents a more complicated sound which in turn represents an idea.
I am coming to the conclusion that the Prime Minister may have fallen into this

pit of confusion and may have imagined that by creating a symbol he would thereby create reality, seeking, I assume, the very worthy reality of national unity. It would appear to me that the Prime Minister has deluded himself into thinking that if he creates a symbol which he will label national unity he will have thereby created national unity.
On the other hand the Leader of the Opposition seems to labour under the delusion that a symbol can destroy reality. Neither of these right hon. gentlemen seems to be seized of the all important fact that first of all there has to be a reality which can be represented by the symbol; that if there were in Canada a reality which could be known as national unity no symbol could destroy it, no symbol could disturb it. But we should bear in mind that no symbol can of itself create reality. Symbols have no intrinsic value of themselves. They have value only as representing something that is of value.
It may be that there has been a poll which suggests that 60 per cent of the Canadian people wish to have a plebiscite on this issue. I must confess I would have some sympathy for them, because I presume this is an expression of their feeling that they have a better grasp of reality than we have here. But I would also suggest that this is a very unsatisfactory way of reaching these conclusions. I would go further, Mr. Speaker, and warn those who are so fervid and so emotional over something that has of itself no intrinsic value whatsoever that they are risking the reputation of the most important democratic institution in our country.
I have observed on several recent trips to the western part of Canada a singular lack of interest in symbols, a complete lack oi interest in the particular design upon which this parliament may finally decide, and a growing impatience with this concentration on symbols to the exclusion of concentration on reality. We were not sent here to play with symbols. We were sent here to create some realities, and I suggest that the Canadian people are seeking from this parliament the creation of the reality of a united, prosperous Canada with a national purpose and a national identity, and we are not going to achieve that by any short-cut of producing a symbol.
I suggest to both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition that they should bear this in mind; that we should leave symbols for the communication of ideas, where they are important and necessary; that the Prime Minister should not delude himself into

thinking he is taking any step toward reality by the creation of a symbol and, equally, the Leader of the Opposition should not delude himself into thinking that because the Prime Minister seeks to substitute one symbol for another this will have the slightest effect on reality.
Furthermore, and I shall turn in a moment to this point, sir, the important point is that it should be accepted by everyone as representing something. I will suggest to you that whatever flag we choose, it will represent reality. It is up to us, as members of parliament, to make sure what the nature of that reality is going to be. It will represent equally well a disunited Canada falling to pieces; it will also represent equally well a united, prosperous Canada with a national purpose.
This flag, whatever it is, will be accepted by the bulk of the Canadian people in a remarkably short space of time as representing Canada. I think it is the duty of members of parliament, it is the duty of the government, to make sure that this symbol, which of itself is not of the slightest importance, has something worthwhile to represent. Let us get on with this and stop making ourselves the laughingstock of the country and the laughingstock in those parts of the world that pay any attention to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if I take the floor today it is for the very good reason that I promised my constituents to express, in due course, their point of view on this famous issue of the flag.
Now that there is hope that this matter will soon be settled I wish to make a few remarks.
Were it only a matter of stating my attitude and that of my constituents, my speech would be rather brief. I would only have to say that it is my duty, as member for Labelle, to vote for the distinctive flag chosen by the committee, and against the union jack as a second flag suggested by the government.
I am very much afraid, however, that it is not that easy; moreover I would not be satisfied if I did not take this opportunity to explain the reasons for my choice.
It seems to me that the flag debate will have been a test for confederation. We will have seen and heard people express freely their ideas, their feelings, their love and sometimes their hate toward the proposed symbols and the ideas which those symbols represent. We will have feared, for a while, that this ideological conflict would deteriorate into a racial or cultural one. But since any test is a source of reward, we will have also seen that,
Canadian Flag
through the worse sentimental crises, it is possible to live side by side in Canada and that, all things being considered, the fathers of confederation were wiser than we thought.
For the first time in this house, the French element has seen the English element get panicky, haggle and recriminate; please note, Mr. Speaker, that I believe my colleagues had not only the right but the duty to act as they did. I know that they will now be in a better position to understand why we, from Quebec, are clinging to certain rights which we believe to be fundamental rights and which we want to uphold at all cost.
I have no doubt the house will also have realized that when I spoke of people expressing themselves freely I had in mind the members of the opposition parties and not the government members, for in the Liberal party there is unanimity. Indeed, the Liberal party has always been a party enjoying unanimity; for better or for worse, Liberals vote as one man. And why blame them if it agrees with them?
Even at the time of conscription, when the province of Quebec strongly opposed such a measure, Quebec Liberals all voted solidly; they were returned. Quebec, like the Prime Minister, was opposed to the acquisition of nuclear weapons, and Quebec Liberals voted solidly for nuclear weapons. Quebec was against the interference of the federal government in the field of education, but the Liberals voted solidly for loans to students. Quebec was against the interference of the federal government in the provincial and municipal fields, but the Liberals gave a solid vote for assistance to municipalities.
And where does the referendum fit into all this?

That will come.
Quebec strongly opposes the union jack as second flag for Canada, but the Liberals voted for such a recommendation in the flag committee, and I am sure they will vote solidly for the union jack when that proposal comes before the house.
Therefore, to grasp what occurred concerning the flag I must note the behaviour of free members, that is the members of the various opposition parties.
It is astonishing to see how public men, with the same degree of sincerity, can take such different stands on fundamental issues. Such attitudes cannot be explained otherwise than through a study of the Anglo-Saxon and Latin-French temperaments, which are altogether different.

Canadian Flag
This brief sociological study will not settle anything, I am sure, but if I could convince the house and the Canadian people that the phenomena which are taking place at the confederation level are not monstrosities, but normal reactions for the two racial groups which founded this country, I would have made quite a step toward the dialogue.
The Latin temperament that French Canada inherited is not a conservative one, in the psychological sense of the word. One has but to study the history of France to find how different it is, say, from that of Britain. Latins have violent, if not revolutionary, reactions. In France, an emperor dethroned a king, a king dethroned an emperor, a revolution dethroned a king, republican regimes came and fell one after another. France today has achieved a certain stability through a president who, with the sovereign consent of the French people, acts much more like a dictator.
In the United Kingdom, on the other hand, when constitutional conflicts did occur, it was always to protect the established principles and traditions-
I am greatly interested by the wanton spirit shown by the hon. member for Labelle, but I have yet to see what his comments have to do with the amendment now before us and the referendum it proposes.
Mr. Speaker, as soon-
Order. I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle and I have the impression that what he has said up to now is just an introduction to his subject.
A lengthy introduction.

Mr. Speaker, in this house, as soon as we try to forget politics a little to underline the reality at the bottom of the whole matter, as soon as we try to study the reactions of hon. members, in other words, as soon as we leave small politics, people claim we are wandering from the subject. I say that on a matter like the flag, if the members of the House of Commons had searched their souls before taking a stupid stand, confederation would not have been endangered.
Mr. Speaker, I shall proceed with my study. I was saying that in Great Britain, for instance, the kingdom has broken up, the empire has distintegrated, the commonwealth is in a bad way but has managed to survive; however, the monarchy still remains as a symbol of stability within order.
What I mean by all this is merely that, for the Latin people, vested interests are only

worth their usefulness, whereas for Anglo-Saxons, traditions are law.

The way
things are going this afternoon it is no wonder we get our papers a little mixed up. The motion for a national plebiscite was defeated by a vote of 9 to 5. In the course of some remarks I made in the house on August 13 last I took strong exception to a majority of the members of the house, 133 in fact, having the responsibility of approving a design for a flag which discarded our heritage of the past and substituted a new flag for Canada. I still object to it. I objected to it in the case of 133 people. But now we are asked to agree to the majority decision of 15 people, so everything I said in connection with the matter at that time is enhanced about nine times.
Let the people decide. It was appropriate then and it is appropriate now. That is what was proposed in the committee, but the motion was defeated by a vote of 9 to 5. By the motion now before us we are asked to agree with that decision and I cannot do so.
Subparagraph (b) of paragraph 5 deals with the motion for the adoption of only one national flag, which was carried by a vote of 14 to nothing. I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that this motion received unanimous support. Yet before the committee's work was completed it was conveniently discarded and completely ignored. The explanation given is that the second flag is to symbolize our membership in the commonwealth and our allegiance to the crown. This has been unnecessary in the past. Why should it be necessary in the future? Are we to consider that the national flag recommended by the committee leads to the conclusion that we will do away with our allegiance to the crown by adopting it? If so, I submit this is another good reason for voting against the

motion now before us and in favour of the amendment seeking a plebiscite.
I also have some comments relative to the vote in committee on the motion that the Canadian red ensign be the national flag of Canada. This was defeated by a vote of 10 to 4. By the motion now before the house we are asked to agree that 10 people can decide to discard the flag which has been used, respected, revered, beloved and admired by the Canadian people generally for a period of nearly 100 years. To me any government which suggests that we should approve the taking of the opinion of 10 people in a matter as important as this are themselves not deserving of public approval and should not be in office in this country.
The Prime Minister and his supporters should welcome a plebiscite as a means of solving this difficult problem. In the course of my remarks on the previous occasion I contended that there should have been a non-partisan approach to this matter, that it never should have been relegated into the area of political partisanship at any time, because it was too important. The Prime Minister may have felt impelled to bring the matter before the house, but may I point out that Mr. Mackenzie King did not do so in 1946 when there was a vote of 23 to 1 in favour of a new flag. No doubt he felt the problem was too contentious.
We are in 1964 now.

In connection with the whole question of the red ensign I ask the government and their supporters these questions. Do they completely ignore the fact that the Canadian Legion wishes to retain the Canadian red ensign as the flag of Canada? Is it a matter of complete indifference to them that the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire are on record in every part of Canada as favouring the red ensign? Is it a matter of complete indifference to them that some 200,000 people signed a petition to retain our present flag? Is it a matter of complete indifference to the government and the members of the government that they must have received thousands of communications from Canadians imploring them not to discard or destroy the flag which we have been using for nearly 100 years?
These are some of the things which we felt should be pointed out. This one was defeated. According to the report, we are asked to express our agreement just because ten people voted against four. I, for one, cannot possibly subscribe to such an idea. The way this mat-

ter has been handled is another great blunder by this government, already noted for its performance in the field of blundering. I cannot support a motion in this parliament that would discard the Canadian ensign from consideration as the national flag of Canada. Remember, the motion is to discard it from consideration as the national flag of Canada. In 1946, as I understand it, a committee reported 23 to 1 to this parliament, to a Liberal government, on a new Canadian flag. Concurrence in that report was never moved by the government of Right Hon. Mackenzie King. He would not accept the responsibility for accepting the committee report at that time. No doubt he had what seemed to him to be good reasons. Right hon. Mr. St. Laurent did not bring the matter before parliament during his term of office as prime minister.
The present Prime Minister decided to have a new flag by act of parliament, giving as his reason that he had promised it during the heat of an election campaign. I contend that is not a good enough reason. It would be much more in the national interest to disregard such a commitment, because the carrying out of a commitment of that nature is much worse than being accused of a broken promise. I declare here and now that I have not and do not prefer any design for the flag of Canada to a greater extent than I do the Canadian red ensign. However, I will say this: I do not rule out the possibility that in the interests of unity in Canada, for the encouragement of a proper attitude by all Canadians from all parts of Canada, an effort should be made to find a somewhat different design more capable of general acceptance. This is the reason I favoured in the committee a design which had incorporated in it the symbols of the founding races of this country, and incorporating also a maple leaf which might be considered as having symbolism with regard to the progress of our country during our growing up period. There it is, Mr. Speaker. There is the design for which I voted. I make no apologies for it. I think it is a very fine compromise.
Now, if it were necessary in the interest of national unity and for the good of the nation that there should be some variation in where these symbols stand, I would be the last one to stand in the way. Some people say we have grown up, and since we have grown up we should run our own show. We should be masters in our own house. I subscribe to that idea. However, it is not necessary to throw out the pictures of our
Canadian Flag
father, mother, grandfather and grandmother in the process. We do not need to do that.
Now, I want to have something to say about this particular feature before dealing with its significance. However before leaving the subject of the Canadian red ensign containing the union jack, I do want to say a word with regard to British justice and its importance to all of us. Many times we hear remarks related to the Canadian Bill of Rights for which my right hon. leader was responsible.
I say that the Canadian Bill of Rights was based on British justice; that was the foundation of the bill of rights. By accepting this motion before the house, and I am now speaking in favour of the amendment, we are asked to do away with every symbol indicating we have British justice in this country. This is a far cry from the type of thing to which we have listened in this house during the last couple of weeks. Many people sleep better at night because they are citizens of a country in which British justice prevails. I cannot bring myself to support a motion which discards the symbolism indicating that situation, so I shall vote for the amendment.
On Monday of this week the Prime Minister stated that the people on this side of the house had been doing their best to prevent a vote on the flag issue. I want to say to him, I want to say to any member of the government or any member of this house, that I reject and resent that assertion. I spoke twice in the previous flag debate. I spoke because I believed what I said, and because a very high percentage of the people of Canada believe as I do. It is my opinion that they still do. In spite of this, the government brings forward a motion which asks us to agree that ten people should rule out of consideration the symbol of those things to which I have just now referred.
Now we come to the report of the committee and we find that the flag designs submitted were divided into three categories. Toward the conclusion of paragraph 6 of that report we find these words:
Elimination by an agreed procedure left only one design in each category.
I want to speak about the word "elimination" and the words "agreed procedure". The procedure was agreed, without a doubt, but the elimination took on the character of a decision based on a previous vote. As a consequence, I want to say that the elimination is something which should be stressed in this house for the benefit of hon. members who may not have given the question of elimina-

Canadian Flag
tion the consideration which it deserves. What did we vote to eliminate? We are voting to eliminate the union jack.
Hear, hear.
This is fine, but I may tell hon. gentlemen that-
You have exposed yourself.

-it
would be the things which they valued most and which are guaranteed to them under the union jack, which would be eliminated if they only knew it. I say they would eliminate the symbols of the Christian heritage of this country.
Oh, no.

This is what is embodied in the union jack. It is the cross of St. George; it is the cross of St. Andrew; it is the cross of St. Patrick, and it goes back to the time of the crusades. This is what those in the far corner, apparently, are favourable to having removed from the national flag of Canada. We are asked to agree to that elimination. I cannot do so.
According to the report, we find that in the process of a vote being taken, the three maple leaf design was retained by a vote of 8 to 6; the single maple leaf design was retained by a vote of 13 to 1; the design containing the union jack and the fleur-de-lis was rejected by a vote of 9 to 5. Yesterday the hon. gentleman who was a member of the committee, and represents Terrebonne, said in this house that there was one time when there was complete unanimity on the design, and it was the present suggestion. Now I know, at least I feel, that he would not deliberately mislead the house.
I refer the house to this particular paragraph because this is the paragraph which applies. It reads as follows:
A vote was then taken to determine the committee's preference between the design containing three maple leaves and the design containing one maple leaf.
All they were doing was voting as between those two designs, and it specifically says so in the report.
The single maple leaf design was retained by a vote of 14 to 0.
Hear, hear.
Fourteen to zero.

Now, if the hon. member can understand, I should like to suggest something to him-that seven Liberals, members of that committee, voted
(Mr. Flemming (Victoria-Carleton).]
against the design which had been submitted to this parliament by the Prime Minister himself. Why did they change their minds. Two or three months ago it had to be three leaves. They were married to the three leaves. But they got divorced awfully quickly; they did not stay together long.
I should like to make a statement on a question of personal privilege. The hon. gentleman has just said that members on this side of the house, all of us-
He said those on the committee.
-were committed to the three maple leaves. I should like him to know that right from the beginning-and I made my views known within the party-I have supported the one maple leaf.

I would accept at its full value any assertion made by the hon. member who has just spoken. If he dissociated himself from the position taken by his party I admire him for publicly saying so. I am speaking in general terms. A few months ago it had to be the three maple leaves, and it could be nothing else.
No.

But in
the committee they changed their minds and voted for one maple leaf-voted against the design submitted by their own Prime Minister.
A question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member raising a question of privilege?

It is a
spurious question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman would wish to allow the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) to state his question of privilege.

Sing "God Save the
Queen" and sit down.

Don't make any jokes about "God Save the Queen".

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who now has the floor has no right to say that we were determined never to consider any other design apart from the three leaf flag.
In so doing, he is not speaking the truth. The government introduced in this house a

proposal for debate and the Prime Minister always said that he was ready to consider all suggestions.
The statement made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is false.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is obvious that the question of privilege of the hon. member for Lotbiniere is ill founded; in fact, it is an argument and not a question of privilege.
He tells falsehoods.

Just
what I expected. Since we are on a question of privilege I hope you will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, if I explain my conception of what a question of privilege is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. May I point out that the question of privilege has been ruled out. I might mention, too, that according to the clock the hon. gentleman's time has expired. However, there were some points raised, taking three minutes or so of the time allotted, and they will be allowed.

I am only anxious to conclude my remarks and I thank you for your consideration, which is exactly what I expect from you.
I believe this whole matter, the committee's report and all the rest, has been mishandled; it is one more blunder in the series of blunders for which the government is famous. I make no apology for saying this. But there is no reason why even at this stage the government could not redeem itself. It could do so by having this amendment carry, by giving its members the right to have a free vote, and letting the report go back to the committee so that the people could decide. Surely this is the right way to settle the matter. It has been stated on many occasions that this is not an urgent question. It does not need to be. I am sure everyone who feels there is a degree of urgency attached to it would be satisfied if it were dealt with at the next general election in the course of a referendum held during that election. My feeling is that the government should seriously consider this course. If they do lose face to a certain extent it will not be nearly as bad as the disruption which I am convinced will follow if this matter is not handled in something like the way I suggest.

Question.
Canadian Flag

Mr. Speaker, if everybody had been unanimous that the motion should come to a vote immediately, I would have resumed my seat. But I saw another Conservative member who was getting to his feet to discuss the matter. Therefore, I should like to take the opportunity to give some of my impressions.
Today, you made a ruling on the amendment now before us. I shall not discuss that ruling, of course. I only regret one thing and it is that I did not ask for a vote on your ruling, because I think it is parliament as a whole that has authority on the management of the business of the house.
But all that is now over and we are discussing the amendment of the Conservatives which reads as follows:
That the words "be now adopted", be struck out and replaced by the following:
That it be referred back to the committee with instructions to strike out paragraph 7 of the said report and substitute therefor the following:
However, as the final vote of the committee did not reveal a sufficient degree of unanimity for the proposed design of a national flag for Canada-
The quality of the French version is to be noted. I think that the Conservative party could not find one French Canadian among its members who accepted to write this amendment. That is why the French version is full of awful errors.
-votre comite recommande alors que le gou-vernement soit autorisc a prendre les mesures ne-cessaires afin de conduire un plebiscite...
Imagine "conduire un plebiscite" instead of an automobile.
... lors de la prochaine Election generate afin que le peuple canadien soit foumi l'occasion...
You may well smile, Mr. Speaker, because it is really funny to hear such jargon.
... qui en est son droit, de declarer son choix pour un drapeau national.
That was concocted by the member for Edmonton West.
Once more, I say that no French Canadian member of the Conservative group agreed to translate the original amendment which was drafted in English.
Mr. Lambert is not a French Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, this is the paradox with which we are faced-and it really is a paradox: That parliamentary committee was created at the special request of the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) after a meeting of the five

Canadian Flag
leaders of the political parties in the House of Commons. This parliamentary committee composed of 15 members had not been mentioned previously. But the Leader of the Opposition told us that, without the establishment of a committee which would study the question of a distinctive national flag, he would not consent to put an end to the debate on the flag issue. At that time, some 65 Conservative members had already spoken in the house.
We asked the leader of the official opposition what kind of a majority he was considering should the Prime Minister and the leader of the other parties agree to the formation of such a committee which would present a majority report. He replied: On 15, 13 to 2. That is not a large majority; it is almost total unanimity.
The leader of the official opposition knew in advance that five of his followers would be sitting on the committee. There were seven Liberals, one N.D.P., one Social Crediter and one member of the Ralliement Creditistes, for a total of 15. The Liberal who acted as chairman, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) did not vote but the others did. After six weeks of sittings, the committee concluded its proceedings by a final vote of ten to four. In other words, one Conservative member voted in favour of the recommendation made by the committee. That was not sufficient.
Now that we have the report, we are getting into a marathon similar to the one we had during the debate on the resolution. It is a Conservative "talkathon".
Mr. Speaker, the amendment deals with the very same issue that the Leader of the Opposition raised during the discussion on the resolution. What the Conservatives want seems obvious: waste the time of the house to prevent the government from taking action and to prevent the passage of legislation. Their game is surely to throw the country into another general election which they themselves would have trouble facing, especially today-I know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker, because even if the Conservatives maintain that the province of Quebec is the only one ready to vote on this issue, I must say that I have been to western Canada to speak to English Canadians, I went to Parry Sound, in Ontario, not long ago, I am going to Toronto next Thursday, to Trinity College, at the Kiwanis club, and in the afternoon, I shall be interviewed on television. Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives can

say what they like, and resort to all the tricks laid down in advance by the Leader of the Opposition-
Hear, hear.

-English speaking Canadians have had enough of this Canadian talk-fest, they are fed up with this waste of time.
An hon. member is interrupting me. Right now I am ready to talk before any association in his riding. I will prove to him that his riding is ready to adopt a flag immediately and without a plebiscite.
One hoax after another has been played on us in the last few days, just as we have been misled since last June with those words: "The public wants a plebiscite."
In 1963, the Conservative members of the province of Quebec said: "We are in favour of adopting immediately a distinctive national emblem." The Liberal members said the same thing throughout Canada and that was part of their election platform, as it was part Of ours. Personally, I was elected with a 12,000-vote majority, and a distinctive national flag figured in my program. The Liberals got the greatest number of seats in Canada. The Conservatives followed suit.
The members of the New Democratic party, at election time declared themselves in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag. But this means nothing to the Leader of the Opposition who is certainly touchy, for instance, when it comes to the matter of unanimous consent with regard to a time limit for debates on an issue such as this, one which has been going on for months and months.
Mr. Speaker, we have been elected and the people who elected us trusted that we would adopt a distinctive national flag, here in the House of Commons.
Today, the Conservatives, to play petty politics, strongly call for a national plebiscite. They want to ask the people who trusted us to select the flag they wanted, to vote on this matter.
I have said, on several occasions, that the design of the flag is of little concern to me. My personal preference is clear: I prefer the flag launched across Canada by the native sons of Canada on the one hand, and by some French Canadians from the province of Quebec, namely the diagonal flag, half red and half white, with a green maple leaf.
However, I do not oppose the adoption of another design, provided it is Canadian, provided it bears a Canadian symbol.
A while ago we heard the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton say that he represents

a population which respects British justice. We have had French justice also. I am the first to recognize that we did have justice under the British empire.
But, Mr. Speaker, let us look what is happening around the world today, let us look at the countries that have always belonged to the British empire, such as Jamaica, Canada and others. Recently, when the members of the commonwealth parliamentary association met in Jamaica, a little country of about 1,800,000 inhabitants, that just won its independence two years ago, the flag flown on the occasion of that meeting was the distinctive national flag of Jamaica. There is a country that is still a member of the commonwealth but it has its own symbol.
People even went further than that. When the Conservative member attended this meeting, and I think perhaps they were two, the national anthem that was sung in Jamaica, during all their stay there, on the occasion of public demonstrations, was not even the national anthem of the British empire or the Queen. It was the national anthem of Jamaica. In fact, it was sung three times, without any attempt being made to sing or to intone the national anthem of England.
I hear those members telling us that the union jack represents British justice. Very well. However, are we not able, after 100 years, to have our own individual symbols as Canadians while continuing to be part of the British commonwealth of nations?
When I go to any social club, I do not wear my neighbour's suit but my own. Why don't we, as Canadians, have our own symbols and why don't we refrain from hanging on to something that we still respect when it is time, not to part with it, but to express our own feelings with our own symbols as a sovereign and independent nation which can take its own decisions.
We have nothing against England nor against the British empire as such. But we object to those backward persons who would like us to go back 150 or 200 years and seek to have the fleur-de-lis on a distinctive Canadian flag.
No.
Do we ask that French symbols be included because we are of French descent.
No.

We ask for nothing like that. We say more: if the Canadian symbol, now represented by the maple leaf on the flag
Canadian Flag
proposed by the committee which considered this question, is not satisfactory, then let us remove the maple leaf and put a beaver, or a sheaf of wheat, or indeed anything else, as long as it is Canadian. But to tell us: pass a red ensign with a union jack in the upper corner and a fleur-de-lis at the bottom to remind us of our forefathers, to remind us of what happened in Canada in 1534, 1608 or 1790, etc., we are fed up with those things.
As I was saying a while ago, not only we French speaking Canadians, but also English speaking Canadians-I noticed it wherever I went-are fed up with it, and I shall prove it Thursday when I visit Toronto.
In my opinion, this amendment tends merely to make us waste our time, to carry on our debate until Christmas and after Christmas till Easter. However, I would like to say another thing to the Conservatives, who every day request a question period in order to speak on the flag. We are now discussing the flag issue-I see that the Conservative house leader is in his seat-I formally warn him that there will be no answers to questions on the order paper, that there will be no question period on orders of the day until the vote has been taken on the report of the committee on the flag. We shall comply with the rules. The unanimous consent of the house will not be granted. We want to know if Conservatives are Canadians, true Canadians, or if they just pretend to be Canadians, from whatever part of Canada they come.
I hear whispers coming from the Conservative opposition. They say that I am in collusion with the Liberals. No, I am not. Moreover, I have not been elected-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Is this man going to be allowed to refer to the opposition as a semblance of Canadians?
I was going to raise the same point, Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman who has raised this question.

Mr. Speaker, I did not hear the remarks of the hon. member; however, he can interpret my words any way he wants and it will not bother me in the least. If the hat fits, wear it. It is as simple as that. If it does not fit, do not wear it.
The plebiscite requested by the Conservatives is but a roundabout means to waste the time of the house. This matter was considered by the house before it was referred

Canadian Flag
to the committee. Now that the committee presented its 10 to 4 majority report to the house, this question of a plebiscite is revived.
I say a plebiscite would only delay the adoption of a flag. We are the elected representatives of the people and we should assume our responsibilities as such.
If there is a majority in the house, the Leader of the Opposition can definitely not make me believe that it does not represent the majority of the Canadian voters. That is what they would want us to believe. They say: "You want to impose closure", and the Leader of the Opposition often says this, as well as some other Conservative members. Some closure, when they have been talking as they have from the very start of the flag debate. It is a Conservative political play. If they think of winning back public favour by so doing they are mistaken, for they are tying around their own necks the rope with which they will hang themselves for sure at the next general election.
Instead of only seeking purely political advantages, let us think and act as Canadians.
I said earlier that during the last election campaign we supported the adoption of a distinctive national flag. We were elected on that plank. Now, we would be asking for a plebiscite on this question? They are not saying that the plebiscite would be held immediately, no, but at the forthcoming general election. Should the next election take place two years hence, we would be dealing with the plebiscite two years from now and then, before ordering the plebiscite, we could still discuss the flag question and, once the plebiscite was over and a government elected, from one of the political parties, there would still be members questioning and discussing the plebiscite, because some will not be satisfied.
Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard of a plebiscite being held in the countries I mentioned a moment ago, which surely belong to the British commonwealth and have won their independence, such as Jamaica, Ghana, India, etc., and England herself? Did some people ask for a plebiscite in those countries, to choose a national flag and a national anthem? Have the duly elected representatives of the people no responsibility in such matters?
Think of those smaller countries I just referred to, Jamaica, Ghana, the African countries, that have won their freedom and independence and are still members of the British commonwealth, with symbols of their
[Mr. Caouette.l
own on their flags, not a union jack or a fleur-de-lis, but, for instance, a true Jamaican symbol. They did not put a banana on the distinctive national flag of Jamaica. It is only with strictly Canadian symbols such as those that we shall enjoy national unity.
Let no one try to make me believe that if I wear my neighbour's hat, I am wearing my own clothes. There is no doubt about it.
The Conservatives will keep on talking endlessly, but they will be held responsible by the Canadian voters. Let me tell you this. Those to whom I appeal in their group are those who have already taken a stand and come from other provinces than Quebec, because I have met several who admitted to me they were anxious to dispose of this matter and to take action, since their electors were after them as they are after us.
Mr. Speaker, that is the wish I make for all of us, that we act in the interests of Canada. It is true that Canada is a member of the British empire but, as Canadians, we should act in the interests of Canada by incorporating our own symbols in our flag, so that we can be identified as Canadians in every part of the world.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? I should like to ask him whether the translation was accurate, in that I understood that member to say that he does not care what is on the flag at all, but mentioned a beaver or a sheaf of wheat as being acceptable, provided the red ensign is destroyed?
I did not say that. I said I wanted a national distinctive flag which could have on it anything which is Canadian, whether it be a beaver, a maple leaf or anything distinctively national.

Would the hon. member permit another question, Mr. Speaker? I wish to ask him whether he would agree with the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), that this flag will not bring about the unity of Canada?
Which flag?
I refer to this proposed flag.
To which proposed flag do you refer? The hon. member for Lapointe has never said anything like that.
I never said that.
You sure did.
I never did.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. If the former minister of labour wishes to lay such accusations, he just has to submit the text.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege. I wish to say that the hon. member for Lapointe on a previous occasion said that a new distinctive flag for Canada would not bring about the unity of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I wish to point out that I have not yet said a single word about the flag, and that I have been absent for 22 days, the time taken by the Conservatives to discuss this question. And it is a good thing I was away, because that debate depressed all the other members in this house.
I wish to state once more that I have never spoken on that subject and, consequently, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) is mistaken.
You made your speech outside the house.

Mr. Speaker, we have just witnessed an example of the reason the people of this country are completely sick and fed up with the party of which the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) is a member. We have listened to him point the finger of scorn at the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and at the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming). Let me suggest to him that if he used those members, of which he is scornful, as examples to follow rather than Hitler, Mussolini, and people of that category, this country would be better off.
Hear, hear.
You would sooner follow Hitler. You said you admired him.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member has no right to lend any motive whatever, and I want to tell him that I shall certainly not follow in the footsteps of his leader, any more than I would have followed those of Hitler or Mussolini whom he just mentioned. It would be better for him if he were minding his own business instead of that of others.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, we heard the hon. member talk about a Canadian flag and suggest that we could have a beaver or a sheaf of wheat on it. Is that not exactly what Adolf Hitler said to the German people when he took their flag away and provided them with the swastika? That represents the same philosophy-destroy your history and tradition, and replace it with something new.
Oh, oh.
Go back to England.
My friend, I am a Canadian.
I do not think you are.
I do not think I am any less a Canadian than you or any other member of this house, and I will stand on that statement.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. May I suggest to hon. members that very little will be accomplished by a shouting contest between members. I invite the hon. member for Cumberland to confine his remarks to the speech which I assume he proposed to make to this house.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the hon. member would permit a question before he proceeds with his speech? Does the hon. member for Cumberland interpret the presence of only one minister of the crown in the house as a desertion of the Prime Minister's stand on the flag?

In view of the fact the Prime Minister's members of the committee deserted his flag completely, I would not be surprised if what the hon. member has suggested is an example of the importance they place on the present flag design. If it should be suggested tomorrow that some other design would be more acceptable and receive a larger degree of support from the country, I am certain the Prime Minister would pass that word along and such a flag would be supported this week. In that event I am sure we would hear all the trained seals say "me too", as usual, and they would stamp their approval on it. At that time we would hear the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) get up and say: I really love this flag. He would say so, no matter what it looked like, provided the Prime Minister approved it.
The speech by the member for Leeds last evening in this house exemplifies the degree

Canadian Flag
of hypocrisy inherent in this whole flag question as far as the government is concerned. Never in the history of this nation have we seen a government as contemptuous of the rights of the people they allegedly represent. It is a government that has displayed on this issue deceit, defiance, delusion, demagoguery, dereliction and a despicable attempt to destroy a dignified symbol that has meant so very much to so very many Canadians of all races, colours and creeds.
What we have witnessed, Mr. Speaker, is this. On May 17 of this year the Prime Minister travelled to the Canadian Legion convention and told the people there that the government was going to have a three maple leaf flag, and that the red ensign was going to be scrapped in favour of this new design which he considered to be more representative and symbolic of this nation's history and tradition.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member says this is wonderful. I hope those members of the opposition will stay and listen to this debate. The Prime Minister stated "I have spoken with a select group of members from the press gallery and told them what I wanted. I told them also how I was going to get what I wanted, by making certain that the members of parliament would not be able to vote on this motion as their consciences indicated, because I was going to make this a government vote involving confidence in the government." We heard the trained seals get up one after the other and say how they supported this flag, how, like the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), they loved it, and then on September 10 the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) finally agreed to set up a committee to determine what the flag design should be.
The committee reports, and what do we learn from the report. We learn that every Liberal member on the committee voted against the design which on May 17 and for every day thereafter until September 10 the Liberal party told the Canadian people was the flag that should be accepted by them without question. We have the committee report before us, Mr. Speaker, and we see that the committee arrived at three designs upon which it voted, the Pearson pennant, the one they now wish us to accept and the one proposed which incorporated our past history and traditions.
I want to say first of all that when the members were appointed to the committee there were those who said that the Conservative members of the committee would go in

there as red ensign men and come out as red ensign men, and that it was useless to set up the committee because there would be no spirit of compromise among the Conservative members appointed to that committee. Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. I was truly amazed when I saw the flag design that had associated with it our past history and traditions because in effect it was a maple leaf flag, about which these people on the other side of the house have talked so much, with a very small emblem in each corner which associated today with the past. For anyone to say that the Conservative members appointed to that committee were not willing to compromise would be absolutely and completely ridiculous. As a matter of fact, if I had been a member of the committee I am very doubtful that I would have been willing to compromise to the degree that was indicated in the design that was accepted as the flag incorporating an association with our past. It departs a long way from the Canadian red ensign.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, as dedicated as the members of the committee were, as willing as they were to attend meetings day in and day out and work, I have no doubt, long and diligently in order to come up with a solution, I say that to my mind the flag committee failed. They failed parliament, they failed the Canadian nation. They had available to them a means of solving this problem but because, no doubt, of word passed down to the Liberal members of the committee it was impossible to produce a flag that would have received the unanimous approval of all members of the committee, and thereby have eliminated any debate in the house.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) said that if unanimous or nearly unanimous approval could be obtained for a flag design there would be no further debate on the matter. Certainly I as a strong advocate of the retention of the Canadian red ensign would not have been happy with such a flag design. Certainly those who wish to remove the union jack from the flag would not have been happy either, but the flag committee would have produced a compromise against which it would have been impossible for any member to argue. But where are we? We are back in the House of Commons because of the regimentation of the Liberal party and the willingness of the members of that party on the flag committee to put their party before the Canadian nation.
I have said on more than one occasion, Mr. Speaker, that the whole point involved in this flag debate is whether or not Canadians are

willing to allow the union jack to be removed from the flag. The hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette) certainly fortified the statements I have made in the past, that they are willing to accept any flag with any kind of design, whether it be the swastika or the black hand of the Mafia or a pumpkin, as long as the union jack is removed.
What could be more ridiculous, idiotic and completely stupid than to consider removing from a flag the nation's history, its traditions and the sacrifices made by generation after generation of Canadians who helped to build this nation and bring it to the point where it is today? I say that such an attitude can only assist in destroying what we have created and that the present government, so willing to do whatever is indicated as desirable by Gallup polls, is not one that is going to strengthen trust in the minds of the people who have some consideration for those who have made a contribution to the building of this nation.
The Prime Minister has put the house in the position where it must do as he asks or he will choke it off and allow no business to be done except to deal with what is apparently his childish pet, a new Canadian flag. The Canadian people must wait for the Canada pension plan, they must wait for the labour code, they must wait for anything else that is of real value and importance to the future of the nation and the way it progresses, because the Prime Minister of the country has the childish attitude that he wants his flag and he wants it now. He is not going to allow parliament to stop him from having it, whether or not he stops the business of this nation. We cannot even ask questions about anything the government is doing now because the Prime Minister wants his flag. What a childish attitude for a man who is supposed to be as big as he is. What a stupid attitude for a man who is responsible for running the affairs of this nation. What a ridiculous attitude for a man who is concerned about unity and about the effectiveness of parliament. The Prime Minister, more than any other man, is destroying the effectiveness of this parliament with this flag issue. Nothing appears to be more important to him than getting a flag so he can say to the people of Canada, "See, I told you that you would have it by Christmas, and here it is." How childish. How ridiculous.

Now, there have been a lot of people who have said-

As I say, there are statements to the effect that people care little about what the flag might be. There are some, but I do not agree that there are a lot. There are certainly some people in this nation who have no great concern about whether or not we have a flag. They might care, sir, if they were to Tealize that this action by this government in producing a new flag is going to cost the Canadian taxpayers a good many millions of dollars, to say nothing of individuals who have a flag now and might desire to have one that does represent this nation.
Here this question lies, unanswered, on the order paper. It will not be answered because of the gag the Prime Minister has applied to this parliament until he gets his childish way and we relent and provide him with a flag.
