Yes.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does he not agree that it would be more honest to tell the truth and say it is the rules which permit questions only before routine proceedings, and that the Prime Minister did offer an opportunity to the official opposition today to have a question period, and they turned it down.

So far as I am concerned, there are no degrees of honesty. You are either honest or dishonest. If the hon. member is calling me a liar, then let him look at Hansard of yesterday where the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) explained to the Prime Minister what v/as going to happen if he did not come forward with a motion that could

receive unanimous approval and thereby allow the ordinary business of this house to be conducted while this debate takes place. The Prime Minister refused. He refused him like the spoiled child he is.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The amendment now before us, Mr. Speaker, is to send the report of the flag committee back to that committee in order that its members might consider the merits of having a national plebiscite carried out to determine through the Canadian people what variety of flag design they consider to be most appropriate as a national flag.
There are many reasons why this seems to be the most logical method of determining a flag for Canada. Certainly we as members of this house have indicated beyond doubt that we are not capable of arriving at a conclusion which would be acceptable to the Canadian people at large while at the same time preventing a deterioration in national unity. Polls have been taken by numerous organizations across this nation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Including one in Waterloo.
The poll in Waterloo South indicated that the Liberals lost their deposit for the first time probably in the history of this nation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The Tories did not do too well.
They may not have done too well but they were certainly an improvement over the Liberals.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: How did they do in Cumberland?
They did very well in Cumberland.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Westmorland.
Let him make his speech.

As I was saying, polls have been taken at various times across this nation by various organizations and on each occasion the majority of those questioned indicated the belief that a plebiscite is the best answer, the best way of determining the kind of flag which would be accepted by all Canadians.

I have before me the result of one of these polls recently carried out by Telepoll, a CTV program. It was forwarded to me by the dominion president of the Canadian corps association who also urged the government to carry out a national plebiscite. The poll in question states that of the 1,134 persons polled across Canada 51.7 per cent favoured a plebiscite, 33.9 per cent wanted parliament to decide and the remainder had no opinion. In the Toronto area, of 150 persons questioned 53 per cent favoured a plebiscite. Many other polls have been taken and most of them show a higher percentage in favour of a plebiscite than the Telepoll to which I have just referred. However, that is the latest poll because it was taken on November 28, and it is an indication of the continued belief in the minds of the people that they should have an opportunity to decide what the design of our flag should be.
There are many reasons why the people should be asked to express their views with regard to a flag design, but the most compelling reason in my mind is the way in which the situation has been handled by the government to date. I refer not only to designs, though in this respect members opposite have shown a readiness to change their views from week to week as necessary, but because the government has unfairly taken so many actions which have proven to be a source of great irritation to many Canadians. I have a telegram here from a Mr. J. A. Pope of Montreal dated November 27. Mr. Pope, in his telegram, has this to say:
The flag on the main administrative building at the Royal Military College used to be the union jack. Subsequently I believe the Canadian red ensign flew proudly over that building. Now it has been replaced by a red and blue flag which is supposed to be the college flag. Since the post offices in Canada and the R.C.M.P. fly the Canadian red ensign I am amazed that someone has authorized the removal of the last vestige of the union jack from the Royal Military College at Kingston, Ontario. As you probably know, an independent country, South Africa, incorporates the union jack in its national flag. Bud Drury must be proud of this action.
That is just one of numerous examples of this type of thing happening across this nation at government instigation or, if not at government instigation, known by the individuals who take the action that the government will applaud them for it. The example of H.M.C.S. Yukon flying the Pearson pennant out at sea is just as glaring an example as the one described in the telegram I have just read. The bumper stickers that were to be distributed by the sticker-licker,
Canadian Flag
the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis), is another example.
Where is he?

I do not know where he is these days. He is probably trying to recoup-his losses from bumper stickers that reproduced the wrong flag. I guess the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) sort of pulled the rug out from under him when he instructed his Liberal-
Order, please. I do not see that it is at all relevant to speak about other hon. members, who we must assume are doing their duty.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member is, nor do I care; but I do know that he endeavoured to publicize in what was certainly a most unsatisfactory manner the former flag design proposed by the government. He used government offices and his position for this endeavour. I certainly see nothing wrong in talking about this as an example of the type of action that has been taken by the government to try and convince Canadians that some sort of a maple leaf flag would be more acceptable to the Canadian nation than the present Canadian red ensign, or even the flag design proposed by the committee which involved an association with our past history and tradition. I believe that all these incidents when added up indicate that this house is no longer capable of producing a flag design that is acceptable to the majority of Canadians, even though it may be acceptable to the majority of the members in this house.
Certainly if it is necessary for the official opposition to stand up for the rights of a majority of the Canadian people, then I say it is their duty to do so. There are some people who suggest that we should now desist from talking about the flag or the flag design that the Canadian people desire. They say, "Don't talk about it any more. While the majority of Canadians still desire the same flag they have had for the last 97 years, the public are getting sick of it and you are going to lose popular support if you keep talking about it and holding up the business of parliament". Mr. Speaker, the first thing the people who put forward this argument should consider is that the government decides the order of business in this house; it is not the official opposition

and if the government desires to hold up the business of the country in order to discuss the flag issue, that is up to them and they must take the responsibility for it.

Canadian Flag
Second, I consider it a matter of principle that we must insist on a flag design which has an association with our past history and heritage. If we believe in this principle, we believe in it today and we will believe in it six months from today; we do not stop believing in it because some people feel that the business of the country is being held up, especially when you know that the government determines the order of business of the house.
I consider it is as important today to insist that the flag of our nation has incorporated in it an association with the past as I did when this issue first came before the house; and I consider that we are as responsible today in insisting that the flag that is adopted by this house must recognize that association with the past as we were when we insisted upon it when the debate began. I certainly hope to see this matter debated until such time as the government is willing to remove the committee report from the business of the house, until such time as it can more constructively be considered, in the light of the more important business that is on the order paper, or until such time as they consider that it is indeed wise to consult the Canadian people and let them determine what we in this house do not seem to be able to determine.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate you on the wise decision you made this afternoon which makes it possible to hold the door open for a compromise on this controversial subject which has been before the House of Commons and the people of Canada for such a long period of time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You can say that again.

I think it is the desire of the house-and this has just been indicated by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne)-that we should as quickly as possible settle in one manner or another this subject of a distinctive national flag. Not only is there a desire in this house for the debate to be completed as early as possible so that we might get on with the more important economic measures that are necessary to deal with the problems that face Canada at this time, but there is also the widespread feeling across this nation. Your wise decision has made it possible for the house to avoid the mistake that was made when this matter was last before us, namely in refusing to resolve it in the only conceivable manner, to my

mind, in which it is possible to achieve resolution at this time; that is to say, by means of referring the matter to the people of Canada in a plebiscite.
When I first entered this debate on August 23, I believe it was, this was the viewpoint I put before the House of Commons. I did so because I was then under the impression that the government, as has been the case in so many other major items of business since it assumed office, had stumbled into this unhappy situation. Nothing that has occurred since that time has changed my viewpoint in this respect. I am still of the opinion that the government has unwittingly blundered into this position and has created the impasse that we now find facing the parliament of Canada and in the first instance, the House of Commons. I am sure that the events of last week, for example, have revealed once again that on basic matters of policy, rather than planning and organizing the business of the country in an orderly fashion the government stumbles and bumbles, to use the classic phrase the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) loved to use when he was a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. It seems to me that here again is a colossal example of the lack of constructive leadership that has marked the record of the administration ever since it assumed office just over a year and a half ago. So I repeat at the outset of my remarks that I hope that we will be able to vote on this matter of a plebiscite and that hon. members will see fit to get this controversial subject out of the House of Commons and into the hands of the people where it obviously belongs.
When the subject was referred to the committee some two months ago it was hoped at that time that an all party committee would be able to come to a compromise solution which would make it possible for all parties and individuals concerned to reach unanimity. It is now obvious that the committee has not been able to achieve this greatly hoped for objective. I was not a member of the committee and therefore I was not privy to all the deliberations which took place. We have had reports from several of the committee members, which I suppose will be supplemented by the statements of other members. We have also had reported leaks in the newspapers of Canada, which unfortunately did nothing to assist the committee in its very difficult deliberations. It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), who has played such a crucial and vital role in this question, was one of those who spoke

to the press prior to the tabling of the report which we now have placed before the house.
I am convinced, as I was convinced when I spoke on this subject before that, as many hon. members have outlined, the only possible way we are ever going to achieve a distinctive national flag acceptable to all the diverse parts and elements of Canada is in the typical spirit of Canadian compromise. Because of the circumstances which have already been referred to-the leaks which tended to introduce partisan considerations into the discussions of the committee-it is unfortunate that we have not been able to reach such a compromise.
I was interested, Mr. Speaker, in the comments of the hon. member for Humboldt-Mel-fort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp). Because of his own personal feelings and his own background, he was one of those who was most enthusiastically dedicated to the retention of the red ensign. It was encouraging to hear him state to the house yesterday that for the sake of national unity he and those from this party who had been associated with him on the committee had been willing to compromise and had voted for one of the three designs which were placed before the committee-the distinctive national flag with the red maple leaf plus the symbols of our basic dual ethnic origins. I think this is a major step forward because, as I have already intimated, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale was one of those who were passionately dedicated to the red ensign.
It was also encouraging to hear my desk-mate, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), indicate that he was willing, in the interests of resolving this subject and removing it from the House of Commons at this stage by means of deliberation within the committee, to accept the maple leaf flag which bore the symbols of our dual ethnic origins. This, Mr. Speaker, is the spirit that must be brought into the discussion by all hon. members if we are ever going to resolve this contentious issue.
Last evening I listened to the hon. member for Leeds extolling the symbolic significance of the maple leaf as a distinctive Canadian symbol which is accepted in all the parts of Canada, as well as being recognized abroad as something which is strongly reminiscent of Canada. I agree with the hon. member in that respect. I have always agreed during the course of this discussion that the maple leaf is an acceptable Canadian symbol. Veterans wear it on their badges. It appears on innu-
Canadian Flag
merable products made in Canada. When we flew with the air force during the war the R.A.F. roundel was modified by having the red maple leaf within the inner circle. But why is it necessary in adding the maple leaf to repudiate all the symbols of the past? That is the point I want to stress throughout my remarks. This seems to me to represent the spirit of nihilism, which is usually identified with those countries who have a revolutionary rather than an evolutionary tradition.
I am sure that all responsible Canadians would agree that the flag which is one of the three which came before the committee, and which bears the symbols of the past, is a distinctive flag acceptable in all parts of the country. Indeed, I would say it would be more distinctive than the one the committee finally presented to the house, because as has already been intimated this flag strongly resembles the flag of Peru. As a matter of fact at a distance it would be quite impossible to distinguish the Peruvian flag from the one that has been supported by the committee. I know this has been disputed by the hon. member for Leeds, but I have checked into the references in this regard and, except for the red maple leaf in the centre white patch, the recommended flag and the flag of Peru are identical. With this flag we would not be achieving the goal that the government has expressed time after time it wishes to achieve, namely the adoption of a distinctive national flag which could not be mistaken for the flag of any other country. Let us be reasonable in this approach, and let us not assume any position from which we will find it difficult to retreat.
One other matter I had hoped would be dealt with by hon. members on the committee is that we are not dealing with one flag only, but with two flags. The comments of the members of the committee which discussed this matter indicate that this situation was in their minds. Unfortunately we are dealing with a so-called distinctive flag and the union jack.
In dealing with this matter the government has never intimated distinctly what its position is in this regard, and this leaves the government open to a charge of political duplicity. We are going to have a flag which removes the traditions and symbols of our past history, while at the same time adopts another flag which reminds us of a time in our national evolution which we should have forgotten over the years.
It is a major breakthrough in this field, that organizations such as the Canadian Legion

Canadian Flag
have finally accepted the red ensign as Canada's national flag. This matter was referred to by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier-Lasalle (Mr. Rock), who drew attention to the fact that it is only within recent years that the Canadian Legion has flown any flag other than the union jack. I suggest the Canadian Legion has moved forward in its thinking and has now accepted the red ensign. The Orange lodge of Canada, one of the most vehement supporters of the union jack, now accepts the red ensign. The I.O.D.E. has moved forward in its thinking to a position of accepting the red ensign as Canada's distinctive national flag.
We have a government which professes to be moving forward in displaying symbols which represent our progress toward national sovereignty, but which offers on the one hand a national flag devoid of any traditional symbols, while on the other hand attempts to reconcile the irreconcilable, by offering the union jack as a symbol of our allegiance to the commonwealth, in spite of the fact the union jack has been superseded by the red ensign and has been accepted by most of these organizations which were enthusiastically devoted to the union jack.
This whole problem is not new to Canadian national life, and of course it is not going to be resolved in one fell swoop. Nor is this the first parliamentary committee which has presented a recommendation to this house on a Canadian flag. In 1945 a parliamentary committee made certain recommendations, and I think it took a more realistic approach to this problem than the approach taken by the latest parliamentary committee. That committee recommended a modified version of the ensign with a maple leaf on the fly. If the government of that day had had sufficient courage, and had not been so concerned with obtaining votes, this modified version would have been adopted, resolving this whole question once and for all.
One thing that has been said before is of such significance that I think it bears repeating. What is now happening under the present circumstances is that the government is catering to the extremist viewpoint, or at least attempting to do so. The government needs to be reminded that it cannot appease or cater to extremism. A responsible government must provide leadership and take a firm stand. This government has not provided this leadership or taken this firm stand, which is the main reason for our difficulties at this time.
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
The Winnipeg Free Press heaved an editorial sigh of relief when the 1945 parliamentary committee report was published, and indicated in an editorial that it felt the problem had been resolved. That editorial states that feeling in these words:
Only two small remnants of extremism survive the earlier controversy. On the one hand, there are still some extreme "loyalists" who want the union jack alone, but to this there are overwhelming practical objections, besides the fact that citizens of the United Kingdom understandably show no enthusiasm for having their flag used by Canadians. On the other hand, there are those who want a flag that does not contain the union jack at all. The Canadian people have continually shown by their actions that the majority feels otherwise.
If I may be allowed to interpolate, this is precisely the feeling of the majority of Canadians today.
The editorial then continues:
Hence the red ensign has been for all practical purposes our national flag since confederation. Notwithstanding the lack of formal authorization, it has ousted all competing flags. It has withstood every effort to discard it. And it surely will withstand any future effort, for this is the standard under which Canadian soldiers were proud to fight and die in both world wars. It is by consent of parliament in 1946 our national flag "until such time as action is taken by parliament for the formal adoption of a national flag." The other day it was consecrated as such on the altar of Westminster Abbey.
In the result it may be said that the Canadian flag question is now settled, finally and irrevocably, except for formal recognition by parliament.
Surely the time has come for this final step. Parliament at the next session should declare the red ensign to be our national emblem.
That is what was said in the Winnipeg Free Press of 1954, and I think it is as pertinent today as it was ten years ago. Let me repeat, the government will not resolve this matter by catering to extremists-those who want nothing but the union jack, and those who want anything else but the union jack. Those are two irreconcilable polarized positions. The government is attempting to bring these two extreme points of view together, and this cannot be done by appeasement.
The proposed flag design now before the house represents the first actual and fundamental departure from tradition that has been put forward at any time during discussions on a national flag. Unfortunately, because of party discipline and solidarity, it seems apparent that regardless of the issue the members of the Liberal party will vote in favour of any government proposal. This fact has been manifested by the actions of the Liberal party throughout the years. To quote the classic phrase, if they do not hang together on controversial issues, they will hang sepa-

rately. This attitude has been demonstrated by the members of that party on many occasions when it seemed almost impossible to believe that solidarity could be maintained.
The Prime Minister has made this issue the subject of a free vote, because the fate of the government is not at stake. I have spoken to many members about this subject, and many from the other side of the house have urged members on this side to continue the fight for a sensible and reasonable solution. I urge those members to vote according to their consciences, in favour of a referral of this matter to the people of Canada, because that is the only possible way we can extricate ourselves from the dilemma into which we have been precipitated by a government motivated by panic reactions.
Oh, tut, tut.

I think that is the only explanation of the present situation. Mr. Speaker, I heard someone say, "tut, tut". I repeat that I believe that is the only explanation possible, if one is to understand the precipitate action taken by the government in dealing with the great majority of controversial matters. As a result of the discussions of Canadian confederation over the past few months, the activities of the bilingual and bicultural commission, the visit of Her Majesty the Queen and the flag debate I have the feeling that today a more moderate mood is beginning to operate in Canada. As I understand the situation concerning the flag, the issue is not whether we shall have a distinctive national flag but what kind of national flag we shall have. With the voice of moderation now being heard in various parts of Canada I think it would be an excellent idea for the government to withdraw from the dilemma in which it has got itself.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You are in the dilemma.

There is cynical laughter from the other side, but the government has repeatedly withdrawn from impossible postures into which it has got itself, and I am sure that events as recent as last week are an indication of this fact. I am trying to be conciliatory in my remarks tonight. Why not use this method which has ever been the method of resolving hopeless divisions in Canada? The government could safely use it as a face saving device.
From the discussion that has gone on in the press, on television and in the house and
Canadian Flag
from the letters we have received surely we now realize that forcing a flag devoid of traditional symbols through the house is as divisive in certain parts of Canada as a distinctive flag with traditional symbols is in other parts of Canada. This is the problem we face and it cannot be resolved just by cracking the whip on the government side and forcing the issue through the house. In other words, what I am trying to say is that unity will not come out of a flag. Rather the reverse is true: A flag can only come out of unity.
The government has proceeded with precipitate haste in response to the extremism of the separatist sentiment that was rampant just a few short weeks ago in this country. It said that something had to be done to heal the wounds in Canadian confederation. I say, Mr. Speaker, that now that the voice of moderation is being heard, surely the time has arrived for the government to take a reasonable viewpoint on this matter. Just to show how the voice of moderation has been heard in various parts of the country, I point out that not so long ago overtones of republicanism surrounded the flag debate. I am not going to go over old controversial issues but we do know that hon. members of this house have even gone so far as to say that in another ten years the issue facing Canada will be whether we remain as a constitutional monarchy or whether we become a republic. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) has publicly uttered this viewpoint both in and outside of the house and it was obvious that this sentiment was present in the unhappy events which surrounded the visit of Her Majesty. That was a shocking experience for Canadians everywhere.
I feel that one of the high points of the current session was the day when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) rose in this chamber and asked all hon. members to join in an address of loyalty to Her Majesty the Queen. That was a unanimous expression of the opinion of the house. One of the voices that spoke at greatest length and in loudest tones that day in support was that of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), and I recall a distinguished member of the press gallery, Mr. Charles Lynch, indicating that this seemed to be a turning away from some of the more extreme viewpoints that had been expressed in the chamber and in other parts of Canada. The leader of the Liberal party in Quebec, a former member of this house, Hon. Jean Lesage, has also been emphasizing over and over again the

Canadian Flag
need for a spirit of compromise and reconciliation if we are going to overcome the present difficulties in Canada.
I am going to take the liberty of quoting from someone outside the house who is not necessarily well known in Canada but I think expresses a viewpoint which reflects the voice of moderation of the ordinary Canadian citizen. I refer to Mrs. Henri Vautelet, a distinguished leader of women in the province of Quebec, a past president of the Quebec federation of Liberal women and a woman with many other public services to her credit. She was speaking in Montreal in the middle of November and here is what the article says:
A prominent French Canadian woman says violence in Quebec province is linked to a world wide pattern of violence and that French Canadians have used their emotions rather than reason in putting their complaints about confederation.
Mrs. Henri Vautelet, former president of the Canadian association of consumers, said the recent outbreak of violence in Quebec was "the idiotic muddling of a lucidly defendable case".
"While I cannot escape the evidence of history that today's strains and stresses on the fabric of confederation are 100 per cent English Canada's responsibility, I feel that French Canada must bear the responsibility for our stupid, sometimes ugly, and usually ineffective and mainly emotional handling of the required presentation of our case."
The article goes on to point out that she was guest lecturer at Loyola college and spoke to students in political science. The article continues:
She said that recent violence in Quebec is a backwash from world wide violence and had little to do with Quebec's resentments.
"Throughout the more civilized world a strange disease of violence, a free floating hate searching for an objective, and a deliberate abandonment to massed hysteria has struck the younger generation. Since Quebec is part of the world, I am astonished that the obvious connection between the rantings of our young separatists and this malady of the age seems to have been largely overlooked. ...
Slogans are not facts but they can be dangerous and substitute too easily, In minds aware of a grievance but a little hazy as to what it really is, for the actual reality of facts."
She pointed to the "masters in our own house" slogan, used by the Quebec Liberal party during the 1962 provincial general election, as an example of an unproved assertion implying needs that no one has yet defined clearly.
"For we are masters in our own house here in Quebec in all but crises of war, and we even have the power to protect our minorities in other provinces and to force a revaluation of our Canadian partnership if we used our existing weapons instead of going off half-cocked over minor and all too often unreal grievances."
I think, Mr. Speaker, that there is the voice of moderation coming from a very distinguished French Canadian woman leader.

I think it indicates that there is no longer any need for panic reaction on the part of the government because we are over the crisis.
Now, I have had many letters reach me on this subject. I am not going to read them into the record, but they have repeatedly presented questions that have never been answered in this house and which I find it difficult to answer myself. Perhaps I could pinpoint the problem as my constituents see it if I put some of these questions on the record. First of all, they ask me why the Prime Minister introduced the flag during the opening ceremony of the biennial meeting of the Royal Canadian Legion at Winnipeg. Was the Prime Minister not aware that this is a memorial service dedicated to the memory of some 200,000 Canadians who have paid the supreme sacrifice in defence of freedoms motivated by the values represented in the symbols that he announced would be removed from the Canadian flag? They keep asking me this question. Why was it done in this abrupt and precipitate manner?
Another question is this one. The Prime Minister suggests he is bringing forward the flag question at this time because of an election promise. Does this imply he feels he must discharge all election promises whether they be foolish or wise? My only aside to this question is that if political parties had to discharge all the promises made during an election campaign the country would be in a very sad and unhappy state.
Another question they ask is why the Prime Minister, if he considered this such an important issue, did not introduce the flag question in the speech from the throne, which is the normal method of outlining the business of the house to be brought forward by the government in any particular session? The only answer I have been able to give in this regard is that there was a panic response to the voice of extremism, as I have pointed out in my earlier remarks.
The fourth question they ask is this: If the committee was looking for a distinctive flag which could not be mistaken for the flag of any other country, why did it choose a flag which closely resembles the flag of Peru? I cannot answer that question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You must have had a letter from John.

Yes, I have a lot of good Johns in my constituency, a lot of good folks, who are seriously concerned about this matter.

Another question I ask is, in a country which has achieved sovereignty by the process of gradual evolution, why has the government suddenly decided to deal with the flag question by the revolutionary process of repudiating the traditional symbols of the past? If I may make an observation on that, I would say we have had several speeches indicating this was the way it was done in the newly emerging nations of Africa. Canada is not a newly emerging nation. We are a nation highly respected in the councils of the world because we have always been a people who demonstrated a spirit of tolerance, good will and mutual understanding.
Another question is, in view of the fact that the restlessness in Canada is a reflection of the fundamental economic changes taking place in Canada, particularly in the province of Quebec where the full impact of the industrial revolution is being felt, why does the government give precedence to issues which divide us rather than concentrate on the basic economic and agricultural problems in Quebec? This question comes from the farm part of my constituency which cannot understand why this issue was hammered by the government all during the month of August. The usual procedure in the house, and I have been here for 13 years, is to tackle a matter for two days and go on to another item of business. Day after day, almost in frantic panic and haste, the government hammered away at this particular issue.
The Tories talked.

Here is one that takes us out into the international field. We hear from the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet), who says it was the Tories who hammered away at this. I just say the government determines the business of this house. It was their decision to set aside every other item of business, and for what reason I do not know.
And the Tories talked.

The hon. member is new to the house, and does not really understand that the opposition can only discuss what the government puts before the house. We have repeatedly asked for consideration of railway and transport matters which the minister knows, since he comes from Manitoba, are matters of great concern to that province. During a speech in Winnipeg two weeks ago the minister made a vicious attack on the Leader of the Opposition. This has been the tactic of hon. members opposite.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I did not deliver an attack on the Leader of the Opposition, I answered the false charges he had made the week previously.
You did not.

I have a clipping here from the Winnipeg Free Press and the headline on it is, "Shrewd, dangerous, Diefenbaker still Canadian Menace,-Teillet." This is exactly what he said. Again, Mr. Speaker, these are the sort of tactics that do not enhance the reputation of public affairs when we deal with personalities rather than policies.
Before the minister interjected, I was dealing with certain questions. We live in a world which has become virtually a whisper gallery or neighbourhood, due to modem means of communication, and yet is tom apart by the poison of narrow nationalism. Under these circumstances, why is the government raising controversial, chauvinistic, nationalistic issues at this time? This is a question I cannot understand. In a day and age when we are moving towards support of NATO, NORAD and the United Nations, when we talk of the necessity of North Atlantic unity and all the rest of it, we suddenly inject the poison of narrow nationalism.
Finally, here is a question that is heard more and more-particularly since the Prime Minister was in the west last week, because he was asked about this question: Will we have a distinctive national flag for Christmas? He said yes. The flag for Christmas promised by the Prime Minister, according to the committee report, is going to be this flag devoid of our traditional symbols. If it is to be regarded as a Christmas present, why does it studiously avoid any of the symbols pertaining to the Person whose advent gave rise to the celebration of Christmas? I think there is a fundamental conflict in this regard. These symbols, as I have already noted, do not denote colonial obsequiousness, but rather they denote that we have slowly evolved out of traditional western Christian civilization. Rather than repudiating these symbols, we should hold them to us as an example of the fact that Canada is still in the vanguard of bringing the benefits of our free institutions to all the people of the world.

I must say to the hon. member that his time has expired.

Carry on.

I am sure many of my constituents will be keenly disappointed, disgusted, even, that the subject of the flag should again be before the house at this time so close to the Christmas season. The large majority of them are very happy with our present flag, the red ensign, and many of them are more concerned about providing for their families. This year a great number of farmers are finding it extremely difficult to do so, owing to unfavourable crop conditions in many districts as a result of the drought; income is lagging far behind the need; many of them were forced to sell their livestock, their basic herds-

I wrote these words myself and I will deliver them myself. These people are very much concerned about their situation-more concerned than is the man who claimed on television the other night to be a great Canadian. I refer to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), whom we see very rarely in this house. I am sure not many farmers in the districts which have suffered from the drought would refer to him as a great Canadian, especially those who were forced to sell their livestock at such low price levels, the lowest in many years. If the Minister of Agriculture was such a true Canadian he would be in the house today, because surely it is an important occasion when we are discussing such a question as the flag of our nation. This absentee member referred to himself as a great Canadian. I think he is well aware that no one else is willing to give him that title.
Why has the government refused to allow a plebiscite on this flag question? Why are they so afraid to have a plebiscite on the issue?
Why are you afraid to have a vote?

Let us stop to think. Had it not been for the official opposition we would today be flying throughout this
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Forgie).]
country the three maple leaf flag, or the Pearson pennant. The flag committee-

speechtext: The hon. member is not only reading his speech but there seems to be someone reading one just behind him, coming to my ear through the earphone.
I cannot conceive of that being a fact.

I can tell the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) that I do not intend to read my speech and I am not listening to anyone behind me. If the hon. member would contain himself he will, I am sure, have an opportunity of making his own speech. But for the official opposition that flag would, by now, be the flag of Canada.
I say it was unnecessary to bring this question before the House of Commons, when there is so much other work which could and should be done. It makes one wonder why the government should be so afraid of letting the people have a say in choosing the flag which is to fly over this great country.
All those who have been following this affair know that the committee was destroyed before it was even set up. Everyone realizes this. In the speech from the throne there was no mention of a new flag design and many members on the other side told me that no proposal for one had been raised in their caucus before the question was introduced in the house. If it was considered so important to change the flag, the intention to do so could very easily have been announced in the speech from the throne. A committee representative of all parties could have been set up to deal with the matter before controversy arose in the House of Commons itself.
I would remind hon. members that when it was introduced in this chamber the Prime Minister stated there would be a free vote. As reported on page 3164 of Hansard of May 12 the right hon. gentleman said:
When the time comes to submit the decision of the government in this matter to the House of Commons I would hope every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictates and that there will be no question of confidence or non-confidence in a party sense.
A few days later the picture changed. The right hon. gentleman was not as strongly supported within his own party on the new proposed flag design as he had thought he was. And a few days later, on May 19, as reported on page 3337, when he was asked by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam

(Mr. Douglas) to say how the matter stood, he replied:
The government must stand or fall on the result of the decision of the house. But we have gone out of our way, and X have gone out of my way personally, to let the members of this party know that in a question so personal, so close to their conscience, so deep in their emotions, as a flag, a member of the Liberal party in voting against the design submitted by the government would not be read out of the party for so doing.
So the picture changed. I heard members from every party except one say, in casual talk, that they were strongly in favour of the red ensign but would agree to some modification. Why did the picture change so completely when the Prime Minister said this decision would be taken as a vote of confidence? All the members on the other side, except one or two, ran for cover. What happened to the members of the splinter parties? Why were they so afraid that they covered up and got behind the government? Mr. Speaker, I could read what some members on the other side of the house have said in this regard. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) is reported as having said, "The people of Canada have never asked for, nor have the people said they want, a flag other than the red ensign". Why should people allow themselves to be scared into accepting a new flag design overnight? Many people have said to me when I have been back home occasionally, "Have you fellows got nothing else to do? What is wrong with the flag we have?" Many people of ethnic groups from all over Europe live in my constituency. They are proud of the flag that we have. In spite of this, I have not heard anyone, when speaking in favour of the red ensign-not even in our party-who was not perfectly willing to accept some modification in the design; but it has been felt that the heritage of our two founding races should be incorporated in the design of a Canadian flag. I believe this was very unselfish on their part.
No one can say that members of parliament have not the right to heed the hundreds of thousands of letters received from many organizations and Canadians. These letters certainly warrant recognition and attention. There have been thousands of postcards and letters received saying, in effect, with regard to the red ensign, "Keep the old flag flying". Thousands of such letters have been received by members of the house, and surely they have warranted recognition on our part. Many organizations have written to members of parliament. Many of us have received requests very recently from such organizations as the Canadian Legion, the I.O.D.E. and 20220-680J

others, which we must recognize. One cannot ignore this vast majority of people who hold something dear to their hearts. If one stops to think, one realizes that had it not been for the official opposition in this House of Commons the Pearson pennant would be flying today. I ask the house, what does it look like when compared with our glorious red ensign?
Now another design has been proposed, and in all fairness to the committee I wonder just what happened during its meetings. I have every respect for the maple leaf, but what would this proposed flag look like when the white background became a little dirty? What would it look like flying outside the House of Commons, compared to the wonderful colours in the flag we are flying here today? I wonder what happened to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), who was a member of the committee. How did he vote when the three maple leaf design was considered? This is the man who has taken so much credit for bringing forward flag designs; the man who went to Winnipeg with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to try to ram down the throat of the Canadian Legion their choice of a flag, whether the Legion liked it or not. Where was the hon. gentleman who introduced this design, who thought he was an expert on designs and should introduce a flag design and nobody else should have anything to say about it, not even the members of his own party, when the vote was taken in committee?
We know that the committee did a wonderful job and put in a great deal of hard work and many, many hours. But as I pointed out, their efforts were defeated before the committee was even set up. Why should we be faced with this issue in the Christmas month? Some people blame the opposition. How can you blame the opposition in this connection? Consider the error we would have fallen into today if it had not been for the official opposition. Consider what would have been flying over this House of Commons. Can you blame the official opposition because the government has seen fit to bring forward this issue again, when so much legislation is pending? I think the government and their supporters had better take another look at some of the fumbling and bungling with regard to the way in which the business of this house has been conducted. I think it is high time people did not have to tolerate such a ridiculous government. People ask what is going on in this session of parliament. One has only to consider the length of time this house has been in ses-

sion and the many things that could have been done and which the government should have done, rather than bringing forward a maple leaf flag. Instead of putting a red maple leaf on this design, they should have put a red herring on it.
Shame.
I think of all summer when we were debating the flag issue, when they were saying we were the ones holding up parliament; in fact, Mr. Speaker, they did not have the legislation ready.
The house leader smiles in acknowledgement.

When I travel through my vast constituency I meet many Indians and Metis. These people are not worrying about the flag we have at the present time, any more than they worried about their treaty rights agreed upon and signed under the union jack and their great mother, Queen Victoria. These people are not worried about the red ensign; but some of them are worried about what they are going to eat.
Will a plebiscite help them?

Many of these people are concerned about what they are going to eat; but they have adopted the red ensign and are proud of it. However, they are wondering about some of the promises of this government. What happened to the Indian claims commission, for example-

-that was shoved down to the bottom of the list?

That is what these people are worried about.
Order. This is extraneous to the subject the house is discussing at the moment.

These people are not worried about a plebiscite; they would be very happy to have a plebiscite on the flag. I think what I have been saying pertains to the question of a plebiscite. However, Mr. Speaker, there are other matters that these people are worried about today more than they are concerned with our debating the flag, which they are proud and happy to live under. I attended an Indian conference and saw how proud and loyal these people are in regard to the red ensign. They are not

concerned about a different flag; they are satisfied with the one they have today. But they are concerned about what they are going to eat this winter. They are concerned about the problems this government promised to do something about. Why should the government be scared of a plebiscite being held?
I heard one member last night challenge us to put this question to a vote. I challenge him to put the question to a plebiscite. I challenge him and the government to go to the people, to call an election, on this issue. Let's have an election on this issue, if they think it is so important and they are afraid of a plebiscite. This is a serious matter. Why are the government fumbling and bungling along? If they are so determined that they are right, let's have an election.
I know it is said we must not fight an election on this issue because the unity of the country will be destroyed. This government has already destroyed the unity of this country, which is at its lowest ebb ever. It is true we do not want an election fought on the flag issue, but if that is the only way the government sees it, let us go to the country. We are not afraid to go to the country on this issue. We know where we stand and we know where the people stand.

I know a lot of people across Canada will be pleased to read that tomorrow. I say to the government: Go to the country on this issue if you want. We are ready to go. speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex Wesi):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to put my thoughts on record in connection with this flag issue. We are now, after a great many perambulations and circumlocutions, considering an amendment to the report of the flag committee. May I begin by expressing my own personal appreciation of the manner in which the flag committee carried out its duties. I refer not only to the representatives from our own party who were on the committee, but from conversations I

have had with various members of the committee I am convinced that a conscientious job of seeking to choose a compromise design satisfactory to the people of Canada was done. The committee succeeded in part and in part only, but they are still entitled to our thanks for the work they did.
The report which was brought in by the chairman was a masterful report. He reported fully, and I am sure that all hon. members of the house had a reasonably full understanding, when the chairman had presented his report, of what went on in the committee. His report was fairly given and I am sure much appreciated.
The amendment to this report advocates the use of a plebiscite in choosing a design for a new Canadian flag. I believe in the principle of a plebiscite and was not converted to this view only recently after the report was brought in. I want to refer to a question I asked on February 24 of this year. As reported at page 136 of Hansard, a time when hon. members will admit we had reached not very far into the 10,000 or so pages of Hansard we have created so far this session, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the following question on the orders of the day:
In view of the government's undertaking to provide the people of Canada with a distinctive national flag, has consideration been given or will consideration be given to allowing the people to make their own choice through a plebiscite or referendum from among several of the most popular designs, including the red ensign?
I had, Mr. Speaker, given some thought to the question of choosing a flag for Canada, and the question I asked was not an idle one. It was not a question intended to embarrass the government. It was an honest question asked for two purposes: first of all, to obtain information as to the attitude of the government to the possibility of holding a plebiscite; and second, to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that others were thinking along these lines. Indeed, I was not the first hon. member in the house to mention it this session; it was mentioned by others even earlier in this session. The Prime Minister answered as follows:
All I can say at the moment, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the procedure which should be followed in this matter is that parliament certainly should be put in a position to decide for or against a particular flag. As to whether it would be desirable to have a popular referendum on this matter so that the people could choose from among a number of designs, I would like to give that matter very careful consideration before agreeing to it.
Canadian Flag
So that my belief that a plebiscite would be a good and satisfactory means for choosing the design for our national flag is not new.
In his speech this evening the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) gave the house the results of some public opinion polls which were held in various parts of Canada and which indicate that a great many people across the country, at least in some parts of the country, are seriously considering the possibility of a plebiscite as a means of choosing a satisfactory flag design.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what does the Conservative party stand for in regard to this issue? I cannot speak for the Conservative party but I can speak for myself. I realize I am not the only one in the Conservative party who feels the way I do; there are many others. I also know that some of my colleagues do not agree with me, and for various reasons. And I do not insist that they should. Our party is democratic and the members of our party, ever since my association with it and since I was elected to this house, have been free to express their own opinions in their own way on every occasion. No pressure has been brought to bear on them at any time by our leader or by members of the government. Our members have been free to go their own way and there has been no unpleasantness and no pressure brought to bear. That statement I can make honestly, and it is true despite suggestions to the contrary which have appeared from time to time in the press.
In the first place I think the purpose of every member of the Conservative party is to promote and maintain national unity. We believe the best way to retain and promote national unity is to devise some means of choosing a flag, as a result of which there would be no losers and no winners.
If hon. members opposite support the government in its method of choosing a flag, a great many people in Canada will have bitter feelings toward a great many other people in Canada, and that is a most unfortunate situation. If we chose a flag through imposition a great many people will feel bitterly disappointed.
I should like to know why the government is in such a hurry to adopt this flag. If the government had argued early this summer that there was some urgency about choosing a flag, that argument might have been understood; but such an argument carries no weight at this time, and a course followed along that line of thinking, with such persistence, will

Canadian Flag
do nothing but create friction and develop a great deal of bitterness between the two founding races of this country.
Since early this summer the flag question has become the centre of activity in this House of Commons, and all the government legislation has been built around it. I do not suggest the government euchred us out of an Easter recess, but we certainly did not have an Easter holiday. We did not have a summer vacation, and I am not sure we are going to have a Christmas break, as things appear at this time. The government can be assured, however, that neither bribe in the way of holidays, nor pressures in the way of threats of an election, will prevent me from using every rule in the rule book to see that we devise a method of choosing a flag which will generate the least possible bitterness in this country, but which will maintain the greatest possible national unity.
I suggest there should be no reason for bitterness between our French speaking and English speaking colleagues in this country. However if we persist in imposing a flag on the people of Canada, I see no opportunity of avoiding a great deal of bitterness. I think we can avoid this bitterness by adopting the suggestion that a plebiscite be held, during the next election in order to save expenses. If we co-operate in this way I am sure we can choose a distinctive national Canadian flag of which all Canadians, French and English speaking, can be proud, while avoiding a a great deal of bitterness. We must avoid rushing into a decision. We must avoid these continual pressures, and we must avoid threats of an election. Let us discontinue the practice of tying our legislative program to the flag issue. The members of this house have been under constant pressure since this matter was first introduced during this session. I am sure the members of the house as well as the people of this country are sick and tired of the whole show.
Hear, hear.

The fact that we have been under pressure and are sick and tired of the whole situation is not something which will prevent me from continuing to discuss this matter, with the hope that a proper and satisfactory solution to the benefit of the people of Canada can be found.
Again, speaking for myself, I suggest that a ballot be prepared for submission to the electors at the next general election containing several suitable compromise designs. In view of all the argument and discussion that

has taken place in this house and across the country about the red ensign and the three maple leaf design, neither of those should appear on that ballot. The presently proposed one maple leaf design might be considered as a suitable compromise for inclusion on such a ballot, because it is the design recommended by the flag committee.
In this regard, three proposed flag designs have been distributed in this house within the last 24 hours. They might be designs suitable for such a ballot. Other designs have been of interest to some of our French speaking colleagues in this party, and I am sure those designs are possibilities for submission to the people on a ballot. I think five or six designs in colour and in miniature should be placed on a convenient-sized ballot so as to allow the people of Canada to express their preference. They could do so by marking the figure 1 beside their first choice, figure 2 beside their second choice, figure 3 beside their third choice and so on. I think the results of such a plebiscite should be calculated on the single transferable voting system. That is, all votes cast for the last choice design could be allotted to the remainder. All the votes cast for the second last design should be allotted then to the remainder, and so on until one design had a clear majority support. That is not a new system of voting, but one that has been used in the province of Alberta for many years in single member constituencies. I think that system has also been used in other provinces. That system, used to calculate the results of a plebiscite as has been suggested, would be a foolproof method. No matter which design illustrated on a ballot-provided they were all reasonably compromise design-was chosen by the majority of the people voting, no one would lose and all French and English speaking citizens could be justly proud of it. This would eliminate or reduce to a minimum all bitterness and controversy. I am glad to associate myself with any other members of the house who are prepared to keep this discussion going, in the hope that reason may prevail, that the government in its wisdom may find it possible to follow some line of approach in choosing a national flag which will be less dangerous to national unity than the method of imposing a flag by a vote in this house.
There have been charges of obstruction levelled against our party and I should like to deal with those charges.
Question.

Not too fast, my friends, not too fast. There have been charges of obstruction and a great deal of criticism, but did you ever stop to think what would have happened if there had been no extended discussion of the flag issue in the house? Have you ever stopped to think what we would have had? We would have had a flag imposed on the people of Canada which even the party that endorsed it would not support in the final analysis. The three maple leaf design was endorsed by the government, but later when they had had a chance to look around and after they had listened to a great many speeches-174 Conservative speeches, was it -on the subject, they decided it was possible to devise and choose a more suitable design, and that is what was done by the committee. So the fact is that the continued discussion did serve a purpose.
The hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) rose in his place this afternoon and said he never did like the three maple leaf design. He made no such statement during the extended discussion of that design. But when the opportunity came to choose a more satisfactory design he was very glad that it was found possible to do so and that a more satisfactory design was recommended by the committee. I say it is just possible that if members of the Conservative party keep on talking for a while we will be able to devise some other design which will bring to government members as well as to all other members of the house, and to all the people of Canada, as much more pleasure as the single maple leaf did as compared with the three maple leaf design. It will possibly be a further improvement over the present proposed design. This is possible.
Why do members criticize us so severely for keeping the discussion alive and continuing to thresh over and reconsider the idea? Much progress has been made. I submit to all members of the house that in this flag issue we are playing for keeps, or we should be playing for keeps. We should not approach the matter lightly. What would have happened if through action of the house we had imposed the three maple leaf design on the country? The country would have had a flag which a great many people did not like and which a great many members of the house did not like. When the sponsors of that flag were faced with a better choice, not one of them stayed with it.
There is no reason at all to suppose that this question is closed. If members of the
Canadian Flag
house will put their minds to it we can just as easily produce a still more satisfactory design. What is the hurry? Why not take our time? After the house has done all it can to provide suitable designs on which the people can vote, why not let the people themselves choose their flag from among the several designs recommended by a committee of the house?
In our amendment we are asking that the flag problem be referred back to the committee. So far as I am concerned I would not say "the" committee but rather "a" committee, because what can we expect if we refer back to the same committee a matter which they in their wisdom have already considered? There were only 15 members of the house on that committee. Why not submit the problem to 15 other members of the house? Set up a new committee with different members on it and let them have a go at the matter. It is very unlikely that they will come up with exactly the same solution as the former committee. I think that would be most wise and that would be my idea of how we should go about this matter. Appoint 15 other members to a committee and let them have a try at choosing a design. If we keep on we will end up with a number of very suitable designs which can be placed on a ballot.
Again I repeat, what is the hurry? If there was hurry last spring then I know of no hurry now. I know that the government of the country promised to bring in a distinctive flag within two years, but surely they have tried. Surely they have made an honest effort to carry out that promise to the electors. If they have not succeeded, at least they have tried and they are entitled to the credit for trying. But there is no hurry now. I can see no need for hurry. So let us take our time and do this thing right. Let us use methods of choosing a design for a new national flag which will tend to prevent friction among the different sections of the country.
I stated that I intended to deal with the topic of obstruction and filibuster. Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 119, contains this statement in paragraph 2 of that citation:
In parliament every comer of the country is represented and no rule should silence elected representatives when they think they have a message to deliver. Freedom of speech is a sacred principle and if there is a place where it should be fully respected that place is the parliament of the nation, and it is the Speaker's responsibility to see that this principle is not infringed upon.
In paragraph 1 of citation 119 we find this opinion:

Canadian Flag
Delays, multiplicity of amendments and even obstruction must not always be regarded as illegitimate political weapons.
I am going to repeat that.
Delays, multiplicity of amendments and even obstruction must not always be regarded as illegitimate political weapons.
In paragraph 2 of citation 119, we find these words:
The mere object of shortening sessions may lead to an undue curtailment of the freedom of speech. The duties of a representative of parliament are too important to be performed in a hurry.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I wonder if the hon. member, while he is looking at Beauchesne, would refer also to citation 149, paragraph (i), which states that a member must not-
-use his right of speech for the purpose of obstructing business of the house.

I have much ground to cover yet, Mr. Speaker, so if our friend does not mind I am going to plow ahead. He will be at liberty to take 40 minutes in due course and make his contribution to the problem of choosing a national flag in some way which will not tend to arouse friction between the various sections of this country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He can be the spokesman from British Columbia. Nobody else will speak.

I am speaking in support of a plebiscite, and bringing forth reasons why a plebiscite is desirable on this matter. These references in Beauchesne indicate the rights of minorities in the House of Commons to challenge the government's right to proceed when in conflict with public interest. There is provision in the rules, however, for the government to override the demands for change of policy by a minority. This is the closure rule. If the government are sure enough of their position, they can invoke closure and answer to the people for their actions. No government can, therefore, successfully contend that they have been prevented from carrying out their responsibilities through the act of a minority opposition.
If the government are unwise in their method of producing a national flag, let them take the steps to start the action suggested. I would say that any charge by the government now or in the future, that a minority are preventing them from carrying out their responsibilities, is completely unfounded. The government are responsible for submitting business to this house, and if the opposition
believe that the government are making a mistake it is their job to use every advantage in the rules, every provision in the rules which is available to them, to prevent the government from making a mistake or taking an unwise action. Surely, hon. members on the government side cannot criticize members sitting on this side of the house for doing the job the people sent them here to do.
Now, in dealing with the flag issue, may I repeat that this is playing for keeps. We do not look forward to having a flag issue or a flag controversy with every change of government. What a situation that would be in this country. This is something which is done once in a generation, once in a lifetime-my colleague says, once in a hundred years. We should not have any talk about changing it again. We are playing for keeps. Why hurry? Why not let us take sufficient time to do the job properly? If the government persists in their present method, then I submit they are planting in Canada the seeds of bitterness for several generations to come. This flag issue is of the utmost importance to our national unity. I believe that the problem should not be approached in haste. No amount of effort no amount of time, and no amount of expense should be permitted to stand in the way of choosing a national flag which is capable of enhancing the national unity of our country.
This afternoon one of the speakers from the southeast corner of the house, I believe it was the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) said that he was elected, and his colleague were elected, on this flag issue. Well, perhaps they were, Mr. Speaker. I do not know what the election issues were in Ville-neuve. I was not anywhere near there. I was in western Ontario, in Middlesex West, with one or two exceptions. This is where my campaign speeches were made. I do not remember making any extravagant promises. My main promise was that I had done my best to carry out my duties and I promised if re-elected I would continue to do just that, to do my very best in carrying out my duties as a member. I was re-elected; but to the best of my knowledge there was no mention made of a new Canadian flag in that area.
It is true the Conservative party, in their national conference, had passed a resolution in favour of a national flag, but that was not an issue in our election. May I call it ten o'clock?
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Wednesday, December 2, 1964
The house met at 2.30 p.m.

subtopic: MR. SCOTT-DECISION ON COMMUTATION OF SENTENCE OF CONVICTED MURDERER
MR. SCOTT-DECISION ON COMMUTATION OF SENTENCE OF CONVICTED MURDERER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to rise on a point of privilege. One Georges Marcotte is at present under sentence of death and is destined to die tomorrow night for the crime of murder. We have been trying all day to obtain from the Minister of Justice an announcement of the decision the cabinet has madp as to whether the sentence is to be commuted to life emprison-ment. The Minister of Justice has declined to make such announcement until such decision has been taken. If the decision is delayed any longer, Mr. Speaker, it will make it virtually impossible for those members of the house who are interested in the case to take any action they might deem appropriate in the light of the decision which the cabinet may have taken. I want to raise as a point of privilege that the failure of the minister to make this decision known to us is an infringement upon our rights as members, and is in effect preventing us from taking the action which we might deem necessary.

subtopic: MR. SCOTT-DECISION ON COMMUTATION OF SENTENCE OF CONVICTED MURDERER

I have listened to a statement but I have not seen any supporting evidence outside of the mere statement that the minister has not informed the hon. member or some other hon. members about this matter. I do not see any question of privilege in that. The minister is simply carrying out his duty, as far as I know.

subtopic: MR. SCOTT-DECISION ON COMMUTATION OF SENTENCE OF CONVICTED MURDERER
