subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, December 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Batten that the sixth report of the special committee on a Canadian flag presented to the house on Thursday, October 29, 1964, be now concurred in, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last evening I was attempting to show cause for submitting the flag issue to the people of Canada in the form of a plebiscite, so that the people across this country can choose the design for a new flag.
By way of a short resume of one or two of the points I covered I should like to state that I, as well as other members in this party and I believe in common with all hon. members in this house, stand for national unity. It is the purpose of parliament to maintain national unity, and we in this party have been searching for ways and means of promoting that unity and avoiding in every possible way discord among our people. If the government follows its present proposal to impose a flag on the Canadian people through a vote in this chamber, there will be discord. The whole issue becomes a party matter. I am sure the party to which I belong as well as other members of the house will agree that if we can devise some means of choosing a flag which will avoid discord and disunity in our nation we should do so.
The Conservative party has moved an amendment to the motion for concurrence in the report of the special committee to the effect that this matter be referred back to the committee with instructions to consider arrangements for submitting this question to the people through a plebiscite. Speaking for myself in this regard rather than for the party-and I should be glad to associate myself with any member of this house who feels the same way-we should continue this discussion with the hope that some better means will be found for deciding upon a flag for the Canadian people than through a government proposal to impose a flag by action of this house.
To show that there is not unanimity in the country, I have permission from my colleague the hon. member for Elgin to place on the record of the house a telegram which he received this morning from radio station CHLO in St. Thomas, Ontario. I may say that

Canadian Flag
this radio station also covers the Middlesex West area. It reads as follows:
Jim McBain, M.P.
House of Commons, Ottawa, Ont.
Jim: Monday and Tuesday, Doug Hinz conducted a straw vote on "High Gear"-
"High Gear" is the name of the program he conducts in the morning hours.
-re the single maple leaf flag design. For your information, Monday's program showed 80 per cent of listeners against it. Tuesday's program 83 per cent against it. Program attracts listeners from 6.30 to 9.15 a.m. Regards.
Barry Kentner CHLO Radio.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SIXTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my support for the amendment moved by representatives of the Progressive Conservative party. However, I must explain that I am giving expression to my personal opinion on this occasion and to what I am very certain is the opinion of the majority of the constituents I have the honour to represent. I must again emphasize that in matters of conscience members of our party are free to express their personal opinions with respect to any issue that comes before the house, and like the members of other parties in the house we are not all of one opinion on this question.
Personally I favour the red ensign as a flag that represents the realities of history which, if we go into our history, we find were given voice in Anglo-Saxon assemblies, in the terms of Magna Carta, in the struggle for freedom during the reigns of Edward III, the Tudors, the Stuarts and James II, in the glorious revolution of 1688, in the reform acts of 1832, in the representation acts passed from 1867 up to 1948, in the mother of parliaments in Great Britain that provides for a government and an opposition, which protects the rights of the minority to free expression and which we are very glad to see has found its counterpart in the parliament of Canada.
However, Mr. Speaker, regardless of my personal opinion and even of some of the very strongly voiced opinions of some of my constituents, we are anxious to adopt a flag that will be acceptable to the great majority of all Canadians. We enter this debate in a spirit of compromise to that end. I spoke of this question on June 30 last, Mr. Speaker, and expressed my criticism of the way the Prime Minister had handled this question. I was particularly critical of his bringing this
(Mr. Thomas.)
flag issue before the remembrance service of the Royal Canadian Legion convention held at Winnipeg earlier this year, and of other speeches he made on this issue. For that reason I urged support for a national flag that provides for the continuity of our history, with the inclusion of the union jack and all it stands for throughout the whole of our history, as well as the inclusion of the fleur-de-lis which stood for so much in the struggle for freedom in France in the days of long ago.
As I said before, we enter this debate in a spirit of compromise with a view to developing finally a national flag that will bring complete unity to the Canadian people. Referring to my own constituency, Mr. Speaker, I must say I have had the wholehearted support of all the Legion branches in my riding, the I.O.D.E. organization throughout the riding, the Orange lodge and a good number of other organizations, including the women's institutes which have expressed their views very strongly with regard to this question. In addition to that, sir, I have had somewhat over 2,000 of my constituents who have informed me in writing of their views with regard to a national flag for Canada, a flag that will contain symbols of our struggle for freedom, for parliamentary institutions in Great Britain, in France and in Canada.
I hear the hon. member for Leeds asking me to name those constituents. I am sorry, I did not hear correctly, Mr. Speaker; it was somebody else over there. Naturally, I could not do that, because I believe that everyone who wishes to speak in this debate should have that opportunity, and then we should vote on the issue.
Before proceeding further I should like to pay tribute to the chairman of the flag committee and the members of that committee. While there have been some criticisms of leaks from that committee I must say that in my opinion they laboured long and laboured in silence. I think there was less in total leakage from the flag committee than from any other committee with which I have had anything to do in this house over a period of 19 years. I think it is only fair to say that.
Unfortunately, from my point of view and the point of view of the majority of my constituents, and I am sure the majority of the Canadian people, the committee did not produce a flag which will be satisfactory. I must say that I am not enamoured with this flag. I do not like this design. I should like a maple leaf with other emblems on the flag as suggested by a speaker from the Progres-

sive Conservative party, which would then include symbols of the founding races of this country and the other groups that have helped to build up this great nation of ours. That is the reason I am supporting the amendment at this time.
There has been a very strong demand for a plebiscite. I have heard pleas for a plebiscite made by the Royal Canadian Legion, the Canadian Corps Association and other veterans groups. In this connection I would like to place on record in part what they have said in this respect. On November 11 the Canadian Legion presented its views to the cabinet with respect to veterans legislation and other matters, and included a copy of the resolution which it adopted at its convention in Winnipeg earlier this year. That resolution reads as follows:
Be it resolved that the delegates to this, the 20th biennial convention of the Royal Canadian Legion assembled at Winnipeg 17th-22nd May, 1964, reiterate the stand taken by the delegates of our 18th and 19th biennial conventions that we urge the government of Canada to, by act of parliament, adopt the Canadian red ensign as the national flag of Canada.
I also have here a very interesting letter from Mr. Heesaker, dominion president of the Canadian Corps Association, which contains the following passage:
Therefore, the Canadian Corps Association, dominion command, again emphatically requests the Prime Minister of Canada, and parliament as a whole, to place this subject before the people, at the next regularly scheduled general election. Let the voters of Canada finalize this matter.
I have received correspondence in similar vein from other veterans organizations, and from reading the papers I understand public opinion polls have been conducted on this issue. I am informed that some 60 per cent of the persons questioned in these polls have asked to have a plebiscite at the next general election in order that they may choose the flag they wish.
We have had nearly 100 years of self government under the British North America Act. So far as I know we are the first country to bring a measure before parliament to change its national flag after nearly 100 years of history. Though that was done by newer members of the commonwealth which obtained their independence in recent years, we are the first country which, having had that long experience of parliamentary government, has brought such a measure before parliament.
I urge members of the government to give consideration to the fact that the veterans of 20220-6814
Canadian Flag
this country have spoken clearly and with one voice on this issue. I am talking about the organized veterans of the country.
No.

Other responsible organizations across Canada have also urged the necessity for a plebiscite, and I ask members of the government to give consideration to their representations.
I am quite sure that the symbols we have at present, the symbols in our red ensign, the symbol of the fleur-de-lis, are very dear to many people because they represent such a great sweep of our histories.
I support the amendment to refer the matter back to the committee so the committee may bring in a report containing two, three or four designs which could be submitted to the Canadian people in a plebiscite at the next federal election. I am confident that if this were done-and it could be done at little extra expense added to the cost of the election-whatever decision was reached would be accepted as a majority decision of the Canadian people made with conviction and in good faith.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in concluding my somewhat brief remarks I urge that when every member has had an opportunity to express his views with respect to this amendment and his views on the remaining portion of the flag debate, we should then return to the realities of present circumstances and deal with legislation that awaits our attention.
They don't have it ready.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit a question.
Willingly.

I ask the hon. gentleman to believe that I raise this question for our edification. He mentioned that the fleur-de-lis was at one time or another a symbol of freedom. I think we all recall the tricolour and even the cross of Lorraine, but I wonder whether the hon. gentleman could remind us of the time in history when the fleur-de-lis was a symbol or emblem of freedom.
I willingly do that, Mr. Speaker. I consulted my good friends the Creditistes as to the history of the fleur-de-lis in the development of French democracy.

Mr. Speaker, of all the many words that have been said on this flag issue and of all the many speeches that have been

Canadian Flag
made, the words Your Honour used, although you are not supposed to make speeches, impressed me more than all the others I have heard. I refer to a few remarks Your Honour made in this house on September 2 last. I believe Your Honour was dealing with a point of order on a subamendment, and you quoted from Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 119(3). I read it in part:
A great deal of latitude must be allowed in the House of Commons which is a forum where every phase of public affairs can be discussed and every member has the right to be heard-
Sometimes we doubt that.
_even if in doing so he sometimes disregards
the rigidity of procedure.
Then you went on to say, Mr. Speaker; and these are the words I refer to in your very short speech:
Basing myself on this principle, and in view of the highly charged emotional context of the issue, it seemed to the Chair that members should be dealt with in a most reasonable fashion.
I would say that if in your wisdom, Mr. Speaker, you could have in some way impressed upon the Prime Minister of this country those two points, this flag debate would have been finished weeks ago.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members on the other side laugh, but let me just repeat what you said, Mr. Speaker:
Basing myself on this principle, and in view of the highly charged emotional context-
I think we would all agree with that. And the flag issue is not the basic issue; the basic issue with which we are dealing, although we may be speaking about a flag, is the unity of this country; and that is very basic.
Hear, hear.

As Your Honour has said, this issue should be dealt with in a reasonable fashion. I contend that this is all the opposition has been trying to do ever since we began this debate. We have asked the Prime Minister to treat it in a reasonable fashion. In fact I am one of those who contend that it is not our place to decide on this flag issue; it is an emotional issue that should be decided by the people. It has nothing to do with the social welfare of the people or the economics of the country. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that if you in your position could even now impress these two points upon the Prime Minister I am sure this debate would be finished today.
Yes?

Some hon. members say "Yes?" The reason we are dealing with this issue now is that it was an election promise. Coming from the west, I wonder about some of the other promises made by hon. members opposite. There are not very many Liberal members in the chamber. One promise that was made in the west that is perhaps more important to the west than the promise of a flag was the $2 a bushel for wheat. When is that promise going to be kept?
Hear, hear.

In fact some of the western members mentioned a figure of $3 a bushel. What has been done about that election promise? I just wish to say a few words on this matter, Mr. Speaker. Instead of the price going up, it has been going down. I refer to the price of Durum wheat mentioned in this house the other day.
Order.

This is in order. I am talking about the promises the government made. They have said the flag was an election promise, and that is the reason the Prime Minister introduced this issue into the house. We contend there is more important business for the House of Commons to deal with than the flag issue.
Hear, hear.

We ask ourselves, why was this issue raised in the first place? Why was it raised at the time it was? Why was it not mentioned in the throne speech, if it was so important? We can give hon. members opposite the answers to these questions. They may have different answers, but we know why this issue was introduced. It was because legislation was not ready.
Oh, oh.

They laugh, Mr. Speaker. Do they want me to point out those pieces of legislation that had to be withdrawn after being introduced into the house? There were two or three such cases, and it is not necessary for me to give the details. I have said before that there is other and more important legislation to be dealt with. Some of this is legislation that could be dealt with in a very short space of time. In our opinion the flag question cannot be dealt with in a very short space of time; as Mr. Speaker has said, it should be dealt with in a reasonable manner. I repeat that all we are asking

is that it be dealt with in a reasonable manner.
Members of the New Democratic party are very anxious that the bill dealing with the labour code be brought before parliament. We are also anxious that this be done.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
In my opinion, you should call to order the member who is speaking at this moment and ask him to keep to the subject under discussion. Furthermore, I would ask you to render your decision immediately, as you did yesterday, and suggest to the hon. member that he confine his remarks to the subject under discussion.

It might be helpful at this time to indicate to the house the understanding of the Chair. The discussion should relate to the amendment. If we assume that a member is going to speak for 40 minutes, I do not see any particular harm in speaking generally for five minutes, but the other 35 minutes should relate to the amendment.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: What about the farmers in Quebec? Why don't you make a speech about that situation? Come on; stand up.
He is not allowed to speak over there.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out once again that your remarks impressed me for this reason. We are speaking on the amendment and raising the question that this whole matter should go to the people in the form of a plebiscite. Because Your Honour made those remarks, to my mind what I have been saying is directly related to the issue before us; in fact, it is the strongest argument that I have.
This is the reason it should be decided by way of a plebiscite. I refer to the two points that Your Honour raised. I do not understand why backbenchers opposite should say it is not relevant. We just wish to deal with legislation that should be dealt with at the present time, and this question has been raised time and again. This is another reason this matter should be decided by a plebiscite, namely that there is important legislation with which we should deal. I refer to the rail line abandonment legislation, for example. That is another matter that is very important to us in the west. Perhaps it is not
Canadian Flag
so important to the people in the east; it appears to me that to some of them the question of a flag is more important. As far as I am concerned, this is a strong reason for this question being decided by a plebiscite.
My second reason for suggesting that the question should be decided by a plebiscite I take from the remarks of the seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Danforth. I refer to just one paragraph of his speech for the moment, in which he said:
I am aware that some members of the committee felt very strongly that a flag ought to contain-
I would point out that he was speaking for the committee:
-the union jack and the fleur-de-lis. That is a view we listened to with the greatest of respect and we explored every possible argument pro and con. I respect that view, but in the end-
I emphasize this last part; the hon. member refers to those in the committee.
-most of us came to the conclusion that by putting emblems such as that on our national flag we would be merely giving ourselves a perpetual reminder of the things that divide us-
Well, Mr. Speaker, whoever heard of the coat of arms of our country being something which would divide us? I submit that this conclusion which was arrived at by the committee is based on a false or erroneous premise. Certainly the union jack will not divide us. I ask the members of this House of Commons, what will the maple leaf do to us? It has already created another faction which did not exist before.
Carried.

To some people-perhaps not to those who are anxious to get this through and are calling "carried"-a national flag represents the deepest emotions of the heart. It means heroism, self-sacrifice, courage and love. I do not think there is anything there which would divide us regardless of which province we come from. I suggest that this is another reason why this issue should go back to the committee and to the people by way of a plebiscite.
Further on in the hon. member's speech he said:
The one thing which it seems to me is significant about the committee report, and which lends great weight to its recommendation, is that if anything can be said it is that this is a parliamentary flag. This is not the flag of any particular party. It is not the flag of any particular individual.
I think had I been helping the hon. member with his speech I would have said "Nor

Canadian Flag
is it the flag of any particular country". It does not, as the hon. member tried to point out, signify unity. Unity is not something which can be legislated, as we all know, any more than a flag can be created by an act of parliament. A flag is merely a bit of coloured cloth until people take it to their hearts, and that cannot be ordered by decree. This flag to many of us is still just a piece of coloured cloth which may come to mean something to us if it is the selection of the people of Canada as a whole.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that the report of the committee is not realistic. It means nothing. In my opinion the flag they have recommended is a nebulous design because it means nothing. The hon. member for Leeds a day or two ago said that the maple leaf represented Canada, and he referred to some publication he had obtained from the parliamentary library. That publication stated that this flag represents all Canada. However, the hon. member neglected to say that the writer of that book died roughly 100 years ago. It did represent all Canada at that time, but not today. When that book was written Canada stopped at the great lakes. Since that time a much larger and greater country has developed, and certainly the maple leaf is not seen west of the great lakes. Therefore in my opinion it does not represent Canada. I would say that each group in Canada should have some representation on the flag to which their hearts are attached.
The hon. member for Kootenay West, who spoke a few moments ago, told us what the union jack meant to him. I have heard members from Quebec say what the fleur-de-lis means to them. I hope I respect that meaning, and in return I would ask those members from Quebec to respect the fact that the union jack means something to me.
I should like to refer to a speech made in this house some time ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who is a returned soldier. He was speaking on what the flag meant to him and referred to the days of liberation after both world war I and world war II; I believe he served in both. The hon. member said the red ensign began to mean something to him when it was waved not by people of Canada but by people liberated by Canadians from oppression and tyranny. As the hon. member said, he realized at that time that the red ensign also meant something to him. I was born an Anglo-Saxon and I served a number of years in the army. Because of those two facts I like the red ensign, and as I say the union jack means

something to me.
At this time I think I should put on record what the red ensign means to our veterans organizations, and I should like to read a letter put out by the president of the Canadians corps. I think this letter was sent to every member of parliament. It is dated November 27, which actually was about three days before this amendment was moved. It is addressed to all members of the House of Commons and reads as follows.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. May I refer to Sir T. Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition, page 470, which reads:
Although it is the duty of the Speaker to interfere in the first instance for the preservation of order, when, in his judgment, the occasion demands his interference, it is also the right of any member who conceives that a breach of order has been committed, if the Speaker refrains from interfering (either because he does not consider it necessary to do so, or because he does not perceive that a breach of order has been committed) to rise in his place, interrupting any member who may be speaking, and direct the attention of the Chair to the matter, provided he does so the moment the alleged breach of order occurs.
May I also refer to page 451 with respect to the subject of relevancy of debate. It says:
Debate must not stray from the question before the house-or anticipate a matter appointed for the consideration of the house.
We have numerous illustrations of this principle being followed, and I would ask the Chair to direct that what we are concerned with here is the question of a plebiscite and nothing else.
Mr. Speaker-

Perhaps I should attempt to answer the point of order. It is all very well to cite principles, if hon. members are able to find citations, but those principles have to be enforced. If I may refer the hon. member to standing orders, standing order 34 (2) says:
Mr. Speaker or the chairman, after having called the attention of the house, or of the committee, to the conduct of a member who persists in irrelevance, or repetition, may direct him to discontinue his speech, and if then the member still continues to speak, Mr. Speaker shall name him, or, if in committee, the chairman shall report him to the house.
In this type of debate, dealing with this type of subject, it seems to me the Chair should at least be given wide discretion, and to follow subsection (2) of standing order 34 is just not called for at this time. I am watching and listening very carefully to the remarks of the hon. member, and I would ask hon. members to trust my judgment to

interfere if and when in my humble opinion it is necessary to do so. Up to the moment, although the hon. member has been speaking quite generally, he is working toward a conclusion and to that extent should be given the benefit of the doubt.

Mr. Speaker, if I could make your job any easier for you perhaps it would help if I read the last paragraph of this letter, which is rather unusual. It says this:
The Canadian Corps Association, dominion command at this time reiterates that no change in Canada's present national flag should be made unless the government is so instructed by the citizens of Canada by means of a plebiscite vote held in conjunction with Canada's next general election.
Everything I am saying is related to the amendment now before the house. I also remind the hon. member for Leeds that this is the first time I have spoken on this issue either inside or outside the house. I could become irrelevant by repeating something he has said in regard to this issue, but I would be off the subject so I will refrain from doing so.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to read what the Canadian corps has to say about what they wish the Prime Minister would do, and I suggest it is exactly the same as we would like the Prime Minister to do. They say:
The right hon. Prime Minister Pearson and some of his associates have, during the past few days, called for British fair play and justice.
The Prime Minister has, therefore, substantiated the veterans of Canada's demand that our present government must not eliminate from Canada, the flag of justice and freedom, the Canadian red ensign.
The Canadian Corps Association, dominion command sincerely hopes that with the latest events in parliament, that the members of the House of Commons will take a closer look at these disclosures and then decide whether to be stampeded by irresponsible people whose only aim is to remove from Canada all the things that we, as Canadians, have been proud of for years.
Perhaps I should say that I read the last paragraph first. At this time on behalf of the Canadian Legion particularly, and veterans generally, I should like to place on record what General Charles Foulkes, former chairman of the chiefs of staff had to say about a cartoon which was detrimental to veterans, as reported in an article in the Toronto Telegram of May 6. The article is headed "Ridicule-how quickly we forget". I believe that statement to be true, and perhaps it is our fault here that we forget so easily. The general had this to say:
A recent cartoon in the Ottawa Citizen depicted two apparently inebriated legionnaires expressing
Canadian Flag
disapproval of the Prime Minister's proposal for a new Canadian flag. While I have no inclination to get into the controversial flag issue, I must take issue with the cartoonist and the Ottawa Citizen for publishing this most insulting cartoon, which attempts to associate the views of the veterans of two wars to those of two inebriates.
Perhaps some of the legionnaires do imbibe a bit too much in their haunts in the various Legion halls, but we should remember that these were the same individuals whom we exhorted to come forward and fight in the mud of France and Flanders. I suspect that many of those who are now poking fun at these old veterans were not too conspicuous in the actual fighting of the last war.
I believe that is true, because of an investigation which was carried out to find out who was responsible for putting this cartoon in the Ottawa Citizen. The general continued as follows:
I rarely speak out on such occasions but to allow such an impression to get abroad that the views of the Canadian veterans can be assumed by such a cartoon is just too much for some of us to take. The newspaper concerned may have forgotten that the men they are lampooning are the same men who withstood the savage attacks at Vimy and Cambria and the Somme. Those of us who saw the fighting in Sicily, Normandy, and Germany are indeed very sympathetic towards the heroes of France and Flanders and take serious umbrage to those like this cartoonist who make fun of the old veteran who still likes his pint of beer, but in his day offered his life in order that we can now enjoy the freedom of the press.
To have affection and pride for a flag and symbol which was once the flag of battle seems to be misunderstood by some, perhaps it is because they never had or wanted to see that emblem in the heat of battle. Be that as it may it hardly behooves any of us who fought under that flag to make jest or fun at his expense. How do we know what he may have suffered or sacrificed while serving under this emblem?
How soon we forget! How easy it is to take a crack at the burned out veteran and his pint of beer and his affection for the flag he fought for. But it was his sacrifice and that of thousands who never came back, that make this free discussion of a Canadian flag possible.
Do what you like about the flag, but don't dare lampoon those who fought to make this free decision possible.
I agree with the general. As a result of the heated argument that has taken place on this issue, and in an attempt to find some solution to our problem, I have read the speeches of many members of this house to ascertain whether I could find some common ground, or a common denominator. I should like to refer to Hansard of November 30, which was last Monday, and particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Danforth, who had this to say:
-it would be preferable to have a distinctive flag that says just one thing, Canada-not French Canada, not English Canada, not ethnic Canada, but Canada.

Canadian Flag
I should now like to turn to another statement by the same member, as recorded in the same volume of Hansard.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I am finding it difficult to pick out anything that is relevant to the amendment now before us in the speech being made by the hon. member. His remarks seem to be relevant to the main motion but without relation to the amendment. Perhaps I should refer again to that citation from Bourinot. The hon. member seems to be anticipating a matter appointed for the consideration of the house which is not the subject matter of the amendment.
According to citation 119 (3) of Beau-chesne's fourth edition, relevancy is not easy to define. However, in view of the number of speeches we have had for so many days, and in view of the decision taken by Your Honour yesterday on the matter of relevancy, I think the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek is out of order and should be called to order.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak on the same point of order. I am not surprised that the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency has attempted to prevent my colleague from speaking, because he is one of those who, in a speech some time ago, recommended that closure be applied.

Order, please. The difficulty of the Chair in attempting to maintain relevancy and avoid repetition is self evident. I do not wish to be involved in one procedural argument after another. Hon. members must discipline themselves to a certain extent.
Perhaps I can help hon. members in this way. It seems to me that the amendment now before us for consideration deals with the holding of a plebiscite. The house has already reached a decision on the subamendment having to do with the four questions that were suggested should be asked through a plebiscite. We do not have to deal with that matter again. The opinion in that regard can be found at pages 6912 to 6920 of Hansard of Monday, August 17.
We are now dealing with the flag question in relation to a plebiscite, and it seems to me the questions to be asked are, should we have a plebiscite or should we not have a plebiscite? What are the reasons for holding a plebiscite? That is the question before the house at the present time, and I am sure hon. members will do their best to help the Chair by trying to be relevant and trying to avoid repetition.

Mr. Speaker, may I remind you that the amendment is even more specific than the question of whether a referendum should be held or not. The subject of the amendment is to refer the report back to the committee with instructions to change a paragraph and replace it by another. The matter of a plebiscite is relevant but it is not the main point of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith).
I must point out to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot that I am not stopping anyone from speaking, but I ask the speakers to restrict themselves to the matter under consideration. I said earlier that I was in favour of closure, and I still am.

Mr. Speaker, I have been trying to establish the reasons why we should hold the plebiscite and I prefaced my remarks by saying that my main reason stemmed from two statements you yourself made in the house. I will repeat them again for the benefit of the hon. member, who I understand believes in closure. The Speaker said that this issue has a highly charged emotional content and should be dealt with in a reasonable fashion. That is all I am asking the House of Commons to do, to deal with this issue in a reasonable fashion, to deal with the people of Canada in a reasonable fashion.
I also said that to my mind, and you may not agree with me, the flag issue is not the basic issue, and I will have something to say about the province from which the hon. member comes in a few moments. I went on to show the reason why I think there is a mutual channel which we can all follow, if we will, in that time and time again the speeches by members on both sides of the house have expressed the desire that we want to be Canadian. I should like to repeat a few remarks that were made by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe). As found on page 10711 of Hansard of November 30 he said:
Do you admit that? This is what we have to consider before going any further in the life of the whole people whom we want to be Canadian, just plain Canadian and not French Canadian, English Canadian, Scottish-Canadian, Irish Canadian, Italian Canadian or German Canadian, no more than American Canadian.
In other words, apparently all of us are of the view that we want to be Canadian and, if so, maybe we are going at this problem the wrong end first. We all say we want to

be Canadian regardless of what country we came from or where our ancestors came from, and we have one thing in common. Can we work from there? Maybe a plebiscite will help us to do so.
For the benefit of some of the Quebec members who may not have travelled extensively in western Canada I am going to read a portion of a letter I have received from a constituent which may startle them. I think we in the House of Commons must face facts if we are going to settle our problems. This constituent's letter reads in part as follows:
This also raises the Quebec question. Surely it is time someone said "enough". The militant group which is supposedly reflecting public opinion in Quebec are like a labour union and every concession is a confession of weakness. They do not set a limit to their aims. All they want is more. Surely there must be enough intestinal fortitude on the part of someone who will say "no, this is it". Surely it is time for Canadians-
Here he repeats something that we all have in common.
-not English Canadians, French Canadians, Scottish Canadians, Russian Canadians, etc., to forget all their previous ancestries and be one thing only and that is Canadian.
You as a member of parliament have a voice in the affairs of Canada and surely there are enough good Canadians of all political and racial backgrounds and creeds in the house who will be prepared to stand up and speak for Canada. If you do not and it is not done soon there will be no Canada as such in our lifetime. This small militant minority cannot be allowed to destroy our heritage for their own peculiar and selfish ends. I can assure you that they are being sponsored from without.
I say again that the flag issue is not the basic issue. The basic issue, and the reason we should have a plebiscite, is to preserve what unity we have in Canada, not to divide us more but to try to bring us together. To me it is apparent that our primary need for unity in Canada today is between the people of the province of Quebec and the people of the other nine provinces. The question that has been asked many times, to which we from the west have not received an answer, is, what does Quebec want?
Quebec.

If we do have a plebiscite we may possibly find out during the course of the plebiscite or during the course of our discussions with other members of the House of Commons what Quebec wants. We have asked this question on numerous occasions and we have had different answers. I am being very frank when I say that some of my people in the west think that Quebec hates the union jack and will accept any emblem on
Canadian Flag
the flag other than the union jack. I am told by some of my colleagues on this side of the house that this is not so. I am also told that the premier of Quebec said: "We do not care what flag the House of Commons chooses; we will not fly it anyway because we have our own flag". I do not know whether that is right, but if it is then I say to the members from Quebec: Why should they try to impose on us in the rest of Canada outside of Quebec a flag we do not want?
Order, please. May I suggest that the hon. member try to restrict himself to the plebiscite, why it should be held, how it should be held, when it should be held.

And the reason why it should be held, Mr. Speaker. That is what I am trying to express. The rest of Canada does not understand Quebec. I have editorials here written by people who are supposed to be authorities in Quebec pointing out what they want, and if this is what they want then certainly the rest of Canada cannot tolerate everything that is written in these editorials. I will not read them.
They do not understand the Conservatives either.
You want closure.

I would say to the hon. member from Quebec who has just interjected that I do not see how he and his party can criticize the rest of us because he entered the house as a member of a party which subsequently split, and now the two groups apparently cannot understand each other.
Where is the hon. member for Three Rivers?
Where is Balcer? Where is Martineau?
Where is Pigeon?
He is here.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to leave the house to attend a meeting of the special joint committee on the Canada pension plan at 3.45?

Mr. Speaker, as my time is rapidly running out I will eliminate some of the remarks I was going to make. I would say that I have been thinking about the decision I must make in regard to this issue and, as I said before, it is an emotional issue. I do not think it is an issue that we as mem-

Canadian Flag
bers of parliament should decide. However, I have tried to assess it and in doing so I have made a summation of what I believe the red ensign stands for. I also have made a summation of the French Canadian viewpoint, as I see it. I have a great number of citizens of French Canadian origin living in my constituency. I would say that they are real Canadians, and I am not taking anything away from the people of Quebec. I say that the majority of them are great Canadians. There are one or two exceptions, but I do not want to name them.
I say that if there is to be a choice of a flag by means of a plebiscite, you should leave the Canadian red ensign as one choice as the veterans have requested. This is a request of certain Legions in our country, you could say the majority. Certainly it is a flag that we have honoured for a number of years. There may be reasons why it should be changed. I know that I am biased; I am prejudiced about it. Since I am prejudiced, I will lean over backwards because I represent a large number of people of French Canadian origin and let them put on this flag any emblem that they desire. I am proud of the contribution the French people have made to Canada. I am particularly proud of the contribution the French Canadians have made to my constituency. They are great constituents. I may not get many of their votes, perhaps 1 will not get any of them. Nevertheless, I represent these people at the moment.
In so far as my summation of the red ensign is concerned, I want to say that when its design is examined dispassionately without prejudice or unreasoned emotion, it can be seen that every desire of our multiple religious, racial and cultural backgrounds is answered. If we aspire to religious and racial tolerance and the attainment of our national objective by negotiation, while maintaining loyalty to ideals rather than narrow nationalism, then our Canadian ensign represents us in a manner that no simple combination of colours or numbers could do. A flag with great depth of meaning capable of representing our complex idealism, it also represents not only our varied traditions and cultures, but also the single aspiration of the Canadian people as a whole, in a manner which a new design could not possibly match.
By understanding the ensign through a study of the elements in the flag, we may better understand ourselves, and will see that all of us can proclaim it as our symbol of unity, the ideal flag for a country like

ours. The ideal of unity by negotiation is also the very basis of our country, Canada. First, our French forefathers negotiated the Quebec Act which guaranteed the religion, language and civil law of the French. Then our British forefathers refused to join in rebellion and decided to settle their differences with their King by negotiation. They knew that the British system of justice was a tradition of great value, and to save it they were prepared to abandon their homesteads and start anew.
I must interrupt the hon. member to inform him that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, since the flag debate was resumed at the beginning of the week hon. members on both sides of the house have expressed their views and I wish to take this opportunity to state mine.
Mr. Speaker, I know that on both sides of the house, among government members as well as within the ranks of the official opposition, or even within the New Democratic party and the Thompson group, there is no unanimity about the adoption of a distinctive national flag. On the other hand, on the government side there is no unanimity on the choice of a distinctive flag, whether it be the three maple leaf design already proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or the single maple leaf design recommended by the committee.
At the outset of the session the Prime Minister himself introduced legislation concerning the adoption of a three maple leaf flag, as well as the union jack, to indicate our membership in the commonwealth and our allegiance to the crown.
Generally speaking the Canadian people did not like the way the Prime Minister-
